modules.label: M1 · The Game and the Loop

lessons.title: The Loop: One Real Trade Through Regime → Scan → Setup → Size → Manage → Review
lessons.note: Walks one actual closed trade through all six stations on screen — that morning's dial reading, the scan hit, the setup name from the catalog, the sizing math, each management decision, and the finished journal entry. Artifact: the printable six-station LOOP card that every later lesson plugs into.

chapters.beat: open on the finished trade's chart and its completed journal entry, then rewind to the morning it began and promise to rebuild the whole trade one station at a time.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a finished trade — the closed chart and its completed journal entry side by side. Tell them: this trade wasn't a hunch that worked; it was six decisions made in a fixed order. Regime, Scan, Setup, Size, Manage, Review. Every UCT trade runs all six, in order — the output of each station is the input of the next. The dial grants permission, the scan supplies the name, the catalog names the trade, the stop sets the size, the rules run the exit, the journal grades the loop. A trade that skips a station is not a UCT trade. Then rewind to the morning this trade began and promise: we're rebuilding it one station at a time, exactly as it happened. By the end of this lesson you'll hold the printed card every later lesson plugs into.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: the finished trade's daily chart beside its completed Journal entry — e.g. NVDA daily, May 2023 earnings-gap swing (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Use NVDA daily, April–September 2023 (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Left panel, the finished chart walked in order: the flat spring base under ≈$30.50 (the pre-earnings high); the May 25, 2023 earnings gap, +26.1% at the open to ≈$38.52 on ≈3.3× average volume, closing +24% on the day; the day-one entry ≈$38.50; the stop ≈$36.60 under the gap day's low (≈5%); the June 20 strength ≈$43.90 where a third came off (≈+2.8R); the 50-day trail and the late-September exit ≈$43 (September closed ≈$43.50). Blended outcome ≈+2.5R. Right panel: the completed 7-field journal entry mocked from exactly those numbers. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Regime and Scan: permission before tickers
chapters.beat: replay that morning's dashboard on screen: the actual 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating reading with its GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, then the nightly scan hit that put this exact name on the list.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay that morning's dashboard. Station one, Regime: the 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating — say the actual number and its band. GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE — a permission band, not a prediction. GREEN means more of the playbook is authorized, not that the market goes up. No number, no trade: permission comes before tickers, every day. Station two, Scan: this name didn't come from Twitter or a hunch — it came off the nightly scan, roughly 3,700 tickers filtered to about ten names in twenty minutes: Stage-2 pass, ADR% of 4 or better, a dollar-volume floor, RS trend up, ranges tightening. It survived every filter, went to the A-list at its pivot, and the alert was armed at the exact trigger price. The market interrupted us; we weren't staring at it.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard replay: the UCT Exposure Rating dial with that morning's score, then the Screener scan-hit row for the trade's ticker
chapters.example_spec: The trade is the NVDA May 25, 2023 earnings-gap swing (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Regime pane: the UCT Exposure Rating dial showing a GREEN-band score — if the dashboard cannot replay May 2023, capture today's dial and caption it 'illustrative of that morning'; SPX closed May 2023 ≈4,180 above a rising 50-day and ran to its ≈4,607 high on July 27, so GREEN is honest. Scan pane: run the Screener with the standard chain — Stage-2 pass, ADR% ≥ 4, dollar-volume floor, RS trend up, tightening ranges — and screenshot NVDA's hit row; verify against May 24, 2023: price ≈$30.50 above all four MAs, RS at highs, base tightening, alert armed ≈$38.20. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Setup and Size: name it from the catalog, then do the math
chapters.beat: call the setup by its catalog name and family, mark the entry and stop on the chart, and work Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % out loud down to the exact share count.
chapters.speaker_notes: Station three, Setup: name the trade from the catalog — its name and its family, one of Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — and which of the four triggers fired it: BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN. Mark entry and stop on the chart. Station four, Size — the arithmetic out loud: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. Hard max 2% of the account per trade; we prefer under 1%. On this trade: 1% account risk with a 5% stop distance means a 20% position — 0.01 ÷ 0.05 = 0.20. On a $10,000 account that's a $2,000 position; at a $50 entry, 40 shares risking $100. Size is derived from the stop, never from conviction.
chapters.on_screen: The trade's daily chart with entry and stop lines drawn, the sizing math written out beside it (same example trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, May 2023, zoomed to the earnings week (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Mark in walk order: the spring base high ≈$30.50; the May 25 gap open ≈$38.52, +26.1% on ≈3.3× average volume; the entry line ≈$38.50 (family: Gaps & Catalysts — day-one gap-and-go over the opening range); the stop ≈$36.60 under the gap day's opening-range low, ≈5% below entry. That 5% distance feeds the on-screen math verbatim: 1% account risk ÷ 5% stop = 20% position; on $10,000 that's $2,000 — ≈52 shares at ≈$38.50, risking ≈$99 (1R ≈ $1.90/share). The trade later resolved ≈+2.5R blended. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Manage and Review: the decisions and the receipt
chapters.beat: step through each hold/trim/exit decision at the bar where it actually happened, then show the finished journal entry that graded the trade — the loop closing on itself.
chapters.speaker_notes: Station five, Manage: step through each decision at the bar it happened. The stop is an appointment, not a debate — placed where the pattern breaks, never moved lower. Breakeven at roughly +1R or the first higher low. First third off at 2-3R into strength; the rest trailed on the line that fits the trade — the 10-day for a fast mover, the 20 or 50-day for a position hold. Never add to losers, no exceptions. Station six, Review: the finished journal entry — all seven fields, filled the day the trade closed: date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-versus-plan, the three-axis grade — Idea, Execution, Preparation — and the annotated screenshot. Zero blank fields, and P&L is not a grade. That review feeds tomorrow morning's read — the loop closing on itself.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal entry for the trade — all 7 fields completed — with the trim and exit bars marked on the chart above it
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, May 25–late September 2023, journal entry beneath (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Mark each decision at its bar, in order: entry ≈$38.50 (May 25); the stop-to-breakeven raise as price tagged ≈+1R ≈$40.40 on the May 30 trillion-dollar push (high ≈$41.93); the first-third trim ≈$43.90 into the June 20 strength (≈+2.8R); the remainder trailed on the rising 50-day all summer, through the August 24 record ≈$50.27; the exit ≈$43 on late September's first decisive close below it (September closed ≈$43.50). Blended ≈+2.5R. Below: the mock journal with all seven fields — date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-vs-plan, Idea/Execution/Preparation grades, annotated screenshot. Zero blanks. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: hand over the printable six-station LOOP card and state the course's architecture out loud: every lesson from here on plugs into exactly one of these six boxes, and you'll know which one before each lesson starts.
chapters.speaker_notes: Hand over the LOOP card. Six stations in order, each with its governing question and the tool that answers it. Regime — what am I permitted to do today? The 0-150 dial. Scan — which names earned the list? The nightly filter chain. Setup — what exactly is this trade? Catalog name plus the five-field card. Size — how much? The formula, 2% hard max. Manage — is the plan intact, and which exit rule fires now? Review — what did this teach, in a form I can aggregate? Print it, keep it beside the platform, and re-fill the walk-through at the bottom for every trade until the loop is reflex. Then state the course architecture plainly: every lesson from here forward plugs into exactly one of these six boxes, and you'll be told which one before each lesson starts. That's the whole course on one page.

lessons.title: Casino Math: Why a 45% Win Rate at 2R Prints Money
lessons.note: R-multiples and expectancy computed live for three trader profiles, including the 90%-win-rate trader who loses money — then a 20-trade on-camera marble-game draw so the member feels 6+ consecutive losers occur inside a profitable system. Artifact: the R-multiple ledger worksheet reused in Module 5.

chapters.marker: The house loses 48% of the hands
chapters.beat: open with the question 'what was your last trade worth in R?' and the claim that a casino never predicts the next hand, it just owns the math of ten thousand of them.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the question: what was your last trade worth in R? Most traders can't answer — they know the dollars, not the units. Then the casino claim: a casino loses roughly 48% of blackjack hands, and it builds marble lobbies anyway. It never predicts the next hand. It owns a small edge and runs it across ten thousand hands, so the outcome of any single hand is irrelevant. That's the frame this whole system runs on: we are the house, not the gambler. You don't need to be right most of the time; you need a positive equation and the discipline to keep dealing. This lesson gives you the unit — R — the equation — expectancy — and a live demonstration that a profitable system can and will hand you six losers in a row.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard title card: 'The casino loses 48% of hands' with a simple edge-per-hand sketch

chapters.marker: R: price every trade in units of risk
chapters.beat: define the R-multiple on one real trade (risk $500, make $1,100 = +2.2R), then re-denominate three past trades from dollars into R on screen so the unit sticks.
chapters.speaker_notes: Define R on a real trade. 1R is the dollars you planned to lose if the stop hits — fixed before entry: shares times stop distance. Risk $500 and make $1,100: 1,100 ÷ 500 = +2.2R. Stopped at plan: −1.0R exactly. Now re-denominate three past trades on screen. A $300 winner where you risked $1,000 is +0.3R — a mediocre trade dressed as a green one. A $250 winner on $100 risked is +2.5R — a great trade that looks small in dollars. A $900 loss on $300 planned risk is −3R — a broken rule, not bad luck. Dollars lie because position sizes differ; R makes every trade comparable to every other. From this lesson on, every trade in this course is priced in R — and so is yours.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard: the R conversion worked three times ($500 risk / $1,100 gain = +2.2R) over three anonymized trade tickets

chapters.beat: compute expectancy live for a 45% winner at 2R, a 60% winner at 1R, and the 90%-win-rate trader who loses money, and let the arithmetic — not opinion — name who eats.
chapters.speaker_notes: The equation: Expectancy = (win% × avg win in R) − (loss% × avg loss in R). Trader one: 45% winner averaging 2R, losers at 1R. (0.45 × 2) − (0.55 × 1) = 0.90 − 0.55 = +0.35R per trade — a hundred trades pays +35R. Trader two: 60% winner at 1R wins, 1R losses. (0.60 × 1) − (0.40 × 1) = +0.20R — profitable, thinner. Trader three: the 90% winner — scalps tiny +0.2R gains and lets losers run to 5R. (0.90 × 0.2) − (0.10 × 5) = 0.18 − 0.50 = −0.32R per trade. Right nine times out of ten, and he eats. Let the arithmetic — not opinion — name who survives: win rate alone tells you nothing. The system you're learning lives in trader one's column.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard table: three traders' expectancy computed line by line (+0.35R / +0.20R / −0.32R)

chapters.beat: run the live 20-trade marble draw at 45%/2R and keep drawing until a streak of 6-plus losers lands, naming the feeling in your gut before revealing the ledger still finishes green.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the marble game live: a bag weighted 45% winners paying +2R, 55% losers costing −1R. Draw twenty, log every result on camera. Keep drawing until a streak of six or more losers lands — at 45%, a 6-plus loss streak inside twenty draws is common, and it will show up. When it does, stop and name the feeling: after loser four your gut says the system is broken; by loser six you want to change something — size up to win it back, or quit. Then reveal the running ledger: even through that streak, the twenty-draw total finishes green, near the expected +7R — twenty draws times +0.35R each. The streak was never information. The bag never changed. Your only job during a streak is to keep drawing at the same size.
chapters.on_screen: Live camera: the marble-bag draw with a running R tally on screen, the 6+ loser streak circled

chapters.beat: fill the first rows of the R-ledger worksheet from the marble draw on screen, and assign it as the standing log you will bring back, filled in, when this exact sheet returns in Module 5.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the first rows of the R-Multiple Ledger from the marble draw, on screen, so the columns are familiar before real money touches them: Date, Ticker, Setup name, 1R in dollars of planned risk, Exit date, Result in R, and Rule Y/N — one question only: did you follow the written plan, win or lose? Then the standing assignment: this ledger is now your permanent trade log. Every trade gets a row, priced in R, nothing else. After every 20 rows you run the expectancy block at the bottom — win rate times average win, minus loss rate times average loss — because that number, not P&L, grades your system. This exact sheet comes back in Module 5, filled in, when we do the risk math for real. Bring it with rows on it.
chapters.on_screen: THE R-MULTIPLE LEDGER toolkit artifact with the marble-draw results entered in the first rows

lessons.title: EARLY WIN: Read Today's UCT Exposure Rating and Write Your Exposure Plan
lessons.note: Screen-records the live dashboard: read today's actual 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating, name its GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, and learn the doctrine that the state is a permission band, not a prediction. Artifact: the one-page max-exposure plan the member re-fills every Monday for the rest of the course.

chapters.marker: A real skill in the first sitting
chapters.beat: promise the early win up front: in the next ten minutes you make a live exposure call off the same dial the firm reads every single morning.
chapters.speaker_notes: Make the promise up front: in the next ten minutes you will make a live exposure call off the same dial this firm reads every single morning — not a toy version, the actual production number. Most courses make you sit through weeks of theory before you touch anything real, and half of all course dropout happens in the first two weeks precisely because nothing real happens. Not here. By the end of this video you'll have read today's 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating, named its permission band, and written a one-page max-exposure plan for the week — the same page you'll re-fill every Monday morning for the rest of the course. One skill, first sitting, used tomorrow morning. Open the dashboard.
chapters.on_screen: The live UCT Intelligence dashboard, Dashboard tab, before zooming to the dial

chapters.beat: screen-record the live dashboard, find today's actual 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating, and say the number out loud with where it sits on the scale.
chapters.speaker_notes: Screen-record the live dashboard and find the UCT Exposure Rating gauge. It's a 0-150 scale — and the number IS the recommended exposure: a reading of 80 means roughly 80% invested is authorized, and readings above 100 mark leveraged territory in gold. Say today's actual number out loud and place it on the scale. The engine builds this score every morning from breadth participation, the distribution-day count, and index moving-average structure — you'll open the hood on all of that in Module 3; today you only need to read the gauge. The dashboard prints the band right beside the score, so there is nothing to interpret: find the number, say the number, note the band. One number, read in ten seconds, before any chart or ticker is opened. That ordering is the discipline.
chapters.on_screen: Live screen-record: the UCT Exposure Rating gauge on the Breadth tile, today's actual reading

chapters.beat: translate today's score into its GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE band on camera and give the band its correct name: a permission band that grants and revokes rights.
chapters.speaker_notes: Translate today's score into its band on camera: GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE. Then give the band its correct name — a permission band. It grants and revokes rights; it does not forecast. Each band maps to concrete things you are allowed to do: how many names you may hold, the ceiling on any single position, and whether you may open new positions at all. GREEN authorizes the full playbook. YELLOW reduces it — fewer names, smaller ceilings. ORANGE parks you: best setups only at minimum size, or nothing. The full regime-by-grade sizing table arrives later in the course; today the skill is the translation itself: number, band, rights. Say it as a sentence — 'the dial reads X, that's this band, which means today I'm allowed to…' — because that sentence is the first station of every trading day you'll ever run.
chapters.on_screen: The dial with the GREEN / YELLOW / ORANGE band scale annotated beside it

chapters.beat: state the doctrine plainly: GREEN does not mean the market goes up, it means more of your playbook is authorized — and show a GREEN day that closed red without costing a rule-follower anything.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the doctrine plainly, straight to camera: GREEN does not mean the market goes up. GREEN means more of your playbook is authorized. The dial measures the health of conditions — participation, accumulation, structure — not tomorrow's direction. Then prove it with a real day: a GREEN morning where the index closed red. The rule-follower lost nothing that day — stops placed by the formula, sizes inside the table, and a red close inside a healthy tape is normal weather. The trader who reads GREEN as a prediction oversizes, skips stops, and gets hurt by ordinary noise. Permission and prediction are different machines: one tells you what you may do, the other pretends to know what happens next. This firm only builds the first kind. If you take one sentence from Module 1, take this one.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily, June 2023 — a healthy-uptrend session that closed red under a green regime (or substitute a firm-logged GREEN-day example)
chapters.example_spec: SPY daily, June 2023 — use Tuesday, June 20, 2023. Walk it: the five-week advance into the June 15–16 push, closing ≈$439.46 on June 16 on ≈1.5× volume, fresh 52-week highs, price stacked above rising 20/50/200-day — unambiguous GREEN conditions (the month closed ≈$443.28); the June 20 red close, ≈−0.5%; the shallow two-day drift that held above the rising 20 EMA; the recovery to new highs — ≈$459.44 on July 27, ≈$457.79 at month-end. Narrate the R-outcome: a rule-follower with formula-sized longs (1% risk each) watched ≈−0.1 to −0.2R of open-profit wiggle, no stops hit, nothing to do. The dial permitted; it never predicted. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: fill in the one-page max-exposure plan live against today's real reading, then install the ritual: this page gets re-filled every Monday morning for the rest of the course, no exceptions.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the Monday Max-Exposure Plan live against today's real reading. Section one: the dial number, its band, and what the inputs said. Section two: what this band authorizes this week — max concurrent names, max single-position size from the table at your best available grade, and whether new buys are allowed: yes, pilot-only, or no. Section three is the sizing table itself — size only from a cell. Section four: portfolio heat — open risk, entry minus stop times shares summed across positions, divided by equity — hard-capped at 10%, no new buy above it. Then install the ritual: this page gets re-filled every Monday morning before the open, for the rest of the course, no exceptions. And it's not a weekly contract — the band can flip mid-week, and a flip kills the page: you write a new one, you don't argue with it.
chapters.on_screen: THE MONDAY MAX-EXPOSURE PLAN toolkit artifact, filled in live against today's dial reading

lessons.title: Where Breakeven Traders Bleed: The Five Leaks and Your Placement Diagnostic
lessons.note: The five leaks that keep a trader at breakeven — no regime filter, oversizing, moved stops, setup-hopping, no review — each shown on a real anonymized trade. Artifact: the 10-question placement diagnostic the capstone reads back. Closes by installing the course guardrail on camera: pilot size or paper ONLY until the M5 sizing gate clears, and no setup traded live until its family drill is passed — the stop is an appointment, not a debate, from day one.

chapters.marker: Breakeven is a diagnosis, not bad luck
chapters.beat: open on the flat equity curve of a real breakeven trader and the claim that five specific, nameable leaks — not one big flaw — are holding it at zero.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a real flat equity curve — eighteen months of work, hundreds of trades, net zero. Breakeven feels like bad luck; it's actually a diagnosis. A breakeven curve means the trader has genuine skill — enough winners to offset the damage — and specific, repeating leaks draining exactly what the skill earns. Not one big flaw: five nameable ones. No regime filter. Oversizing. Moved stops. Setup-hopping. No review. Every breakeven trader is bleeding from at least one; most bleed from two or three. This lesson shows you each leak on a real anonymized trade, then hands you a ten-question diagnostic that locates yours. Write the result down honestly — the capstone module reads this exact page back to you, and your playbook isn't finished until your journal proves the primary leak is plugged.
chapters.on_screen: An anonymized flat 18-month equity curve hovering at zero (or substitute a firm/member example curve)
chapters.example_spec: Build the curve in a spreadsheet and chart it as one thin line hovering at zero, axis in R, fully anonymized. Ledger recipe: 140 trades, January 2022–June 2023; 50% winners averaging +0.9R, losers −1R — genuine skill — then salt in the leaks: one ≈−8R oversized loser in the May 2022 selloff and another in the September 2022 selloff; a six-trade losing run of counter-trend longs during June 2022's ORANGE tape; a churny setup-hopping stretch across Q1 2023. Net after 18 months ≈ 0R. The visible shape to point at: grind up, cliff, grind up, cliff, flat — skill earning exactly what the leaks drain. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Leak one and two: no regime filter, oversizing
chapters.beat: show a real anonymized trade opened long into a hostile tape, then one where a single oversized loss erased eleven disciplined wins, naming each leak at the bar where it bled.
chapters.speaker_notes: Leak one, no regime filter: a real trade opened long into a hostile tape — the dial deep in ORANGE, distribution stacking — a clean chart in a market that had revoked permission. The setup wasn't wrong; the calendar was. It bled from the first bar. Leak two, oversizing: a journal showing eleven disciplined wins averaging under +1R each — then one position sized at many times normal that gave it all back in a single trade. Do the arithmetic out loud: eleven wins at roughly +0.8R is about +9R earned; the oversized trade, planned as −1R, realized near −10R because the size was ten times what the formula allowed. One trade erased three months. Skill was never the problem in either chart — the leak sits before the entry, in permission and in size.
chapters.on_screen: Two anonymized trade charts side by side: a long opened on an ORANGE tape, and the single oversized loser next to its 11-win journal streak (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Left, leak one — AAPL daily, spring 2022: the late-March rally to ≈$179 (March closed ≈$174.61); the long ≈$175 in the first week of April while the tape was hostile — SPX had already broken from its January 4, 2022 high ≈4,819 to ≈4,115 by February 24 and was printing lower highs, a dial deep in ORANGE; the stop ≈$166 hit within days (−1R); the slide to ≈$137 by the end of June. Clean chart, revoked calendar. Right, leak two — UPST daily at its November 9, 2021 earnings: held at ≈10× formula size, it gapped −22.6% overnight, from a ≈$314 close to a ≈$243 open, closing ≈$257 — the planned −1R realized ≈−10R — beside a mocked journal strip of eleven +0.8R wins (≈+9R) it erased. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Leak three and four: moved stops, setup-hopping
chapters.beat: a real trade whose stop got moved twice on the way to a −3R exit, then a journal that cycled four setups in six weeks with none of them mastered.
chapters.speaker_notes: Leak three, moved stops: a real trade planned at −1R. Price approached the stop; the trader moved it lower to 'give it room.' It kept falling; he moved it again. Final exit: −3R — three times the planned loss, on purpose, in two decisions. A stop that moves away from price is not a stop; it's a story. Leak four, setup-hopping: a journal that cycled four different setups in six weeks — breakouts, then gappers, then reversals, then back — none reaching twenty logged reps. Every switch resets the learning clock to zero, so this trader has been a beginner four times instead of competent once. Mastery of one setup takes a market cycle of reps; sampling four takes forever. Both leaks compound quietly: moved stops make losers bigger, and hopping keeps the winners from ever getting good.
chapters.on_screen: The −3R trade chart with all three stop placements marked, beside a journal view showing 4 setups cycled in 6 weeks
chapters.example_spec: Moved-stop chart: PYPL daily, February–March 2022. Walk it: the February 2 earnings crash — a −20.4% gap to an open ≈$140, closing ≈$132.57 on ≈7× volume, a ≈−25% day; the falling-knife entry ≈$120 mid-February; the planned stop ≈$112 (1R ≈ $8); stop moved to ≈$104 as price approached; moved again toward ≈$96; final exit ≈$96 in March with the slide still running into the mid-March low near ≈$90. Draw all three stop placements as dated horizontal segments. Realized ≈−3R on a planned −1R, via two deliberate decisions. Beside it: a mocked journal view cycling four setups in six weeks — breakouts, gappers, reversals, breakouts again — none reaching twenty logged reps. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Leak five, then your placement diagnostic
chapters.beat: the no-review trader repeating an identical mistake three months running, then take the 10-question placement diagnostic live and file the result — the capstone reads this exact page back to you.
chapters.speaker_notes: Leak five, no review: a trader repeating the identical mistake — buying extended, far past the pivot — in October, in November, and again in January. No journal, so no pattern; no pattern, so no fix; the same tuition paid monthly. Now take the placement diagnostic, live: ten Y/N questions against your last twenty REAL trades, two questions per leak — Q1 and Q6 locate the regime leak, Q2 and Q7 oversizing, Q3 and Q8 moved stops, Q4 and Q9 setup-hopping, Q5 and Q10 no review. Pull the journal, not the memory — a flattered diagnostic sends the wrong leak to your capstone. The scoring rule: two-out-of-two on any leak means that leak owns you; ties go to the leak that cost the most dollars. File the finished page — the capstone opens by putting this exact sheet back in front of you.
chapters.on_screen: THE PLACEMENT DIAGNOSTIC toolkit artifact — the ten-question Y/N table, filled in live

chapters.beat: state the course rules and sign them: pilot size or paper ONLY until the Module 5 sizing gate clears, no setup traded live until its family drill is passed, and from day one the stop is an appointment, not a debate.
chapters.speaker_notes: Read the course rules out loud and sign them on camera, so the member does the same. Rule one: pilot size or paper ONLY until the Module 5 sizing gate clears — that gate is ten sizing problems at a 100% pass bar, deliberately stricter than every other checkpoint, and nothing after Module 5 is traded live until it's cleared. Rule two: no setup is traded live until its family drill is passed — watching the lesson authorizes nothing. Rule three, from day one: the stop is an appointment, not a debate — placed where the thesis dies, before entry, and kept. These aren't training wheels; they're the difference between tuition and destruction. Every blown-up account you'll ever hear about broke one of these three while 'still learning.' Initial the guardrail line on the diagnostic page. The market will still be here when you've earned size.
chapters.on_screen: The guardrail signature line at the bottom of the Placement Diagnostic, signed on camera
