lessons.title: One Bar, One Auction: Candles, Close Position, and the Volume Witness
lessons.note: OHLC anatomy, close-position quality (a close in the top 40% of the range means buyers won the day), and volume as the witness — the same +5% day on 3× average volume versus 0.4×, and why only one is evidence. Closes with 10 cover-the-answer reps calling buyer vs seller control.

chapters.beat: open on a single candle and make the claim: this shape records an entire day's fight between buyers and sellers, and by the end of this lesson you can read the verdict at a glance.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a single candle, blown up full screen. Make the claim: this one shape records an entire day's fight — every buyer and seller who showed up, who held control at each phase, and who won at the bell. A candle isn't decoration; it's a compressed auction transcript. By the end of this lesson you'll read the verdict at a glance: who won the day, how decisively, and whether the crowd showed up to witness it. That glance-speed read is the atomic skill under everything in this course — bases, breakouts, gaps, and reclaims are all just sequences of these glyphs. We build it in four steps: anatomy, then the close-position rule, then the volume witness, then ten timed reps. No pattern interpretation yet — first you learn to read the display before anyone argues about what it means.
chapters.on_screen: A single daily candle enlarged full-screen, unlabeled (any liquid name — e.g. one NVDA daily bar)

chapters.beat: dissect a real bar on screen into open, high, low, close, body, and wicks, saying what each piece reveals about who held control and when they lost it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Dissect one real bar. Open: where the auction started — the overnight consensus. High: the buyers' furthest advance before sellers stopped them. Low: the sellers' deepest push before buyers stepped in. Close: the final verdict — the price both sides accepted at the bell, the single most important number on the bar. The body, open to close, is the day's net ground gained or lost. The wicks are failed excursions — territory visited and surrendered. A long upper wick says buyers advanced and were repelled; a long lower wick says sellers broke ground and lost it back. Then read the same bar as a story: opened here, buyers pushed to the high, sellers took it back to the low, and the close tells you who held the field when it ended. Every bar on every chart tells this story.
chapters.on_screen: One real daily bar annotated live: O, H, L, C, body, and both wicks labeled with arrows
chapters.example_spec: Use the NVDA daily bar of May 30, 2023 — the day it tagged a $1-trillion valuation intraday and faded — enlarged with its volume (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Walk the anatomy in order: open ≈$40.51, gapped up on post-earnings euphoria; high ≈$41.93 — the buyers' furthest advance, printed early; low ≈$40.04 — the sellers' answer; close ≈$40.19, pinned near the low at ≈8% of the range. The body is small; the long upper wick is the story — buyers advanced ≈3.5% past the open and surrendered all of it. Green versus the prior session, yet sellers held the field at the bell. Volume above average, just under the ≈2× May 31 printed: a witnessed fight. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: teach the quality rule with three real bars closing top, middle, and bottom of range: a close in the top 40% of the day's range means buyers won the day.
chapters.speaker_notes: The quality rule, with numbers: a close in the top 40% of the day's range means buyers won the day. Compute it on three real bars. Range equals high minus low; close position equals close minus low, divided by range. Bar one closes at 92% of its range — buyers won decisively; sellers had a whole session to knock it down and couldn't. Bar two closes mid-range near 50% — a draw; the day produced information for neither side. Bar three closes at 10% of range — sellers won, even if the bar printed green earlier. Note what the rule ignores: the open, and whether the day was up or down. A stock can rise 3% and still close at the bottom of its range — that's a warning, not strength. The close's position in the range IS the verdict.
chapters.on_screen: Three real daily bars side by side closing at ~90% / ~50% / ~10% of range, close-position math computed under each
chapters.example_spec: All three bars from NVDA daily, 2023–24, one name throughout (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Bar one, ≈98% close: February 22, 2024 — gapped +11.2%, range ≈$74.55–78.60, close ≈$78.54 on ≈1.8× average volume; buyers won outright. Bar two, ≈50%: pick a quiet consolidation day from the September 6–20, 2023 chop whose close sits mid-range — take the cleanest one. Bar three, ≈10%: August 24, 2023 — gapped +6.6% to a record ≈$50.27 intraday after blowout earnings, closed ≈$47.16 on ≈2.4× volume, barely green against the ≈$47.11 prior close and at the bottom of its range: the up-day the sellers won. Compute (close − low) ÷ (high − low) under each bar. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: put the same +5% day on screen twice, once on 3× average volume and once on 0.4×, and explain why only one of those two days counts as evidence of anything.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the identical +5% day on screen twice. Version one: 3× average volume. Version two: 0.4× average volume. Same price change, opposite meaning. Volume is attendance — how much real money voted. The 3× day is evidence: institutions participated, real size changed hands, and the move now has a constituency that must defend it. The 0.4× day is an empty room: a handful of small orders drifted price higher, nobody committed, and there is nothing underneath when it gets tested. The rule this installs permanently: price makes the claim, volume is the witness, and an unwitnessed claim doesn't count as evidence of anything. Every signal you learn in this course — breakout, gap, reclaim — will be put on trial with this same question. A move on 3× volume gets a verdict; a move on 0.4× gets dismissed.
chapters.on_screen: The same +5% daily bar shown twice with its volume pane: once at 3× average volume, once at 0.4× (pull a real pair — e.g. an NVDA high-volume gap day vs a quiet low-volume drift day)
chapters.example_spec: Hold the ticker constant so only volume differs (NVDA prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Heavy version: NVDA, January 8, 2024 — ≈+6% to a new all-time high close ≈$52.20, clearing the November 20, 2023 high ≈$50.55, on volume well above its 50-day average but below the ≈2.3× of the period's heaviest days (verify the multiple on your platform). Light version: hunt NVDA's quiet drifts — the December 26–29, 2023 holiday sessions or the July 2023 summer chop — for an up-day of similar percent size on under-half average volume; take the lightest, and if NVDA lacks a clean sub-0.5× specimen, pull it from AMD in the same holiday window. Show each bar with its volume pane and the 50-day volume average drawn. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Ten reps: who won the day
chapters.beat: run 10 cover-the-answer bars calling buyer versus seller control before each reveal, and set the pass bar: the call should be fast and felt, not deliberated.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run ten cover-the-answer reps. For each: show a bare bar with its volume, cover what came next, and demand the call in two seconds — buyers or sellers, and does the witness confirm? Then reveal. Format matters: say the call out loud BEFORE the reveal, every time — silent nodding grades nothing. Use the three cues under each rep: where did it close in its range (top 40% means buyers won), how big was the body versus the wicks, and was volume above or below average? On a miss, name which of the three cues you misread. The pass bar: the call should be fast and felt, not deliberated — if you're still computing at rep ten, run the set again tomorrow. This is perception training and speed is the point: ten bars a day for a week and the read becomes automatic.
chapters.on_screen: A 10-bar drill sequence: single bars with volume, answer covered then revealed one at a time
chapters.example_spec: Build ten reps from documented bars (NVDA and NFLX split-adjusted). Three buyer-won (close in the top 40%, heavy volume): NVDA Feb 23, 2023 (+13.0% gap, ≈$23.44→$23.66); NVDA Feb 22, 2024 (≈$75.03→$78.54, ≈1.8×); ANET Aug 1, 2023 (≈$44.38→$46.40, ≈6.4×). Three seller-won: NFLX Apr 20, 2022 (−29.7% gap, ≈15.8×); PYPL Feb 2, 2022 (−20.4%, ≈7×); COIN May 11, 2022 (−24.9%, ≈5.4×). Two deceptive: NVDA Aug 24, 2023 (green print, ≈10% close position) and COIN Jun 6, 2023, which gapped −19.8% to ≈$47.10 and closed ≈$51.61 near its high on ≈4× volume. Two low-volume drifters where 'no evidence' is the honest call. Labels hidden, two-second calls, pass ≈8/10. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The Moving-Average Stack: 9 EMA, 20 EMA, 50 SMA, 200 SMA — What Each Line Is For
lessons.note: The firm's four lines and their distinct jobs — 9 EMA momentum leash, 20 EMA swing trend, 50 SMA institutional line, 200 SMA bull/bear divide — shown stacked on a leader and tangled on a chopfest. Artifact: the exact four-slot MA template configured live on the dashboard chart.

chapters.beat: open on a naked chart and add the firm's four lines one at a time, promising that by the end each one carries a distinct job title, not decoration.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a naked chart — price and volume only. Add the firm's four lines one at a time: the 9 EMA, the 20 EMA, the 50 SMA, the 200 SMA. Make the promise: by the end of this lesson each line carries a distinct job title — none is decoration and none is redundant. The 9 EMA is the momentum leash. The 20 EMA is the swing trend. The 50 SMA is the institutional line. The 200 SMA is the bull/bear divide. Two are exponential — the fast pair, weighted toward recent price because their job is responsiveness. Two are simple — the slow pair, deliberate because their job is context. This exact four-slot stack is the firm's standard: every chart in this course wears these four lines and no others, and by the end of this lesson, so will yours.
chapters.on_screen: A naked daily chart with the four MAs added one at a time (use a clean Stage-2 leader — e.g. NVDA daily 2023)

chapters.marker: The fast pair: 9 EMA and 20 EMA
chapters.beat: show the 9 EMA as the momentum leash a hot leader rides and the 20 EMA as the swing-trend line beneath it, each doing its job on a real advancing stock.
chapters.speaker_notes: The 9 EMA is the momentum leash: when a leader is at its hottest, price rides the 9 — touching it, bouncing, never closing meaningfully below. Show it on a real advancing stock: weeks where every dip finds the 9 and the stock never lets you in cheaper. The day a hot name closes hard below its 9 is the first sign the leash slipped — not a sell signal by itself, but notice served that the momentum phase is ending. The 20 EMA beneath is the swing-trend line: the level an orderly uptrend respects between thrusts. Pullbacks to a rising 20 on quiet volume are rest; a lost 20 is a broken swing. Job titles, restated: the 9 tells you how hot, the 20 tells you whether the swing is intact. When flags arrive later in the course, the 20 EMA is the disqualifier line — remember it.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, first half of 2023 — price riding the 9 EMA through the advance, the 20 EMA catching the deeper pullbacks

chapters.marker: The slow pair: 50 SMA and 200 SMA
chapters.beat: the 50 SMA as the institutional line where big money defends its inventory, and the 200 SMA as the bull/bear divide that no serious long trade fights.
chapters.speaker_notes: The 50 SMA is the institutional line. Big money builds positions over weeks, and its average cost tends to live near the 50 — so that's where it defends its inventory. Show real touches: a leader pulling back to a rising 50 on drying volume and getting bought, repeatedly. That's not magic; it's institutions protecting their basis, and two or three defended touches confirm who's underneath. The 200 SMA is the bull/bear divide — the market's long-term memory. Above a rising 200, a stock is innocent until proven guilty; below a falling 200, guilty until proven innocent. The firm's rule is blunt: no serious long trade fights the 200. Every stock you will ever buy in this course is above it. The fast pair times; the slow pair judges eligibility — and eligibility always comes first.
chapters.on_screen: A leader's daily chart with two defended 50 SMA touches marked, then zoomed out to price above a rising 200 SMA (e.g. MSFT daily 2023-2024)

chapters.beat: put a leader with 9 over 20 over 50 over 200 in clean rising order beside a chopfest where all four braid together, and read the verdict: stacked means tradeable, tangled means walk away.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two charts, side by side. Left: a leader with the full stack in clean rising order — 9 over 20 over 50 over 200, all four sloping up, evenly separated like lanes. That geometry means every timeframe of buyer agrees: momentum, swing, institutional, and secular demand all pointing the same way. Every strategy in this course works on that chart. Right: a chopfest — all four lines braided together, crossing weekly, price whipping through the whole cluster. That braid means nobody agrees; every rally gets sold, every dip gets bought, and both sides get stopped out. No setup in the catalog works there. Read the verdict out loud: stacked means tradeable, tangled means walk away. This one-glance filter will disqualify half the charts you ever open — and that free, instant 'no' is worth more than most entries.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: NVDA daily 2023 in clean 9>20>50>200 order vs INTC daily 2022 with all four MAs braided

chapters.beat: configure the exact four-slot MA template live on the dashboard chart, slot by slot, so every chart the member opens for the rest of the course wears these four lines.
chapters.speaker_notes: Configure the template live on the dashboard chart, slot by slot. Open any chart, open chart settings, and fill the four MA overlay slots exactly: slot one — EMA, period 9. Slot two — EMA, period 20. Slot three — SMA, period 50. Slot four — SMA, period 200. Type matters: the fast pair is exponential and the slow pair is simple; a 9 SMA or a 50 EMA is a different tool and not the firm's. Save, and the settings persist to your account — every chart you open anywhere on the platform now wears these four lines automatically. Verify on a fresh ticker: pull one up cold and confirm all four lines paint. From this moment through the capstone, every chart you and I look at together wears this exact stack. Same lines, same jobs, no exceptions.
chapters.on_screen: The live dashboard chart-settings panel — the four MA overlay slots configured to 9 EMA / 20 EMA / 50 SMA / 200 SMA

lessons.title: Three Lines That Matter: Trend, Support, Resistance — and None That Don't
lessons.note: Drawing discipline on five real charts, including overhead supply and why a breakout into it fails; over-annotation diagnosed as a named beginner failure. Ends with 10 draw-it-yourself reps checked against the reveal.

chapters.beat: open on the same chart twice, one buried under a spiderweb of drawings and one wearing exactly three lines, and ask which trader knows what to do at tomorrow's open.
chapters.speaker_notes: The same chart, twice. Left: buried under a spiderweb — every swing connected, fibs on fibs, a dozen horizontals, three channels. Right: the identical chart wearing exactly three lines — one trendline, one support, one resistance. Ask the question and let it hang: which trader knows what to do at tomorrow's open? The spiderweb trader has a drawing for every outcome, which means he has a decision for none — whatever price does, some line 'explains' it, and no line obligates him. The three-line trader has three prices where he must act, and everywhere else he does nothing. Lines are not art and not analysis theater; each one is a pre-commitment to a decision. If a line doesn't tell you to do something when price touches it, it shouldn't exist. Three lines, three decisions — that's what this lesson installs.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: the same daily chart drowned in ~30 drawings vs wearing exactly 3 lines (any liquid name — e.g. AAPL daily)
chapters.example_spec: AAPL daily, January 2023–January 2024. Right panel, exactly three lines: the rising trendline under the January–July 2023 swing lows, anchored at the January 3, 2023 low ≈$124.17; the support zone ≈$166–172 — the August and October 2023 defended lows, the most-touched shelf on the chart; the resistance zone ≈$198–200 — the July 2023 high and the December 14, 2023 high ≈$199.62, twice rejected. Left panel, the identical chart buried under ≈30 drawings: every minor swing connected, fib fans, a dozen stray horizontals, three channels — build it deliberately ugly. Close on the contrast: the three-line chart dictates buy ≈$170, wrong below ≈$164, profit into ≈$198; the spiderweb dictates nothing. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Drawing discipline, charts one through three
chapters.beat: draw the trendline, support, and resistance on three real charts while stating the rules: most-touched levels win, zones beat exact prices, and a line no one traded at is not a level.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the three lines on three real charts, stating the rules as the pen moves. Rule one: most-touched levels win — a line with four or five touches is a level the market has repeatedly voted on; a line connecting two random points is a coincidence. Rule two: zones beat exact prices — draw support as a band roughly a percent thick, because the market remembers areas, not pennies, and an exact-price line trains you to be wrong by a nickel. Rule three: a line no one traded at is not a level — no volume, no reaction, no wicks fighting at that price means delete it; you're decorating. On each chart: the trendline on the governing swing lows, support at the most-defended zone below, resistance at the most-rejected zone above. Three charts, nine lines total, every one earning its place out loud.
chapters.on_screen: Three real daily charts drawn live, one at a time — trendline, support zone, resistance zone on each
chapters.example_spec: Chart one — SPY daily, 2023: trendline under the March/May/June swing lows; support ≈$404–410, the May basing shelf around the May 4 low ≈$403.74; resistance ≈$457–460, the July 27 high ≈$459.44 with September's failure just beneath it. Chart two — TSLA daily, 2023: trendline under the January–June advance off the January 6 low ≈$101.81; support ≈$152–160, the April–May shelf; resistance ≈$299–300, the July 19 high ≈$299.29. Chart three — META daily, 2023: trendline under the recovery's swing lows; support ≈$279–290, October's defended zone (low ≈$279.40 on October 26); resistance ≈$325–330, the July 27 and pre-earnings-October highs. Count touches out loud — three-plus or it isn't drawn. Nine lines total. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Overhead supply: the ceiling of trapped buyers
chapters.beat: chart four: shade the zone of old holders waiting to sell out even, then show the breakout that ran straight into that ceiling and died.
chapters.speaker_notes: Chart four is the one that costs traders real money. Shade the zone where a stock traded heavily before a decline — everyone who bought there is underwater, and most have exactly one plan: sell when it gets back to even. That's overhead supply — a standing army of sellers with resting orders at their break-even. It doesn't show up as a line; it shows up as a ceiling. Now play the failure: the stock bases, sets up beautifully, breaks out on volume — directly into the shaded zone. The breakout stalls within days and dies, not because the pattern was wrong but because its path ran into a wall of trapped inventory. The pre-trade check this installs: look LEFT and up before any breakout — how much trading happened above the pivot, and how recently? A clean sky above beats a perfect base below.
chapters.on_screen: A real failed breakout into shaded overhead supply — e.g. PYPL daily 2022: a bounce/base attempt dying into the heavy 2021 congestion above (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: PYPL daily, 2022, with 2021–22 context visible. Shade the overhead supply first: the February–April 2022 congestion ≈$95–125, where heavy volume traded after the February 2 crash and before the June collapse to ≈$67.58 on June 30 — every buyer there trapped, waiting to sell even. Then the trap: the June–July base ≈$70–90; the August 3 breakout gap through ≈$90, opening ≈$101.14 and closing ≈$97.92 on ≈3.6× volume (earnings plus the Elliott stake) — textbook, except the path led straight into the shaded zone. The rally died at ≈$103.03 on August 16 at the zone's lip, rolled over, and broke the pivot; breakout buyers ≈$92 with stops ≈$84 took the full −1R by late October, and PYPL closed December ≈$71.22. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: chart five: name the spiderweb as the beginner failure it is, then erase it live, line by line, down to the three that actually govern the trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Chart five: the spiderweb itself. Name it honestly — over-annotation is a named beginner failure, not a style preference. It comes from a real anxiety: every line feels like insurance against missing something. But drawings are decisions, and thirty decisions is zero decisions. Erase it live, line by line, interrogating each one. How many touches? Two — delete. Did anyone trade there? No volume, no reaction — delete. Does this fib cluster obligate me to any action? No — delete. Keep only what survives: the trendline the trend actually obeys, the support zone with the most defended touches, the resistance zone with the most rejections. What remains is three lines — and suddenly the chart says something: here I'd buy, here I'm wrong, here I take profit. The eraser did more analysis than the pencil ever did.
chapters.on_screen: The spiderweb chart erased live, drawing by drawing, down to the surviving three lines
chapters.example_spec: The same AAPL daily, January 2023–January 2024, wearing the ≈30-drawing spiderweb built for chapter one's split screen. Erase live, interrogating each drawing: two-touch micro-trendlines — coincidence, delete; fib fans — no volume, no reaction at any level, delete; stray intraday horizontals nobody traded at — delete; redundant channels — delete. The three survivors, revealed in order: the rising trendline under the January–July 2023 swing lows off the January 3 low ≈$124.17; the support zone ≈$166–172 with its August and October defended touches; the resistance zone ≈$198–200, capped by the December 14, 2023 high ≈$199.62, twice rejected. End on the clean chart's sentence: buy ≈$170, wrong below ≈$164, profit into ≈$198. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run 10 draw-it-yourself reps with the answer covered, checking each against the reveal, with the pass bar stated: your three lines land inside the instructor's zones, every time.
chapters.speaker_notes: Ten draw-it-yourself reps, answer covered. For each chart: pause the video, draw your trendline, your support, and your resistance — commit ink before the reveal — then uncover the instructor's version and compare. The grading standard is zones, not pixels: your three lines land inside the instructor's zones, every time. That's the pass bar. If your support sits at a level the instructor's version doesn't even acknowledge, re-run the three rules — touches, zones, traded-at — and find which one you skipped; that's the miss to log, not 'I was off by forty cents.' Expect the first three or four to be humbling and the last three to converge — this skill compounds fast because the rules are few. If you fly through it, re-run the set on ten fresh charts from tonight's scan. Your pen, every chart, from here forward.
chapters.on_screen: The 10-chart drill: each chart blank for the member's own drawing, then revealed with the instructor's three lines overlaid
chapters.example_spec: Pre-build ten answer keys, mixing trend directions, one daily chart each: MSFT 2023 (trendline under the March–July advance; resistance ≈$366, the July high); GOOGL 2023; NFLX 2023 (support ≈$29–31, the winter-into-spring shelf; resistance ≈$48.50, the July 19 high — prices split-adjusted 10:1, ≈10× these at the time); DKNG 2023 (trendline under the January–September advance, ≈$15 to ≈$32); XOM 2022 (the uptrend inside a down year); TSLA 2022 (downtrend line on the lower highs); AAPL 2022; COIN 2023 (support ≈$70–77 autumn zone; resistance ≈$114, the July high); AMD 2023 (resistance ≈$130, the June high, broken in December toward ≈$147); SMCI 2023. Grade attempts on zone overlap, not pixels. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The Weekly Decides, the Daily Times: Multi-Timeframe Alignment
lessons.note: The same stock on weekly, daily, and 60-minute with the rule stated plainly: no daily-timeframe entry against a weekly downtrend. Eight aligned-or-not drills with the answer covered.

chapters.beat: open the identical ticker on weekly, daily, and 60-minute side by side and let the member feel the verdict flip with the zoom before any rule is named.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open the identical ticker three ways at once — weekly, daily, 60-minute, side by side — and don't state any rule yet; let the member feel the verdict flip with the zoom. The weekly shows a clean multi-year uptrend stair-stepping above a rising 200 — a stock you'd own. The daily shows a sharp three-week pullback below the 20 EMA — a stock you'd worry about. The 60-minute shows a violent bounce off yesterday's low — a stock you'd chase. Same company, same price, three opposite feelings — and a trader with no hierarchy acts on whichever screen happens to be open, which is why the same person can be bullish at breakfast and bearish by lunch. The problem isn't that timeframes disagree; they always disagree. The problem is having no rule for which one outranks the others. That rule is this lesson.
chapters.on_screen: One ticker in a 3-pane grid: weekly, daily, and 60-minute side by side (e.g. META across late 2023)

chapters.beat: read the weekly chart first and ask it exactly one question: is this stock in an uptrend I am permitted to buy, or not — nothing else lives on this timeframe.
chapters.speaker_notes: Read the weekly first, always — and ask it exactly one question: is this stock in an uptrend I am permitted to buy, or not? Nothing else lives on this timeframe. You don't hunt entries on a weekly, you don't set stops on a weekly, you don't measure targets on a weekly. It is the eligibility court, and its evidence is structural: price above a rising 200, the stack in order, higher highs and higher lows across months, no heavy overhead supply pressing down from above. If the weekly answers yes, the stock enters the pool and the lower timeframes get to speak. If it answers no, the analysis is OVER — no daily pattern, however beautiful, reopens the case. This is deliberately boring: one question, one binary answer, ten seconds. The weekly decides. Everything after it merely times.
chapters.on_screen: The same ticker's weekly chart alone, full screen, with the single yes/no question overlaid: 'Uptrend I'm permitted to buy?'

chapters.beat: with the weekly's permission granted, drop to the daily to locate the entry and to the 60-minute to refine it, all on the same stock's real move.
chapters.speaker_notes: With the weekly's permission granted, drop down one level at a time on the same stock's real move. The daily is where the entry lives: the base, the tightening pullback, the pivot — the exact price where the trade begins and the structure that puts the stop underneath it. The daily answers where and when. Then, optionally, the 60-minute sharpens: inside the daily setup, intraday structure refines the fill — an opening range holding above the pivot, intraday volume confirming the break — shaving entry cost and tightening risk. But keep the hierarchy straight: the 60-minute refines an entry the daily already found, on a stock the weekly already approved. It never originates a trade. Three screens, three jobs, one direction of authority: the weekly decides, the daily times, the 60-minute sharpens — and authority never flows upstream.
chapters.on_screen: The approved ticker stepping down: daily chart with pivot and stop marked, then the 60-minute showing the entry morning's structure
chapters.example_spec: META, November 2023 — the lesson's ticker, stepped down. Weekly permission already granted: the full 2023 recovery above a rising long-term line. Daily: the October pullback bottomed ≈$279.40 on October 26 on ≈3.5× volume; the early-November base built under ≈$325–330 — the July 27 and pre-earnings-October swing-high zone. Mark pivot ≈$330 and stop ≈$310 under the last daily higher low; the entry bar is the mid-November close through the pivot (note the month itself closed ≈$327.15, a retest of it). Then that morning's 60-minute: opening range holding above ≈$330, intraday volume expanding on the break. Outcome: ≈$360 by mid-December (≈+1.5R, first trim) and ≈$390 by late January — January closed ≈$390.14 — for ≈+3R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The rule, and the trade it saves you from
chapters.beat: state it plainly: no daily-timeframe entry against a weekly downtrend, then show a seductive daily setup that died for exactly that reason.
chapters.speaker_notes: State it plainly and write it on the screen: no daily-timeframe entry against a weekly downtrend. No exceptions for beautiful patterns. Then show the trade this rule exists to prevent: a seductive daily setup — a tight multi-week base, a clean pivot, even a volume breakout — sitting inside a weekly making lower highs beneath a falling 200. The daily says buy; the weekly says this is a bear-market rally in a broken stock. Play it forward: the breakout runs a few days, hits the weekly's overhead supply, rolls over, and takes out the stop — not because the entry was mistimed, but because the trade fought the tide that actually governs. Counter-trend daily setups fail at a rate no entry skill overcomes. The rule costs you a few winners a year and deletes an entire category of loser. Take that exchange every time.
chapters.on_screen: NFLX daily, March-April 2022 — a clean-looking daily bounce setup inside the weekly downtrend, marked where it died (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: NFLX, March–April 2022 (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Weekly first: the November 17, 2021 top ≈$70.10; the January 21, 2022 earnings gap −21.2% to an open ≈$40.04; lower highs beneath a falling long-term line; heavy overhead supply across ≈$40–70. Daily, the seduction: the mid-March bounce off ≈$33 rallying ≈20% in two weeks to ≈$39–40 by March 29 — higher lows, a reclaim-shaped base. Mark the tempting entry ≈$38.50 over the late-March highs, stop ≈$35.50 under the last higher low. Forward: the rally died at the falling weekly structure, the stop hit for −1R within two weeks, and on April 20 NFLX gapped −29.7% and closed ≈−35% on the day, ≈15.8× volume. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run eight aligned-or-not calls with the answer covered, each graded on one binary question: does this daily entry have weekly permission, yes or no.
chapters.speaker_notes: Eight reps, answer covered, graded on one binary question: does this daily entry have weekly permission — yes or no? For each: show the daily setup first and let the member judge the pattern, then reveal the weekly and demand the call before showing the outcome. The set is deliberately built to sting: several of the eight are gorgeous daily patterns inside broken weeklies — the exact bait that costs real money — and a couple are mediocre-looking dailies inside powerful weekly uptrends, the unglamorous trades that actually pay. Grade only the binary. Not 'would this have worked' — one counter-trend winner proves nothing except that roulette sometimes pays. On a miss, name what you ignored on the weekly: the falling 200, the lower highs, the overhead supply. Eight for eight, called fast and felt, closes the lesson.
chapters.on_screen: The 8-rep drill: daily setup shown first, weekly revealed second, aligned-or-not stamped on each
chapters.example_spec: Pre-build eight daily-first, weekly-reveal pairs. The bait — gorgeous daily, broken weekly, correct call NO: NFLX March 2022 bounce ≈$33 to ≈$39; PYPL August 2022, the August 3 gap (+12.8%, ≈3.6× volume) that died at ≈$103.03 on August 16; COIN March 2022, a rally holding ≈$190 before April closed ≈$112.71; COIN August 2022, the August 4 gap opening ≈$106.10 and closing ≈$88.90 on ≈4× volume. The unglamorous — mediocre daily, powerful weekly, correct call YES: META October 2023 pullback to ≈$279.40; NVDA September 2023 chop above its rising 200-day; MSFT August 2023 drift to the 50-day; DKNG October 2023 ≈$27.62 shakeout. Daily shown first, call demanded at the weekly reveal; grade the binary only. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The Winners Gallery: 25 Monster Charts, No Rules Yet
lessons.note: Pure perception training on 25 annotated past monsters — repeated exposure to what right looks like before a single buy rule exists — then 10 guess-before-you-check reps. Artifact: the downloadable 25-chart Winners Gallery model book, re-annotated in the capstone and recycled in the Module 10 drill. Build the gallery inside the product's Model Book (year-organized curated monsters) rather than a static download, and run the guess-before-you-check reps on Model Book charts with the setup labels hidden.

chapters.marker: See it a hundred times before you name it
chapters.beat: open with the training claim: your eyes learn what right looks like through repeated exposure, and this whole lesson happens before a single buy rule exists.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the training claim plainly: your eyes learn what right looks like through repeated exposure — the way a cashier learns counterfeit bills by handling thousands of genuine ones, not by studying forgeries. This whole lesson happens before a single buy rule exists, on purpose. We're about to page through twenty-five of the biggest winning stocks of past cycles, annotated, and the assignment is simply to look. No pivots, no triggers, no sizing — those come in the setup modules, and they'll land ten times harder because your eyes will already recognize the shape they formalize. This is the firm's version of the classic hundred-chart model book: perception before tactics. By the tenth chart you'll start seeing the repetition yourself; by the twenty-fifth you won't be able to unsee it. That itch — 'these all look the same' — is the lesson working.
chapters.on_screen: A fast montage of annotated monster charts flipping past (SMCI 2023, NVDA 2023, TSLA 2020…)

chapters.marker: Your gallery lives in the Model Book
chapters.beat: tour the product's Model Book of year-organized curated monsters and show that the 25-chart Winners Gallery is built inside it, a living artifact, not a PDF that dies in a downloads folder.
chapters.speaker_notes: Tour the Model Book on the dashboard: the firm's curated library of the best stocks in history, organized by year — click a year, get that cycle's monsters; click a stock, get its full chart with the firm's annotations on it. The 25-chart Winners Gallery is built inside this product surface, not exported to a PDF that dies in a downloads folder. That matters for three reasons. The charts are live — you can zoom, scroll, and change timeframes instead of squinting at a static image. The gallery grows — new monsters get added as cycles produce them. And it's the same surface you'll use for the rest of your time here, so today's reps build the habit of living in it. Open it now, find the gallery, and remember the path — you will re-annotate these exact charts yourself in the capstone.
chapters.on_screen: The Model Book tab on the live dashboard — year pills, the stock gallery, one monster opened with its annotations

chapters.beat: page through the first dozen annotated monsters saying almost nothing beyond the recurring shape: quiet base, tightening range, ignition, sustained advance.
chapters.speaker_notes: Page through the first dozen monsters saying almost nothing — deliberately. Let the charts do the teaching, and only name the recurring shape once it repeats on its own: a quiet base, sometimes months long, where nothing happens and nobody cares. Then the range tightens — each pullback smaller than the last, the chart coiling. Then ignition: a decisive break on obvious volume. Then the part that makes the money — a sustained advance that runs further and lasts longer than seems reasonable, stair-stepping up the moving averages for months. Quiet base, tightening range, ignition, sustained advance — four beats, twelve different stocks, different years, different industries, same biography. Resist the urge to lecture; when the presenter talks less, the member's pattern-matching works harder. By chart eight or nine they're saying the four beats before you do. That's the goal of this pass.
chapters.on_screen: Model Book charts advancing one by one — the first 12 annotated monsters, minimal commentary (e.g. ELF 2023, PLTR 2024, ANET 2023…)
chapters.example_spec: Fix the first-pass dozen, in this order: NVDA 2023, SMCI 2023, ELF 2023, CELH 2022–23, ANET 2023, AXON 2023, PLTR 2023–24, DKNG 2023, TSLA 2020, ENPH 2020, ZM 2020, SHOP 2020. Every chart carries the same four beats to tap silently: quiet multi-month base, tightening range, ignition on heavy volume, months-long advance stair-stepping the moving averages. Name numbers once, on the archetype, and let the rest rhyme: NVDA's spring 2023 base under ≈$30.50, the May 25 earnings gap open ≈$38.52 (+26.1%) on ≈3.3× volume, the run to the ≈$50.27 record on August 24 — prices split-adjusted 10:1, ≈10× these at the time. Minimal commentary after chart three. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the remaining charts and let the common tells surface on their own: volume drying up before the move, closes stacking in the top of their ranges, the four lines falling into order underneath.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the remaining charts slower and let the finer tells surface on their own. First: volume drying up before the move — in the final weeks of each base the volume bars shrink to a trickle; sellers are exhausted, supply has changed hands, the stock has gone quiet. Then the mirror: volume exploding on ignition day, often 3× average or more — the witness showing up exactly when the claim is made. Second: closes stacking in the top of their daily ranges through the advance — bar after bar finishing in the top 40%, the buyers-won verdict from lesson one repeating for weeks. Third: the four lines falling into order underneath — 9 over 20 over 50 over 200, the stack from lesson two, forming before the big move and holding through it. Nothing here is new; the gallery is where the course's pieces reveal they were always one picture.
chapters.on_screen: The remaining gallery charts with the tells highlighted: dry-up volume shaded inside the base, top-of-range closes marked, the MA stack ordering underneath
chapters.example_spec: The remaining thirteen, spanning cycles so the same biography lands across decades: MNST 2004–06, TASR 2004, AAPL 2004–05, GOOGL 2005, CMG 2010–11, NFLX 2013, TSLA 2013, NVDA 2016–17, CROX 2021, SE 2020–21, MELI 2020, UPST 2021, META 2023. Warn on screen that the old names read tiny today: AAPL's 2003 low prints ≈$0.34, GOOGL's 2004 debut ≈$2.40, CMG's 2008 low ≈$0.74 after its 50:1 split. On each, highlight three tells in order: the volume dry-up in the base's final weeks (bars toward ≈half average); closes stacking in the top 40% of daily range; the 9>20>50>200 ordering forming underneath. Worked anchor: UPST 2021 — base under ≈$130 into mid-August, earnings ignition, August close ≈$229, September ≈$316, peak ≈$401.49 on October 15. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run 10 guess-before-you-check reps on Model Book charts with the setup labels hidden, then set the standing appointment: this gallery gets re-annotated in the capstone and its charts return in the Module 10 placement drill.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run ten guess-before-you-check reps on Model Book charts with the setup labels hidden. Show each chart up to a decision point, cover what follows, and ask only the perception question: is this coiling to go, or not? Commit out loud, then reveal the label and the resolution. There's no grading rubric yet — no rules exist to grade against, and that's the point: you're measuring whether your eyes learned the shape, and after twenty-five annotated monsters, most members surprise themselves. Then set the two standing appointments out loud. One: this gallery gets re-annotated by YOU in the capstone — your own pivots, your own notes, graded. Two: these same charts return in the Module 10 placement drill, where you'll name families and setups on them. Today you just looked. Soon you'll have names for everything you saw.
chapters.on_screen: Model Book drill mode: a gallery chart with its setup label hidden, revealed after the member's call
chapters.example_spec: Freeze ten Model Book charts at a decision point, labels hidden. Coiling-to-go (call YES), leading with the four that have verified bars: ELF April 2023 tightening before the May 25 earnings gap (+10.7%, open ≈$95.70, close ≈$104.15 on ≈5.2× volume); CELH's ≈$30–33 early-2023 coil before May closed ≈$41.84; AXON's mid-2023 flat base near ≈$186 before the August 9 gap (+12.7%, ≈4.8×); DKNG's May 2023 flag off the May 5 gap close ≈$24.58. Then NVDA late-January 2023, SMCI January 2023, PLTR October 2023, TSLA October 2019. Foils (call NOT): INTC mid-2022, the braided declining mess; RIVN mid-2022, a wide loose bounce under falling averages. Demand the call in seconds, then reveal label and resolution. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

modules.label: M3 · The Regime Engine: Stages, the Dial, and the Permission System

lessons.title: The Four Stages of Any Stock: One Life Cycle on One Chart
lessons.note: Stage 1-4 traced across a single three-year chart of a recent monster — basing, advancing, topping, declining as one perceptual gestalt, no buy rules yet. Artifact: the one-page life-cycle diagram members annotate on three more tickers as homework.

chapters.marker: Every monster has the same biography
chapters.beat: open on the ending: the full three-year chart of the recent monster zoomed out to its entire run, and promise that by the end of this lesson the member can name the four chapters of that story on any chart, no buy rules required.
chapters.speaker_notes: Start zoomed all the way out on the finished story: three years of one monster stock, its entire run on one screen. Every big winner you will ever trade lived this same four-chapter biography — Stage 1 basing, Stage 2 advancing, Stage 3 topping, Stage 4 declining. Same shape, different ticker, every cycle. Here is the promise for the next twelve minutes: by the end you can name which chapter any chart is in, on sight, with zero buy rules — because this lesson is perception training, not tactics. And connect it forward: the 0-150 dial you read in Module 1 is this exact lens applied to the whole market. Today we build the lens on a single stock, where the chapters are easiest to see. Keep the 9/20/50/200 template from Module 2 on — the lines do the narrating.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI weekly, 2021-2025, fully zoomed out — one complete four-stage life cycle: neglect, ~10x advance, the 2024 top, the decline (or substitute a firm-tracked monster)
chapters.example_spec: Keep SMCI weekly, 2021-2025 (prices split-adjusted for the October 2024 10-for-1 — ≈10× these at the time). Left to right: 2021-2022 Stage 1 chop ≈$3.5-7 around a flat 200-day; Stage 2 from the early-2023 breakout ≈$10 (base low ≈$6.28, October 2022) riding a rising 50-over-200 to the March 8, 2024 top ≈$122.90; Stage 3 — flattening averages and 30-40% churn April-August 2024 (monthly closes ≈$86, $78, $82, $70, $44); Stage 4 — the October 30, 2024 gap of −29% on ≈3× volume under a now-falling 200-day, down to the November 15 low ≈$17.25. Buying the ≈$10 breakout, stop ≈$8, banked well over +20R before Stage 3. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Stage 1, basing: the boring part everyone skips
chapters.beat: scrub back to the flat left edge of the same chart and show price chopping sideways across a flattening 200 SMA, naming neglect and quiet accumulation as one visual gestalt.
chapters.speaker_notes: Scrub back to the flat left edge of the same chart. This is Stage 1: price chopping sideways for months, crossing back and forth over a FLATTENING 200 SMA, volume dead, headlines silent. Nobody cares — and that is the point. Neglect and quiet accumulation are one visual gestalt: big money building a position slowly enough that price barely moves. The tells, stated plainly: the 200-day has lost its slope, price straddles it in both directions, ranges gradually tighten, and rallies die without follow-through. You do not buy Stage 1. Not because it can't work — because it costs you time, and time is the one thing a swing trader budgets. Your money belongs in Stage 2, and Stage 1's only job is to tell you where the NEXT Stage 2 will be born. Watchlist material, not buy material.
chapters.on_screen: Same SMCI weekly scrubbed to the 2021-2022 left edge — sideways chop across a flat 200 SMA (NVDA weekly 2022 works equally well)

chapters.marker: Stage 2 and Stage 3: the advance and the top
chapters.beat: trace the advancing phase where price rides a rising 50 above a rising 200, then the topping churn where the averages flatten and wide, sloppy swings replace clean pullbacks.
chapters.speaker_notes: Trace the advance: price breaks out of the base and rides a rising 50 SMA above a rising 200 SMA — higher highs, higher lows, pullbacks that are orderly and shallow, finding the moving averages and bouncing. Stage 2 is the ONLY stage this system buys. Every setup family you will learn in Modules 7 through 10 assumes Stage 2 as its precondition. Then trace the top: the character change is unmistakable once you know it. The averages flatten. Clean pullbacks become wide, sloppy 15-20% swings in both directions. Huge volume with no net progress — that churn is distribution, holders handing inventory to latecomers. Stage 3 often LOOKS exciting; the daily ranges are huge. But the trend engine has stalled, and a stock that stops making progress on heavy volume is telling you the biography is entering its third chapter.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI weekly, 2023 through early 2024 — the clean 50-over-200 advance rolling into wide, sloppy topping churn

chapters.marker: Stage 4, decline: why 'it's cheap now' is the trap
chapters.beat: walk the decline under a falling 200 SMA and mark the three spots a bargain-hunter buys on the way down, the lesson's built-in counter-example.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the decline: price under a now-FALLING 200 SMA, lower highs, failed bounces. Now mark the three spots on this chart where a bargain-hunter said 'it's down 40%, it's cheap' — and show what happened after each one: lower. Cheap is not a level; it is a story the declining chart tells at every price on the way down. State the rule with no hedge: we do not go long a stock trading under a falling 200 SMA. Ever. Not for a bounce, not because we loved it in Stage 2. And give the arithmetic that makes the trap lethal: a stock down 50% must double just to get back to even — the hole is always deeper than the discount looks. Stage 4 is where the next Stage 1 eventually forms. Your job is to wait for that, not to catch this.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI weekly, mid-2024 into 2025 — the falling-200 decline with three 'it's cheap now' buy points marked, each followed by lower prices

chapters.marker: The life-cycle diagram and your three-ticker homework
chapters.beat: hand over the one-page Stage 1-4 diagram artifact and assign the drill: annotate the complete cycle on three more tickers before the Stage-2 Gate lesson.
chapters.speaker_notes: Hand over the artifact: the one-page Stage 1-4 life-cycle diagram — the idealized arc with each stage's tells written on it. Basing: flat 200, price straddling it, ranges tightening. Advancing: rising 50 over rising 200, orderly pullbacks. Topping: flattening averages, wide sloppy swings, churn volume. Declining: falling 200, lower highs, no long trades. Then assign the drill, with a rep count, not a vibe: before the Stage-2 Gate lesson, annotate the COMPLETE cycle — all four stages, boundaries marked at the bar where the evidence turned — on three more tickers of your choosing. Big past winners work best; pull candidates from the Model Book's year galleries. This is the same guess-before-you-check muscle from Module 2, now with a vocabulary. The next lesson converts this perceptual skill into eight binary questions, so bring calibrated eyes.
chapters.on_screen: The one-page Stage 1-4 life-cycle diagram artifact, full screen, with the three-ticker homework written at the bottom

lessons.title: The Stage-2 Gate: Eight Yes/No Questions — Fail One, Skip the Stock
lessons.note: The purely mechanical trend gate: eight binary criteria (price above a rising 50 and 200, 200-day rising for a month+, within striking distance of highs, RS confirming, etc.) with zero judgment allowed. Runs five live tickers through the printed gate card, including two that fail on exactly one criterion.

chapters.marker: Why a gate and not an opinion
chapters.beat: open with two charts that both 'look great,' reveal one is actually Stage 3 topping, and state the premise: eyes lie, binary questions don't, and this gate allows zero judgment.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with two charts side by side. Both 'look great' — strong runs, near highs, bullish feel. Then reveal: one is a healthy Stage 2 leader; the other is Stage 3 topping, flattening averages hidden under the excitement. Your eyes just failed, and that is the premise of this lesson: eyes lie, binary questions don't. The Stage-2 gate is a purely mechanical trend screen — eight questions, each answerable only yes or no, zero judgment allowed. It answers exactly one thing: is this stock ELIGIBLE to be traded at all. Not 'is this a good entry' — that is a different skill, taught later. Eligibility comes first and it is binary. The doctrine that makes it work: fail one question, skip the stock. Any gate that bends to enthusiasm isn't a gate — it's an opinion with paperwork.
chapters.on_screen: Side-by-side: a clean Stage 2 leader (NVDA daily, mid-2023) vs. a Stage 3 look-alike topping after a huge run (DOCU daily, late 2021)

chapters.marker: The eight yes/no questions, read off the card
chapters.beat: walk the printed gate card line by line: price above a rising 50 and 200, the 200-day rising for a month-plus, within striking distance of highs, RS confirming, and the rest — each answerable only yes or no.
chapters.speaker_notes: Read the printed gate card line by line, and after each line say what a yes looks like on the chart. Is price above the 50 SMA? Above the 200 SMA? Are both rising? Has the 200-day been rising for at least a month — not a one-week wobble, a sustained slope? Is price within striking distance of its highs — a stock 40% off its high is repairing, not leading? Is the RS line confirming — outperforming the market, not just rising with it? Then the card's remaining structural checks, each one binary. Here is the discipline that gives the card teeth: if you find yourself debating a line, the answer is no. Hesitation IS information. Eight yeses or the stock doesn't pass — there is no seven-and-a-half on this card.
chapters.on_screen: The printed eight-question Stage-2 gate card, full screen, read line by line

chapters.marker: Five live tickers through the gate
chapters.beat: run five current-market names through the card at speed on camera, stamping all eight boxes for each in real time.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now speed. Pull five current-market names — real tickers from this week's tape, not curated heroes — and run each through the card on camera, stamping all eight boxes out loud in real time. The performance point of this chapter is pace: a practiced gate check takes under a minute per stock, because every question is a glance — price versus a line, a slope, distance from highs, the RS pane. Narrate the rhythm: 'above the 50, yes; above the 200, yes; 200 rising a month-plus, yes...' Let some pass and some fail naturally; don't stack the deck. What the member should absorb is that this is not analysis — it is inspection. Analysis is what you earned the right to do AFTER the gate says yes. Expect roughly a third of decent-looking charts to fail on at least one line; that is the gate doing its job.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard charts with the 9/20/50/200 template — five current-market tickers run through the printed card live, boxes stamped on camera
chapters.example_spec: Preferred: five uncurated names from this week's scan. Guaranteed fallback — set all charts to June 15, 2023: NVDA ≈$43 split-adjusted (≈$430 at the time; 10-for-1 in June 2024) — all eight yes, above rising 50/200, near highs, RS leading; ELF ≈$110 — all eight yes (May close $104.02, June close $114.23); KO ≈$61 — multiple fails, flat-to-rolling 200-day, sliding from its April 24 high $64.99 to $55.08 by October 2; PLTR ≈$15 — seven yes, one no, its 200-day not rising a month-plus; DKNG ≈$26 — seven yes, one no, ≈65% under its 2021 high ≈$74. Read exact levels off the charts. NVDA ran ≈+1.5R into the July high ≈$48, ≈+2R by August 24 ≈$50.27. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: slow down on the two tickers that fail on exactly one line and enforce the doctrine out loud: fail one, skip the stock — there is no 'but it's close.'
chapters.speaker_notes: Slow down on the two names that failed exactly one line — because this is where every member will want to negotiate. One fails only on '200-day rising for a month-plus'; one fails only on striking distance of highs. Everything else is a yes, and the chart is seductive. Say the doctrine to camera: fail one, skip the stock. There is no 'but it's close.' Then justify it with the asymmetry: skipping costs you nothing — the scan universe is roughly 3,700 tickers and tomorrow's list is full — while overriding the gate costs you the gate itself, because a rule you bend once is not a rule, it's a mood. And the statistical truth underneath: a stock failing exactly one Stage-2 criterion is disproportionately often early Stage 3 or late Stage 1 — the two most expensive places to be wrong.
chapters.on_screen: The two one-criterion failures, each chart shown with its single failed line highlighted red on the gate card
chapters.example_spec: Use the two one-criterion failures from the June 15, 2023 fallback set. PLTR daily: everything yes — price ≈$15 above a rising 50-day ≈$11, at 52-week highs, RS surging since the May 9 earnings gap (+19%, ≈3.4× volume, ≈$7.70 to ≈$9.55) — except the 200-day ≈$9 is only just flattening out of decline, failing 'rising a month-plus.' It later worked (≈$20.24 by August 1), which is exactly why the doctrine gets said over a seductive chart. DKNG daily: ≈$26, rising 50 over rising 200, RS strong — but ≈65% below its 2021 high ≈$74, failing striking distance alone. Highlight each failed line red. No entry or stop is drawn: a gate fail is no trade, 0R by definition. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Your gate reps: ten names, card in hand
chapters.beat: close with the assignment: run ten tickers from tonight's scan through the printed card, and the pass bar is that every skip cites the exact criterion that failed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the assignment, specified as a literal rep count: take ten tickers from tonight's scan output and run every one through the printed card, boxes stamped, before the next lesson. The pass bar is not 'did you find winners' — it is that every skip cites the exact criterion that failed, by name. 'Skipped, 200-day not rising a month' is a rep; 'skipped, didn't like it' is not. This is how the gate becomes reflex: ten reps with the card in hand, then the card lives beside your platform permanently — it is also the first checklist line on the five-field setup card you'll meet in Module 7, so this exact skill gets recycled every trade from here forward. Next lesson, we lift this same lens off the single stock and point it at the entire market.
chapters.on_screen: Tonight's real nightly-scan output list on the Screener, with the printed gate card beside it

lessons.title: Same Lens, Bigger Chart: Staging the Indexes
lessons.note: The stage lens lifted to SPY, QQQ, and IWM — perceptual index staging as its own graded skill, with two historical sequences called stage by stage. Sets up the mechanical counts, which get their own lesson next.

chapters.marker: The market is just a bigger stock
chapters.beat: open by placing the Module lesson-one life-cycle diagram beside a SPY weekly and showing the same four chapters playing out at index scale.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the Stage 1-4 life-cycle diagram from lesson one physically beside a SPY weekly chart and let the shapes rhyme. The market is just a bigger stock: it bases, it advances above a rising 50 and 200, it churns wide and sloppy at tops, it declines under a falling 200. Same four chapters, same MA evidence, same tells — the only difference is scale and consequence. When one stock enters Stage 4, you lose a candidate; when the INDEXES enter Stage 4, most of your playbook loses permission. That is why this module lives here, early: every downstream decision — which setups are eligible, how large you size, whether you may buy at all — consumes the market's stage. This lesson makes index staging a graded skill of its own, by eye first. The mechanical counts that harden it come next lesson.
chapters.on_screen: The Stage 1-4 life-cycle diagram beside SPY weekly, 2021-2023 — a full market cycle mirroring the single-stock arc

chapters.marker: Staging SPY, QQQ, and IWM today
chapters.beat: call the current stage of all three indexes live on the dashboard, narrating the 50/200 structure and slope evidence behind each call.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now do it live, with today's actual charts — no curation, whatever the market gives you. Pull SPY weekly and call its stage out loud, narrating only the evidence: where price sits relative to the 50 and the 200, the slope of each, the character of recent pullbacks — orderly or sloppy. Then QQQ, same narration. Then IWM. Commit to a stage call on each one; a hedged call is a failed rep, and the member needs to see you commit on an uncooked chart. The three answers will often differ, and say why that matters: QQQ is growth and momentum — closest to what we trade; SPY is the broad benchmark; IWM is the small-cap risk appetite gauge. Staging all three every week is the habit being installed here — it feeds directly into the Monday max-exposure plan you started in Module 1.
chapters.on_screen: Live dashboard charts — SPY, QQQ, and IWM weekly with the 9/20/50/200 template, staged on camera today

chapters.marker: Historical sequence one, called stage by stage
chapters.beat: replay a past index cycle from top through decline into the new base, stamping each stage transition at the bar where the evidence actually turned.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay 2021 into 2023 and stamp each transition at the bar where the evidence actually turned — not where hindsight says the top was. Late 2021: price still at highs but the 50-day flattening, swings widening — Stage 3 character. Early 2022: the break below a flattening 200 that then turns down — Stage 4 begins, and every long-side permission goes with it. Through 2022: lower highs, failed bounces under the falling 200 — Stage 4 persists no matter how sharp the bear rallies feel. October 2022: the low that holds, the chop that follows, the 200 flattening out — Stage 1 basing. Into 2023: price reclaims the averages, the 50 turns up and crosses back over — Stage 2 resumes. The lesson inside the replay: the evidence turned at identifiable bars. Nobody needed to predict; they needed to read.
chapters.on_screen: SPY weekly, 2021-2023 replay — stage-transition boundaries stamped at the exact bars where the 50/200 evidence turned

chapters.marker: Historical sequence two: when the indexes disagree
chapters.beat: work a second sequence where QQQ and IWM sit in different stages on the same day, and what a split tape means for which stocks are even eligible.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work 2023 as the split-tape case: by spring, QQQ was in a confirmed Stage 2 — rising 50 over rising 200, orderly pullbacks, megacap tech leading — while IWM chopped sideways in a Stage 1-3 hybrid, going nowhere for months. Same day, same market, two different stages. What a split tape means, practically: eligibility narrows to where Stage 2 actually lives. In 2023 that meant growth and tech names could pass the gate while small-cap breakouts kept failing — not because their patterns were drawn wrong, but because their neighborhood had no trend engine. So the rule: your candidates must be in Stage 2 themselves AND belong to the part of the tape that is in Stage 2. A split tape is not a red light; it is a narrower map. The dial's inputs, next lesson, absorb exactly this.
chapters.on_screen: QQQ weekly vs. IWM weekly, 2023, side by side — confirmed Stage 2 against months of sideways chop on the same dates

chapters.beat: grade the member's own stage calls on two covered index charts, then name what's coming: the distribution and follow-through counts that turn this perceptual skill into arithmetic.
chapters.speaker_notes: Grade the skill before leaving it. Put up two covered index charts — ticker and dates hidden, chart paused mid-history — and have the member call the stage on each before the reveal, evidence named: price versus the 50 and 200, slopes, pullback character. Two committed calls, then uncover and score. A miss is fine; a hedge is the only failure. Then name precisely what this skill still lacks: perception tells you the stage, but it cannot tell you the DAY the stage changed — and exposure decisions live on days, not vibes. That precision comes from two mechanical counts: distribution days, which call tops by arithmetic, and follow-through days, which announce bottoms the same way. That is the entire next lesson, and it is the module's drill material. Perception first, mechanics second — you now have the first half.
chapters.on_screen: Two covered index charts (tickers and dates hidden) for graded stage calls, then the reveal
chapters.example_spec: Covered chart A: QQQ weekly, paused August 2008 ≈$46, ticker and dates hidden. Answer: Stage 4 — lower highs since the October 2007 top ≈$55, price under a rolled-over 200-day, bounces dying at the falling averages. Covered chart B: SPY weekly, paused April 2013 ≈$159 (March close $156.67, April close $159.68). Answer: Stage 2 — rising 50-day over rising 200-day, shallow orderly pullbacks since the late-2012 base ≈$142. Grade only the committed call plus cited evidence. No entries in this drill, but note the stakes: B's read keeps a rider in a trend that reached ≈$171 by August 2013; A's read forbids longs into QQQ's fall to ≈$25.05 on November 21, 2008 — ≈-46%, 0R risked.
