lessons.title: Distribution Days and Follow-Through Days: The Counts That Call Tops and Bottoms
lessons.note: The mechanical rules on their own: the cluster rule (4-6 distribution days inside ~25 sessions kills an uptrend) and the follow-through day (day 4-7 off the low, up big on higher volume). One fully-worked historical top and one bottom, counts stamped bar by bar — this is the module's drill material.

chapters.beat: they count down: open with a market top that looked perfectly healthy on price alone, then reveal the distribution days that had been stacking underneath it for weeks.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a market top that looked perfectly healthy on price alone: the Nasdaq in November 2021, sitting within reach of all-time highs, no crash, no headline panic. Then reveal what price alone never showed — the distribution days that had been stacking underneath it for weeks: repeated sessions where the index fell on volume heavier than the day before. Institutions were selling into strength while the index level stayed polite. That is how tops actually happen: not a bell, a countdown. Big money cannot exit in one day; it distributes over weeks, and volume is the fingerprint it cannot hide. This lesson gives you the two mechanical counts of the regime engine — the one that calls tops and the one that announces bottoms — both pure arithmetic, both readable by anyone willing to count. These counts feed the dial directly.
chapters.on_screen: Nasdaq Composite daily, November-December 2021 — index near highs while heavy-volume down days quietly stack beneath it

chapters.marker: The distribution day and the cluster rule
chapters.beat: define an index down-day on volume heavier than the prior session, then state the kill rule as arithmetic: 4-6 distribution days inside ~25 sessions ends an uptrend, no opinion involved.
chapters.speaker_notes: Define the unit first: a distribution day is an index down-day on volume heavier than the prior session. Down on lighter volume doesn't count — no urgency. Up on heavy volume doesn't count — that's the opposite signal. Down, on MORE volume than yesterday: institutions selling with intent. One distribution day means nothing; markets shrug them off weekly. The kill rule is the cluster: four to six distribution days inside roughly 25 sessions ends an uptrend. Not 'weakens' — ends. No opinion involved, no judgment call, no 'but earnings season.' A day also ages out: once it falls outside that rolling ~25-session window, it drops from the count. So the number you carry each morning is simple: how many distribution days sit inside the current window. The dashboard tracks it, and it is one of the five scorecard numbers you'll assemble in Module 4.
chapters.on_screen: The distribution-day definition and 4-6-inside-~25-sessions cluster rule as an on-chart annotation, with the dashboard's distribution-day count beside it

chapters.marker: One historical top, counts stamped bar by bar
chapters.beat: replay the full topping sequence stamping D1, D2, D3 on each qualifying bar until the cluster fires, marking the exact session the uptrend legally died.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the late-2021 Nasdaq top and stamp it live: find each qualifying bar — down day, volume above the prior session — and mark it D1, D2, D3, narrating the check both ways ('down, but volume lighter — doesn't count'). Let the tension build exactly the way it did in real time: the index still near highs at D3, still respectable at D4. Then the cluster fires — the count reaches the kill threshold inside the window — and you mark the exact session the uptrend legally died. Say 'legally' deliberately: from that bar forward, the trend is guilty, whatever the index price says, and permissions contract accordingly. Then show the payoff: the January 2022 break that followed. Members who watched the count knew weeks before members who watched price. That gap — count versus price — is the whole value of the mechanic.
chapters.on_screen: Nasdaq Composite daily, November 2021-January 2022 — D1 through the cluster stamped bar by bar, the kill session flagged, the January break after it

chapters.marker: The follow-through day: how bottoms announce themselves
chapters.beat: define day 4-7 off the low, up big on higher volume, then stamp a real historical bottom the same way — including the earlier rally attempt that never followed through and failed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Bottoms announce themselves with the mirror count. After a decline makes a low, some bounce begins — call that day one of a rally attempt. Most attempts fail; you commit nothing to a bounce. The signal is the follow-through day: on day 4 through 7 off the low, the index rises BIG — a decisive thrust, not a drift — on volume higher than the prior session. Early strength off a low is routine; strength that returns with power nearly a week in is institutions committing. Stamp the 2020 sequence: the March 23 low, an earlier rally attempt that faded without ever following through, then the genuine follow-through in early April — day-counted, volume-checked, on camera. Two honesty notes: a follow-through day does not guarantee the bottom, but no durable bottom in decades has started without one. And it re-opens buying at pilot size only — never full exposure on day one.
chapters.on_screen: S&P 500 daily, February-April 2020 — the March 23 low, the failed earlier rally attempt, and the early-April follow-through day stamped with its day count

chapters.beat: this is the module's rep material: assign the member to stamp both counts on two fresh covered sequences, feeding directly into the 12-turn graded drill in the Permission System lesson.
chapters.speaker_notes: This lesson is the module's rep material, so the assignment is the lesson. Two fresh covered sequences — index charts with dates and outcomes hidden. Sequence one is a topping tape: stamp every qualifying distribution day, maintain the rolling count, and mark the exact session the 4-6-inside-~25-sessions cluster fires. Sequence two is a bottoming tape: identify the low, number the rally-attempt days, disqualify anything before day 4, and stamp the follow-through day — or state, with evidence, that none occurred; some covered sequences won't have one, and calling 'no signal' correctly is a passing rep. Work with the answer covered, commit in ink, then reveal and grade. These two sequences feed directly into the 12-turn graded drill in the Permission System lesson — the module's 80% checkpoint — so treat them as the dress rehearsal. Counting on dead charts now is what makes the count automatic on live ones.
chapters.on_screen: Two covered index sequences (dates hidden) — one topping tape for distribution stamps, one bottoming tape for the follow-through call
chapters.example_spec: Topping tape: Nasdaq Composite daily, September 3-October 10, 2018, dates hidden. Qualifying distribution days stack through late September with the index near ≈8,100; the 4-6-inside-~25-sessions cluster fires in the first days of October — mark that session; the index then loses ≈20% into December. Bottoming tape: S&P 500 daily, December 2018-January 2019. Low: December 24 ≈2,351. December 26's ≈+5% surge is rally-attempt day 1; the follow-through prints January 4, 2019 — day 7, ≈+3.4% on higher volume, index closing ≈2,532. These are index points, not share prices — no split adjustment. Read exact levels off the charts. A pilot buy after that FTD, risking ≤1R, rode the 2019 uptrend for multiples of that risk. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Inside the UCT Regime Dial: What Feeds the 0-150 Exposure Rating and What Flips It
lessons.note: The proprietary engine end-to-end: the breadth, distribution-count, and index MA-structure inputs behind the daily 0-150 score, read on two replayed real dashboard mornings — one GREEN, one ORANGE — naming exactly what changed between them. Core doctrine on camera: GREEN means more of your playbook is authorized, not that the market goes up.

chapters.beat: open the live dashboard on today's 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating and state the claim: everything built in this module compresses into this dial every single morning.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open the live dashboard on today's actual UCT Exposure Rating — the 0-150 dial — and read it out loud, with its band. Then make the claim this lesson exists to prove: everything built in this module compresses into this one number every single morning. The stage lens, the index staging, the distribution count, the follow-through logic — the dial is all of it, computed daily, so that your first market decision each day takes ten seconds instead of an hour. The score maps to a GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE permission band, and the discipline is order-of-operations: you read this number BEFORE you open a single stock chart. Not after, not alongside — before. Tickers are question three; permission is question one. By the end of this lesson the dial stops being a black box, because you will have seen exactly what feeds it and exactly what flips it.
chapters.on_screen: The live dashboard dial — today's actual 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating with its GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE band

chapters.beat: walk the input families one at a time: breadth participation, the distribution-day count from last lesson, and index MA structure, showing where each one lives on the dashboard.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the input families one at a time, and point at where each one lives on the dashboard — this is a tour, not a formula dump. Family one: breadth participation — what fraction of stocks are actually above their key moving averages, how many made 4% up-days versus down-days, net new highs versus new lows. The index can be carried by five megacaps; participation can't lie. It lives on the Breadth Monitor. Family two: the distribution-day count from last lesson — the running tally of heavy-volume selling inside the rolling window. Family three: index MA structure — where SPY and QQQ sit relative to the 9/20/50/200 stack and which direction those lines slope. Healthy participation, a quiet count, and rising structure push the score up; deterioration in any family drags it down. Three families, one number, every morning at 7:35 when the Morning Wire ships.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard Breadth page tour — Monitor participation columns, the distribution-day count, and the SPY/QQQ MA structure panel

chapters.beat: re-open a real recorded GREEN dashboard morning and read the inputs aloud: what breadth said, what the count said, what the MA structure said, and the score they combined into.
chapters.speaker_notes: Re-open a real recorded GREEN morning — an actual dashboard capture, not a mock-up — and read the inputs aloud the way a member should every day. Breadth: strong participation, healthy percentages above the key averages, 4% up-days outnumbering down-days, net new highs positive. The count: distribution days low inside the window — no cluster building, institutions not leaving. Structure: SPY and QQQ above rising 50s and 200s, the stack in order. Then the score they combined into, and its GREEN band. Now say what GREEN authorized that morning — full playbook eligibility, normal sizing rights, new buys permitted — and note, deliberately, what it did NOT say: it did not say the market goes up today. It said the environment supports your setups. Hold this morning in memory; the next chapter puts its opposite beside it.
chapters.on_screen: A real recorded GREEN dashboard morning — dial score, Breadth Monitor readings, and MA structure read aloud together
chapters.example_spec: Pull the dial's stored history for the week of June 12, 2023 (any morning that week). Walk the inputs in order: structure — SPY ≈$434 and QQQ ≈$358 early that week, closing Friday June 16 at ≈$439.46 and ≈$367.93 on the window's heaviest volume (≈1.5×), both above rising 50- and 200-days, stack in order; breadth — percent above the 50-day expanding through the 50s-60s as small caps join, net new highs positive and growing, 4% up-days outnumbering down-days; count — ≈1-2 distribution days, none recent. Dial: GREEN. What the permission was worth: A+ breakouts under that band resolved ≈+2R to +3R into the July highs (SPY $459.44 on July 27, QQQ $387.98 on July 19). Read exact readings off the Breadth Monitor history. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The ORANGE morning, and exactly what changed
chapters.beat: replay the real ORANGE morning beside it and name, input by input, what flipped between the two dates so the score stops being a black box.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the real ORANGE morning, side by side with the GREEN one, and go input by input naming exactly what flipped between the two dates. Breadth: participation collapsed — the percent of stocks above their key averages fell hard, 4% down-days swamped up-days, net new lows took over. The count: the distribution cluster fired — heavy-volume selling stacked inside the window until the uptrend legally died, exactly the mechanic from last lesson. Structure: the indexes lost their rising 50s; slopes rolled over. Each deterioration dragged the score down through YELLOW into ORANGE. This is the demystification moment: the dial did not 'decide' anything — the tape changed, measurably, input by input, and the score followed. A member who can name what flipped will trust the dial on the mornings it disagrees with their hopes. That trust is the entire point of this chapter.
chapters.on_screen: The GREEN and ORANGE dashboard mornings side by side — each input family's before/after readings called out
chapters.example_spec: Beside the June 12, 2023 GREEN capture, pull Monday September 26, 2022. Name the flips input by input: breadth — percent above the 50-day in single digits (washout zone) versus the GREEN morning's 60s, net new lows in the thousands versus positive net highs, 4% down-days swamping up-days; count — the distribution cluster fired weeks earlier (late August), uptrend legally dead; structure — SPY ≈$364 under falling 50- and 200-days versus above rising ones. Dial: deep ORANGE. Outcome of obeying it: flat through the final ≈4.5% flush into the October 13 low ≈$348.11 (September closed ≈$357.18), and flat across the whole slide from the August peak — several R of drawdown never taken. Read exact readings off the Breadth Monitor history. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close with the core doctrine straight to camera: GREEN means more of your playbook is authorized, not that the market goes up — and a member who trades GREEN as a prediction has missed the module.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close straight to camera with the module's core doctrine, stated without decoration: GREEN means more of your playbook is authorized. It does not mean the market goes up. The dial is a permission system, not a prediction machine — it tells you what you are ALLOWED to do, never what will happen. GREEN days close red; that costs a rule-follower nothing, because sizing and stops were built for exactly that. ORANGE days close green; standing aside cost you one day of someone else's gains and none of your capital. If you catch yourself thinking 'the dial says up' — stop. You have missed the module, and the tuition for that misunderstanding is charged in real money, because a trader who treats permission as prophecy sizes up on conviction instead of rules. Next lesson maps each band to its concrete rights: position count, size ceilings, and whether you may buy at all.
chapters.on_screen: The dial full-screen with the doctrine as a title card: 'GREEN = more playbook authorized. Not a prediction.'

lessons.title: The Permission System: What GREEN, YELLOW, and ORANGE Each Let You Do — Plus 12 Regime Turns
lessons.note: Each state mapped to concrete rights — position count, size ceiling, and whether you may open new names at all (the full sizing table lands verbatim in Module 13). Ends with 12 historical regime turns as cover-the-answer drills graded on a printed rubric, 80% to close the module.

chapters.marker: Three states, three sets of rights
chapters.beat: open with the same A+ chart shown under GREEN and again under ORANGE, and land the punchline: the chart didn't change, your permissions did.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with one A+ chart — a textbook setup, tight and ready — shown twice: once under a GREEN regime, once under ORANGE. Then land the punchline: the chart didn't change; your permissions did. Under GREEN, that A+ setup supports a position up to 20-25% of the account. Under ORANGE, the identical chart caps at 8% — and if it honestly grades a B instead of an A+, it is not a smaller trade, it is NO trade. Same pixels, different rights. This is the lesson where the dial stops being a mood ring and becomes a rulebook: each band grants and revokes three specific things — how many names you may hold, how large any one may be, and whether you may open new positions at all. Setups answer 'what'; the regime answers 'whether' and 'how much.' Never let the chart's quality argue against the band's rights.
chapters.on_screen: The same A+ setup chart shown twice — labeled GREEN (20-25% authorized) and ORANGE (8% max, B = skip)
chapters.example_spec: Use META daily, January 2023, as the A+ chart shown under both bands. Find: the November-December 2022 base ≈$112-124 built off the $88.09 November 4 crash low; volume drying through December; the mid-January trigger bar through the ≈$124 pivot on expanding volume; stop structure under the last December contraction ≈$115. Entry ≈$124.50, stop ≈$115 — read exact levels off the chart. Label showing one GREEN (January 2023 was post-follow-through: 20-25% ceiling) and showing two ORANGE (8% max; a B-grade version is no trade). Outcome: the February 2 earnings gap — +19.8%, open ≈$183.38, close ≈$188.77 on ≈4.1× volume, ≈$197 intraday — roughly +7R on initial risk. Same pixels, different rights. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: What each band lets you do
chapters.beat: map GREEN, YELLOW, and ORANGE to their concrete rights: position count, size ceiling, and whether you may open new names at all, noting the full regime-by-grade sizing table lands verbatim in Module 13.
chapters.speaker_notes: Map the rights concretely. GREEN: the full playbook is authorized — a 5-10 name book at full rights, new buys permitted, and your best grade sizes to the table: GREEN plus A+ equals a 20-25% maximum position. YELLOW: rights reduced — trim position count, and the ceiling drops to 15% for an A+. ORANGE: best names only, smallest size — 8% for an A+, and a B-grade setup in ORANGE is always a skip; no cell in the table, no trade. State what never changes across bands: every position still obeys Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, hard-capped at 2% with under 1% preferred, and total portfolio heat stays capped at 10%. The band sets the ceiling; the formula sets the size under it. This full regime-by-grade sizing table lands verbatim in Module 13 — today you learn to read it; there you'll trade it.
chapters.on_screen: The regime sizing table full-screen: GREEN+A+ 20-25% · YELLOW+A+ 15% · ORANGE+A+ 8% · B-in-ORANGE SKIP, with the 2% formula and 10% heat cap beneath

chapters.beat: walk a single historical regime turn end to end, showing rights expanding rung by rung as the state improved and contracting the day it downgraded.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk one historical regime turn end to end — October 2022 into 2023 works cleanly. Start in the ORANGE: exposure parked, the trader flat and running the routine. The follow-through day prints — day 4-7 off the low, up big on higher volume — and buying re-opens at PILOT size only. That is the first rung of the ladder: pilot, half, full, overweight — and each rung must be PAID FOR by the last; you add exposure only after existing exposure is working. As the state improves through YELLOW toward GREEN, rights expand rung by rung: more names, bigger ceilings. Then show the other direction, because it is faster: the day the state downgrades, new-buy rights are revoked immediately, pending orders are cancelled, and open positions get managed to their existing plans — not panic-sold, managed. Rights expand on a ladder and contract on a trapdoor. That asymmetry is deliberate.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily, October 2022 through spring 2023 — the follow-through day, then the pilot→half→full ladder annotated rung by rung

chapters.beat: run 12 historical regime turns cover-the-answer style, calling the state and the rights it grants at each turn, graded against the printed rubric.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the module's graded drill: twelve historical regime turns, cover-the-answer style. For each turn the member sees the tape up to a decision point — dates hidden, outcome covered — and must call two things in ink before the reveal: the regime state, with the evidence named (participation, the distribution count, index structure), and the rights that state grants — position count, size ceiling, new buys or not. Then uncover, and grade against the printed rubric: state correct, evidence cited, rights correct. Twelve turns is enough to cover the whole zoo: clean tops, V-bottoms, failed follow-throughs, split tapes, downgrades that reversed. Run two or three on camera at full narration so the member sees the standard, then let them work the rest alone. The instruction is a rep count, not a suggestion: all twelve, in ink, before the reveal, every time.
chapters.on_screen: The 12-turn drill: a covered historical index chart at a decision point, with the printed grading rubric beside it
chapters.example_spec: Build the 12 covered turns from these SPY/QQQ/IWM daily decision points, dates hidden: (1) late-January 2018 top; (2) the January 20, 2016 SPY low ≈$181.02, the February retest (QQQ 2/8, IWM 2/11) and the FTD; (3) September-October 2018 cluster top; (4) December 2018 low, day-7 FTD January 4, 2019; (5) February 2020 trapdoor; (6) failed late-March 2020 rally attempt, then the genuine early-April FTD; (7) September 2020 downgrade; (8) the November 9, 2020 breadth-thrust upgrade (IWM +8.1% gap); (9) the divergent top — IWM 11/8/21 ≈$244.46, QQQ 11/22/21 ≈$408.71, SPY not until 1/4/22 ≈$479.98; (10) the May 2022 FTD that failed within days; (11) August 2022 downgrade at the falling 200-day; (12) October 2022 low into the 2023 split tape (QQQ Stage 2, IWM chop). Rights, not entries, are graded — a correct ORANGE risks 0R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: score the drill on camera, state the pass bar of 80% on the rubric to proceed, and prescribe the remediation loop for misses: rewatch the counts lesson, retake the turns you got wrong.
chapters.speaker_notes: Score the drill on camera and state the terms plainly: the pass bar is 80% on the printed rubric to close this module and proceed. Grade one member-style attempt out loud so the standard is visible — state right but rights wrong is a miss; state right with no evidence cited is a miss; a hedged call is a miss. Under 80%, the remediation loop is specific, not punitive: rewatch the Distribution Days and Follow-Through Days lesson — misses almost always trace to the counts — then retake only the turns you got wrong. Mastery here is not optional, because every module after this one ASSUMES you can read the regime: the scan filters by it, the setup grades consume it, the sizing table is keyed to it. And flag what's coming: one lesson remains in this module, and it covers the hardest permission of all — the months when the answer is nothing.
chapters.on_screen: The drill scored on camera against the rubric — 80% pass bar and the remediation loop written on screen

lessons.title: Cash Is a Position: The Off-Season Playbook
lessons.note: What you actually DO through a months-long ORANGE tape: the scorecard and nightly scan still run, the A-list stays fresh, reps continue on replay — but exposure stays parked. The discipline math of missing nothing (the leaders that set up in the base of a bear are caught by the routine, not by being positioned), and the trap of boredom trades quantified with one real drawdown-avoidance example. (~12 min)

chapters.marker: The months where doing nothing is the trade
chapters.beat: open on a real months-long ORANGE stretch in the dial's history and say the uncomfortable part out loud: this system will sometimes tell you to hold no stocks for a quarter.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on the dial's own history through 2022 and let the member see it: month after month of ORANGE. Then say the uncomfortable part out loud, because no one selling a trading course ever does: this system will sometimes tell you to hold no stocks for a quarter. Not a week — a quarter. And that instruction is not the system failing; it is the system working. 2022 took the Nasdaq down roughly a third; the trader who was simply ABSENT beat almost everyone who showed up every day. Cash is a position — it has a return profile (zero), a risk profile (zero), and there are entire regimes where zero is the best available trade. The skill this lesson teaches is not patience as a virtue; it is the off-season as a PLAYBOOK — specific work, done daily, while exposure stays parked.
chapters.on_screen: The dial's 2022 history — a months-long ORANGE stretch — beside the Nasdaq's 2022 decline

chapters.beat: show that the five-number scorecard and the nightly scan still run every day and the A-list stays fresh, while exposure stays parked: the work continues, the risk doesn't.
chapters.speaker_notes: Show the routine running on an ORANGE morning, unchanged from a GREEN one. The five-number scorecard still gets filled before the open: dial score, percent above the 50-day, net new highs and lows, the 4% counts, the distribution-day count. The nightly scan still runs — Stage-2 pass, the movement and liquidity filters, the tightening ranges. The A-list stays fresh: names at pivots, alerts armed, stale names deleted. The only line that changes is exposure: parked. Say the principle exactly: the work continues; the risk doesn't. This distinction is what separates an off-season professional from a lapsed hobbyist — the hobbyist stops watching because there's nothing to buy, then needs weeks to rebuild context when the turn comes. The professional's routine costs twenty minutes a night and means the turn finds them already loaded. The next chapter proves that's not a platitude.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard on an ORANGE morning — scorecard filled, nightly scan run, A-list current, zero open positions

chapters.marker: You miss nothing: leaders base in the bear
chapters.beat: pull two past leaders whose bases formed during the ORANGE tape and show the nightly routine catching both long before the follow-through day, no position required.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here is the arithmetic of missing nothing. Pull NVDA and META weekly through 2022: both spent the ORANGE tape carving Stage 1 bases — tightening ranges, flattening 200s, quiet volume — while the indexes ground lower. Now overlay what the nightly routine saw: both names passing more scan filters as their bases tightened, both landing on the B-list ('right pattern, needs time'), both promoted toward the A-list as pivots formed — all BEFORE the market's follow-through day, all without a dollar at risk. When the dial turned in early 2023, the routine-running trader didn't scramble to find the new leaders; they were already annotated on the list with entries and stops drawn. The next generation of monsters builds its bases DURING the bear. The routine catches them by default. You are not positioned in the base — you are positioned the day permission returns.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA and META weekly, 2022 into early 2023 — Stage 1 bases forming through the ORANGE tape, breakouts after the turn

chapters.beat: price one real boredom trade against the drawdown the routine-only trader avoided by sitting out, putting an actual dollar figure on the itch to 'just do something.'
chapters.speaker_notes: Now price the itch. Take one real boredom trade — a long opened into an ORANGE tape for no reason the playbook recognizes — and run its cost honestly: even 'kept small' at an 8% position with a 5% stop, that's 0.4% of the account gone per itch, and boredom trades never come alone; they come in strings, against a hostile tape, where even good setups fail at elevated rates. Then put the real number beside it: the routine-only trader who sat out 2022 avoided an index drawdown on the order of 25-30%. State the recovery arithmetic that makes avoidance so valuable: down 25% requires plus 33% just to get even. The boredom trader enters the new bull digging out of a hole; the disciplined trader enters it at high-water mark with a ranked list. 'Just do something' has a dollar figure. It is always negative.
chapters.on_screen: One real anonymized boredom trade into a hostile tape, priced against the 2022 drawdown the sidelined trader avoided (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Stand-alone example: AMD daily, August 2022. The tape is ORANGE — no-new-buys — but the summer rally is seductive. The boredom trade: buying AMD ≈$102 mid-August as it rallies straight into its falling 200-day just overhead, stop ≈$94 under the August shelf — read exact levels off the chart. Post-Jackson Hole (August 26) the tape breaks; the stop hits within days for -1R, AMD closes September at ≈$63.36 and bottoms ≈$54.57 on October 13. Price the itch: an 8% position with an 8% stop is ≈0.64% of the account per itch, times the string such trades come in — against the ≈20% index drawdown into that October 13 low the sidelined trader skipped entirely. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close with the off-season assignment: keep the scan, the scorecard, and chart-replay reps running through the next ORANGE stretch, and the artifact is a fresh, ranked A-list on the day the dial turns.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the off-season assignment — specific, not aspirational. Through the next ORANGE stretch, three things run without interruption. One: the nightly scan and the five-number scorecard, daily — twenty minutes, non-negotiable. Two: chart-replay reps — the market isn't producing live setups, so drill dead ones: covered-chart stage calls, gate checks, count-stamping on historical tapes. The off-season is when skill compounds fastest, precisely because no money is at risk while you rep. Three: A-list maintenance — bases tracked, pivots drawn, entries and stops annotated, stale names cut. The deliverable is concrete: on the day the dial turns — the follow-through day that re-opens buying at pilot size — you hand yourself a fresh, RANKED A-list with levels already drawn. That list is this lesson's artifact and the off-season's entire point: the work was never paused; only the risk was.
chapters.on_screen: A fresh ranked A-list with annotated entries and stops — the artifact waiting for the day the dial turns
chapters.example_spec: Mock the artifact as the ranked list a routine-runner held on Friday January 6, 2023 — the week permission returned. Row 1: NVDA — Stage 1 base under the December 2022 high ≈$18.50 split-adjusted (≈$185 then; 10-for-1 in June 2024); entry over that pivot, stop under the last contraction ≈$16; the mid-January breakout ran to ≈$27.78 by the March close, ≈+5R. Row 2: META — pivot ≈$124, stop ≈$115 (this module's A+ example); ≈$188.77 after the February 2 gap. Row 3: SMCI — tightening base, pivot ≈$9 split-adjusted (≈$90 then), stop ≈$7.50; ≈$11.92 by April 18. Each row carries name, theme, pivot, stop, RS note, alert armed — read exact levels off the charts and hand-annotate the printed list. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

modules.label: M4 · Breadth, Relative Strength, and Leadership: The Confirmation Layer

lessons.title: The Market's X-Ray: Percent of Stocks Above the 50-Day and 200-Day
lessons.note: Reading the internal participation the index price hides, with the working thresholds (sub-20% = washout territory, 70%+ = overheated) on the dashboard's Breadth Monitor. Includes two historical extremes where the internals diverged from the index before the index moved.

chapters.marker: The index price hides the patient's vitals
chapters.beat: open with a session where the index closed green while most stocks fell, and introduce % above the 50-day and 200-day as the X-ray underneath the price.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with a session where the index closed green while most stocks fell — 2021's second half produced them constantly: SPY printing new highs on the backs of five megacaps while the average stock was already 20% off its high. That is the trap of cap-weighting: the index is a weighted average, and a handful of trillion-dollar names can carry it while the army retreats underneath. So we X-ray it. Percent of stocks above their 50-day moving average, and percent above their 200-day — two numbers that count every soldier equally. The index tells you where the GENERALS are; participation tells you whether anyone is following them. A rally the troops aren't joining is a rally on borrowed time, and the index price alone will never tell you that. This module is the confirmation layer: every signal now needs a witness, starting with the market itself.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily near highs, late 2021, beside the Breadth Monitor's % above 200-day showing the average stock already in retreat

chapters.beat: draw the two lines on the dashboard's Breadth Monitor history: sub-20% is washout territory, 70%+ is overheated, and locate today's actual reading between them.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the two working lines on the Breadth Monitor's history and make them permanent furniture in the member's head. Sub-20% of stocks above the 50-day: washout territory — selling so indiscriminate it historically marks the neighborhood of durable lows, not the start of new declines. Fear is finishing, not beginning. Seventy percent and above: overheated — participation so complete there's little fuel left to convert; not a sell signal by itself, but the tape's cold-start potential is spent and chase-entries stop paying. Between the lines is the working range where trend, not extreme, drives decisions. Then locate today's actual reading between them, live, and say what it implies for this week's permissions. One warning: these are context thresholds, not triggers — sub-20 doesn't mean buy tomorrow; it means start watching for the follow-through mechanics you learned in Module 3.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard Breadth Monitor history with the 20% washout and 70% overheated lines drawn, today's reading located between them

chapters.marker: Historical extreme one: internals bottom before price
chapters.beat: replay a washout where % above the 50-day turned up from under 20 while the index was still making lower lows, marked to the exact sessions.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay autumn 2022 and mark the sessions. Into the October low, percent of stocks above the 50-day collapsed under 20 — washout territory, the indiscriminate stage of selling. Then the tell: as the index made its FINAL lower lows in October, the participation number refused to confirm — it turned UP from under 20 while price was still falling. Fewer stocks were making new lows on each index low; the selling was exhausting from underneath. Internals bottomed BEFORE price, by weeks, and the divergence was visible to anyone watching this one number. Now connect it to the machine the member already knows: this is why breadth participation feeds the 0-150 dial — the X-ray improves before the patient looks better. You don't buy the divergence itself; you let it put you on alert for the follow-through day that makes the turn official.
chapters.on_screen: Breadth Data Charts — % above 50-day vs. SPY, September-November 2022, the internals upturn marked against the index's final lower lows

chapters.marker: Historical extreme two: rot under a rising index
chapters.beat: walk the mirror case where participation bled for weeks beneath the index's new highs before the break, the divergence price alone never showed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the mirror image — the one that saves accounts rather than makes them. November-December 2021: the S&P grinding out fresh record highs, financial television celebratory, and underneath it the percent of stocks above the 200-day bleeding lower week after week. Every new index high came with FEWER stocks participating — the army deserting while the generals advanced. Price alone showed nothing but strength right up until the January 2022 break; the X-ray showed rot for weeks beforehand. This is the divergence that matters most for a swing trader, because tops are where oversized positions get trapped: when new index highs stop being confirmed by participation, your posture changes — tighten stops, stop initiating chase entries, respect the distribution count from Module 3 as it starts to stack. Rot under a rising index is the market whispering before it shouts. The number heard it first.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily printing new highs, November-December 2021, beside the % above 200-day bleeding lower for weeks before the January break

chapters.marker: Read it every morning in ten seconds
chapters.beat: close on the Breadth Monitor as the daily habit: where both percentages live on the dashboard and how this number slots into the five-number scorecard built at module's end.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close by converting the concept into furniture. Show exactly where both percentages live on the dashboard's Breadth Monitor, and demonstrate the full daily read in real time: glance, two numbers, done — ten seconds. The questions those ten seconds answer: Is participation confirming the index, or diverging? Is either working threshold — sub-20 washout, 70-plus overheated — in play? Has the number changed character this week? That's it; no analysis session, no hour of charts. Then place it in the bigger habit this module is building toward: percent above the 50-day is one of the five numbers on the morning scorecard you'll assemble at module's end — dial score, this number, net new highs/lows, the 4% counts, the distribution count. Five numbers before the open, every trading day. This lesson delivered the first one after the dial. The next lesson delivers two more.
chapters.on_screen: The Breadth Monitor with both participation percentages highlighted — the ten-second morning read, timed on camera

lessons.title: The Leading Edge: Net New Highs/Lows and the 4% Up/Down Day Count
lessons.note: New highs minus new lows as the earliest regime tell — one bottom where net new highs flipped positive before price confirmed, marked to the session — plus the specific warning of expanding new lows underneath a rising index, and the daily 4%-up vs 4%-down count as the day's true character.

chapters.marker: The earliest tell in the toolkit
chapters.beat: open with the claim that net new highs minus new lows flips before price does, and promise one historical bottom marked to the exact session as proof.
chapters.speaker_notes: Make the claim first, prove it second: net new highs minus new lows is the earliest regime tell in this toolkit — it flips before price does. The logic is structural. To make a new 52-week high, a stock must have ALREADY repaired its entire chart — base built, trend resumed, buyers in control for months. New highs are therefore a roster of finished turnarounds, and that roster starts growing before the index — dragged by its laggards — can show it. Mirror logic on the downside: expanding new lows are damage the index hasn't priced yet. One number, new highs minus new lows, positive or negative, read daily. The promise for this lesson: one historical bottom marked to the exact session where this number flipped positive while price still looked broken — plus the warning version that fires under rising indexes, and a second number that reads each individual day's true character.
chapters.on_screen: The net new highs minus new lows series on the Breadth Monitor, with the claim as a title card: 'This number flips before price'

chapters.marker: The bottom, marked to the session
chapters.beat: replay that low on camera: stamp the bar where net new highs flipped positive, then the later bar where price finally confirmed, and measure the lead time between them.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the 2022-2023 turn on camera and stamp it. Through the October 2022 low, new lows swamped new highs — the net number deeply negative, as it should be at a bottom. Then stamp the first bar where net new highs flipped positive and HELD: early January 2023, while the index was still grinding under its falling 200-day and the headlines were still calling rallies bear traps. Then stamp the later bar where price finally confirmed — the index reclaiming its averages and breaking the downtrend later that month. Measure the gap between the stamps on screen: weeks of lead time, visible to anyone reading one number. Then the discipline, stated flat: the flip is an ALERT, not an entry. It tells you to lean in, refresh the A-list, and watch for the follow-through mechanics from Module 3. Early information is only an edge if it changes preparation, not if it triggers impatience.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily with net new highs/lows, October 2022-February 2023 — the positive flip stamped in early January, price confirmation stamped weeks later, lead time measured

chapters.marker: The warning underneath a rising index
chapters.beat: show expanding new lows while the index climbed, the specific divergence that says an advance is hollowing out from beneath.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the same instrument pointed the other way. Late 2021: the index climbing to record highs while the new-low count EXPANDED underneath it — hundreds of stocks breaking to 52-week lows during index all-time highs. Sit with how abnormal that is: a healthy advance should be starving the new-low list, and instead it was feeding it. That specific divergence — expanding new lows under a rising index — says the advance is hollowing out from beneath: leadership narrowing to a handful of giants while the broad market quietly enters its own private bear. It is the sister signal to the participation rot from last lesson, and together with a stacking distribution-day count it forms the classic top signature. Posture response, not panic response: no new chase entries, tighten what's extended, respect the counts. The index's price will eventually tell the truth. This number tells it first.
chapters.on_screen: SPY daily at record highs, November-December 2021, beside the expanding new-lows count — hundreds of 52-week lows under an all-time-high tape

chapters.marker: The 4% up/down day count: the day's true character
chapters.beat: define the daily 4%-up versus 4%-down count and read a deceptive session where the index finished flat but the count screamed one-sided.
chapters.speaker_notes: The third instrument reads a single day. Count the stocks that moved up 4% or more today; count the stocks that moved down 4% or more. Those two counts are the day's true character, because 4% moves are conviction moves — real buying or real selling, not drift. Now read a deceptive session with it: the index closes flat, headlines say 'quiet day' — but the count shows 4%-down days swamping 4%-up days by multiples. That was not a quiet day; that was broad, urgent selling hidden under a flat cap-weighted average. The mirror also matters: a flat index with lopsided UPSIDE counts is quiet accumulation. One-sided counts stacking day after day tell you which side is actually winning the war beneath the index. Both counts live on the Breadth Monitor — up 4% today, down 4% today — and they take five seconds to read.
chapters.on_screen: The Breadth Monitor's up-4%/down-4% columns on a flat-index session where the count was heavily one-sided
chapters.example_spec: Use Monday, November 22, 2021. SPY tags a fresh intraday record ≈$473, reverses, and closes ≈-0.3% — a shrug on the surface. Underneath, rate-sensitive growth is massacred: high-multiple software and recent IPOs down 5-15% on the day, so the down-4% count swamps the up-4% count by multiples — read the exact counts off the Breadth Monitor history. Walk it in order: the near-flat index close, then the two count columns, then the roster of -4% names. The day's true character was broad urgent selling. SPY squeezed to one last record $479.98 on January 4, 2022 before breaking, its heaviest volume day landing January 24, 2022 (≈2.7×); refusing fresh growth longs there saved multiple R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Two more numbers for the scorecard
chapters.beat: add net new highs/lows and the 4% counts to the member's morning read, then run cover-the-answer reps on three covered tapes calling which side actually led each day.
chapters.speaker_notes: Bank the two additions formally: net new highs/lows and the 4% up/down counts now join the morning read, alongside the dial and percent above the 50-day from last lesson. The scorecard being assembled at module's end is now four-fifths built — the distribution-day count from Module 3 completes it. Then drill before leaving: three covered tapes — multi-day stretches with the index price VISIBLE but the internals hidden. For each day, call which side actually led — buyers or sellers — from the price action alone, in ink. Then reveal the 4% counts and the net new highs number, and grade yourself. The member will get several wrong, and that is the lesson landing: the index misleads, the counts don't. Every miss is a day the internals told a different story than the surface — exactly the days these numbers exist to catch.
chapters.on_screen: Three covered-tape drills — index price visible, internals hidden — with the 4% counts and net new highs revealed after each call
chapters.example_spec: Cover the internals on three stretches, index price visible. (a) November 8-December 3, 2021: SPY grinds to its ≈$473 November 22 record, then eases to ≈$453 — barely -3% on the surface — while net new lows expand and 4% down-days dominate; IWM had already topped $244.46 on November 8. Answer: sellers led nearly every day. (b) December 28, 2022-January 13, 2023: directionless chop in the ≈$380s (December close $382.43), but net new highs flip positive in early January and 4% up-days cluster — answer: buyers quietly led; SPY closed January at $406.48. (c) August 24-September 2, 2020: SPY vertical to highs (August close $349.31) while participation narrows — answer: hollowing, days before the September 3 break. Grade each daily call against the revealed counts. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The RS Line: Divide by SPY, Spot Leadership Before Price Confirms
lessons.note: Constructing the RS line and reading its slope, with the highest-value tell in the toolkit: the RS-line new high arriving roughly two weeks before the price new high, shown on three real leaders. Eight leader-or-laggard cover-the-answer reps.

chapters.marker: Leadership shows in the ratio before it shows in price
chapters.beat: open with the highest-value tell in the toolkit: the RS-line new high arriving roughly two weeks before the price new high.
chapters.speaker_notes: Lead with the highest-value tell in this entire toolkit: the RS-line new high that arrives BEFORE the price new high — roughly two weeks before, on the real leaders you'll see in this lesson. Here is why the ratio runs early. The RS line is the stock's price divided by SPY. A stock still finishing its base can be massively outperforming the market the whole time — falling less on red days, rising more on green ones — and the ratio records that outperformance daily while the raw chart still looks unfinished. Institutions accumulating a future leader push the ratio to new highs while price is still capped by the base's ceiling. So the RS line at a new high with price still basing is the footprint of accumulation you can see for free. Learn to read one line's slope and you'll routinely know the leaders a fortnight early.
chapters.on_screen: A leader's daily chart with RS line pane — the RS-line new high flagged roughly two weeks before the price new high
chapters.example_spec: Use NVDA daily, December 2022-May 2023, RS pane on (price ÷ SPY). All levels split-adjusted for the June 2024 10-for-1 — ≈10× these at the time. Find: the post-October base off the ≈$10.81 low; the RS line breaking to fresh 52-week highs in January while price still sat well under its own highs; the April-May flag ≈$26-28 where the RS line prints new highs in early May while price stays capped under ≈$28; then the May 25 earnings gap — +26.1%, open ≈$38.52, close ≈$37.98 on ≈3× volume — carrying price to new highs. The RS-line high led the price high by two-plus weeks. Flag both bars. Entry ≈$28.50 over the flag high, stop ≈$26.20; ≈$46.73 by the July close, ≈+8R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Build the line: divide by SPY
chapters.beat: construct the RS line on camera as price divided by SPY and teach slope reading, including the gold case: an RS line rising while the market falls.
chapters.speaker_notes: Construct it on camera so it never feels like a black box: take the stock's price, divide by SPY's price, plot the ratio. That's the whole indicator — no parameters, no settings, nothing to optimize. Then teach the reading, which is entirely slope. Rising RS line: outperforming the market — and note it can rise even on a down day, if the stock fell less than SPY. Flat: moving WITH the market, no leadership information. Falling: lagging, even if the price chart is going up — rising slower than SPY is still losing the race. Then the gold case, the one to burn in: an RS line rising while the market FALLS. That stock is being accumulated against the tide — someone is buying it while everything gets sold — and when the market turns, those names lead the new advance. That is precisely how the 2023 leaders announced themselves during the 2022 bear.
chapters.on_screen: The RS line constructed live on the dashboard chart — price ÷ SPY — with rising, flat, falling, and rising-in-a-falling-tape slope cases shown
chapters.example_spec: Construct price ÷ SPY live on NVDA daily, spring 2023 — the rising case (April close $27.75 to May $37.83, split-adjusted). Flat case: BRK.B daily, H1 2023 — price drifts with the market, ratio flat, no leadership information. Falling-ratio case: KO — it holds near its highs ($64.70 December 13, 2022; $64.99 April 24, 2023) while the ratio already bleeds, then price follows down to $55.08 by October 2, 2023. Gold case: META daily, November-December 2022 — SPY slides into its late-December low (close $382.43) while META's RS line rises off the $88.09 November 4 bottom; that against-the-tide accumulation preceded the ≈$124 breakout (stop ≈$115) to the $326.20 July 2023 high — roughly +18R on initial risk. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Three real leaders, three early tells
chapters.beat: mark the RS-line new high and the later price new high on each of three real leaders, measuring the roughly two-week lead every time.
chapters.speaker_notes: Prove the two-week lead three times, marked to the bar. NVDA, early 2023: RS line pushing to new highs in the first months of the year while price was still working through its base — the RS-line high printed, and the price new high followed with the May earnings breakout; mark both bars, measure the gap. META, early 2023: same sequence — ratio leading through the base, price confirming later; stamp and measure. SMCI, late 2023 into January 2024: RS line at new highs ahead of the price breakout that began its vertical run; stamp and measure. Roughly a two-week lead, three different stocks, three different months. Then say what a member does with the tell, concretely: an RS-line new high on a name still in its base is an A-list PROMOTION signal — draw the pivot, arm the alert, get there before the crowd's confirmation does.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA (early 2023), META (early 2023), SMCI (Dec 2023-Jan 2024) — RS-line new high and later price new high stamped on each, lead time measured

chapters.beat: counter-example: a stock printing price highs on a flat-to-down RS line, and why the missing witness disqualifies it from the A-list.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the counter-example, because the tool matters most when it says no. Pull a defensive name grinding to 52-week price highs during a roaring growth tape — a staple like KO through 2023 sits at highs on the raw chart while its RS line versus SPY drifts flat-to-down the entire time. The price chart says strength; the ratio says this stock is losing the race to the market itself, just losing it slowly and politely. That missing witness disqualifies it from the A-list — full stop. The doctrine: we do not buy price highs without RS confirmation, because a laggard at highs has no institutional sponsorship fueling further outperformance; it is rising because everything is rising, and it will fall faster than it rose when the tide goes out. Price tells you what a stock did. RS tells you whether anyone is choosing it. Buy the chosen.
chapters.on_screen: KO daily 2023 at price highs with its RS line vs. SPY flat-to-down beneath — the missing witness highlighted

chapters.beat: close with the drill: eight charts with answers covered, call leader or laggard from the RS line alone before each reveal, and review every miss by naming which slope cue was misread.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the drill, cover-the-answer format as always: eight charts, price pane HIDDEN, RS line alone visible. For each, call it — leader or laggard — in ink, before the reveal. Forcing the call from the ratio alone is the point: it proves the RS line carries enough information by itself, and it breaks the habit of letting a pretty price chart overrule the witness. After each reveal, grade — and review every miss by naming which specific slope cue was misread: a flat line mistaken for rising, a late rollover missed, a rising-in-a-falling-tape gold case not recognized, a new-high-in-the-ratio not spotted while price still based. Naming the misread cue is what converts a miss into a rep. From this lesson forward, the RS pane stays on the template permanently: RS confirming is already a line on the Stage-2 gate card — now you know exactly how to read it.
chapters.on_screen: Eight covered charts showing the RS line only — leader-or-laggard calls before each reveal
chapters.example_spec: Prepare eight charts, RS pane only, price hidden. Leaders: NVDA (January-June 2023), SMCI (November 2023-February 2024), CELH (February-July 2023 — $28.08 April low to $65.35 by the August close), META (2023, $120.34 to $353.96) — each ratio in a persistent uptrend making higher highs. Laggards: PFE, VZ, PYPL, and DIS (April-October 2023: $102.50 down to the $78.73 October 4 low while SPY held up) — ratios in steady decline even during index rallies. SMCI doubles as the gold-case check: its RS line pushed to new highs through the choppy autumn-2023 tape before price broke out ≈$29 split-adjusted (≈$290 then; 10-for-1 October 2024) and ran to the March 8, 2024 top ≈$122.90 — a >20R trend from a standard entry. After each reveal, name the slope cue. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Volume as the Witness: Confirmation as Its Own Verdict
lessons.note: Confirmation graded as a standalone skill: does this signal have a witness? Breakouts, gaps, and reclaims each shown twice — once with expanding volume, once without — and the pass/fail verdicts that follow. The dry-up-then-expansion sequence as the single most reliable tell in the system. Records once, serves both courses (fills UCT Foundations' volume-witness slot).

chapters.marker: Does this signal have a witness?
chapters.beat: open with the standing question this lesson installs, and the same breakout shown twice: once with a crowd behind it, once in an empty room.
chapters.speaker_notes: Install the standing question this lesson exists to build: does this signal have a witness? From today forward, every signal — every breakout, gap, and reclaim — gets asked that question before a dollar moves, and the witness is volume. Open with the demonstration: the same breakout shown twice. Version one clears the pivot with a crowd behind it — volume expanding to multiples of average, real money committing at the moment of decision. Version two clears the identical pivot in an empty room — volume at a fraction of normal, nobody home. Price did the same thing in both; only one of them is EVIDENCE. Module 2 planted this idea in one chapter; this lesson grows it into its own graded skill, deliberately — confirmation dies as a discipline when it's a bullet point inside a breakout lesson. Price makes claims. Volume is the witness that corroborates or contradicts. No witness, no verdict, no trade.
chapters.on_screen: The same breakout shown twice — once on expanding volume, once in an empty room — with the standing question as the title card
chapters.example_spec: Crowded room: ELF daily, May 25, 2023 — a multi-month base resolves post-earnings, gapping +10.7% to open ≈$95.70 and closing ≈$104.15 on ≈4.8× average volume; entry ≈$96, stop ≈$88 under the breakout-day low — read exact levels off the chart; ≈$114.23 by the June close (≈+2R) and ≈$139.85 by August 31 (≈+5R). Empty room: COIN daily, August 4, 2022 — the same visual, the range top cleared to ≈$106 with a ≈$116.30 print, but the 3.6× volume all belonged to sellers: it closed ≈$88.90, back under the level. Anyone who chased was -1R inside a session; COIN closed ≈$35.39 in December. Same price behavior at the pivot; only the witness differed. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the identical pivot break on 3× average volume versus 0.4×, with the verdict spoken for each: one is evidence, one is noise, and only one gets traded.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the breakout on trial formally. The identical pivot break, two exhibits: one on 3× average volume, one on 0.4×. Speak the verdict for each, in the courtroom register. Exhibit one: 3× average volume through the pivot — institutions committing size at the exact price where the pattern resolves; this is evidence, and it gets traded. Exhibit two: 0.4× average — the same price print with nobody behind it; this is noise, and low-volume breakouts are where failed breakouts live, because there's no committed buying underneath to defend the level on the first retest. Then arm the member practically: average volume means the 50-day average, and you judge the break's volume against it AT the moment of decision — projecting intraday pace when needed, not waiting politely for the close while the entry runs away. Same chart pattern, opposite verdicts, and volume alone was the difference. One gets traded. One gets skipped.
chapters.on_screen: The identical pivot break as two exhibits — 3× average volume vs. 0.4× — verdicts stamped TRADE and SKIP
chapters.example_spec: Reuse the lesson-open pair as the formal exhibits so demo and trial match. Exhibit one, TRADE: ELF, May 25, 2023 — measure breakout-day volume against the 50-day average on your platform, ≈4-5× (the tape shows 4.8×); gap open ≈$95.70, close ≈$104.15; entry ≈$96, stop ≈$88 under the breakout-day low; outcome ≈+2R by the June close ≈$114.23, ≈+5R by the August 31 high ≈$139.85. Exhibit two, SKIP: COIN, August 4, 2022 — the +31% gap clears ≈$100 and prints ≈$116.30, but closes ≈$88.90, back under the level, on 3.6× volume that belonged entirely to sellers; nobody defends it, -1R immediately and ≈-60% to ≈$35.39 by December. Stamp TRADE and SKIP on screen. Read exact levels and multiples off the charts. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run a gap and a reclaimed level each twice, with and without expanding volume, issuing the pass/fail verdict on all four exhibits.
chapters.speaker_notes: Same court, two more signal types, four exhibits. A gap up on enormous volume — NVDA's May 2023 earnings gap is the canonical case: a rip higher on volume many times average that never looked back, institutional repricing that stuck. Verdict: pass. The same-sized gap on thin volume: an ambush with nobody behind it — thin gaps get faded and filled because no real money defends them. Verdict: fail. Then reclaims: a broken support level retaken on expanding volume — buyers aggressively repurchasing the level, trapped shorts fueling the move; that reclaim holds. Pass. The same reclaim drifting back above the level on quiet volume — a technicality, not a statement, and it fails on the first test. Fail. Four exhibits, one unchanged question: did real money show up at the moment that mattered? The signal type changes; the witness requirement never does.

Exhibit two, heavy-but-distributional gap (fail): BABA, March 28, 2023 — the reorganization gap opens ≈$95.35, closes ≈$98.40 on 5.5× volume, the window's heaviest, yet fully fills within four weeks and slides to ≈$79.55 by the May close: the volume was supply. Exhibit three, witnessed reclaim (pass): META, November 10, 2022 — retakes the broken ≈$97 shelf, open ≈$107.12, close ≈$111.87 on ≈2.2× volume, holds permanently. Exhibit four, quiet gap (fail): META, December 13, 2022 — +6.5% to ≈$122.13, closes red ≈$120.15 on ≈1.2× volume, handed straight back. chapters.marker: Dry-up then expansion: the single most reliable tell
chapters.beat: trace the sequence on a real base where volume bled dry into the lows and expanded through the break, and name it the system's highest-confidence witness.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the sequence that outranks every single-bar signal in this system: dry-up, then expansion. Trace it on a real base. As the base matures, volume BLEEDS — each pullback quieter than the last, until the final contraction trades at a fraction of average. That dry-up is sellers finishing: everyone who wanted out is out, supply exhausted, the stock going quiet because there's nothing left to sell. Then the break — and volume EXPANDS through the pivot as committed buyers meet an empty shelf of supply. Scarcity meeting demand is what launches stocks. NVDA into May 2023 is the textbook print: months of drying volume through the base, then the earnings-week expansion that resolved it. Name it plainly as the system's highest-confidence witness: the full sequence — quiet INTO the level, loud THROUGH it — is the signature this entire method hunts for, and you will meet it again in every base lesson in Module 7.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, January-May 2023 — volume drying up through the base, then expanding through the earnings-gap breakout; the dry-up-then-expansion sequence annotated

chapters.marker: Confirmation is its own graded skill
chapters.beat: close with five covered signals where the member must issue the pass/fail verdict from the volume pane alone, and the bar is committing to the verdict BEFORE seeing what price did next.
chapters.speaker_notes: Grade it like the standalone skill it is. Five covered signals: chart visible up to the signal bar, volume pane visible, everything AFTER covered. For each, the member issues the verdict — pass or fail — from the volume pane alone, in ink, before seeing what price did next. That ordering is the entire bar: committing to the verdict BEFORE the outcome is what separates a confirmation discipline from outcome-worship, because a witness assessment has to stand on the evidence at the moment of decision, not on how the story ended. Some well-witnessed signals will have failed anyway, and some empty-room signals will have worked — grade the verdict against the EVIDENCE, not the outcome; that's expectancy thinking from Module 1 applied to confirmation. From here forward the volume check is a permanent field: the five-field setup card in Module 7 carries 'volume witness required — Y/N' on every trigger. This lesson is why.

(3) ELF, August 2, 2023 — gap +15.5% to ≈$134.60 on ≈5× volume — pass on the evidence, yet it stalled near ≈$139.85; the verdict is still correct. (4) AAPL, late-March 2023 drifting to recovery highs ≈$165 on sub-average volume — fail on the evidence; it kept rising to ≈$198 by July. (5) META, November 10, 2022 volume reclaim of ≈$100 — pass; it worked hugely. Grade verdicts against evidence, never outcomes. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Group Before Stock: Rank the Themes, Then Build the Five-Number Morning Scorecard
lessons.note: The Theme Tracker workflow — rank sectors and themes by RS, pick the two hunting grounds, pull the top names inside each — then assemble the permanent morning habit: dial score, % above the 50-day, net new highs/lows, 4% counts, distribution-day count — five numbers in under three minutes. Artifact: the scorecard worksheet filled live against that morning's real data. Record against the live Morning Wire: build the five numbers by hand once for understanding, then show the Wire shipping every one of them at 7:35 AM — the Wire is your scorecard, filled in.

chapters.beat: open with a mediocre chart from a leading theme outrunning a beautiful chart from a lagging one: the case for ranking groups before picking stocks.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the comparison that breaks most retail traders' mental model: a mediocre chart from a leading theme against a beautiful chart from a lagging one. 2023 supplied it perfectly — a middling AI-infrastructure name with an average base outran pristine setups in solar, where the whole group bled all year. The textbook chart in the dying group failed; the C-plus chart in the leading group paid. The reason is structural: a large share of any stock's move is group move. Institutions allocate to THEMES — they buy the story, then distribute across its names — so when a theme is being accumulated, its whole roster gets a tailwind that forgives imperfect patterns; when a theme is being sold, no pattern is clean enough to fight the outflow. So the order of operations inverts permanently: rank the groups FIRST, then hunt inside the winners. Hunt where the food is. This lesson also assembles the module's capstone habit — the five-number morning scorecard.

Lagging theme, textbook chart: ENPH — its tidy late-2022 consolidation near ≈$300-320 (high $339.92, December 5, 2022) looks pristine after a monster run, but solar is bleeding; it resolves DOWN — the April 26, 2023 gap of −19% on ≈6.7× volume, then ≈$79.58 by the October close, ≈-75% — and breakout attempts stopped out ≈-1R fast. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: rank sectors and themes by RS on the dashboard live, pick the two hunting grounds, and pull the top names inside each from that morning's real data.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the workflow live on the dashboard's Theme Tracker with that morning's real data — this is a repeatable procedure, not a concept. Step one: rank. Sort the sectors and themes by relative strength across a couple of horizons — persistent leaders, not one-day pops; the leaders and laggards columns do the work for you. Step two: choose exactly TWO hunting grounds — the two strongest themes. Two is deliberate: focus is the edge, and three-plus hunting grounds regresses to hunting everywhere, which is hunting nowhere. Step three: expand each chosen theme and pull its top names — strongest RS within the strongest groups, the leaders inside the leadership. That shortlist is your scan's priority lane and your A-list's feeder. Total cost: about two minutes each morning. Note the compounding: theme leadership persists for weeks and months, so most mornings this confirms yesterday's map — and the mornings it CHANGES are exactly the mornings you most need to know.
