modules.label: M5 · Risk Math, First Pass: R, the Formula, and the 2% Ceiling

lessons.title: The 2% Ceiling and the Arithmetic of Ruin
lessons.note: Why 2% account risk is the hard max (prefer under 1%): the recovery table (−25% needs +33%, −50% needs +100%) and losing-streak survival math at 2% versus 10% risk per trade. Artifact: the printable ruin table members keep beside their platform. Includes the gap-risk segment the stop cannot protect: the worked case where a 5% stop yields a 20% position at 1% account risk — then the stock gaps −30% overnight and the realized loss is 6× plan. That arithmetic, not the stop, is why the sizing table caps position size at all.

chapters.marker: Right on the stock, dead in the account
chapters.beat: open with the trader who nailed the thesis and still blew up on size, and name the module's claim: survival is arithmetic, not talent.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the trader who called the stock perfectly and still blew up. He bought a leader before a monster run — the thesis played out — but he risked 10% of his account per attempt, took three shakeouts before the real move started, and was down over 30% before the run began. Right on the stock, dead in the account. This module's claim: survival is arithmetic, not talent. There is no market opinion, no conviction, no chart pattern anywhere in the next six lessons — just numbers that decide whether you get to keep playing. The rules you leave with: 2% of the account is the hard maximum risk on any single trade, and under 1% is the preference. Everything else in this lesson is the proof of why those numbers and not larger ones.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: two equity curves from the same entries — 1% risk survives to the run, 10% risk is down 30% before it starts (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: META daily, Aug 2022–Feb 2023. Trades in order: four failed bottom-buys down the Stage-4 trend — ≈$170 (mid-Aug), ≈$150 (mid-Sep), ≈$130 (late-Oct, the bar before the Oct 27 −24.5% gap to an $97.98 open on 7× volume), ≈$97 (early-Nov bounce off the Nov 4 low $88.09) — each stopped 6–7% lower. Then the real entry: the early-January breakout back through the ≈$122 December gap level (Dec 13 open $122.13), entry ≈$124, stop ≈$116, held through the Feb 2 2023 earnings gap (+19.8%, open $183.38, close $188.77) for ≈+8R. Plot the same five signals twice: at 1% risk the account enters the winner ≈−4% and finishes at new highs; at 10% it is ≈−34% first and the identical winner leaves it underwater. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The recovery table, drawn by hand
chapters.beat: build the hole-vs-climb-out table live (−10% needs +11%, −25% needs +33%, −50% needs +100%) and mark the line where recovery stops being realistic.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the table live, one row at a time, and make members do the division with you. Lose 10% and you hold $90 of every $100 — getting back to even needs $10 of gain on a $90 base: +11%. Manageable. Lose 25% and you need +33% just to reclaim breakeven. Lose 50% and you need +100% — a double, which most traders never produce in a year, just to get back to where you started. Lose 70% and the climb is +233%. Mark the line between −25% and −50%: below it, recovery stops being a trading problem and becomes a career problem. The hole always grows faster than the ladder out of it — that asymmetry, not fear, is why the ceiling exists.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard: the hole-vs-climb-out table (−10%/+11%, −25%/+33%, −50%/+100%) drawn row by row

chapters.beat: run the same 10-loss streak at both risk levels on screen (2% leaves you at −18%, 10% leaves you at −65%) and show that only one of those accounts still gets to play the next hand.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the identical 10-loss streak twice on screen. At 2% risk per trade, each loss leaves 98% of the account: 0.98 to the tenth power is 0.817 — down about 18%. Painful, recoverable, still in the game; the recovery table says roughly +22% gets you home. At 10% risk, each loss leaves 90%: 0.90 to the tenth is 0.349 — down 65%, needing a +187% climb that effectively never happens. Same trades, same entries, same system — the only variable was size. And Module 1's marble draw already proved a 6-plus loss streak lives inside a healthy 45%-win system, so a long losing stretch is not a tail risk, it's an appointment. One account keeps its seat at the table; the other is gone. Size is the difference.
chapters.on_screen: Spreadsheet: two compounding rows, ten straight losses at 2% (→ −18%) vs 10% (→ −65%)

chapters.marker: The loss the stop cannot catch
chapters.beat: work the gap case in full: 1% account risk on a 5% stop yields a 20% position, the stock gaps −30% overnight, and the realized hit is −6% of the account — 6× plan — which is why the sizing table caps position size at all.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the loss the stop cannot catch. Work the case in full: 1% account risk on a 5% stop gives a 20% position — 0.01 ÷ 0.05 = 0.20. Legal, textbook, exactly what the formula lesson will teach. Then the company reports after the close and the stock opens down 30%. Your stop never printed; the first trade of the day is 30% below it. The realized hit is 30% of a 20% position: −6% of the account — six times plan on a trade you sized correctly. This is why the sizing table caps position size at all: a tight stop can justify a monster position on paper, but no stop protects you overnight. The position-size ceiling is gap insurance, and it is why 20-25% is the maximum even at GREEN + A+.
chapters.on_screen: NFLX daily, April 2022 — the −35% overnight earnings gap that opened far below any stop (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NFLX daily, Jan–Apr 2022 (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the Jan 21 2022 −21.2% earnings gap, open ≈$40.04, starting the Stage-4 downtrend; the March bounce toward the declining 50-day; the drift into Apr 19, closing ≈$34.90 while holding through earnings; then the Apr 20 open ≈$24.52 — a −29.7% overnight gap on 14× volume. Mark the textbook plan: entry ≈$34.90, 'protective' stop ≈$33.15 (5% below → a legal 20% position at 1% account risk), and show the first print of the day landing ≈$8.60 below that stop. Outcome: the planned −1R realized as ≈−6R — ≈6% of the account — before the market opened. Position-size ceilings are gap insurance; stops are not. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The ruin table you keep beside your platform
chapters.beat: hand over the printable ruin table artifact and lock in the rule as spoken doctrine: 2% is the hard ceiling, under 1% is the preference, no market opinion ever overrides it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Hand over the printable ruin table and tell them where it lives: taped beside the platform, not in a downloads folder. It carries the recovery rows and the streak math you just watched. Then state the rules as spoken doctrine, no hedging: 2% of the account is the hard ceiling on any single trade — not a target, a ceiling. Under 1% is the preference, and it is where you will live until the Module 5 sizing gate clears and your journal says you have earned more. No market opinion ever overrides it: not conviction, not a sure thing, not making back yesterday's loss. The dial can be GREEN, the chart can be perfect, and the ceiling is still 2%. Close by pointing forward: the next lesson turns this ceiling into an exact share count with one formula.
chapters.on_screen: The printable ruin table artifact held up beside the trading platform

lessons.title: The Formula: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % — Worked Five Times
lessons.note: The firm's exact formula worked on five real tickers at 1% account risk — the canonical case: a 5% stop yields a 20% position; a 10% stop yields a 10% position — with size always derived FROM the stop, never the reverse. Artifact: the position-size calculator sheet with five solved rows and three blank rows to complete before the next lesson.

chapters.marker: Size is an answer, not a feeling
chapters.beat: open with two traders buying the same breakout, one sizing on conviction and one on arithmetic, and state the whole lesson in one line: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two traders buy the same breakout at $50. One says 'I really like this one' and buys 300 shares; the other solves an equation and buys 40. Only one knows what he is risking. The whole lesson is one line: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. Every term is knowable before entry — the stop comes from the chart, the account risk comes from the ceiling lesson (2% hard max, under 1% preferred), and position size is just the algebra: Position Size % = Account Risk % ÷ Stop Distance %. Size is the OUTPUT. It is never an input, never a feeling, never a conviction level. Say the sequence the whole firm sizes by: stop first, distance second, size last. We now run it until it is boring.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, with Position Size % isolated on the second line

chapters.beat: derive the formula on the whiteboard and work the two anchor cases at 1% account risk: a 5% stop yields a 20% position, a 10% stop yields a 10% position — wider stop, smaller size, same dollars at risk.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the two anchor cases at 1% account risk. Case one: entry $50.00, structural stop $47.50 — a 5% stop distance. Position size = 1% ÷ 5% = 20% of the account. On $10,000 that is $2,000, 40 shares, and if the stop hits you lose 40 × $2.50 = $100 — exactly 1%. Case two: entry $20.00, stop $18.00 — a 10% stop. Position size = 1% ÷ 10% = 10%: $1,000, 50 shares, and the stop costs 50 × $2.00 = $100 again. Twice the stop, half the size, identical dollars at risk. That is the whole machine: the formula converts any stop the chart demands into the same fixed loss. Wide stops do not make trades riskier — oversizing them does.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard: the two anchor cases side by side — 5% stop → 20% position, 10% stop → 10% position, both risking $100 on $10K

chapters.marker: Five real tickers, five real stops
chapters.beat: work the formula on five live charts spanning a tight-stop liquid leader to a wide-stop high-ADR mover, saying the same three-step sequence out loud each time: stop first, distance second, size last.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run five live charts at 1% account risk, saying the same three-step sequence out loud each time: stop first, distance second, size last. Span the spectrum: a liquid mega-cap leader with a tight 3% stop under a shelf — 1 ÷ 3 gives a 33% raw answer the sizing table will cap; a 5% stop → 20%; a 6% stop → 16.7%; an 8% stop → 12.5%; and a high-ADR mover whose honest stop is 12% away — 1 ÷ 12 ≈ 8.3%. Convert each to dollars and shares on screen, rounding shares DOWN every time. The point the five reps hammer: the entry never decides the size, the stop does — and the wilder the stock, the smaller you are in it, automatically, without willpower.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard Charts: five current names spanning tight-stop mega-cap (e.g. AAPL) to high-ADR mover (e.g. MARA), formula worked on each
chapters.example_spec: Prep these five charts (bar-replay or static), matching the script's stop ladder: AAPL Jun 2023 — entry ≈$178 over the flat ≈$177 May shelf, stop ≈$172.70 (3% → 33% raw, table-capped); MSFT Nov 2023 — entry ≈$370, stop ≈$351.50 (5% → 20%); META May 2023 — entry ≈$250 on the shelf above the Apr 27 gap ($239.89 open), stop ≈$235 (6% → 16.7%); DKNG Jun 2023 — entry ≈$25, stop ≈$23 under the Jun 1 low $23.19 (8% → 12.5%); MARA late-Oct 2023 — entry ≈$9.30 over the range high, stop ≈$8.20 (≈12% → 8.3%). Say 'stop first, distance second, size last' on each; convert to dollars and shares, rounding down. All paid ≥2R: AAPL $193.97 and META $286.98 by Jun 30, DKNG $31.78 in July, MARA $23.49 by December. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: demonstrate the inverted version (pick the position size you want, then back-fit a stop inside the noise to justify it) and show on one of the same five charts how that stop gets hit by ordinary wiggle.
chapters.speaker_notes: Demonstrate the inversion that kills accounts. Take one of the same five charts. The trader wants a 25% position — conviction is high. Run the formula backward: at 1% account risk, a 25% position requires a 4% stop, so he draws one 4% under his entry — inside a stock whose average daily range is 5%. That stop is not an invalidation level; it is an accounting fiction sitting where ordinary noise lives. Show the next two weeks of bars: the thesis never broke, structure never failed, and the wiggle stopped him out anyway — then the stock ran without him. Picking size first and back-fitting the stop converts a good trade into a coin flip. The stop must mark where you are WRONG. If the honest stop makes the size small, the size is small.
chapters.on_screen: Same chart with the back-fit 4% 'stop' drawn inside the average daily range — hit by a wiggle that never broke structure
chapters.example_spec: DKNG daily, Jun–Aug 2023: entry ≈$25 over the June pivot, honest structure stop ≈$23 just under the Jun 1 swing low $23.19 (8%). The trader wants a 25% position, so at 1% risk he back-fits a 4% 'stop' ≈$24 — inside a stock whose average daily range runs ≈5%. Find, in order: the entry bar; two or three ordinary red days in the next fortnight whose lows wick through ≈$24 while the ≈$23 structure low never trades and no close breaks the pivot; then the run to ≈$33.60 on the Aug 4 gap-up (+12%, open $33.59, 3.8× volume) — June closed $26.57, July $31.78. Outcome: the back-fit stop pays −1R and forfeits ≈+4R; the structural stop keeps the trade. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Your calculator sheet: five solved, three blank
chapters.beat: walk the position-size calculator artifact row by row, then assign the three blank rows as required homework to complete before the Sizing Gate checkpoint.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the position-size calculator sheet row by row. Five rows are solved — the canonical pair plus the three chart cases — each showing the full chain: entry, stop, stop distance %, account risk target, position size % (risk ÷ distance), position dollars, shares rounded down, dollars at risk. Three rows are blank, and they are required homework: pull three names from tonight's scan, place an honest structural stop on each, and complete every column before the next lesson. Bring the finished sheet to the Sizing Gate checkpoint — the gate's ten problems are these same rows with the answers hidden, and the pass bar there is 100%. If any blank row takes you more than sixty seconds, rewatch this lesson now; the gate does not grade effort.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: The Sizing Gate — Ten Problems, 100% to Pass
lessons.note: The course's hard gate on its most dangerous skill: ten worked sizing problems — mixed stop widths, mixed account sizes, one deliberate skip-because-the-structural-stop-is-too-wide case — solved on camera after the member attempts each cold. The bar is 100%: any miss means rewatch the formula lesson and retake. Nothing after this module is traded live until this gate clears.

chapters.beat: open by naming what this checkpoint really is: the course's hard gate on its most dangerous skill, because a trader who sizes wrong one time in ten is not 90% safe, he is unsafe.
chapters.speaker_notes: Name what this checkpoint is before problem one: the course's hard gate on its most dangerous skill. Every other module gates at roughly 80% — this one is 100%, and the exception is deliberate. A trader who sizes wrong one time in ten is not 90% safe; he is unsafe, because the one oversized trade is the one the recovery table punishes. A chart-reading error costs you a trade; a sizing error costs you the account that would have taken every future trade. So the terms are absolute: ten problems, ten correct, no partial credit — and nothing after this module is traded live, not pilot size, not one share, until this gate clears. It is the only test in the course where a miss means stop, not close enough.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE toolkit card — header and its 'Ten problems. 100% to pass.' tagline

chapters.beat: explain the mechanics before problem one: pause the video, solve each problem cold on your own sheet, then watch it solved on camera; copying the on-screen work is passing someone else's gate.
chapters.speaker_notes: Explain the mechanics before any math. Fold the printed card to cover every ANSWER line. For each problem: pause the video, solve it cold on scratch paper, then uncover and grade. Copying the on-screen work is passing someone else's gate — the market administers the real retake at full size. The toolkit: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, rearranged to Position Size % = Account Risk % ÷ Stop Distance %; then Position $ = Position Size % × Account, and Shares = Position $ ÷ Entry, always rounded DOWN. Three hard limits apply to every problem: account risk ≤ 2% (under 1% preferred); the regime × grade ceiling — GREEN + A+ 20-25%, YELLOW + A+ 15%, ORANGE + A+ 8%, B in ORANGE is a skip; and total portfolio heat ≤ 10%.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE card — 'How This Gate Works' section plus the regime size-ceiling table

chapters.beat: work five problems live at a fixed account size with stops from 3% to 12%, narrating the same stop-distance-size sequence every time until it sounds boring.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the first five at a narrated cadence — the same sequence every time until it sounds boring. Problem 1: $10,000 account, GREEN, A+, 1% risk, entry $50.00, stop $47.50. Stop distance 5%; 1% ÷ 5% = 20% → $2,000 → 40 shares → $100 at risk. Problem 2: entry $20.00, stop $18.00 — 10% stop → 10% position → $1,000 → 50 shares, the same $100. Problem 3: $8,000, YELLOW, 0.5% risk, 4% stop → 12.5% → $1,000 → 40 shares → $40 — under the 15% YELLOW ceiling. Problem 4: $25,000, GREEN, 2% risk, 8% stop → 25% → $6,250 → 50 shares → $500 — legal, but pinned at BOTH the 2% hard max and the top of the GREEN ceiling; nothing may be added. Problem 5: $50,000, 1% risk, 4% stop → 25% → 156 shares, because 156.25 rounds DOWN. Always down.
chapters.on_screen: Doc-cam working problems 1-5 from THE SIZING GATE card, answers covered then revealed

chapters.beat: work four problems across different account sizes ($5K to $250K to prove the formula doesn't care), then the deliberate trap: a structural stop so wide that the only correct answer is skip the trade, not shrink the stop.
chapters.speaker_notes: Problems 6 through 8 change the account size to prove the formula does not care: $100,000 in ORANGE at 0.5% risk with an 8% stop → 6.25%, just under ORANGE's 8% ceiling — in ORANGE it is small and A+ or nothing; $250,000 at 1% with a 6% stop → 16.7% → 208 shares, roughly $2,496 at risk. Problem 9 is the ceiling lesson: $50,000, 1.5% risk on a 3% stop says a 50% position — but GREEN + A+ caps at 25%. Cap it: the table always outranks the formula, because a stop cannot catch an overnight gap. Then problem 10, the deliberate trap: $8,000 account, honest structural stop 15% away. The formula yields a meaningless 13-share position; forcing a real one risks 3%, over the hard max. The only correct answer is SKIP — never shrink the stop to force the math.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE card problems 6-10, with #9's ceiling cap and #10's SKIP circled

chapters.marker: The pass bar and the retake
chapters.beat: state the gate terms to camera: 10 for 10 or it's a miss, any miss means rewatch the formula lesson and retake with fresh numbers, and nothing after this module gets traded live until this gate clears.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the terms straight to camera. Ten for ten. Nine is a miss, and a miss is not a judgment — it is a routing instruction: rewatch the formula lesson, then retake this gate with fresh numbers on a written date. Log the attempt number on the card; there is no shame in attempt two and no credit for attempt zero. Self-grade the checklist before scoring: every size derived FROM the stop, nothing over 2%, every share count rounded down, the regime ceiling checked on all ten, and #10 marked SKIP — not a tighter stop. Until the 'Gate cleared on' line is dated, nothing after Module 5 gets traded live; pilot size and paper remain your whole world. The market does not grade on a curve. Neither does this.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE card — 'Score & Retake' block with the 'Gate cleared on' line highlighted

lessons.title: Where the Stop Actually Goes: Structure, Percent, ATR — Invalidation, Not Comfort
lessons.note: The same entry sized three ways under a structure stop, a fixed-percent stop, and an ATR stop, unified by the iron rule: the stop marks the price where the thesis is wrong, then the size is derived. Includes the case where the structural stop is too wide for 2R and the correct answer is skip, not shrink the stop.

chapters.marker: The stop marks where you're wrong
chapters.beat: open with the iron rule spoken plainly: a stop is the price at which the trade's thesis is dead, never the loss that feels tolerable, and everything else in this lesson is just three ways to find that price.
chapters.speaker_notes: The iron rule, spoken plainly: a stop is the price at which your trade's thesis is dead — never the loss that feels tolerable. Those are different numbers, and confusing them is one of the five leaks from Module 1. If you bought a base breakout, the thesis is 'the breakout is real'; the price that proves it false sits below the structure that launched it, not 2% under your fill because 2% feels safe. Everything in this lesson is just three ways to find that thesis-death price — structure, fixed percent, ATR — and the order of operations never changes: invalidation first, size second, derived through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. You do not choose the stop. The chart chooses it; you only choose whether the trade is worth taking at that stop.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI daily, Jan-Feb 2024 — a flat-base breakout with the thesis-death level marked under the pivot area (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, Aug 2023–Feb 2024 (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the Aug 2023 high ≈$35.70, the bar before the Aug 9 −14.5% gap, starting the five-month flat base; the October low ≈$22.60; the Dec–Jan tightening between ≈$27 and ≈$31; the mid-January breakout through the ≈$30.50 December swing high; then the Jan 19 2024 preannouncement gap (+11.6%, open $34.76, close $42.34, 4× volume) straight through the ≈$35.70 base pivot. Entry ≈$30.70. Mark two candidate stops: the 'tolerable-loss' 2%-under-fill line ≈$30.10 (wrong — inside ordinary noise) versus the thesis-death level ≈$27 under the final contraction low (right). Outcome: SMCI cleared ≈$100 (=$1,000 pre-split) by early March — ≈+18R against the honest stop. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: on a real breakout chart, place the stop under the pivot-area low where the pattern is objectively broken, then derive the position size from it with the formula on screen.
chapters.speaker_notes: On the real breakout chart, place the structure stop where the pattern is objectively broken: under the pivot-area low — the last contraction low before the break. Above that level, any pullback is normal retesting; below it, the base has failed and there is nothing left to be right about. Measure it live: entry at the pivot, stop under that low — call it 6% away. Then derive the size on screen: at 1% account risk, 1% ÷ 6% = a 16.7% position — dollars, shares rounded down, done. The structure stop is the firm's default because it is the only one of the three that reads the actual battlefield: it goes wider on loose patterns and tighter on coiled ones, automatically sizing you down in sloppy stocks and up in clean ones.
chapters.on_screen: Same SMCI breakout chart — stop placed under the final contraction low, sizing math overlaid

chapters.marker: Percent and ATR on the same entry
chapters.beat: size the identical entry two more ways (a fixed-percent stop and an ATR-multiple stop), line all three sizes up in one table, and show that the entry never changed — only the invalidation logic did.
chapters.speaker_notes: Size the identical entry two more ways. A fixed-percent stop — a flat 8% under every entry — is simple and consistent but blind: needlessly wide on a tight coil, inside the noise on a volatile name. An ATR stop — say 2× the 14-day ATR below entry — adapts to the stock's actual volatility: if ATR is 2.5%, the stop sits 5% back and the formula gives a 20% position at 1% risk. Line all three up in one table: structure 6% → 16.7% position; percent 8% → 12.5%; ATR 5% → 20%. Same entry, three sizes — because the entry never changed, only the invalidation logic did. Whichever method you use, the sequence is identical: the stop is chosen for a reason you can say out loud, and the size falls out of the formula.
chapters.on_screen: Three-column table: structure vs fixed-percent vs ATR stop on the same entry, each with its derived position size

chapters.beat: show the failure case: dragging the stop tighter so the formula spits out a bigger position, placing it inside normal noise, and getting stopped on a wiggle that never threatened the thesis.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the failure case, performed live. The trader looks at the honest 6% structural stop, does not like the 16.7% position it allows, and drags the stop up to 3% — presto, the formula now 'permits' 33%. But that 3% stop sits inside the stock's ordinary daily range: nothing about the thesis dies there, only his patience. Replay the bars: an intraday wiggle — a normal, meaningless rotation that never threatened the base — tags the stop and he is out with a real loss on a trade that was never wrong. Worse, he was double size when it happened. This is comfort-stop surgery: mutilating the invalidation level to justify the position you wanted. The formula is honest; feed it a lie and it returns a bigger, faster way to lose.
chapters.on_screen: Same chart with the dragged-in 3% stop getting wicked out by ordinary daily range while structure holds

chapters.beat: work the case where the honest structural stop is so far away the trade can't pay 2R, and close on the decision sequence the member leaves with: invalidation first, size second, and if the two can't agree, the answer is no trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Last case: the honest structural stop is simply too far away. A high-ADR name with a loose base puts the thesis-death level 15% below entry, and the nearest realistic target does not pay 2R against that risk — the trade cannot pay you enough for what it demands. The wrong answers: shrink the stop to where it fits (comfort surgery in reverse), or take it anyway and hope. The right answer is no trade. Close on the decision sequence the member leaves with, in order: invalidation first — where is the thesis dead? Size second — what does the formula allow at that stop? And if the stop and the payoff cannot agree, the answer is skip. There will always be another bus. There is only one account.
chapters.on_screen: MARA daily, late 2023 — a wide, loose structure whose honest stop sits ~15% away and can't pay 2R (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: MARA daily, Nov 2023–Jan 2024, framed at the Jan 2 2024 blow-off. Find, in order: the parabolic ≈$8.50 → ≈$26.60 run (Nov close $11.97, Dec 4 gap-open $15.33, Dec 29 close $23.49, Jan 2 open $26.64); the wide, loose late-December 'structure' — 20% swings, no tight contraction; a candidate entry ≈$27 over that high; the only honest invalidation, the last defensible swing low ≈$22.50, roughly 16% away. Do the math on screen: 2% ceiling ÷ 16% stop ≈ 12% max position, and 2R demands ≈$36 from an already-extended parabola with no basing under it. Verdict: SKIP. Proof: Jan 2 closed $22.93, −14% from its own open, and MARA printed $17.73 by Jan 31 (≈−33%), never reaching $36. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Only Take Trades That Pay: The 2R Minimum, Expectancy, and the One Commandment
lessons.note: Expectancy = (win% × avg win in R) − (loss% × avg loss in R), computed on the Module 1 marble log including a 38%-win-rate system that prints money, installing the entry filter: no trade without 2R to the first target. Closes with the zero-exception commandment — never add to losers — and the account math of one doubled-down loser versus ten disciplined stops.

chapters.beat: open with the provocation: a system that loses 62% of the time made money all year, and prove it on screen with (38% × 2.5R wins) − (62% × 1R losses) = +0.33R per trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the provocation: here is a system that loses 62% of the time and made money all year. Prove it on screen: expectancy = (38% × 2.5R average win) − (62% × 1R average loss) = 0.95 − 0.62 = +0.33R per trade. A third of an R, every trade, on average — over 100 trades that is +33R, and at 1% risk per trade that is roughly a third of the account, while being WRONG nearly two trades out of three. Meanwhile the 90%-win-rate trader from Module 1 — tiny wins, occasional multi-R disasters — bleeds. Win rate is the number amateurs brag about; expectancy is the number accounts compound on. This lesson gives you the equation, then installs the two rules that keep your own expectancy positive: the 2R minimum and the one commandment.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard: (38% × 2.5R) − (62% × 1R) = +0.33R per trade, worked digit by digit

chapters.marker: Expectancy from your own marble log
chapters.beat: bring back the Module 1 marble-game log and compute Expectancy = (win% × avg win in R) − (loss% × avg loss in R) on its actual numbers, so the member grades a system they personally traded.
chapters.speaker_notes: Bring back the Module 1 marble-game ledger — the one you filled during the live draw — and grade it with the real equation: Expectancy = (win rate × average win in R) − (loss rate × average loss in R). Count the wins, compute the rates, average the R columns, and run it. At the marble game's 45% and 2R, that is (0.45 × 2.0) − (0.55 × 1.0) = 0.90 − 0.55 = +0.35R per trade — the system you personally sat through, including that gut-churning 6-loss streak, was printing a third of an R the whole time. This is the ledger's standing job from here on: every 20 rows, run the expectancy block. That number — not P&L, not win rate — is the grade of your system, and later, of you.
chapters.on_screen: THE R-MULTIPLE LEDGER artifact — the EXPECTANCY SELF-CALC block filled from the Module 1 marble draw

chapters.beat: install the rule live on a chart: measure entry-to-stop, project it 2× to the first target, and if 2R doesn't fit under the nearest resistance, the trade is declined before it ever gets sized.
chapters.speaker_notes: Install the entry filter live on a chart. Measure entry to stop — entry $50, stop $47.50, risk $2.50. Project it forward: the first target must sit at least 2× that risk above entry — $55.00 — BELOW the nearest overhead resistance. If old supply sits at $53, the trade pays at most 1.2R and it is declined before it is ever sized; you do not shrink the stop to fix the ratio, you pass. Why 2R is the line: at a realistic 40-50% win rate, 1R winners are a treadmill — (0.45 × 1) − (0.55 × 1) is negative. The 2R floor is what makes your loss rate affordable: every trade must pay for at least two of its own failures. The market offers thousands of trades; you only need the ones that pay.
chapters.on_screen: Chart with entry/stop marked and the 2R projection dying under overhead resistance — e.g. PYPL daily, mid-2023 rally into supply (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: PYPL daily, May–Aug 2023. Find, in order: the slide into the ≈$61 late-May/early-June low (May closed $61.99 after the May 9 −7.9% gap); the June–July rally to ≈$76 (Jul 31 close $75.82); a plausible entry ≈$75 over the mid-July pivot with stop ≈$71 under the last higher low (risk ≈$4 = 1R); then project 2R to ≈$83 and watch it die — the declining 200-day sits ≈$75–78 and the Feb 2023 breakdown shelf ≈$76–81 caps the move, so the trade pays ≈1.2R at best. The filter declines it before sizing; you never shrink the stop to fix the ratio. Proof: PYPL topped ≈$77, then the Aug 3 earnings gap opened $66.70 (−8.9%, 3.4× volume) straight through the stop — taken ≈−2R, filtered 0R; $58.46 by September. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: One doubled-down loser vs ten disciplined stops
chapters.beat: run the account math side by side: ten honest 1R stops cost −10R, while one loser averaged down and gapped through the stop erases more than all ten combined.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the account math side by side. Left column: ten honest stops, ten disciplined −1R exits, −10R total — at 1% risk the account is down about 10%, fully recoverable per the ruin table (+11% to home). Right column: one trade, planned at 1R. It drops 1R; instead of stopping he 'improves his average' and doubles the position. It drops again; he adds again. He is now triple size with no stop honored — and the overnight gap does what gaps do. A −30% gap on what has become a 60% position is −18% of the account: one trade erased more than all ten disciplined losers combined, plus the year's edge. The stops were the cheap column. Losses are the business's inventory cost; averaging down is setting the warehouse on fire.
chapters.on_screen: Split-screen slide: ten −1R stops (−10R) vs the averaged-down, gapped-through loser (−18R) — pair with PTON daily, Nov 2021 (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: PTON daily, Oct 2021–Jan 2022, beside the ruin slide (update it to −10R vs −20R). Find, in order: the downtrend from the Aug 3 2021 high ≈$123; a late-October 'value' buy ≈$92 with planned stop ≈$87 (1R, ≈20% position); the stop ignored and average-downs ≈$89 and ≈$87 — now ≈60% of the account with no stop honored; the Nov 4 close $86.04; then the Nov 5 earnings gap opening $57.13 and closing $55.64 on 5.2× volume (read exact levels off the chart). A −33.6% gap on a 60% position ≈ −20% of the account, ≈−20R — twice what ten disciplined −1R stops (−10R) cost. Aftermath for the closer: $35.76 at December's close, ≈$27 by late January. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close by writing 'never add to losers' as the single zero-exception rule of the entire system, and tie it back to expectancy: adding to a loser is manually growing the avg-loss term of your own equation.
chapters.speaker_notes: Write it on screen and box it: NEVER ADD TO LOSERS. It is the single zero-exception rule of the entire system. Not in GREEN, not on A+ setups, not when you are sure, not to fix your average. Tie it back to the equation so it is math, not morality: expectancy = (win% × avg win) − (loss% × avg loss). Adding to a loser does exactly one thing arithmetically — it grows the average-loss term of your own equation, by hand, in real time. You are manually engineering negative expectancy onto a system that may have been fine. Adding to WINNERS — after a new setup forms, sized by the same formula — is a different, later lesson and completely legal. Down is never a reason to buy. Say it once out loud, then we are done.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: 'NEVER ADD TO LOSERS' boxed above the expectancy equation with the avg-loss term circled

lessons.title: Running This System Under $25K: PDT, Cash Accounts, and Settlement
lessons.note: The pattern-day-trader rule and how this course's own doctrine consumes day trades (a breakout bought at 10 AM and stopped at 2 PM is one), cash-account settlement timing as the workaround, and the honest adjustments for a small account: fewer concurrent names, wider-timeframe stops, and why the 2% ceiling matters MORE, not less, when the account is small. (~10 min)

chapters.marker: The rule that punishes your discipline
chapters.beat: open with the trap: under $25K in a margin account, the pattern-day-trader rule allows 3 day trades per rolling 5 days, and a correctly executed stop can be the thing that burns one.
chapters.speaker_notes: The trap, stated plainly: in a margin account under $25,000, the pattern-day-trader rule allows only 3 day trades in any rolling 5-business-day window. A day trade is buying and selling the same security in the same session — and here is the sting: a correctly executed stop can be the thing that burns one. Trip the limit and the broker flags and restricts the account until it is funded to $25K. So the rule does not just cap gambling — it can punish your discipline, taxing exactly the behavior this course demands: honoring the stop fast. This lesson is the honest operating manual for running the UCT system under $25K: what the rule actually counts, the cash-account workaround, and the adjustments that make the system fit a small account instead of fighting it.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the PDT rule — margin account under $25K = 3 day trades per rolling 5 business days

chapters.marker: How our own doctrine consumes day trades
chapters.beat: walk the concrete case from the note: a breakout bought at 10 AM and stopped out at 2 PM the same day is one day trade, so the system's best practice (honor the stop fast) collides with the rule.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the concrete case. Your A-list alert fires at 10:00 AM; you buy the base breakout at the pivot, exactly per plan. The breakout fails — sellers swamp it — and at 2:00 PM your stop executes. Same security, same session: that is one day trade, and you did nothing wrong. Do it three times in a week — three failed breakouts, three honored stops — and the fourth correct stop is the one the rule blocks or flags you on. That is the collision: the system's best practice, cut losses fast, is exactly what the rule counts. What you must NEVER do is 'save' a day trade by holding a broken trade overnight — that converts a planned −1R into gap lottery. The stop is still an appointment. The fix is structural, not behavioral: the next two chapters.
chapters.on_screen: 5-minute chart of a real failed morning breakout — bought at 10 AM, stopped at 2 PM, labeled 'one day trade' (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute chart, Aug 24 2023 — the session after the blowout earnings (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the gap-up open $50.22, +6.6% over the $47.11 prior close, already through the July high ≈$48; the 9:30–10:00 opening consolidation topping ≈$50.30; the 10 AM alert-style breakout buy ≈$50.35 with stop ≈$49.10 under the opening-range low; then the all-day fade — lower highs from late morning, the stop executing in the early afternoon, close $47.16 on 2.4× volume, below the prior close. Outcome: an honest, correct −1R — and same security, same session means one of the three day trades a sub-$25K margin account gets per rolling five days is consumed by doing everything right. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: show settlement mechanics on a real example: cash accounts have no PDT rule, but sale proceeds must settle before reuse, so the workaround is splitting capital into rotating settled tranches and never spending unsettled funds.
chapters.speaker_notes: The workaround: the PDT rule applies to margin accounts. A cash account has no day-trade limit — but it has its own physics: you trade only with settled cash, and equity sale proceeds settle the next business day (T+1). Show it on a real example: a $10,000 cash account split into two $5,000 tranches. Monday you buy and stop out of a trade in tranche A — those proceeds settle Tuesday morning. Tuesday you trade tranche B while A settles; Wednesday A is back online. Rotating settled tranches means you always have dry powder without ever spending unsettled funds — which matters, because trading on unsettled proceeds triggers a good-faith violation, and a few of those get the account restricted anyway. Cash account plus tranche rotation: the discipline tax removed, the stop always honorable.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: two-tranche T+1 settlement calendar — Mon trade A, Tue trade B while A settles, Wed A is live again

chapters.beat: lay out the three adaptations without sugarcoating: fewer concurrent names, stops planned on the daily/weekly timeframe so exits rarely happen same-day, and patience as a structural requirement rather than a virtue.
chapters.speaker_notes: The three honest adjustments, no sugarcoating. One: fewer concurrent names — two or three positions, not eight; a small account splits into meaninglessness beyond that, and fewer names means fewer stops competing for your day-trade or settlement budget. Two: plan stops on the daily and weekly timeframe — enter on the daily trigger with the stop at daily structure, so a same-day stop-out is the exception, not the routine; swing structure naturally spaces entry and exit across days. Three: patience becomes structural, not aspirational — you physically cannot churn, so you take only A-grade setups from the A-list and let the B-grade ideas go. None of this handicaps the system. The system IS daily-timeframe swing trading; the small-account constraints just remove the option of doing it wrong.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the three small-account adjustments — fewer names, daily/weekly stops, A-grade only

chapters.marker: Why 2% matters MORE when you're small
chapters.beat: close on the psychology-and-math of small accounts: the temptation is to oversize your way to $25K faster, but the ruin table from lesson one shows the small account is exactly the one that cannot afford the drawdown.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close on the psychology and the math together. The small-account temptation is always the same sentence: 'I'll never reach $25K risking 1% — let me size up and get there faster.' Run the ruin table against that logic one more time. At 10% risk, the ordinary 6-loss streak — the one the marble draw produced on camera — leaves 0.90 to the sixth power, about 53% of the account: down 47%, needing +88% to recover, on an account with no cushion and maximum emotional loading. The big account can survive a stupid stretch; the small account is exactly the one that cannot afford the drawdown. So the ceiling binds HARDER when you are small: 2% hard max, under 1% preferred, no exceptions for ambition. Small accounts do not die from growing slowly. They die from trying to grow fast.
chapters.on_screen: The printable ruin table artifact with the 6-loss-at-10% row (−47%, +88% to recover) highlighted

modules.label: M6 · The Scan Engine: Watchlists That Feed the Loop

lessons.title: The Nightly Scan: 3,700 Tickers to 10 Names in 20 Minutes
lessons.note: The actual filter chain run live on the Screener with a running clock — Stage-2 pass, ADR% ≥ 4 (low-ADR names filtered entirely), a dollar-volume floor, RS trend up, tightening ranges — explaining each filter by showing the garbage it removes. Artifact: the exact filter settings plus that night's real 10-name output list.

chapters.beat: open by starting a visible on-screen timer over the full Screener universe and framing the promise: this funnel replaces years of unstructured chart flipping with a repeatable nightly workflow.
chapters.speaker_notes: Start the visible timer at 0:00 over the full Screener universe — roughly 3,700 tickers — and make the promise: twenty minutes from now this list will be ten names, and you will know exactly why each survived. This funnel replaces the thing that consumes most traders' evenings: unstructured chart flipping, hoping to stumble onto something. The scan is THE LOOP's second station — Regime granted permission this morning; Scan decides which names have earned a place on your list tonight. Five filters, applied in a fixed order, each explained by showing the garbage it removes: the Stage-2 trend gate, ADR% ≥ 4, a dollar-volume floor, RS trend up, and tightening ranges. Same chain, every night, twenty minutes. The clock is running.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard Screener over the full ~3,700-ticker universe with an on-screen countdown timer at 0:00

chapters.beat: apply the Stage-2 trend pass first and scroll through what it removed: downtrends, basing wrecks, and Stage-4 falling knives that no setup lesson will ever make buyable.
chapters.speaker_notes: Apply the Stage-2 trend pass first, because it deletes the most. This is Module 3's eight-question gate as a screen: price above a rising 50 and 200, the 200-day rising for a month-plus, within striking distance of highs, RS confirming — fail one, gone. Then scroll the corpses so members see what died: downtrends grinding under a falling 200; basing wrecks that need months more repair; Stage-4 falling knives that look cheap. Say the point out loud: no setup lesson in this course will ever make these buyable. A perfect flag on a Stage-4 stock is a perfectly drawn trap. The gate typically cuts the universe by three-quarters or more before any judgment happens — which is exactly why it goes first: it is binary, mechanical, and cannot be argued with.
chapters.on_screen: Screener with the Stage-2 pass applied — scrolling the removed downtrends and Stage-4 charts

chapters.beat: layer on the movement filter (low-ADR names filtered entirely — a stock that can't move 4% a day can't pay 2R on a swing) plus the dollar-volume floor, showing the illiquid and the comatose getting cut.
chapters.speaker_notes: Layer on the movement filter: ADR% ≥ 4 — average daily range of at least 4%. The logic is arithmetic, not preference: a stock that cannot move 4% in a day cannot reach a 2R target inside a swing hold. Low-ADR names are filtered ENTIRELY, not deprioritized — a beautiful setup on a stock that does not move is a parking spot, not a trade. Then the dollar-volume floor: enough daily dollar volume that your full position enters and exits without moving the tape or eating a wide spread. Scroll what these two cut: the comatose mega-caps that drift one percent a week, and the illiquid micro-caps where the spread IS your stop. What survives is the tradeable middle: stocks that move, in size you can actually trade.
chapters.on_screen: Screener with ADR% ≥ 4 and the dollar-volume floor layered on — the comatose and the illiquid dropping out

chapters.beat: add the final two filters and watch the list collapse to the survivors: names outperforming the market whose pullbacks are contracting into a coiled, scannable pivot.
chapters.speaker_notes: Add the final two filters and watch the list collapse to survivors. RS trend up: the stock is outperforming SPY over the scan window — Module 4's ratio line applied as a screen. In a universe where most names track the index, outperformance is the fingerprint of institutional accumulation, and it shows in the ratio before it shows in price. Then ranges tightening: recent pullbacks contracting, each swing smaller than the last, volatility compressing into a coil — the pre-breakout signature you stared at across the Winners Gallery: quiet base, tightening range, ignition. Restate the chain's logic: Stage 2 says the trend is real, ADR says it can pay, dollar volume says you can trade it, RS says big money agrees, tightening says the move may be soon. From 3,700 to a handful.
chapters.on_screen: Screener final pass — the survivors, with one chart open showing contracting pullbacks coiling into a pivot
chapters.example_spec: Run the final screener pass live as scripted; for the open chart use NVDA daily, Sept 2023–Jan 2024 (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: pullbacks contracting in sequence — ≈−22% (Aug–Oct, ≈$50.30 down to the Oct 31 low $39.23), ≈−10% (Nov–early Dec), ≈−6% (mid-Dec) — each low higher; volume drying into late December; the RS line versus SPY rising throughout while SPY only regained its July level in December; the range tightening under the Nov 20 pivot high $50.55; then the Jan 8 2024 ignition bar through it. Entry ≈$50.60, stop ≈$47.50 under the last contraction low. Outcome: NVDA ran to ≈$95 (=$950 pre-split) by the Mar 8 high $97.40 — roughly +14R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: stop the clock, hand over the exact filter-settings artifact plus that night's real 10-name output list, and assign the drill: run this exact chain yourself tonight and bring your ten to the next lesson.
chapters.speaker_notes: Stop the clock — under twenty minutes — and hand over both artifacts: the exact filter settings, so the chain is reproducible click for click, and tonight's actual 10-name output list, so you can check your own run against a known answer. Then the drill, stated as a rep count, not a suggestion: run this exact chain yourself tonight, on tonight's data, and bring your ten names to the next lesson. They will not match this list perfectly — a day passed, data moved — but most should overlap, and every name on your list must have all five filter reasons attached. From tonight forward this is a standing appointment: the nightly scan runs every market night, even in ORANGE when you cannot buy anything — because the leaders of the next leg are basing in this list right now.

lessons.title: Watchlist Architecture: A-List, B-List, and the Weekend Deep Scan
lessons.note: A-list = at a pivot within 1-2 days with an alert set at the exact trigger price; B-list = right pattern, needs time — plus the full Sunday routine (theme review, weekly-chart sweep, ten charts annotated with exact entry and stop levels) that produces Monday's plan. Artifact: the weekend scan template built live from a real Friday close.

chapters.marker: A watchlist is a promotion system, not a pile
chapters.beat: open with the 80-ticker graveyard list every member already has, and replace it with the two-tier architecture where every name has a status and an expiry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the list every member already owns: 80 tickers, accumulated over months, no statuses, no expiries — a graveyard where good ideas go to be forgotten. A watchlist is not a pile; it is a promotion system. Every name on it must have a status — how close is it to actionable — and an expiry — the condition under which it leaves. Two tiers do all the work. The A-list: names at a drawn pivot, actionable within 1-2 days, alert armed at the exact trigger price. The B-list: right pattern, needs time. Names are promoted when they tighten toward the pivot and deleted when structure breaks. That is the whole architecture: the scan feeds the B-list, the B-list feeds the A-list, and the A-list feeds THE LOOP's Setup station — nothing lingers, nothing goes stale.
chapters.on_screen: Watchlists page: a bloated 80-ticker list beside the clean two-tier A-list/B-list structure

chapters.marker: The A-list: at the pivot, alert armed
chapters.beat: define the A-list precisely on a live chart: within 1-2 days of a drawn pivot, with an alert set at the exact trigger price, so the market interrupts you instead of you staring at it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Define the A-list precisely on a live chart. Membership requires three things. One: a drawn pivot — an exact trigger price on the chart, to the tick, not 'around 50.' Two: proximity — the name is within 1-2 days of that pivot; it could fire tomorrow. Three: an alert armed at the exact trigger price, set right now, on camera. The alert is the point of the whole structure: the market interrupts YOU. You are not staring at quotes all day — the A-list watches itself and rings when a name does the one thing you pre-decided matters. An A-list name with no alert is just a wish. Cap the list where your attention actually reaches: a handful of names, each with a pivot, each armed.
chapters.on_screen: Live chart with the pivot drawn to the tick and the Watchlists alert popover armed at that exact price
chapters.example_spec: Prefer a current A-list name sitting within ≈2% below a clean flat pivot and arm the real alert live. If none qualifies, bar-replay NVDA daily to Jan 5 2024 (prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time): draw the pivot to the tick at the Nov 20 2023 intraday high $50.55 (=$505.48 at the time — read the exact print off your platform, 'to the tick, not around 50.55'); show the December touches that respected it (proximity: within 1–2 days of firing); arm the Watchlists alert ≈$50.56, a penny above, on camera. Step the replay to Jan 8 2024 — the alert fires intraday and the bar closes ≈$52.25. Planned trade: entry ≈$50.60, stop ≈$47.50; the armed alert caught an eventual ≈+14R winner. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The B-list and the promotion rules
chapters.beat: define the B-list (right pattern, needs time) and demonstrate both moves: a B-name tightening into its pivot gets promoted, and an A-name that broke structure gets deleted, not demoted.
chapters.speaker_notes: The B-list holds right-pattern-needs-time names: correct Stage-2 context, correct structure forming, but the coil is not tight enough or the pivot not close enough to arm. Then demonstrate both moves live. Promotion: a B-name whose pullbacks have contracted into its pivot area — draw the trigger, arm the alert, move it up; it earned A-list status by tightening, not by you getting impatient. Deletion: an A-name that broke structure — lost its pivot low, cracked its key support, whatever its invalidation was. It gets DELETED, not demoted. A broken chart back on the B-list is sentiment, and sentiment is how 80-ticker graveyards form. If it repairs itself, the nightly scan will find it again — that is the scan's job, not your memory's. Lists stay small because the exits are ruthless.
chapters.on_screen: Watchlists: a tightening B-name promoted with alert armed, and a structure-broken A-name deleted on camera
chapters.example_spec: Bar-replay Jan–Feb 2024 for both moves (SMCI prices split-adjusted 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Promotion: SMCI on the B-list through early January — show the Dec–Jan range tightening between ≈$27 and ≈$31 under the ≈$30.50 swing-high pivot; in the Jan 8–16 window the contraction narrows, so promote it to the A-list on camera and arm the alert ≈$30.60, stop ≈$27. It fires within days and the Jan 19 preannouncement gap (+11.6%, open $34.76, close $42.34) carries it to ≈$100 (=$1,000 pre-split) by early March — a ≈+18R promotion. Deletion: PYPL on the A-list holding a base near ≈$60 (December close $61.41, January close $61.35); the Feb 8 2024 earnings gap opens $57.98, −8.3% on 4.4× volume, and closes $56.13 through the range low — structure broken, DELETE on camera, not demote. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the full weekend routine in order: theme and sector review, the weekly-chart sweep of the universe, then ten charts annotated on camera with exact entry and stop levels — which IS Monday's plan.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the full weekend routine in order — this is the big one, and it produces Monday's plan. First, theme and sector review: which groups led the week, read off the Theme Tracker, so you know where the RS lives. Second, the weekly-chart sweep of the universe: weekly bars hide the daily noise and show which bases actually built cause this week — this is where next month's A-list comes from. Third, the output: ten charts annotated on camera with exact entry and stop levels — pivot to the tick, structural stop marked, each one a pre-written trade card waiting for a trigger. Say the punchline plainly: those ten annotated charts ARE Monday's plan. When Monday opens you are not deciding anything; you are executing decisions made Sunday, in the calm, with no positions on and no tape running.
chapters.on_screen: Sunday sweep: Theme Tracker rankings, then weekly charts, then ten daily charts annotated with exact entry and stop

chapters.marker: The weekend template, built from a real Friday close
chapters.beat: build the weekend scan template artifact live from an actual Friday close, and set the standing drill: this routine runs every Sunday, and Monday morning you only trade what it produced.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build the weekend scan template live from an actual Friday close so members watch the blank page become the plan: theme rankings filled in, the weekly sweep's candidates listed, the ten annotated names with entries and stops, the A-list and B-list updated, alerts armed. Then install the standing drill: this routine runs EVERY Sunday, and Monday morning you only trade what it produced. That last clause is the discipline payload — if a ticker is not on the sheet, Monday-you does not touch it, because Monday-you is the worst decision-maker you employ: rushed, tape-hypnotized, FOMO-loaded. Sunday-you, calm and flat, already made the good decisions. The premarket-routine lesson adds the morning layer on top, but its raw material is this page. No Sunday scan, no Monday trades. That simple.

lessons.title: From Alert to Fill: Order Types, Buy-Stops, and Slippage
lessons.note: Every entry trigger in the catalog presupposes you can place a buy-stop — this lesson finally teaches it. Market vs limit vs stop vs stop-limit on a real platform, the buy-stop-above-the-pivot workflow with an alert as backup, where slippage actually comes from, and the two fills — one clean, one chased — with their cost difference in R terms.

chapters.beat: open with the gap this lesson closes: every entry trigger in the setup catalog says 'buy above the pivot,' which silently presupposes an order type most retail traders have never placed — the buy-stop.
chapters.speaker_notes: Name the gap this lesson closes: every entry trigger in the setup catalog — BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, RED TO GREEN — says some version of 'buy above the pivot.' That instruction silently presupposes an order type most retail traders have never placed: the buy-stop — a resting order that sits ABOVE the market, dormant, and triggers only when price rises through your level. Most members have only ever used market orders — buy now at any price — and maybe limits. Neither can execute 'buy the moment $50.10 prints, without me watching.' The buy-stop can. By the end of this lesson you will have placed all four order types on a real platform and wired the buy-stop into the A-list workflow, so your entries execute your plan instead of your reflexes.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the four catalog entry triggers, each reading 'buy above…' — with the words BUY-STOP revealed beneath

chapters.marker: Four order types on a live platform
chapters.beat: place a market, limit, stop, and stop-limit order on a real platform on camera, stating in one sentence each what it guarantees and what it sacrifices (price certainty vs fill certainty).
chapters.speaker_notes: Place all four on a live platform, one sentence of truth each. Market order: guarantees the fill, sacrifices the price — you WILL own it, at whatever the book offers; fine for liquid exits, dangerous for entries in fast tape. Limit order: guarantees the price, sacrifices the fill — you will never pay more than your limit, and the stock can run without you by a penny. Stop order — our buy-stop: dormant until your trigger price trades, then it converts to a MARKET order — guarantees participation in the breakout, accepts slippage on the fill. Stop-limit: triggers at your stop price but fills only within your limit band — bounds the slippage, accepts the chance of no fill in a gap. Every order is the same trade-off in different clothes: price certainty versus fill certainty. Know which one each situation needs.
chapters.on_screen: Real broker order ticket — placing market, limit, stop, and stop-limit orders on camera

chapters.beat: run the full A-list workflow live: draw the pivot, set the buy-stop a few cents above it, arm the price alert as the backup, and let the trigger fire without you watching the tape.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the full A-list workflow end to end. Draw the pivot on the chart — exact, to the tick, say $50.00. Place the buy-stop a few cents above it — $50.10, clear of round-number noise — with the position size already computed from the structural stop through the Module 5 formula. Then arm the price alert at the trigger as the backup layer: if the order fails, expires, or you pulled it premarket for an earnings check, the alert still tells you the pivot fired. Now close the platform. That is the point — the trigger fires without you watching the tape. You cannot hesitate, chase, or freeze if the decision executed while you were at work. The order IS the discipline: you wrote the plan Sunday, sized it by formula, and the market executes it against itself.
chapters.on_screen: Chart with pivot at $50.00, buy-stop resting at $50.10 on the broker ticket, dashboard alert armed as backup
chapters.example_spec: Keep the $50.00/$50.10 schematic on the slide — say out loud it is an invented round number — then demo on a real chart: NVDA daily, first week of Jan 2024, pivot at the Nov 20 2023 high $50.55 (=$505.48 at the time; prices split-adjusted 10:1 — read the exact tick off your platform). On the broker ticket place a buy-stop ≈$50.60, a few ticks above the pivot, sized by the Module 5 formula against a stop ≈$47.50 under the December contraction low at 1% account risk. Arm the dashboard alert at the same price as backup, then close the platform on camera. Step to Jan 8 2024: the resting order fills ≈$50.60 as NVDA trades through, closing ≈$52.25 — no chasing. Outcome: ≈+14R by the Mar 8 high $97.40. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: break slippage into its real sources on screen — spread, thin books, fast tape, and market orders chasing a running price — and show which order types are exposed to each.
chapters.speaker_notes: Break slippage into its real sources so it stops being a mystery tax. The spread: you buy the ask and sell the bid — on a liquid leader that is a cent; on a thin name it can be half a percent before anything happens. Thin books: your order eats through the visible size and fills the remainder higher. Fast tape: on a breakout, everyone's buy-stops trigger together and the book reprices between your trigger and your fill. And market orders chasing a running price — the self-inflicted kind. Map exposure by order type: market orders are exposed to all of it; buy-stops are exposed at the moment of trigger, because they become market orders; stop-limits cap it but can miss; plain limits have zero slippage and maximum miss-risk. This is also why the scan's dollar-volume floor exists — liquidity was pre-filtered before you ever placed the order.
chapters.on_screen: Level 2 / time-and-sales view: the spread, a thin book, and a breakout print sweeping several price levels
chapters.example_spec: Record live between 9:35 and 10:00 AM on any session — Level 2 and time-and-sales do not replay. Split screen two real names: AAPL (thick book — penny-wide spread, thousands of shares stacked at every level) versus that morning's top premarket gapper under ≈50M float from the Movers feed (thin book — 20–40 cent spread, a few hundred shares per level). Capture, in order: the spread on each; the book depth difference; then, on the gapper, price approaching its obvious premarket-high pivot and the breakout print sweeping three or four ask levels in one transaction. Price it in R: on a planned $0.50 risk unit, that ≈$0.15 sweep is ≈0.3R paid before the trade begins — slippage is a ladder, not a fee. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: compare the two real fills from the note side by side: the clean buy-stop fill at the pivot versus the chased entry 3% higher, and translate the difference into R terms to show the chase silently shrank the trade's payoff before it began.
chapters.speaker_notes: Compare the two real fills in R terms. The plan: pivot $50.00, structural stop $47.50, first target $55.00 — risk $2.50, reward $5.00, a clean 2R trade. Fill one: the buy-stop fires at $50.10 — pennies of slippage, plan intact. Fill two: the trader had no resting order, saw the breakout an hour later, and chased the fill 3% higher at $51.50. Same stop, same target — but risk is now $4.00 and reward is $3.50: the 2R trade became roughly 0.9R before the first bar closed. That is below the 2R minimum from Module 5, which means the chased version is a trade the system DECLINES. Nothing about the stock changed; the entry mechanics silently destroyed the payoff. That is the lesson: the buy-stop is not a convenience — it is what keeps the R you planned.
chapters.on_screen: Side-by-side table: fill at $50.10 (2R intact) vs chased fill at $51.50 (0.9R — below the minimum)

lessons.title: The 30-Minute Premarket Routine
lessons.note: The full sequence with a clock: five-number scorecard → Exposure Rating → gaps and movers → earnings check → A-list trigger confirmation → a 3-5 name focus list with alerts armed. Artifact: the timestamped one-page daily prep sheet used in every trade walkthrough that follows. Anchor the routine to the product: Morning Wire first, scanner candidates second, your A-list alerts last — the member's routine IS the dashboard walk.

chapters.marker: Your routine IS the dashboard walk
chapters.beat: open with the on-screen clock at 0:00 and the anchor rule: Morning Wire first, scanner candidates second, your A-list alerts last — the same walk every morning, in the same order.
chapters.speaker_notes: Clock on screen at 0:00. The anchor rule before anything else: your routine IS the dashboard walk — Morning Wire first, scanner candidates second, your A-list alerts last, the same order every morning. Why that order: the Wire sets permission — regime before tickers, always; the scanner surfaces what changed overnight; and your A-list is where your money actually acts — you arrive at your own names carrying full context. Thirty minutes, timestamped stations, and at the end a one-page prep sheet that every trade walkthrough in the rest of this course opens with. The routine's job is to make 9:30 boring: by the open, every decision that could be pre-made has been made, and you are an executor, not an improviser. Start the clock.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard home with an on-screen clock at 0:00 — the Morning Wire tab queued first

chapters.beat: fill the five-number market-health scorecard live from the Morning Wire and read the Exposure Rating, so the day's permission level is decided before any individual chart is opened.
chapters.speaker_notes: Minutes 0-8: fill the five-number scorecard straight from the Morning Wire — it ships at 7:35 AM with every number in it. One: the dial score, today's 0-150 UCT Exposure Rating, and its band — GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE. Two: percent of stocks above the 50-day. Three: net new highs minus new lows. Four: the 4%-up versus 4%-down day count. Five: the distribution-day count. Write them down — writing is the commitment device — and the dial's band decides the day's permission level BEFORE any individual chart is opened: what you may buy, how large, or whether today is watch-only. Permission, not prediction: a GREEN read does not say the market goes up; it says more of your playbook is authorized. Regime station complete, before you have seen a single ticker.
chapters.on_screen: Morning Wire at 7:35 AM — the dial reading and the five scorecard numbers highlighted in the brief

chapters.beat: sweep the gaps-and-movers feed and the scanner candidates for anything that changed overnight, then run the earnings check to confirm nothing on your list reports today or tomorrow undisclosed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Minutes 8-18: what changed overnight. Sweep the gaps-and-movers feed: anything gapping hard — is one of them yours? A gap through your pivot changes the trade, and a gap in a theme-mate changes the context. Then the scanner candidates: fresh names the nightly chain surfaced, noted for tonight's list — not impulse-bought this morning. Then the earnings check, non-negotiable: confirm nothing on your list reports today or tomorrow undisclosed. A pre-report position turns your structural stop into a coin flip — Module 5's gap lesson made the math plain: 1% planned risk became a 6% realized loss when the stock gapped 30% through the stop. Any name inside the earnings window gets its alert suspended and a note on the prep sheet. Two minutes of checking versus six times plan. Cheap insurance.
chapters.on_screen: Movers sidebar gaps feed, then scanner candidates, then the Calendar earnings check run against the A-list

chapters.marker: Confirm the A-list, arm the alerts
chapters.beat: re-verify each A-list trigger against premarket price, cut the list to a 3-5 name focus list, and confirm every survivor has its alert armed at the exact trigger price.
chapters.speaker_notes: Minutes 18-27: your names. Re-verify each A-list trigger against premarket price. Did an overnight gap put a name already through its pivot? Then the clean trigger is gone — it moves to the watch column, not to a chase. Did one break down premarket? Delete it. From what survives, cut to a 3-5 name focus list — the names genuinely in play today. Five is the ceiling because attention is the real constraint at the open; ten focus names is zero focus. Then confirm every survivor has its alert armed at the exact trigger price and, where the plan calls for it, the buy-stop resting from the order-types lesson — sized through the formula, stop pre-placed. Each focus name carries an if-then sentence: 'If $50.10 prints on volume, I am in with 40 shares, stop $47.50.' No sentence, no slot.
chapters.on_screen: Watchlists A-list against premarket quotes — cut to a 3-5 name focus list, every alert re-armed at its trigger

chapters.beat: stop the clock and hand over the timestamped one-page daily prep sheet artifact — the same sheet every trade walkthrough in the following modules will open with — and set the drill: run the full 30-minute routine five market mornings in a row.
chapters.speaker_notes: Stop the clock at minute 30 and hand over the artifact: the timestamped one-page daily prep sheet — the five numbers and band at the top, overnight notes, the 3-5 name focus list with trigger, stop, and size for each, alerts confirmed. This exact page opens every trade walkthrough in the modules that follow: when we dissect a trade, the first exhibit is always the prep sheet from that morning — because a trade without prep is just a reaction. Then set the drill as a rep count: run the full 30-minute routine five market mornings in a row, sheet completed and timestamped, before the first setup-family module. Five mornings makes it a habit; the habit makes the open boring; and boring at 9:30 is exactly what a professional looks like.
chapters.on_screen: The timestamped one-page daily prep sheet artifact, completed at minute 30

modules.label: M7 · Setup Family I: Bases & Breakouts

lessons.title: How to Learn a Setup: The Five-Field Card, Setup Functions, and the Four Entry Triggers
lessons.note: Every play in the catalog gets the same card — context, pattern, trigger, stop, failure mode — is classified by function (opens a position, adds to a winner, or exits one), and fires as one of the firm's four entry types: BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN. Artifact: the full setup-to-entry-type mapping table members pin above their desk.

chapters.beat: open the full setup catalog on screen and make the promise: master this one card format today and every setup lesson that follows is just five blanks filled in differently.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open the firm's setup catalog on screen — four families: Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims. Here is the promise of this lesson: every play in this catalog is taught on exactly one card format with five blanks — Context, Pattern, Trigger, Stop, Failure mode. Master that skeleton today and every setup lesson that follows is just five blanks filled in differently. This is deliberate. Traders fail by collecting setups like baseball cards and hopping between them; the card forces every play into the same falsifiable structure, so learning setup number nine costs a fraction of what setup number one cost. You are not memorizing a catalog. You are learning one skeleton and a set of costumes. Say that sentence back before we start.
chapters.on_screen: The Model Book / Setups library — the full setup catalog grid grouped by the four families

chapters.marker: The five-field card, filled in live
chapters.beat: write a complete card for the Flat Base Breakout on camera (context, pattern, trigger, stop, failure mode) and show why each field must be falsifiable, not a vibe.
chapters.speaker_notes: Write a complete card on camera for the Flat Base Breakout. Context: GREEN band, Stage 2, RS line at highs, a five-week flat base under $50. Pattern plus Trigger: tight range $46 to $49.80, BASE BREAKOUT over $50.00 — buy-stop at $50.10, valid only on expanding volume through the pivot. Stop: $47.50, under the final contraction low, where the pattern is objectively broken — that is 5.2% stop distance, and at 1% account risk the formula gives 0.01 divided by 0.052, roughly a 19% position. Failure mode: closes back inside the base within three days on rising volume — exit, don't argue. Then the 2R check: first target $55.30 under the next resistance equals 2.0R — it passes. Hammer the standard: every field must be a number or level you can be proven wrong about. 'Looks strong' is not an entry. A blank or hedged field already reads SKIP.
chapters.on_screen: THE FIVE-FIELD SETUP CARD toolkit card — the worked Flat Base Breakout example rows

chapters.marker: What is this setup FOR? The three functions
chapters.beat: sort a handful of catalog names into the three piles on screen (opens a position, adds to a winner, exits one), answering the question every member asks: when would I ever use this one?
chapters.speaker_notes: Every setup in the catalog answers a second question beyond 'what does it look like': what is it FOR? Sort a handful of catalog names into three piles on screen. Pile one, opens a position: Flat Base Breakout, Episodic Pivot, Cup & Handle — these start trades in names you don't own. Pile two, adds to a winner: a 20 EMA Pullback in a name you already own is not a new trade, it's an add — that distinction gets its own lesson in Module 8. Pile three, exits one: climax and parabolic rules exist to get you OUT, not in. This function column answers the question every member asks — 'when would I ever use this one?' — and it prevents the classic error of using an add-on pattern to initiate, or an exit signal as an entry. The function goes on the card next to the family.
chapters.on_screen: Setup catalog names sorted live into three labeled columns — Opens / Adds / Exits (slide over the Model Book grid)

chapters.marker: The four entry triggers, drawn to the dollar
chapters.beat: mark BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, and RED TO GREEN on four real daily charts, each with the exact price where the order goes in.
chapters.speaker_notes: Every entry in this system fires as one of exactly four triggers, and each one is a specific dollar price, not a feeling. On four real daily charts, mark them. BASE BREAKOUT: buy-stop a few cents above the drawn pivot of a completed base. PREV DAY HIGH BREAK: buy the move through yesterday's high, on volume. PREV LOW RECLAIM: price undercuts a prominent prior low, then reclaims it — you buy the reclaim, not the undercut. RED TO GREEN: the stock opens down, then crosses back up through yesterday's close — buy the cross. On each chart, write the exact price where the order goes in. Note for members: the Morning Wire's Top 5 picks print an Entry Type field using these exact four labels every single morning — this lesson is the decoder ring for that field.
chapters.on_screen: Four daily charts in a 2×2, one per trigger, each with the exact trigger price marked (pull from Model Book examples, or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Four charts, one per trigger. BASE BREAKOUT: SMCI daily, Nov 2023–Jan 2024 — flat base ≈$27–31 (prices split-adjusted, 10:1 Oct 2024 — ≈10× these at the time); buy-stop ≈$30.60 over the pivot. PREV DAY HIGH BREAK: NVDA daily, May 26 2023 — the day after the May 25 +26.1% earnings gap (open ≈$38.52 adj); buy through that gap day's high ≈$39.50 adj on volume. PREV LOW RECLAIM: META daily, Nov 2022 — the undercut of the late-October low ≈$93 down to the Nov 4 low $88.09, then buy the reclaim ≈$93. RED TO GREEN: CELH daily, early Jun 2023 — opens down, buy back through the prior close ≈$43 adj (3:1 split Nov 2023 — ≈$129 then). Write each order price on the chart; all four resolved ≥ +2R within weeks. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: assemble the full setup-to-entry-type mapping table live, row by row, and tell members to print it and pin it above their desk before the flagship lesson.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now assemble the artifact: the setup-to-entry-type mapping table, row by row. Each row is one catalog setup, its family, its function — opens, adds, or exits — and which of the four triggers fires it: BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN. Fill several rows on camera so the pattern of the table is obvious: Flat Base Breakout — Bases & Breakouts — opens — BASE BREAKOUT. U&R — Reversals & Reclaims — opens — PREV LOW RECLAIM. Kicker Candle — Gaps & Catalysts — opens — RED TO GREEN. Tell members to print it and pin it above their desk before the flagship lesson, because from here forward the course will name a setup and expect them to answer with its trigger without looking anything up. The wall chart is how that reflex gets built.
chapters.on_screen: The setup-to-entry-type mapping table built row by row (printable table slide), final artifact shown complete

lessons.title: Field Weeks: How You'll Trade This Course — Pilot Size, Paper, and the Family Assignments
lessons.note: The application protocol for the whole setup tier: after each family module, one field week — run the nightly scan, find 2-3 live candidates of THAT family, write the five-field card and entry/stop for each, log them in the Journal, and grade the outcome against plan. Pilot size or paper only until the M5 sizing gate and the family's own drill are both cleared. This is where watching becomes trading.

chapters.marker: Why watching never made anyone a trader
chapters.beat: open with the honest claim: the setup tier is graded on what you DO in the live market each week, not on videos completed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Say the honest thing first: no one has ever become a trader by finishing videos. Watching builds recognition; only reps in the live market build reflexes. So the setup tier is graded on what you DO each week, not on completion percentage. After each of the four family modules there is one field week — a week of live-market work on that family only, logged and graded. The videos teach the skeleton; the field week is where your eyes, your scan, and your Journal do the actual learning.
