If you are tempted to binge all four family modules and 'do the practice later,' understand that this is precisely the failure mode the course is built to prevent. One family, one field week, then the next family. That pacing is the curriculum.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard Journal tab — an empty field-week log ready to be filled

chapters.marker: The field-week protocol, all five steps
chapters.beat: walk the loop on screen: run the nightly scan, find 2-3 live candidates of THIS family, write the five-field card with entry and stop for each, log them in the Journal, grade the outcome against plan.
chapters.speaker_notes: The protocol is the same every time, five steps. One: run the nightly scan every night of the week — the same funnel from Module 6. Two: from the output, find two to three live candidates of THIS family — during the base-family field week, only Bases & Breakouts count. Three: write the five-field card for each, with an exact entry price and an exact stop. Four: log every card in the Journal, whether it triggers or not — a candidate that never fires is still a graded rep, because the grade is on the plan, not the outcome. Five: when the week closes, grade each outcome against the plan: did you take the trigger you wrote, honor the stop you wrote, and manage by the rules? That plan-versus-execution comparison is the entire point of the week.
chapters.on_screen: Screener nightly-scan output side by side with the Journal entry form

chapters.beat: the hard rule — state the gate plainly: no real size until BOTH the Module 5 sizing gate and the family's own drill are cleared, and define exactly what pilot size means in dollars of risk.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the gate with no softening: no real size until BOTH gates are cleared — the Module 5 sizing gate, which is ten problems at 100%, no partial credit, and the family's own drill at 80%. Until then, field weeks run at pilot size or on paper. Define pilot size in dollars of risk, not shares: your normal preference is under 1% account risk per trade — pilot is a quarter of that or less, roughly 0.25% of equity. On a $10,000 account that is about $25 on the line — small enough that the outcome cannot matter and the process is all that's being trained. Paper is equally acceptable and carries zero shame. What is not acceptable is real size before the gates, because the most expensive lessons in trading are the ones you pay tuition on before you can do the arithmetic.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE toolkit card (Score & Retake section: 'nothing after Module 5 is traded live until this line is filled in')

chapters.beat: open an actual Journal entry from a field week and grade it on camera: the card, the entry/stop, what happened, and the verdict versus plan.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open an actual Journal entry from a field week and grade it on camera so members see the standard. Read the card aloud: setup name and family, the context, the trigger price, the stop, the failure mode. Then the record: where it filled, what happened bar by bar, where it exited. Now the verdict — and here is the reframe that matters: this trade is graded on plan-adherence, not P&L. A trade stopped out at exactly minus 1R, at the written stop, at the planned size, grades as an A. A winner that was entered early, sized on feel, or held past a violated stop grades as an F that happened to get paid. Fill the grade axes — idea, execution, preparation — and the one-line verdict. This is what every one of the member's own entries must look like by Friday.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal — one completed field-week trade entry with annotated screenshot and grade (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Reconstruct the journal entry from DKNG daily, May–Aug 2023. Card fields to read aloud: Flat Base Breakout, Bases & Breakouts; context — Stage 2, GREEN mid-2023 tape, RS strong; base ≈$21–25 from the May 4 low $21.07 through mid-June; trigger buy-stop ≈$25.30 over the range high; stop ≈$23.20 under the last contraction (≈8%); failure mode — close back inside on volume. Record: filled mid-June, breakeven stop near +1R, first third sold 2–3R into the July run (July closes $31.78), remainder trailed out into the Aug 4 peak $34.49; blended ≈ +2.5R. Verdict: A on idea, execution and preparation — every decision matched the written card; the grade is plan-adherence, not the P&L. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: lay out the calendar (one field week after each of the four family modules) and close on the line that names the stakes: this is where watching becomes trading.
chapters.speaker_notes: Lay out the calendar so nobody can claim confusion. Module 7, Bases & Breakouts, then field week one. Module 8, Momentum & Trend, then field week two. Module 9, Gaps & Catalysts, then field week three. Module 10, Reversals & Reclaims, then field week four. Each family is gated the same way: 80% on that family's replay drill PLUS a completed field log — two to three carded candidates, journaled and graded against plan — before the next family opens. Not calendar time, not videos watched: demonstrated work. And close on the line that names the stakes, straight to camera: this is where watching becomes trading. Everything before this point was preparation. The field weeks are the course.
chapters.on_screen: A four-row calendar slide: family module → its field week → the 80%-plus-field-log gate to the next family

lessons.title: FLAGSHIP — Flat Base Breakout: Contractions, Dry-Up, Pivot, and the Tick-Exact Buy
lessons.note: Full anatomy of the coil: each pullback smaller than the last, volume drying up into the base, drawing the pivot to the tick, buying the break on the volume threshold, initial stop under the final contraction low sized through the Module 5 formula. Three real trades: two winners and one failed breakout where the 1R loss is taken on camera. Script in three chaptered segments with a micro-check between each — one recording, three sittings if needed.

chapters.beat: the coil, read left to right — trace a real base contraction by contraction, showing each pullback smaller than the last and volume drying up into the base, then set the micro-check: mark the contractions on a fresh chart before continuing.
chapters.speaker_notes: Read a real base left to right, contraction by contraction. What you are looking for: each pullback smaller than the last — a first pullback of maybe 15-20%, then 8-10%, then a final tight one of 3-5%. That shrinking sequence is supply drying up: everyone who wanted out has sold, and sellers who remain demand higher prices. Confirm it in the volume pane — volume bleeds dry into the right side of the base. Quiet is good; quiet means the float has moved into strong hands. Remember Module 4: dry-up then expansion is the single most reliable tell in the system, and the dry-up half happens here, inside the coil. Then set the micro-check: pause the video and mark the contractions yourself on a fresh chart before continuing. Do not skip it — segment two assumes you did it.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI daily, Nov 2023–Jan 2024 — the flat base under $300 with each contraction bracketed and the volume dry-up visible (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, Aug 2023–Jan 2024 (prices split-adjusted — 10:1 Oct 2024, ≈10× these at the time). Left to right: the early-August 2023 high ≈$35.7 and the ≈37% October correction to ≈$22.6 (October closes $23.95) — the first, widest pullback; the November recovery (close $27.35); then a ≈10% December dip to ≈$26.6 (December closes $28.43); finally the tight ≈4–5% early-January contraction, closes clustering ≈$28.5–31. Volume bleeds dry through December into January — mark it in the volume pane. Bracket the shrinking sequence ≈37% → ≈10% → ≈4%. The base resolves Jan 19 2024: opens +11.6% at ≈$34.76 and closes ≈$42.34, a +36% day on ≈4.6× average volume. Member micro-check chart: AXON daily, Aug–Nov 2023. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: drawing the pivot to the tick — put the exact pivot price on the chart and define the volume threshold that makes the break buyable versus the break you walk away from.
chapters.speaker_notes: The pivot is a specific price, not a zone: the high of the final contraction — the ceiling the base has been pressing against. Draw it to the tick. In the worked example the base ranges $46 to $49.80, so the pivot is $50.00 and the buy-stop goes at $50.10 — a few cents through, never anticipating. Then the second half of buyable: the volume threshold. The break must print clearly expanded volume through the pivot — recall the Module 2 exhibit: the same plus-5% day on 3× average volume is evidence, on 0.4× it is noise. A break of your pivot on dead volume is the break you walk away from, even though price touched your number. Price says when; volume says whether. Both, or no trade — your buy-stop can be cancelled faster than a loss can be recovered.
chapters.on_screen: The same base with the pivot line drawn at $50.00 to the tick, buy-stop $50.10 marked, volume pane below
chapters.example_spec: The $46–$49.80/$50.00/$50.10 numbers are the generic card graphic — keep them there. On the real SMCI chart (split-adjusted; 10:1 Oct 2024, ≈10× these at the time), draw the pivot at the high of the final early-January contraction ≈$30.50 — to the tick off your platform — with the buy-stop a few cents through ≈$30.60. Volume pane below: December–January dry-up at roughly half average volume, then the Jan 19 2024 break printing ≈4.6× average — the expansion that makes it buyable. Contrast exhibit: point at a quiet mid-December poke toward the range high — price without volume, the break you walk away from. Outcome preview: Jan 19 gapped +11.6% to ≈$34.76 and closed ≈$42.34, +36% on the day. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Stop and size in one motion
chapters.beat: place the initial stop under the final contraction low and size it live through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % (2% hard max), then set the micro-check: recompute the size with a wider stop.
chapters.speaker_notes: Stop and size are one motion because size is DERIVED from the stop, never chosen first. The initial stop goes under the final contraction low — the price where the coil is objectively broken. Worked in full: entry $50.10, stop $47.50, stop distance 5.2%. The formula: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. At 1% account risk: 0.01 divided by 0.052 equals roughly a 19% position. Check the table cell — GREEN plus A+ allows 20-25%, so 19% fits. The 2% hard max is never touched. Micro-check before segment three: recompute with the stop under the whole base low at $46.90 — 6.2% distance, 0.01 divided by 0.062, a 16% position. Wider stop, smaller size, identical dollars at risk. If that took you more than a minute, rewatch the Module 5 formula lesson tonight.
chapters.on_screen: THE FIVE-FIELD SETUP CARD toolkit card — the worked stop and sizing rows ($47.50 → 5.2% → ~19% at 1% risk)

chapters.beat: two winners, end to end — walk both real winning trades from scan hit through pivot buy to exit, narrating each management decision at the bar it happened.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk both winners through THE LOOP, station by station, narrating each decision at the bar where it happened. The scan hit put the name on the list; the A-list alert was armed at the pivot; the buy-stop filled on the expansion bar — no chasing, the order was waiting. Then management by rule, not mood: stop moved to breakeven at roughly plus 1R or the first higher low; first third sold at 2 to 3R into strength, while the tape was paying up; the remainder trailed on the moving average, exited only when the trail line broke. At every decision, say what the bar showed, what the rule said, and what was done — that three-beat cadence is the teaching. Two different charts, identical process. The trades look smart in hindsight; on the day, they were just rules being followed in order.
chapters.on_screen: Two winning flat-base trades end to end — e.g. SMCI Jan 2024 and CELH Jun 2023 base breakout (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Winner one: SMCI — buy-stop ≈$30.60 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Oct 2024, ≈10× at the time) over the January pivot, stop ≈$28.50 under the final contraction low. Jan 19 2024 opens ≈$34.76 and closes ≈$42.34 (+36%), triggering the breakeven move immediately; first third out at 2–3R; remainder trailed on the 20 EMA to the Feb 22 close $97.55 and the Mar 8 high $122.90 — outcome ≈ +8R or better. Winner two: CELH daily, May–Aug 2023 (3:1 split Nov 2023 — ≈3× at the time): base ≈$40–46 after the May 10 +10.6% gap; entry over the pivot ≈$46, stop ≈$41; the Jun 23 break prints ≈4.9× volume and August closes $65.35 — ≈ +4R trailed. Narrate scan hit → armed alert → fill → managed exit on both. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The failed breakout, 1R paid on camera
chapters.beat: work the third real trade to its failure, take the planned 1R loss without flinching, and name the lesson: the loss was the system working, not the system breaking.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the third trade — the one that fails — worked with exactly the same calm. Same scan hit, same card, same buy-stop through the pivot. Then the failure mode from the card arrives: the stock closes back inside the base on rising volume within days, and the stop hits. Take the planned 1R loss on camera without flinching, and say what it is: the loss was the system working, not the system breaking. Go back to Module 1's casino math — a 45% win rate at 2R prints money, which means the majority of your trades losing 1R each is BUDGETED. This loss was in the budget. Journal it the same day: the ledger row reads minus 1.0R, Rule column Y — and a Y row at minus 1R is a better trade than an N row that got paid.
chapters.on_screen: RBLX daily, Nov 2021 — a failed base breakout with entry, the close back inside the base, and the −1R stop-out bar marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: RBLX daily, Nov–Dec 2021. Find: the Nov 9 earnings day — gaps +29.4% to open ≈$99.60 and closes ≈$109.52, +42% on the day at 4.3× volume — then the run to the Nov 22 high $141.60; then the short two-week high base ≈$120–141. Entry: buy-stop ≈$135 over the base's interior swing high, filled on the late-November push; stop ≈$119 under the base low. The card's failure mode arrives on schedule: the first sessions of December close back inside the base on rising volume, and the Dec 15 −9.0% gap (open ≈$98.01) knifes through the stop — mark the −1R stop-out bar. Ledger row: −1.0R, Rule column Y. RBLX closes February 2022 at $51.57, −64% from the high. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Bull Flag: The Flagpole, the Quiet Drift, and the Trendline Break
lessons.note: A sharp advance, then a brief orderly pullback on lighter volume, entered on the break of the flag's upper trendline with the stop under the flag low — with the numeric depth and duration bounds that separate a flag from a rollover. One textbook flag next to one that lost the 20 EMA: the disqualifier, not a dip to buy.

chapters.beat: open with why a sharp advance followed by a rest is the market's most natural continuation, and why the pole's strength is half the setup.
chapters.speaker_notes: The flag is the market's most natural continuation, but the trade is earned by the pole, not the flag. A sharp advance — the pole — proves demand: institutions paid up aggressively enough to move the stock 20% or more in days. The rest that follows is those buyers digesting, not distributing. Without a real pole, a sideways drift is just chop wearing a flag costume. The firm's scanner quantifies this — prior momentum is credited in tiers, and a pole in the 20%-plus range is what puts a name on the list at all. So the first question on any flag candidate is backward-looking: how strong, how fast, and on what volume was the advance? A violent pole on heavy volume followed by a quiet drift is the signature. A limp pole disqualifies the pattern before you draw a single line.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily, Oct–Dec 2019 — the earnings-gap flagpole before the flag (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: TSLA daily, Oct–Dec 2019 (prices split-adjusted; 5:1 2020 and 3:1 2022 — ≈15× these at the time). Find: the Oct 24 2019 earnings gap +17.1%, ≈$17 → open $19.89, close $19.98, on ≈2.2× average volume; then the continuation pole into early November ≈$23.1 — a ≈36% advance in under three weeks, the demand proof that earns the trade. Contrast it with the limp sideways drift preceding the report: no pole, no flag. Then the rest: the November drift ≈$21.1–23.1 on visibly lighter volume — the flag the following chapters trade. Outcome preview: the December resolution ran to the Feb 4 2020 high $64.60 (≈$970 contemporary) — roughly +190% from the flag. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: state the numeric depth and duration bounds that separate a brief orderly pullback on lighter volume from a rollover, and show one chart of each.
chapters.speaker_notes: A flag is numerically bounded, or it isn't a flag. Duration: brief — days to roughly two or three weeks. Longer than that and you're in base-building territory, judged by base rules. Depth: shallow — the drift gives back no more than about a third of the pole, and critically, it holds the rising 20 EMA. Volume: lighter than the pole — the pullback prints below-average volume, sellers unenthusiastic. Now the contrast chart: a pullback that retraces half the pole or more, on EXPANDING volume, with wide sloppy bars — that is not a flag resting, that is a rollover beginning, and the same shape-at-a-glance becomes a completely different object once you check the numbers. One chart of each on screen. The bounds are the lesson: orderly, shallow, quiet, brief — or it's not this setup.
chapters.on_screen: Side by side: a textbook shallow flag on light volume vs a deep rollover on expanding volume (Model Book pair)
chapters.example_spec: Textbook flag: NVDA daily, May–Jun 2023 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Jun 2024, ≈10× then). Pole = the May 25 earnings gap +26.1%, open $38.52, close $37.98 on ≈3.1× volume; flag = the following one-to-two-week drift ≈$37.5–41 — gives back well under a third of the pole, holds the rising 20 EMA, prints below-average volume; resolves toward ≈$44 by mid-June (June closes $42.30), ≈ +2R from a trendline entry. Rollover contrast: UPST daily, Oct–Nov 2021 — pole into the Oct 15 high $401.49, then a 'flag' retracing over half the pole to the Nov 10 close $256.59 on EXPANDING volume with wide sloppy bars, then breaks; holders rode −73% into January ($109.01). Same glance, opposite numbers. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: draw the flag's upper trendline on a real chart, mark the exact break entry, and place the stop under the flag low sized through the Module 5 formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the flag's upper trendline — the declining line across the drift's highs — and the entry is the break of that line: buy-stop just above it. The stop goes under the flag low, the price that says the rest failed and the pole is being unwound. Then size it through Module 5. Worked: if the flag low sits 4% below the entry, Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % gives 0.01 divided by 0.04 — a 25% position at 1% account risk. Notice what just happened: the formula output landed exactly at the GREEN plus A+ ceiling of 20-25%. The table always outranks the formula — a tight stop never licenses a monster position, because no stop catches an overnight gap. Cap it at the cell. Tight-stop continuation entries hit this ceiling constantly; expect it.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily Dec 2019 flag — upper trendline, break entry, stop under the flag low, sizing math on screen (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Same TSLA Nov–Dec 2019 flag (split-adjusted, ≈15× then). Draw the declining trendline across the drift's highs from the ≈$23.1 pole high; the break comes mid-December. Entry: buy-stop just above the line, filling ≈$23.90 (≈$359 contemporary). Stop: under the flag's final low ≈$23.00 — ≈4% distance. Run the math on screen: 1% ÷ 4% = 25% position, landing exactly at the GREEN + A+ ceiling — cap it at the cell, the table outranks the formula. Outcome: the December close $27.89 is already ≈ +4R; the run into the Feb 4 2020 high $64.60 (≈$970 contemporary) is ≈ +45R on the initial 90-cent risk. Say aloud that the tight stop is what makes the multiple that large. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the real winner from flagpole through drift to breakout and exit, checking every field of the five-field card as it fills.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the real winner start to finish, and fill the five-field card as each field proves itself on the chart. Context: Stage 2, GREEN band, RS line confirming, a 20%-plus pole on heavy volume. Pattern: a one-to-two-week drift, shallow, holding the 20 EMA, volume drying up. Trigger: the break of the flag's upper trendline — write the exact price. Stop: under the flag low — write it, compute the distance, derive the size. Failure mode: a close below the 20 EMA, which is the next chapter. Then narrate the trade through: the fill on the break, breakeven near plus 1R, the first third off at 2 to 3R into strength, the trail on the remainder. The card fills itself when the chart is right — and when a field won't fill cleanly, the chart is telling you it isn't right.
chapters.on_screen: The completed five-field card filling in beside the worked flag chart (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Fill the card against the same TSLA Nov–Dec 2019 trade (split-adjusted, ≈15× then). Context: Stage 2, post-earnings tape, RS line at highs, a ≈36% three-week pole. Pattern: the November drift giving back under a third of the pole, holding the rising 20 EMA, volume drying up. Trigger: the trendline break ≈$23.90. Stop: ≈$23.00, ≈4% — 25% position at 1% risk, capped at the cell. Failure mode: a close below the 20 EMA. Then narrate: mid-December fill, breakeven near +1R, first third off at 2–3R into the late-December ≈$26–28 zone (December closes $27.89), trail the remainder into the January–February run and out near ≈$43; blended ≈ +14R — the 4% stop is why. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The 20 EMA loss is a disqualifier
chapters.beat: put the failed chart beside the textbook one and hammer the rule: a flag that loses the 20 EMA is a dead setup, not a better price to buy.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the failed chart beside the textbook one and hammer the rule until it's boring: a flag that closes below the 20 EMA is a dead setup, not a better price. The 20 EMA is the swing-trend line from Module 2 — the line a resting leader is defended at. When the drift loses it, the premise 'strong hands digesting' is falsified; what you're looking at is distribution. The beginner's instinct is the opposite — 'I liked it at $60, I love it at $55' — and that instinct is how a continuation pattern becomes a bagholding. There is no discount entry inside a broken flag. The name goes off the card entirely; if it later rebuilds a proper base, it re-enters the funnel as a base, judged by base rules. Preview Module 8's language: leaders bounce off that line like tennis balls; the ones that splat through it are eggs.
chapters.on_screen: Two charts side by side: the textbook flag vs one that closed below the 20 EMA and rolled over (Model Book pair)
chapters.example_spec: Left chart: the TSLA Nov–Dec 2019 textbook flag from this lesson. Right chart: COIN daily, Nov 2021–Jan 2022. Find on COIN: the run into the Nov 9 2021 high ≈$368 (that session closed ≈$357), a few flag-looking drift days, then the Nov 10 candle — gaps −8.4% to open $327.22 and CLOSES $328.60, decisively below the rising 20 EMA ≈$335 — mark it as the disqualifier. Then show what 'I loved it at $310' bought: COIN closed December at $252.37 and January at $190.15, with a Jan 24 low ≈$173 — averaging into the broken flag absorbed ≈ −4R past any honest stop. The name re-entered the funnel only after rebuilding a proper base, judged by base rules. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Cup & Handle: The Multi-Week Base and the Handle's Low-Volume Shakeout
lessons.note: The rounded recovery to prior highs and the shallow low-volume handle, bought over the handle high — with the measured criteria (minimum cup duration in weeks, handle forming in the upper half of the base). One real multi-week example annotated week by week so the member sees how slowly a good base actually builds.

chapters.marker: The pattern that pays you for patience
chapters.beat: open with why the biggest breakouts come from the longest bases, and what the rounded recovery to prior highs says about supply changing hands.
chapters.speaker_notes: The biggest breakouts in the Winners Gallery come from the longest bases, and the Cup & Handle is the archetype: a decline, a rounded bottom, and a patient recovery back toward the prior highs, traced over months. Explain what the rounding actually is: supply changing hands. Everyone who bought the old high and suffered through the decline sells on the way back up — to institutions accumulating quietly. By the time price returns to the highs, the float has migrated from weak hands to strong ones, and that migration cannot be rushed; it takes weeks by nature. That's why the pattern pays you for patience: the time IS the cause, and the cause is what funds the eventual move. A chart that recovers too fast hasn't transferred any supply — hold that thought for the next chapter.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA weekly, Apr–Oct 2016 — the multi-month cup with handle before the 2016–17 run (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA weekly, Feb–Nov 2016 (split-adjusted; 4:1 2021 and 10:1 2024 — ≈40× these at the time). Walk left to right: the early-2016 correction low ≈$0.65 (≈$26 then); the rounded multi-month recovery through spring and summer; the return to the highs, where Aug–Oct consolidates ≈$1.39–1.78 — the cup's rim, Aug 2 low $1.39, October close $1.78 — with a shallow, quiet late-October handle ≈$1.65–1.78. Volume improves up the right side and dries into the handle. Name the mechanism: months of supply migrating from trapped holders to accumulating institutions. Resolution: Nov 11 2016 gaps +17.8% to open $1.99 and closes $2.20 — +30% on the day, 3.8× volume — launching the run to $3.02 by Feb 7 2017. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: state the minimum cup duration in weeks and the recovery-to-prior-highs requirement, and disqualify one too-short, too-sharp imposter on screen.
chapters.speaker_notes: Bound it numerically. Duration: the cup needs a minimum of roughly seven weeks — under that, you don't have a base, you have a dip. Shape: a rounded recovery, not a V — the right side climbs back to within striking distance of the prior highs, ideally on improving volume. Depth: proportionate to the market; a cup that gives back so much it undercuts the whole prior advance is damage, not digestion. Now disqualify the imposter on screen: a three-week V-shaped snapback that touches the old high. It fails the duration test and the shape test — no time passed, no supply transferred, and every buyer from the old high is still sitting overhead waiting to sell at breakeven. That overhead supply, from Module 2, is exactly what a real cup spends seven-plus weeks dissolving. Fail the measurements, skip the stock.
chapters.on_screen: Two charts: a qualifying seven-week-plus rounded cup vs a three-week V-shaped imposter
chapters.example_spec: Qualifying cup: the same NVDA 2016 weekly structure — count ≈20-plus weeks from the spring recovery through the October rim ≈$1.78 (split-adjusted, ≈40× then); rounded right side, recovery to within a few percent of the prior high on improving volume — passes duration, shape and depth. Imposter: SMCI daily, Mar–Apr 2024 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Oct 2024, ≈10× then). Find: the Mar 8 2024 peak $122.90, a two-week collapse toward ≈$85 (Mar 19 gaps −11.2% to open $88.86), then a roughly three-week V-shaped snapback to ≈$105 — no time passed, no supply transferred, every high-price buyer still overhead. The V failed at the rim: SMCI closed August 2024 at $62.47, −49%, and any breakout buyer paid ≈ −1R with no follow-through ever coming. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: define the handle as a shallow drift forming in the upper half of the base on drying volume, and show why a deep or low-in-base handle kills the setup.
chapters.speaker_notes: The handle is the pattern's final exam: a shallow drift-down forming in the UPPER HALF of the base, on drying volume, typically a week or two. What it does mechanically: shakes out the last impatient holders just below the obvious high, right before the move — you'll recognize this as the same shakeout logic the whole reversal family is built on. Two disqualifiers, both hard. A DEEP handle — one that retraces sharply on heavy volume — says supply is still aggressive; that's not a shakeout, it's selling. A LOW-IN-BASE handle — forming in the bottom half of the structure — says the recovery failed before it finished. Draw the base's midpoint line on the chart and check where the handle sits; above the line on quiet volume passes, anything else kills the setup. Shallow, high, and quiet — all three or none.
chapters.on_screen: Zoom of the handle with the volume pane showing dry-up; the base's midpoint line drawn to prove the handle sits in the upper half

chapters.marker: One real base, annotated week by week
chapters.beat: step through the actual multi-week example one weekly bar at a time so the member feels in real time how slowly a good base builds.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now slow the whole thing down to real speed. Step through the actual example one weekly bar at a time — click, annotate, click, annotate — and let the member feel how little happens each week. Week three: nothing. Week six: still rounding. Week nine: right side building, volume still quiet. This tedium is the point of the chapter: on a static chart the finished cup looks obvious, but living through it is twelve-plus weeks of a stock doing approximately nothing, and that is exactly when impatient traders leave — which is who they're handing their shares to. Connect it to Module 3's off-season doctrine: bases like this one form during dead and ORANGE tapes, and the nightly scan plus a fresh A-list is how you're positioned to own the breakout you'd otherwise have stopped watching for.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA weekly 2016 stepped bar by bar with per-week annotations (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Step the same NVDA 2016 weekly chart bar by bar (split-adjusted, ≈40× then). Scripted stops: the May 13 2016 earnings week — the +10.1% gap, open $0.98, close $1.02 on 5.6× volume, that starts the right side; June — rounding ≈$1.10–1.18, annotate 'nothing happening'; July lifting to $1.43; the Aug 12 2016 earnings week — the pop to $1.58 (Aug 15 high $1.59) on 3.8× volume, completing most of the recovery; September — the quiet pullback to the Sep 12 low $1.43, volume still muted; October — the rim ≈$1.65–1.78 and the drift into the handle. Roughly twenty-six weekly bars where each week looks like nothing — then the Nov 11 breakout candle. Narrate the tedium; the tedium is the lesson. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: mark the exact trigger above the handle high, place the stop, run the sizing formula, and fill the five-field card as the leave-with artifact.
chapters.speaker_notes: The trigger is exact: a buy-stop just above the handle high — that's the BASE BREAKOUT trigger on the wall chart. The stop goes under the handle low, the price where the shakeout turned into a breakdown and the thesis died. Then the one motion from the flagship: derive size from the stop. Worked cleanly: handle high $50, entry $50.10, handle low $47.50 — about a 5% stop distance, and at 1% account risk the formula gives 0.01 divided by 0.05, a 20% position, inside the GREEN plus A+ cell of 20-25%. Run the 2R check against the nearest overhead resistance before sizing anything. Then fill the five-field card on camera as the leave-with artifact: context, the measured cup, the qualifying handle, trigger, stop, and the failure mode — a break of the handle low, or a breakout that dies back inside the handle.
chapters.on_screen: THE FIVE-FIELD SETUP CARD filled for Cup & Handle beside the annotated chart, entry and stop lines drawn
chapters.example_spec: Card numbers stay generic ($50 / $50.10 / $47.50); draw the real lines on NVDA 2016 (split-adjusted, ≈40× then). Trigger: buy-stop just above the handle high ≈$1.78 (≈$71 contemporary). Stop: under the handle low ≈$1.63 — ≈8%, so 1% ÷ 8% ≈ a 12% position. The break arrives via the Nov 11 2016 earnings gap from a $1.69 prior close: the buy-stop fills on the open $1.99 (≈$80) — note the gap-through honestly and re-anchor the stop under the gap-day low. Run the 2R check against the clean air above the old high. Outcome: $2.79 by Dec 29 (≈$112) — ≈ +5R on the planned 15-cent risk in seven weeks, far more on the 2017 trail to $3.02. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: IPO Base: A New Issue's First Consolidation — Short, Shallow, Explosive
lessons.note: Why IPO bases resolve violently (no overhead supply, small float) and the adjusted rules: shorter base tolerance, wider ADR, smaller size, plus the still-locked-up float risk. One recent IPO winner worked from listing day through its first breakout, and one failed IPO base beside it.

chapters.beat: open with the structural reason: no overhead supply and a small float mean nobody above is waiting to sell at breakeven, so resolution is violent in both directions.
chapters.speaker_notes: The structural reason first, because it explains every adjusted rule that follows. A recent IPO has NO overhead supply — there is no crowd of trapped buyers from years past waiting overhead to sell out at breakeven, because the stock has no past. And the float is small — most of the shares are still locked up with insiders, so the tradable supply is thin. Combine those and you get the setup's signature: when a new issue's first consolidation resolves, it resolves violently, because there's nothing overhead to slow an advance and nothing underneath to cushion a failure. That cuts both ways, and the whole lesson is built on respecting both edges of that sword: the same physics that produce the explosive winners produce fast, ugly failures. You trade this family for the asymmetry — but only with the adjusted rulebook.
chapters.on_screen: ARM daily, Sep 2023–Feb 2024 — from listing day through its first base and breakout (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: ARM daily, Sep 2023–Feb 2024 (no splits). Find, in order: the Sep 14 2023 IPO — priced $51, opens ≈$56, closes $63.59 on the heaviest volume of the run, then the Sep 15 spike to ≈$69; the sloppy price-discovery slide to the Oct 20 low $46.50 — label it untradeable; the recovery and the first real consolidation, Dec–Jan, roughly ≈$60–78, tightening through late January. Then the chapter's point — Feb 8 2024: a +22.6% opening gap to $94.41 closing $113.89, +48% on the day at ≈9× volume, extending to the Feb 12 high $164.00 within three sessions. No overhead supply and ≈90% of the float still locked. Then flag the sword's other edge: the October slide was equally fast downhill. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the three deviations from the standard base rules on screen: shorter base tolerance, wider ADR allowance, and smaller position size to pay for the volatility.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three deviations from standard base rules, all consequences of youth and thin float. One: shorter base tolerance — a new issue can't have printed a seven-week cup; its first valid consolidation may be only two to four weeks, and that's acceptable HERE and only here. Two: wider ADR allowance — these names routinely move far beyond the scanner's 4% ADR floor, so expect wide daily ranges and place stops on structure, not on hope of tightness. Three: smaller position size, and note the formula does most of this automatically: a wider structural stop mechanically shrinks the position — at 1% account risk, a 10% stop is a 10% position, where a 5% stop would have been 20%. On top of that mechanical shrink, cut the risk input itself — take 0.5% instead of 1% — because gap risk on a thin float is exactly what the sizing ceiling exists for.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the three IPO adjustments (shorter base, wider ADR, smaller size) beside the standard base rules, with the 10%-stop → 10%-position math

chapters.beat: show where to find the lock-up expiration date and the still-locked float, and make checking it a mandatory pre-entry step on the card.
chapters.speaker_notes: One check is mandatory before any IPO entry, and it lives on the card: the lock-up expiration. Insiders and early investors are typically barred from selling for about 180 days after the IPO. On that date, a locked float — often several times the tradable shares — becomes free to sell. That is a scheduled supply event sitting on the calendar, and buying a thin-float breakout two weeks in front of it is volunteering to be the exit liquidity. So the pre-entry step: find the IPO date, count 180 days forward, confirm the exact expiry in the prospectus or a filings search, and write the date on the five-field card next to the earnings check. No entry into the unlock window. This is thirty seconds of homework that removes one of the only fully forecastable disasters in the catalog — take the thirty seconds.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard Calendar / ticker detail with the IPO date shown and the lock-up expiry counted ~180 days forward

chapters.beat: work the recent real IPO from its first day of trading through its first consolidation and breakout, marking pivot, entry, and stop.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the real winner from its first day of trading. Day one through the first weeks: wide, sloppy price discovery — untradeable by our rules, and say so. Then the first real consolidation forms: a short base, two to four weeks, range tightening, volume drying up — the same coil grammar as the flagship, compressed in time. Draw the pivot at the high of that range to the tick, place the buy-stop just above it, and demand the volume witness on the break exactly as always. Stop under the base low; because the stop is structurally wider on a name like this, walk the sizing out loud: 1% risk on an 8% stop is 0.01 divided by 0.08 — a 12.5% position, ORANGE-ceiling territory even in a GREEN tape by choice. Then the resolution: the violent advance that the no-overhead structure promised.
chapters.on_screen: ARM daily — pivot, entry, and stop marked on the first base, breakout bar highlighted (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Same ARM chart. Mark: pivot ≈$78 at the late-January range high (Feb 7 closes $77.00), buy-stop ≈$78.30; stop under the base low ≈$72 (≈8% — 1% ÷ 8% = 12.5% position, then halve the risk input to ≈0.5% per the IPO rulebook). The break arrives as the Feb 8 2024 earnings gap and the stop order fills on the open $94.41 — teach the slippage honestly: thin-float IPO breaks gap through pivots, which is exactly why size is pre-shrunk. Re-anchor the stop under the gap-day low ≈$93. Outcome: the Feb 12 high $164.00 is ≈ +11R on the planned $6.30 risk unit, the Feb 12 close $148.97 ≈ +8R, and a rules-based trail into late February exits near $141 for ≈ +7R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The failed IPO base beside it
chapters.beat: put the real failure next to the winner, show where it broke plan, and demonstrate how the smaller-size rule turned a violent move into a survivable loss.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the mirror image, side by side. Same anatomy on the left edge: recent listing, first consolidation, drawn pivot, buy-stop, fill. Then the difference: the break fails, the stock knifes back through the base low, and the exit executes at the structural stop. Here's the teaching point — mark where it broke plan: nowhere. The plan contained the failure. Because the smaller-size rule was applied — reduced risk input on an already-wide stop — the violent move produced a survivable, budgeted loss instead of a crater. Run the arithmetic on screen: at 0.5% account risk, even a gap through the stop that doubles the planned loss costs 1% of the account — annoying, not fatal. That is the whole IPO family in one sentence: you cannot control the violence, so you pre-shrink the consequence. Log both trades; the failure is the more instructive Journal entry.
chapters.on_screen: RIVN daily, Nov–Dec 2021 — the failed first base beside the ARM winner, stop-out marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: RIVN daily, Nov 2021–Mar 2022, beside the ARM winner. Find: the Nov 10 2021 IPO — priced $78, opens ≈$107, closes $100.73; the frenzy spike to the Nov 16 high $179.47; then the first two-to-three-week consolidation, a loose ≈$100–130 range (November closes $119.76). Entry: the early-December push through the range's interior high ≈$122 (also show the ≈$130 buy-stop that never fills). Stop: under the range low ≈$98, at the 0.5% IPO risk input. The failure: Dec 17 2021, the session after the first earnings report, gaps −8.2% to open $99.92 and closes $97.70 — the stop executes ≈$98–100, a planned −1R costing ≈0.5% of equity. RIVN closes January at $65.74 and bottoms $33.46 on Mar 15: the pre-shrunk consequence beside the crater avoided. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Launchpad: Consolidating on Top of the Stacked Averages, Then Launching
lessons.note: A momentum burst, then a rest that sits on the full stacked 9>20>50>200 cluster; higher-low entry with the stop below the pad. The stack-check comes first — the same pattern without stacked, rising MAs is explicitly NOT a Launchpad — and one current-market candidate is assessed live.

chapters.beat: open with the image: after a momentum burst, price parks flat on top of the full moving-average cluster like a rocket on its pad.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the image, because the image IS the setup: after a momentum burst, price goes flat — but instead of drifting back down to find support, it parks directly on top of the full moving-average cluster, like a rocket sitting on its pad. All four of the firm's lines — 9 EMA, 20 EMA, 50 SMA, 200 SMA — rise up underneath the resting price until the stock is sitting on the whole stack at once. That configuration is rare, and its rarity is information: it means the advance was strong enough, and the rest shallow enough, that every timeframe of buyer — momentum, swing, institutional — is holding at the same place at the same time. When that coiled rest resolves upward, all four cohorts are already positioned underneath it. That's the launch.
chapters.on_screen: PLTR daily, Aug–Oct 2024 — flat consolidation sitting on the stacked averages, then the launch (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: PLTR daily, Aug–Nov 2024 (no splits). Find: the Aug 5 washout close $24.09, then the Aug 6 earnings burst — gaps +12.3% to open $27.05 — extending to ≈$31.5 by late August (August closes $31.48) — the fuel; then the rest: a flat shelf ≈$29–32.5 into early September while the 9 and 20 EMAs rise underneath to meet price, the 50 SMA climbs through ≈$27–28, and the 200 SMA rises far below ≈$22 — all four stacked, all rising, price parked on the cluster, volume quiet. Then the launch: Sep 9 gaps +7.8% and closes $34.60, Sep 20 prints $37.20 on 7.2× volume, October closes $41.56, and the Nov 5 earnings gap closes $51.13. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: verify 9 over 20 over 50 over 200, all rising, on screen, and show the identical-looking pattern WITHOUT the stack that is explicitly NOT a Launchpad.
chapters.speaker_notes: Before anything else — before the pattern, before the trigger — verify the stack, because the stack is the setup's precondition, not decoration. On screen, check all four: 9 EMA over 20 EMA over 50 SMA over 200 SMA, in that order, and ALL of them rising. Each line has the job title from Module 2 — momentum leash, swing trend, institutional line, bull/bear divide — and the Launchpad requires all four employed and pointing up. Then the counter-exhibit: an identical-looking flat rest where the averages are braided together or the 200 is flat — and say it flatly: this is NOT a Launchpad, whatever the price bars resemble. Same shape, no stack, no setup. This is the Stage-2 gate discipline applied at pattern level: a binary check, zero judgment, and failing one line means the name is judged as something else entirely.
chapters.on_screen: Two charts: the candidate with 9>20>50>200 all rising vs an identical-looking rest with tangled averages — labeled NOT a Launchpad
chapters.example_spec: Stack pass: the same PLTR late-August 2024 shelf ≈$29–32.5 — tick 9 > 20 > 50 > 200 on screen, all four rising. Counter-exhibit: RIVN daily, Jun–Oct 2023. Find: a genuine momentum burst (≈$14 in early June to the Jul 27 high $28.06) followed by an almost identical-looking flat rest ≈$22–26 (August closes $22.73, September $24.28) — but the averages fail: the 200 SMA sits flat-to-declining near price and the 50 is still braided; the stack never formed. Label it NOT a Launchpad, whatever the bars resemble. Outcome proves the gate: PLTR's pad launched ≈ +30% into October and ≈ +60% by the Nov 5 gap, while RIVN's lookalike broke down on the Oct 5 −10.5% gap and closed October at $16.22 — a stack-blind buyer ate ≈ −2R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: trace the burst-then-rest sequence on a real chart, showing the tightening range sitting on the averages while volume goes quiet.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now trace the sequence itself on the real chart. First the burst: a sharp momentum advance — that's the fuel, same logic as the bull flag's pole. Then the rest, and this is where you slow down: the range tightens bar by bar, the closes cluster, and volume goes quiet — the dry-up signature from Module 4, meaning nobody is selling into the pause. Meanwhile the averages do the work: the 9 and 20 rise up underneath until price is literally resting on them, with the 50 and 200 climbing below in formation. Point at the compression: tight range, quiet volume, rising floor. The pad is a coil where the spring is being loaded by the averages themselves — every session that passes at the same price makes the floor higher and the eventual break cleaner.
chapters.on_screen: Zoom on the pad: tightening range and clustered closes, volume pane going quiet, the 9/20 EMAs rising to meet price

chapters.marker: The higher-low entry, stop below the pad
chapters.beat: mark the higher-low trigger, place the stop under the pad, and size it through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %.
chapters.speaker_notes: The trigger: inside the pad, wait for a higher low — a pullback low above the prior low, proof the floor is rising — and buy the break of the swing high that follows it. Mark the exact price; a buy-stop or armed alert sits there, per the standard workflow. The stop goes below the pad — under the pad's low, where the whole resting structure is objectively broken and the stack is about to be lost. Then size it, out loud, through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %: if the pad low sits 6% below the entry, then at 1% account risk it's 0.01 divided by 0.06 — roughly a 17% position, inside the GREEN plus A+ 20-25% ceiling with room to spare. Two percent hard max as always; under 1% preferred. Entry, stop, size — one motion, no improvisation.
chapters.on_screen: Entry and stop drawn on the pad: higher-low trigger marked, stop below the pad low, sizing math (1% ÷ 6% ≈ 17%) on screen

chapters.beat: pull up a current-market chart cold and run the full Launchpad checklist on camera, ending with a stated pass or fail and why.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close by doing the job cold, on camera, the way the member will do it during the field week. Pull up a current-market chart — no rehearsal — and run the full Launchpad checklist in order. One: stack check — 9 over 20 over 50 over 200, all rising? Two: was there a genuine momentum burst? Three: is the rest tightening on quiet volume, sitting ON the averages? Four: is there a higher-low trigger you can price to the tick? Five: does the stop below the pad give a distance the formula can size within 2%, and does 2R fit under the nearest resistance? Then end with a stated verdict — pass or fail — and the reason, in one sentence. Members should notice the verdict is fast: with binary checks, most charts fail in seconds, and that speed is the skill.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard chart — a live current-market candidate run through the five-line Launchpad checklist, verdict stated on camera
chapters.example_spec: First choice: pull that morning's scanner leaders and run the checklist cold on the top stack-qualified name — the verdict genuinely unrehearsed. If the live tape offers no candidate, run this chart cold, as if live: AXON daily, Sep–Nov 2024. The five checks in order: stack 9>20>50>200 all rising — pass; a genuine summer burst from the Aug 5 low $279.02 through the Aug 7 earnings gap (+11.9%, close $349.24) to ≈$365 — pass; a tightening September–October shelf ≈$390–430 sitting on the 9/20 with quiet volume — pass; a higher-low trigger priceable to the tick over ≈$432; stop under the pad low ≈$395 (≈8%), sizeable within 2% with 2R clear overhead. Verdict: PASS — the Nov 8 gap closed $603.18 and Dec 6 printed $698.67, ≈ +4.6R to +7R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Base Failure Modes + 20 Replay Reps
lessons.note: The three killers — late-stage bases, wide-and-loose structure, breakouts into overhead supply — each on a real failed chart, plus the shakeout-versus-failure decision rule for the day after entry. Module gate: 20 graded chart-replay reps against the family rubric at 80%, opening with a 60-second sizing recall to keep the formula warm. Then the field week: one week live — scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry/stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome vs plan. 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next family.

chapters.beat: open cold: recite and work Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % (2% max) on one ticker in under a minute, keeping the Module 5 formula warm before anything else.
chapters.speaker_notes: Start the timer, cold. Recite it: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % — 2% hard max, under 1% preferred, size always derived FROM the stop. Now one ticker in under a minute, the Sizing Gate's own numbers: $50,000 account, entry $80.00, structural stop $76.80. Stop distance: $3.20 on $80 is 4%. Position: 1% divided by 4% is 25% — $12,500. Shares: $12,500 divided by $80 is 156.25 — round DOWN, 156 shares. Dollars at risk: 156 times $3.20, $499 — right at 1%. Timer stops. This recall opens the lesson because mastery is perishable: the formula must stay warm through the entire setup tier, and if that took you longer than the minute, that's your signal to rewatch the Module 5 formula lesson before tonight's scan.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE toolkit card — problem 5 ($50,000 · entry $80.00 · stop $76.80) worked live against a 60-second timer

chapters.marker: The three killers on real charts
chapters.beat: walk one real failed chart each for late-stage bases, wide-and-loose structure, and breakouts into overhead supply, naming the tell that was visible BEFORE entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three failure modes kill more base trades than everything else combined, and each one was visible BEFORE entry. Killer one: the late-stage base. A leader's third or fourth base in a long run is obvious to everyone — and obvious is dangerous; by then the story is fully owned and the failure rate climbs steeply. Count the bases left to right before you buy one. Killer two: wide-and-loose structure. A real base tightens — each pullback smaller, closes clustering; a structure whose swings stay wide and sloppy never transferred supply, and its 'pivot' is just the top of chop. Killer three: the breakout into overhead supply — Module 2's ceiling of trapped buyers; a pivot sitting directly under a zone of old trapped holders is a breakout into a wall of sellers waiting to get out even. On each chart, name the tell that was on screen before the buy.
chapters.on_screen: Three failed charts in sequence — e.g. ZM Oct 2020 late-stage base, a wide-and-loose structure, a breakout into overhead supply (Model Book pulls, or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Killer one, late-stage: ZM daily, Sep–Nov 2020 — count the bases up from the 2019–20 run (this is the third/fourth); the Sep–Oct base ≈$370–480 breaks out to the Oct 19 high $588.84, then Nov 9 gaps −13.4% to open $433.00 and closes $413.24, −17% on the day, breaking it. Tell: the base count. Killer two, wide-and-loose: PTON daily, Mar–Oct 2021 — a sloppy ≈$85–130 range whose swings never tighten; the late-June push toward ≈$129 is the top of chop, and it rolls over. Tell: no contraction sequence. Killer three, overhead supply: UPST daily, Jul–Aug 2022 — a ≈$23–33 base directly beneath the collapse zone from ≈$70–401; the August attempt over ≈$33 dies within days ($14.02 by Nov 9). Each failure ≈ −1R, each visible before entry. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Shakeout or failure? The day-after rule
chapters.beat: teach the decision rule for the morning after entry: what price action says hold through the shake versus take the stop now, on two contrasting real examples.
chapters.speaker_notes: The hardest morning in this family is the day after entry, when the breakout pulls back in — so make the decision mechanical. Hold through the shake when: price is still holding the pivot area, the pullback volume is QUIET, and the stock reclaims the pivot intraday — that's a shakeout, weak hands being cleared, and your stop under the final contraction low is untouched and stays untouched. Take the exit when: the stock CLOSES back inside the base on RISING volume — that is the five-field card's written failure mode arriving on schedule, and you don't wait around inside a failed pattern. Two contrasting real examples on screen, called in real time. And the frame that governs both: the stop is an appointment, not a debate. The day-after rule tells you whether the appointment is near; it never, ever moves it.
chapters.on_screen: Two day-after charts side by side: a quiet shakeout that reclaimed the pivot vs a close back inside the base on heavy volume
chapters.example_spec: Shakeout side: TSLA daily, Nov 2019 (split-adjusted, ≈15× then). After the Oct 24 breakout over ≈$20, mid-November drifts back toward the pivot ≈$21–22 on visibly quiet volume, holds above it, and reclaims the highs — the stop under the final contraction was never touched, and holders collected the run into the Feb 4 2020 high $64.60, roughly +190%. Failure side: RBLX daily, early Dec 2021 — the days after the late-November entry, price CLOSES back inside the ≈$120–141 base on rising volume; the rule says exit, the stop pays ≈ −1R, and RBLX closes February 2022 at $51.57, −64% from the Nov 22 high $141.60. Same anxious morning, opposite mechanical answers. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: demonstrate the mechanics live: chart replay with the answer covered, grade each rep against the family rubric, and state the pass bar of 80% to close the module.
chapters.speaker_notes: Demonstrate the drill mechanics so there's zero ambiguity about the homework. Chart replay, answer covered: scroll a historical chart to the right edge of a base and stop. Now grade yourself against the family rubric before revealing what happened: Did you mark the contraction sequence? Did you draw the pivot to the tick? Is your stop at the structural invalidation — the final contraction low — not at a comfortable distance? What's your volume verdict on the break — evidence or noise? And is it a buy, a watch, or one of the three killers? Then reveal, score the rep, next chart. Twenty reps, scored honestly, and the pass bar to close this module is 80% — sixteen of twenty. Below that, the remediation is targeted: rewatch the specific chapter your misses cluster on, then retake with fresh charts.
chapters.on_screen: Chart replay on the dashboard with the answer covered — one full rep demonstrated, the family rubric visible beside it
chapters.example_spec: Demo rep chart: AXON daily, Aug–Nov 2023. Scroll to the right edge in early November, answer covered, and grade against the rubric aloud: the Aug 3 low $175.37, then the Aug 9 earnings gap +12.7% (open $198.12, close $200.44, 5× volume); contraction sequence ≈13% into the Sep 26 low $189.12 → ≈4% in late October, closes clustering ≈$200–213 (October closes $204.49); pivot drawn to the tick at the range high ≈$213; stop ≈$200 under the final contraction low (≈6% distance); volume verdict — dry through October, expansion required on the break; none of the three killers present. Call: BUY on a volume break of ≈$213. Reveal: Nov 8 closed $229.58 on 3.6× volume and December closed $258.33 — ≈ +3.5R trailed. Score the rep, next chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: assign the week: scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry and stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome versus plan — 80% on the drill plus the completed field log opens Family II.
chapters.speaker_notes: Assign the week that closes the family. Every night: run the nightly scan — the full funnel. From it, card two to three LIVE Bases & Breakouts candidates: a complete five-field card each, with an exact entry price and exact stop, logged in the Journal whether they trigger or not. Any fill runs at pilot size or paper — both gates still govern: the Module 5 sizing gate at 100% and this module's drill at 80%. At week's end, grade every outcome against plan — plan-adherence, not P&L. The gate to Family II, Momentum & Trend, is both together: 80% on the replay drill PLUS the completed, graded field log. Not one or the other. The drill proves your eyes; the field log proves your process. Bring both, and the next family opens.
chapters.on_screen: Screener nightly-scan output beside a blank five-field card and the Journal field-week log

modules.label: M8 · Setup Family II: Momentum & Trend

lessons.title: FLAGSHIP — 20 EMA Pullback: Qualify the Touch, Buy the 9 EMA Remount
lessons.note: The family's core motion at full depth: a bullish trend pulls back to the rising 20 EMA, a candle holds it, and the remount of the 9 EMA is the buy — qualifying checklist (trend intact, volume quiet on the pullback, RS line holding), stop under the pullback low, tennis-ball action separating leaders from laggards. Includes one chart that kept slicing the 20 EMA: the skip signal, not a better price. Artifact: the pullback-qualification checklist.

chapters.beat: open with the family's core image on two real charts: a leader hits the rising 20 EMA and bounces like a tennis ball, a laggard hits it and splats — this lesson teaches you to tell them apart before the bounce.
chapters.speaker_notes: This family lives on one image, so open with it on two real charts. A leader in a true uptrend pulls back to its rising 20 EMA and bounces off it like a tennis ball — buyers were waiting at the line, the reaction is immediate and firm. A laggard hits the same line and splats like an egg — no bid shows up, the line gives way, the 'support' was decoration. Same moving average, same touch, opposite outcomes — and the entire flagship lesson is learning to tell the tennis ball from the egg BEFORE the bounce, using checks you can run in advance rather than a bounce you can only see in hindsight. Recall the line's job title from Module 2: the 20 EMA is the swing-trend line. This setup is simply the disciplined way to buy a leader at it.
chapters.on_screen: Two charts: NVDA daily Mar–Jul 2023 bouncing off every rising 20 EMA touch vs a laggard splatting through the same line (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Tennis ball: NVDA daily, Mar–Jul 2023 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Jun 2024, ≈10× then). Mark each rising-20-EMA touch and the immediate bounce: the Apr 14 low $26.22, the early-May dip to $27.24, the June 26 pullback ≈$38.7 — every touch bought within a bar or two; the trend runs from a $23.22 February close to a $46.73 July close, ≈ +100%. Egg: DIS daily, Feb–Sep 2023. After the Feb 9 spike to $118.18 that closed back at $110.36, every touch of the flattening 20 EMA gives way — the March, April and May retests each slice through with no bid, the line flips to resistance, and DIS bleeds to the Sep 27 low $79.22. Same line, same touch, opposite outcomes. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Qualify the touch: the three checks
chapters.beat: run the qualifying checklist on a real pullback: trend intact, volume quiet on the pullback, RS line holding — and reject one candidate that fails a single check.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three checks qualify a touch, run in order, all binary. Check one — trend intact: the stack holds, 9 EMA over 20 EMA over 50 SMA over 200 SMA, price still making higher highs; the pullback is a rest inside an advance, not the first leg of a top. Check two — volume quiet on the pullback: the down days print BELOW-average volume; quiet selling is digestion, loud selling is distribution, and the volume pane tells you which in two seconds. Check three — RS line holding: from Module 4, price over SPY; the RS line should hold its uptrend through the pullback — a stock whose RS breaks while price rests is being rotated out of. Then reject one live candidate that passes two checks and fails one, and say the doctrine: fail one, skip the stock. Same gate logic as Stage 2 — no 'but it's close.'
chapters.on_screen: A live pullback on the dashboard chart with the three checks ticked; a second candidate failing the RS-line check, skipped on camera
chapters.example_spec: First choice: run the three checks on a live pullback from that day's scanner leaders, and skip a second live candidate that fails one check, on camera. Historical fallback pair, run as if live: PASS — NVDA daily, late Jun 2023 (split-adjusted, ≈10× then): stack intact and rising; pullback to ≈$38.7 on below-average volume; RS versus SPY still climbing (NVDA $23.22 → $46.73 February to July while SPY went $396 → $458) — three ticks, qualified, and it resolved ≈ +3R into mid-July. REJECT — DIS daily, Apr 2023: price pulls into its 20 EMA ≈$98–102 looking buyable, but the RS line has been rolling over since February — one check fails, skip the stock; DIS closed July at $88.89 and bottomed $79.22 in September, so the skip preserved the R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The hold candle and the 9 EMA remount buy
chapters.beat: mark the candle that holds the 20 EMA, buy the remount of the 9 EMA to the tick on a real winning trade, and place the stop under the pullback low sized through the formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: The entry has two parts, and impatience ruins both. First, the hold candle: the bar whose low tags the rising 20 EMA and holds it — closing in the upper part of its range; Module 2's verdict rule applies, a close in the top 40% of the day's range means buyers won that day at the line. That candle is evidence, not entry. Second, the buy: the remount of the 9 EMA — the momentum leash. Price crossing back above the 9 says the pullback is over and momentum has resumed; a buy-stop sits just above that remount level. The stop goes under the pullback low. Work it on the real winner: entry $102, pullback low $97 — a 4.9% stop distance, so at 1% account risk, 0.01 divided by 0.049 is roughly a 20% position, inside the GREEN plus A+ cell. Hold candle, remount, stop, size — in that order, every time.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily 2023 — hold candle at the 20 EMA, 9 EMA remount entry, stop under the pullback low, sizing math on screen (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, Jun–Jul 2023 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Jun 2024, ≈10× then); the $102/$97 pair in the notes is the generic worked example. On the chart: the June 26 hold candle — its low tags the rising 20 EMA ≈$38.7 and it closes in the top of its range, buyers winning the day at the line. Then the 9 EMA remount over the next sessions — buy-stop just above, filling ≈$41. Stop under the pullback low ≈$38.7 — ≈5.5%, so ≈an 18% position at 1% risk, inside the GREEN + A+ cell. Outcome: ≈$48 by mid-July (July closes $46.73) — ≈ +3R; first third at 2–3R, trail the rest. Read exact levels off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The slicer: skip signal, not sale price
chapters.beat: walk the chart that kept slicing through the 20 EMA and name the doctrine: repeated slicing disqualifies the name entirely, it does not offer a better entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the chart this lesson exists to protect you from: the slicer. Price cuts down through the 20 EMA, closes below it, pokes back above, slices through again — three, four times. Each slice looks, to a hopeful eye, like a cheaper entry into the same 'uptrend.' Say the doctrine plainly: repeated slicing DISQUALIFIES the name entirely — it does not offer a better price. A defended line gets defended; when institutions are actually accumulating a leader, the 20 EMA touch is met with an immediate bid — the tennis ball. Slicing means no one of size is defending, which means the trend claim itself is broken, whatever the higher highs looked like last month. The slicer goes off the list. If it later builds a proper base, it re-enters the funnel through Family I, judged by base rules — not through this setup at a discount.
chapters.on_screen: A chopfest chart slicing through the 20 EMA repeatedly — the Model Book contrast pull for this lesson
chapters.example_spec: Slicer exhibit: BABA daily, Jan–Oct 2023. Find: the January rally toward ≈$121 that makes the 'uptrend' claim, then the behaviour that voids it — price slices down through the 20 EMA in February, pokes back above in March, slices again in April, briefly reclaims in May, slices again: four-plus crossings, no touch ever met with an immediate bid. Each slice looked like a cheaper entry — ≈$105, ≈$95, ≈$85 — and BABA bottomed $77.77 on May 31, −36% from January. Say honestly that a July squeeze to $102.50 briefly rewarded the averaging, then failed again to an $82.54 October close. State the doctrine: repeated slicing disqualifies; re-entry only through Family I as a rebuilt base. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: build the artifact on screen field by field and assign it: no 20 EMA Pullback gets bought in your field week without this checklist filled in first.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build the artifact on screen, field by field, because during the field week no 20 EMA Pullback gets bought without it filled in first. The fields: Stack intact — 9 over 20 over 50 over 200, all rising, Y or N. Higher highs still in place, Y or N. Pullback volume below average, Y or N. RS line holding, Y or N. Hold candle printed at the 20 EMA with an upper-range close, Y or N. Then the numbers: 9 EMA remount trigger price, exact. Stop, at the pullback low, exact. Stop distance percent, position size from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % at your risk level, 2% hard max — and the regime-table cell check. Any N anywhere, any blank number: the checklist already reads SKIP. Print it, keep it beside the platform, and fill one per candidate, every time.
chapters.on_screen: The pullback-qualification checklist artifact built line by line — the lesson's printable card

lessons.title: EMA Crossback: The Re-Entry After the Extension
lessons.note: Kell's re-entry: after an extension, price crosses back into the 9/20 EMAs and either reclaims them (the long re-entry) or rejects them (the short) — both directions worked on the same template. Framed as the tool for re-entering a trend you exited too early: the most common regret trade, done correctly.

chapters.beat: open with the most common story in trading: you sold the leader too early, watched it run, and either chased it or sulked; Kell's crossback is the third option, done correctly.
chapters.speaker_notes: Start with the most common story in trading, because every member is living it. You owned the leader. You sold — early, for a reason that felt smart. Then it ran for weeks without you, and you did one of two things: chased it extended and got shaken out at the worst prices, or sulked and refused to ever touch it again. Both are emotional answers to a structural question. The crossback — Kell's re-entry — is the third option: a defined, repeatable template for getting BACK into a trend you exited too early, at a price and moment where the trade makes structural sense again. Frame it this way on camera: this lesson doesn't fix the early exit — Module 12 works on that. It fixes what you do AFTER the early exit, which is where the real damage usually happens.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily, 2020 — an early exit marked, then the extension that kept running without you (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: TSLA daily, Jun–Aug 2020 (prices split-adjusted; 5:1 Aug 2020 and 3:1 2022 — ≈15× these at the time). Mark the early exit: sold late June ≈$64 (≈$960 contemporary) after a strong run — 'up big, taking it.' Then the extension that ran without you: TSLA stretches to the Jul 13 high ≈$119.7 (≈$1,795) — ≈ +87% in under three weeks, far beyond the 8%-over-the-20-EMA EXTENDED flag. Freeze there and name the two bad answers: chasing that high into the ≈ −24% three-day shakeout that followed, or sulking while it added another ≈39% into the Aug 31 close $166.11 (≈$2,492). The structural third option — the crossback re-entry — is marked in chapter three. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The template: extension, then cross back in
chapters.beat: define what qualifies as an extension away from the 9/20 EMAs and mark the moment price crosses back into the EMA zone, where the decision window opens.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two conditions define the template, in order. First, the extension: price stretches well away from the 9 and 20 EMAs — use the firm's working number, the scanner flags a name more than 8% above the 20 EMA as EXTENDED, and that's the zone we mean: momentum has outrun its own leashes, and chasing there is buying someone else's exit. You do nothing during the extension except watch. Second, the cross back in: gravity does its work and price returns INTO the 9/20 EMA zone. That crossing — price re-entering the band between the two EMAs — is where the decision window opens, and only there. Mark the moment on the chart. Nothing is bought yet; the crossback is a location, not a trigger. What price does next — reclaim or reject — is the trade, and that's the next two chapters.
chapters.on_screen: The chart with the 9/20 EMA zone shaded, the >8%-extended stretch marked, then the cross back into the zone circled

chapters.beat: work a real chart where price crosses back and RECLAIMS the 9/20 EMAs, entering the re-entry with trigger and stop on screen.
chapters.speaker_notes: The long side: price crosses back into the EMA zone and RECLAIMS it — closes back above both the 9 and the 20, buyers defending the band on contact. That reclaim is your re-entry trigger: buy-stop above the reclaim bar's high. The stop goes under the crossback low — the lowest point of the return move; if that low breaks, the reclaim failed and the thesis is dead. Then the same one motion as always: entry to stop, say it's a 5% distance — at 1% account risk, 0.01 divided by 0.05, a 20% position, checked against the regime-table cell. Notice what the structure just gave you: a defined re-entry at a BETTER technical location than your emotional chase would have been, with a tighter, more honest stop. That's the whole value of the template — it converts regret into a plan with numbers on it.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily 2020 — the reclaim of the 9/20 with the re-entry trigger and stop under the crossback low marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Same TSLA 2020 chart (split-adjusted, ≈15× then). After the Jul 13 spike ≈$119.7, price crosses back into the 9/20 EMA zone: the late-July pullback prints the crossback low ≈$91 (≈$1,366) inside the band, and July closes $95.38. The reclaim: the first sessions of August close back above both EMAs — buy-stop above the reclaim bar's high fills ≈$100 (≈$1,500). Stop under the crossback low ≈$91 — ≈9%, so ≈an 11% position at 1% risk, checked against the regime cell. Outcome: the run into the Sep 1–2 2020 peak ≈$155 (≈$2,320 contemporary) — ≈ +6R in five weeks, at a better technical location than any chase. Read exact levels off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The reject: the short side of the same template
chapters.beat: on the same template, show price rejecting the EMAs instead, and name it as the short — every rule identical, direction inverted.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now run the identical template in the mirror. After a downside extension — price stretched far BELOW the 9/20 EMAs — the bounce carries price back up into the zone. The decision window opens the same way. But this time price REJECTS: it fails at the underside of the 9 and 20, sellers defending the band from above, and rolls back over. That rejection is the short-side trigger, with the protective stop above the rejection high — every rule identical to the long reclaim, direction inverted, nothing new to memorize. Be explicit about scope, because it matters: today this is RECOGNITION — you must be able to name a reject on sight. Short-side EXECUTION — the smallest sizing in the catalog, buy-stop protection, borrow mechanics — formally arrives in Module 10, where shorts are taught properly. See the mirror now; trade it later.
chapters.on_screen: The mirrored chart: a downside extension, the bounce into the 9/20 zone, and the rejection at the underside of both EMAs
chapters.example_spec: Mirror chart: NFLX daily, Jan–Apr 2022 (prices split-adjusted — 10:1 Nov 2025, ≈10× these at the time). Find: the Jan 21 2022 earnings collapse — gaps −21.2% from a $50.81 close to open $40.04, closing $39.75 on 6.2× volume — leaving price extended far BELOW the declining 9/20 EMAs; then the bounce carrying price up INTO the zone, highs ≈$43–45.8 (Jan 31 closes $42.71) tagging the underside of both; then the reject — the bounce fails at the band, prints lower highs, and rolls over through March toward ≈$33. Mark the short trigger under the rejection low with the stop above the rejection high ≈$45.8. Resolution: Apr 20 gaps −29.7% and closes $22.62 (≈$226 then) on 14× volume — ≈ +3R. Recognition only; execution in Module 10. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close with the discipline rule: the crossback re-enters a still-intact trend you exited early; if the trend checks fail, your early exit was right and the card stays blank.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the discipline rule that keeps this setup from becoming a revenge-trade license. The crossback re-enters a trend that is STILL INTACT — before the trigger means anything, the trend checks must pass again, fresh: Stage 2 holding, the stack in order, higher highs alive, RS line confirming. If those pass, your early exit was merely early, and the reclaim is an earned re-entry. But if the trend checks FAIL — the stack is breaking, RS is rolling, the structure is topping — then hear this clearly: your early exit was RIGHT. The market took you out of a deteriorating name and your emotions are trying to buy it back. In that case the card stays blank, and the blank card is the win. Re-entry is earned by the chart, never owed to your regret. Write that on the card's context line.
chapters.on_screen: Trend-intact checklist overlaid beside the crossback chart; one failed-check example shown and left untraded
chapters.example_spec: Overlay the trend-intact checklist beside the TSLA reclaim — every check green, re-entry earned. Failed-check contrast: ZM daily, Oct 2020–Feb 2021. The early exit came in the $500s; after the Oct 19 high $588.84, price crosses back into the 9/20 zone in November — the location prints — but run the checks fresh: the stack is breaking (9 under 20, 50 flattening), higher highs died with the Nov 9 bar (gap −13.4% to $433.00, close $413.24, −17% on the day), and the RS line is rolling hard as money rotates out of stay-at-home names. Fail, fail, fail: the card stays blank. The Dec 1 gap −9.1% follows, December closes $337.32, and ZM is under $200 by December 2021 — the blank card banked ≈ +4R of avoided loss. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Wedge Pop & Wedge Drop: One Coil, Two Resolutions
lessons.note: The descending coil taught once, then both resolutions on the same chart's full cycle — the Wedge Pop that starts the up-cycle and the Wedge Drop mirror that breaks the down-cycle open, every rule inverted side by side. Recognition only on the short side here: short-side EXECUTION (sizing smallest, buy-stop protection, borrow mechanics) waits for M10, where shorts formally arrive.

chapters.beat: open on the same chart's full cycle and make the claim: the tightening wedge is the market's turn signal at BOTH ends of a move, and you're about to learn it once for both.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put one chart's full cycle on screen — base, advance, top, decline — and make the claim that organizes the lesson: the tightening wedge is the market's turn signal at BOTH ends of a move. Near the bottom of a decline, a descending wedge that resolves upward — the Wedge Pop — is what starts the new up-cycle. Near the top of a rally, a rising wedge under the averages that resolves downward — the Wedge Drop — is what breaks the down-cycle open. Same compression, two doors. And here's why you learn them together in one sitting: they are one pattern with one grammar, and once you can read the coil itself, the direction of resolution is just which door opens. Circle both wedges on the cycle chart now, before any rules, so the member's eye holds the symmetry for the rest of the lesson.
chapters.on_screen: COIN daily, Jan–Jul 2023 — one chart's full cycle with both wedges circled (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: COIN daily, Dec 2022–Apr 2023, extending the left edge so both wedges fit.
