Circle wedge one, the Pop: the Dec 2022–early-January descending coil above the Jan 6 low $31.55 — converging swings, shrinking bars, 9/20 EMAs flattening overhead, volume bleeding dry — resolving upward mid-January (January closes $58.48) and starting the up-cycle to the Feb 2–3 peak $87.63 (Feb 2 closes $81.46 on 2.5× volume). Circle wedge two, the Drop: after that top, the mid-February low ≈$56 and the late-February bounce wedging UPWARD toward ≈$68 on fading volume beneath the now-flattening averages, then breaking its lower trendline in early March into the ≈$56–59 zone by Mar 13. One chart, one grammar, two doors — the next chapters trade each. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: draw the descending wedge anatomy against the 9/20 EMAs: the tightening range, the shrinking bars, and the averages flattening overhead.
chapters.speaker_notes: Teach the anatomy once, on the descending version, against the 9 and 20 EMAs. Three features. First, the tightening range: the down-move's swings compress — each bounce weaker, each decline shallower, the highs and lows converging toward an apex. Second, shrinking bars: the daily ranges themselves get smaller as energy drains from both sides — sellers exhausted, buyers not yet committed. Third, the averages: the 9 and 20 EMAs flatten overhead, their downslope going horizontal as the decline loses rate. Confirm with the volume pane: volume bleeds out through the coil — the dry-up half of Module 4's most reliable sequence, dry-up then expansion. When you see all three plus the volume drain, you have a loaded coil. Which way it fires is not knowable inside the coil — and you never need to know; you trade the resolution, not the prediction.
chapters.on_screen: Zoomed descending wedge with the 9/20 EMAs flattening overhead and the volume pane bleeding dry

chapters.marker: The Wedge Pop: starting the up-cycle
chapters.beat: on the cycle chart, work the pop that reclaims the averages and opens the new up-cycle, with trigger, stop, and the sized entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: On the cycle chart, work the pop. The trigger: price breaks the wedge's upper trendline and RECLAIMS the 9 and 20 EMAs — the flattened leashes flip from ceiling to floor, and the expansion volume shows up right where the dry-up sequence said it should. Entry on the reclaim break — buy-stop above it, exact price written. The stop goes under the wedge low: if the coil's floor gives way after the pop, the resolution failed and the thesis is dead there, not at a comfortable round number. Size it in one motion: say the wedge low is 6% below entry — at 1% account risk, 0.01 divided by 0.06, roughly a 17% position, checked against the regime cell. Then let the chart make the argument: this pop is the exact bar the whole up-cycle — the one we circled in chapter one — started from.
chapters.on_screen: COIN daily — the pop entry through the upper trendline, stop under the wedge low, sizing math on screen (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Same COIN chart, January 2023. The trigger: mid-January, price breaks the wedge's upper trendline and RECLAIMS both EMAs — the reclaim bar closes back above the 9 and 20 ≈$38–40; buy-stop above it fills ≈$41, with expansion volume printing right where the dry-up sequence said it should. Stop under the wedge low ≈$35 (the Jan 6 extreme $31.55 is the wider variant) — ≈15% distance on a volatile name, so 1% ÷ 15% ≈ a 7% position; the formula shrinks size automatically. Outcome: the up-cycle runs to the Feb 2 close $81.46 and the $87.63 peak — ≈ +7R available, ≈ +4R on standard management — and this pop is the exact bar the chapter-one circle started from. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The Wedge Drop: every rule inverted
chapters.beat: scroll the same chart forward to the rally's end and lay the Drop beside the Pop rule-for-rule: bounce wedging upward beneath the averages, then the break that opens the down-cycle.
chapters.speaker_notes: Scroll the same chart forward to the rally's end and build the mirror rule-for-rule, saying each inversion out loud. The coil: instead of a downmove compressing, the bounce wedges UPWARD — rising, narrowing pushes on fading volume — beneath the now-flattening averages; price is grinding up into the underside of the 9/20 instead of coiling above them. The trigger: instead of an upside reclaim, it's the break of the wedge's LOWER trendline — the failure of the last weak push. The invalidation: instead of the wedge low, it's the wedge HIGH — above the pattern, not below it. The resolution: the break that opens the down-cycle, on the same chart whose up-cycle the Pop began. Lay the two rule sets side by side in a two-column table as you go: every row identical, every direction flipped. One grammar, two doors — now proven on one chart.
chapters.on_screen: The same chart scrolled forward — the upward-wedging bounce under the averages and the breakdown, beside a two-column Pop/Drop rule table

chapters.beat: set the boundary explicitly: members must name the Wedge Drop on sight from today, but short-side execution (smallest sizing, buy-stop protection, borrow mechanics) formally arrives in Module 10 — then drill it by marking both wedges on a fresh cycle chart.
chapters.speaker_notes: Set the boundary explicitly, because scope discipline is part of the doctrine. From today, members must NAME a Wedge Drop on sight — in the drill, in the field week, on any chart shown cold. But nobody shorts one yet: short-side EXECUTION — the smallest sizing in the catalog, buy-stop protection placed above, borrow mechanics — formally arrives in Module 10, where the short-side mirror is taught properly. Recognition now, execution later; seeing the pattern early and trading it early are different privileges, earned separately. Then the drill that closes the lesson: hand the member a fresh full-cycle chart, unmarked, and have them find and mark BOTH wedges — the Pop that started the up-cycle and the Drop that ended it — with triggers and invalidation levels drawn. If they can do that on a chart they've never seen, the coil grammar is installed.
chapters.on_screen: A fresh, unmarked full-cycle chart — the member's drill canvas, answer covered
chapters.example_spec: Drill canvas: UPST daily, Apr–Nov 2023 — a fresh full cycle not used elsewhere. Presenter's answer key: wedge one, the Pop — the spring descending coil above the May 3 low $11.93, bars shrinking, 9/20 flattening overhead, volume dry; it resolves upward with the May 10 earnings gap (+39.4%, open $19.64) and runs the up-cycle to the Aug 1 high $72.58 — a reclaim entry ≈$14.50 with stop ≈$12 is ≈ +12R on a late-July trail, ≈ +23R at the peak. Wedge two, the Drop — after the Aug 9 collapse (−17.3% gap, close $34.03 on 4.1× volume), the Aug–Sep bounce wedges upward ≈$30 → $36 on fading volume, then breaks its lower trendline: October closes $24.03 and the Nov 8 gap −27.6% closes $21.38. Member marks both wedges; grade against this key. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Adding to Winners + 20 Family Reps
lessons.note: The ADD doctrine: when a continuation setup in a name you already own means pyramiding smaller — only once the core position is above breakeven, with the combined risk still inside the 2% formula and the stop moved to protect the blend. Closes with 20 replay reps mixing all four family members, recycling two Stage-2 gate questions from Module 3. Then the field week: one week live — scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry/stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome vs plan. 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next family.

chapters.beat: open with the reframe from the five-field card's function column: a 20 EMA Pullback in a name you ALREADY own isn't a new trade, it's an ADD — and adds have their own rules.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the reframe that the five-field card's function column set up back in Module 7. A 20 EMA Pullback appears in a name you ALREADY own. Same stack, same quiet pullback volume, same hold candle, same 9 EMA remount. But this is not a new trade — it is an ADD, and adds have their own rules, because the question has changed. A new trade asks 'is this a good entry?' An add asks 'do I increase exposure to a position I already have, and what does that do to my total risk?' Same pattern on the chart, different decision in the account. Traders who miss this distinction pyramid winners into oversized positions with stale stops and give back months of work in a week. The function column exists precisely for this moment: read the pattern, then ask what it's FOR — here, it's for adding, governed by three gates.
chapters.on_screen: THE FIVE-FIELD SETUP CARD's function framing beside a chart of an owned name printing a fresh 20 EMA Pullback
chapters.example_spec: Owned-name chart: NVDA daily, May–Jul 2023 (split-adjusted; 10:1 Jun 2024, ≈10× then) — deliberately the flagship's own chart, reread through the function column. The position: core owned from the May 25 earnings-gap entry ≈$38.9 (that day gapped +26.1%, opening $38.52 on 3.2× volume), stop long since moved to breakeven, comfortably above water by late June. Then the fresh signal prints: the June 26 touch of the rising 20 EMA ≈$38.7, quiet pullback volume, hold candle, 9 EMA remount ≈$41 — an identical pattern to a new entry, but in a name already held. Freeze there and pose the chapter's question: not 'is this a good entry?' but 'do I add, and what does that do to total risk?' The add resolved ≈ +3R (July closes $46.73). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: state the doctrine on screen: the core position must be above breakeven, the add is pyramided SMALLER than the core, and the combined risk must still fit inside Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % under the 2% cap.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three gates, all mandatory, in order. Gate one: the core position must be ABOVE BREAKEVEN. You only add to a trade that has already proven itself — adding to a loser is the zero-exception commandment from Module 5, and adding to a flat trade is just doubling an unproven bet. Gate two: the add is pyramided SMALLER than the core — each layer smaller than the last, never inverted. A 20% core takes maybe a 10% add; an inverted pyramid puts your biggest money at your worst prices. Gate three: the COMBINED position must still fit the math — total risk through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % stays under the 2% hard cap against the blended stop, and portfolio heat — the sum of entry-minus-stop times shares across every open position, divided by equity — stays under the 10% cap. All three gates or no add. Two of three is a skip.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the three ADD gates with the formula and the 10% portfolio-heat line from THE LOOP CARD's Size station

chapters.beat: work a real add with numbers: compute the blended cost basis, move the stop to protect the blend, and show the disaster version where an unmoved stop turns a winner into a full loser.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the arithmetic that makes gate three real. Core: 100 shares at $50, stop $47.50 — $250 at risk, 1% of a $25,000 book, wait — keep it simple: $250 planned risk. The stock works; you add 50 shares at $60 on the pullback. Blended cost: 100 times 50 plus 50 times 60, divided by 150 shares — $53.33. Here is the disaster version, on screen: leave the stop at $47.50. Your risk is now 150 shares times $5.83 — roughly $875, three and a half times the original plan, and a stop-out from here turns a winning position into a full-size loser. The rule: when you add, the stop MOVES to protect the blend — up under the pullback low that justified the add, say $52. Now 150 shares times $1.33 is about $200 of risk on a profitable blend. Compute it every add. The add and the stop move are one action.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard math: 100 sh @ $50 + 50 sh @ $60 → $53.33 blend; unmoved $47.50 stop = ~$875 at risk vs moved stop ≈ $200

chapters.beat: run the drill mechanics live: 20 replay reps mixing all four family members (20 EMA Pullback, EMA Crossback, Wedge Pop, Wedge Drop) plus two recycled Stage-2 gate questions from Module 3, graded at the 80% bar.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the drill mechanics live so the homework is unambiguous. Twenty chart-replay reps, answer covered, mixing all four family members in random order: 20 EMA Pullback, EMA Crossback, Wedge Pop, Wedge Drop. For each rep, before the reveal: name the setup, state whether it qualifies — the three touch checks, the extension threshold, the coil anatomy — mark the trigger price, and place the stop at the structural invalidation. Interleaved deliberately, because you can ace each setup in isolation and still freeze when a live chart doesn't announce which lesson it belongs to. And two of the twenty questions are recycled Stage-2 gate questions from Module 3 — mastery is perishable, and the eligibility gate must stay warm underneath every setup skill. The pass bar is 80% — sixteen of twenty. Misses get targeted remediation: back to the specific chapter, then fresh charts.

chapters.speaker_notes: Assign the closing week, same protocol as Family I, new family. Every night: run the nightly scan. From the output, card two to three LIVE Momentum & Trend candidates — pullbacks qualifying on the checklist, crossbacks in still-intact trends, wedges with real coils — each with a complete five-field card, exact entry, exact stop, logged in the Journal whether it triggers or not. Adds count as reps here too: if an owned name prints a qualifying pullback, run the three ADD gates on paper and log the decision. Everything at pilot size or paper until both standing gates are cleared — the Module 5 sizing gate at 100% and this family's drill at 80%. At week's end, grade every log against plan. The gate to Family III, Gaps & Catalysts: 80% on the drill PLUS the completed, graded field log. Both. Then the gaps open.

modules.label: M9 · Setup Family III: Gaps & Catalysts

lessons.title: FLAGSHIP — Episodic Pivot: Day One of a New Trend
lessons.note: A neglected stock gaps 10%+ on massive volume from a surprise the market has not priced: the premarket homework (float, overhead supply, does the gap clear the base), the opening-range-high entry, the day-low stop, partials into strength, trailing on the 10/20-day — with the pacing rule delivered on camera: EP mastery is measured in earnings seasons, not weeks. Artifact: the premarket gap checklist; two winners plus one faded EP taken for the planned loss. Script the premarket-homework segment (float, overhead supply, gap-clears-base, season clock) as a clean self-contained chapter — it doubles as UCT Foundations' premarket-homework lesson via a clip.

chapters.beat: open on a neglected stock the morning it gapped 10%+ on massive volume from a surprise the market had not priced, then fast-forward the months-long trend it started, and name the thesis: you are not chasing a gap, you are buying day one.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here is the definition, and every word is load-bearing: a NEGLECTED stock — flat or forgotten, no crowd in it — gaps 10% or more on massive volume because of a surprise the market has not priced. Not a leader everyone owns. Not a 4% drift. Ten-plus percent, on volume multiples of normal, on genuinely new information. That combination is day one of a new trend, and that is the thesis of this setup: you are not chasing a gap, you are buying the first day institutions are forced to build a position that takes weeks. Show the gap morning, then fast-forward the months-long trend it started. The gap looks extended on day one. It is actually early. That reframe — extended is early when the information is new — is what this whole lesson installs.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI daily, January 2024 — the +30%+ pre-announcement gap EP that trended for weeks (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, November 2023–March 2024 (prices split-adjusted for the 10:1 of October 2024 — ≈10× these at the time). Walk it: a quiet, neglected base ≈$25–31 through late 2023; then the January 19, 2024 gap on the pre-announced blowout quarter — opens ≈$34.75 against a ≈$31.15 prior close (+11.6%), closes ≈$42.35, up ≈36% on the day, on ≈3× average volume. Fast-forward the trend it started: ≈$80 by the February 16 close and the ≈$122.90 high on March 8 — 'extended is early' when the information is new. Entry ≈$38.60 over the opening-range high, stop ≈$34.50 at the day low; the 10/20-day trail paid ≈+10R by mid-February. Read exact levels off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: work float, overhead supply, and does-the-gap-clear-the-base on one real premarket gap while filling the premarket gap checklist on camera, and start the season clock out loud: this homework is the whole edge.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three checks before the open, filled on the checklist while you talk. One: float — a small float means the forced buying has nowhere to hide; note the share count. Two: overhead supply — scroll left; every holder trapped above the gap price is a future seller. The best EPs gap into clean air. Three: does the gap CLEAR the base — the open must print above the entire prior consolidation, not inside it; a gap that opens mid-base is a trade for someone else. Then start the season clock out loud: EPs cluster in earnings season, roughly four windows a year, so tonight's homework list comes from the reporting calendar. This homework is the whole edge — the entry itself takes thirty seconds; the ten premarket minutes are the trade.
chapters.on_screen: The premarket gap checklist artifact beside the Calendar's earnings feed for that morning

chapters.beat: mark the opening range on the intraday chart, buy the break of its high on volume, set the stop at the day low, and size it live through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % under the 2% max.
chapters.speaker_notes: Mechanics, to the tick. Let the opening range form — the first minutes of trade. Your buy-stop goes just above the opening-range high, and it fires only on volume. Your stop is the day low: if a 10% gap on massive volume trades back below where the day started, the surprise is being rejected and the thesis is dead. Now size it with the formula: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. Say the gap opens at $50, the opening-range high is $52, the day low is $48.75 — entry $52.10, stop distance about 6.4%. At 1% account risk: 0.01 ÷ 0.064 ≈ a 15.6% position. On a $50,000 account that is $7,800, 150 shares, roughly $500 at risk. Stop first, distance second, size last — same sequence as every trade in this course.
chapters.on_screen: The same EP's 5-minute intraday chart, gap morning — opening range, buy-stop, and day-low stop marked
chapters.example_spec: SMCI 5-minute, January 19, 2024 gap morning (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). In the notes' order: gap open ≈$34.75 vs. ≈$31.15 prior close, a +11.6% gap; let the opening range form — high ≈$38.50, low ≈$34.50 at the day low (read exact prints on your platform); buy-stop just over the opening-range high ≈$38.60, firing only on volume; stop at the day low ≈$34.50 — stop distance ≈10%, so 1% account risk gives ≈a 10% position by the formula. Day one closes ≈$42.35 (≈+0.9R) on ≈3× average volume; the 10/20-day trail converted it into a multi-week ≈+10R hold into February. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Two winners and one faded EP
chapters.beat: replay both winners with partials into strength and the trail on the 10/20-day, then the faded gap exited for exactly the planned loss, managed with the same calm as the winners.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk both winners with the management rules spoken at the bar they applied. Move the stop to breakeven at roughly +1R or the first higher low. Take the first third off at 2-3R into strength — you sell some when it feels best, not when it feels worst. Trail the remainder on the 10/20-day moving averages — that is the EP's trail, and it is what converts a good gap into a multi-week trend hold instead of a scalp. Then the third chart: a gap that passed the homework and still faded. The stop hit at the day low, the planned 1R was paid, done. Same calm, same voice as the winners. Roughly half of EPs fail — the math works because the winners pay multiples of the disciplined 1R the failures cost.
chapters.on_screen: PLTR daily, November 2024 earnings-gap EP with the 10/20-day trail drawn, plus one faded gap (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Winner: PLTR daily, November 2024 — base ≈$40–45 into the November 4 report (prior close ≈$41.40); November 5 opens ≈$47.86 (+15.6%) and closes ≈$51.13, up ≈23% on the day, on ≈4× average volume. Entry ≈$52 over the opening-range high, stop ≈$46.50 under the gap-day low (read exact); breakeven at +1R, first third off at 2–3R ≈$63–69, 10/20-day trail through the ≈$80.55 December 20 close, trail exit ≈$76–80 for ≈+4–5R. Faded EP: SPCE daily/5-minute, July 12, 2021 (Branson-flight morning) — gaps to ≈$52, early pop ≈$55–57 triggers the entry, then fades all day to close ≈$40.70; the day-low stop pays the planned −1R calmly. SPCE reverse-split 1-for-20 in 2024, so a current chart shows ≈20× those prices. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The mastery clock and your checklist
chapters.beat: deliver the pacing rule to camera (EP mastery is measured in earnings seasons, three to four of them, not weeks — the membership is where those reps happen) and hand off the premarket gap checklist as the artifact the member fills every gap morning.
chapters.speaker_notes: Deliver the pacing rule straight to camera: EP mastery is measured in earnings seasons, not weeks — three to four of them. That is a year of deliberate reps, because the setup only appears in clusters four times a year and no amount of rewatching substitutes for live seasons. That is exactly what the membership is for: every season, the Morning Wire and the scanner surface the gap candidates, and you run this same checklist against live names with the firm. Hand off the artifact: the premarket gap checklist gets filled every gap morning from now on — float, overhead supply, gap-clears-base, season context — before any entry is planned. And restate the guardrail: this setup is not traded live until the family drill at the end of this module is passed. Pilot size or paper until then.

lessons.title: Power Earnings Gap: Institutions Repricing in Real Time
lessons.note: Blowout numbers gap an established leader above its base on huge volume — what separates a PEG from an ordinary earnings pop (magnitude of beat, guidance raise, gap clearing the entire base) and from an EP (known leader vs neglected name, which changes the hold horizon). One real earnings morning walked from the print to the entry, next to one ordinary pop that faded.

chapters.marker: Why institutions can't finish in one day
chapters.beat: open on a real established leader gapping above its base on blowout numbers and huge volume, and frame the PEG: funds repricing a business in real time, which is why the move continues.
chapters.speaker_notes: A Power Earnings Gap is an ESTABLISHED leader gapping above its base on blowout numbers and huge volume. The logic is mechanical, not mystical: when a business reports results that change what it is worth, funds must reprice it — and a fund that needs to move hundreds of millions of dollars cannot finish buying in one session without destroying its own fill. So the gap day is not the move; it is the start of the repricing. That is why a true PEG continues for days and weeks instead of fading — the buyers are still there tomorrow, working orders. Open on the real example: the print hits, the stock gaps clear of a multi-month base on volume several times normal, and the follow-through is institutions finishing what they started.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, May 2023 — the guidance-blowout earnings gap above the base that never looked back

chapters.marker: PEG versus an ordinary earnings pop
chapters.beat: the three separators on the chart: magnitude of the beat, a guidance raise, and the gap clearing the ENTIRE base, with each one checked against the live example.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three separators, each checkable before you commit a dollar. One: magnitude of the beat — not a penny over consensus, a blowout that changes the estimate curve. Two: a guidance RAISE — the beat tells you about last quarter; the raise tells you the repricing has a future, and it is the raise that forces analysts to move numbers and funds to chase. Three: the gap clears the ENTIRE base — price opens above every consolidation high, so there is no trapped supply overhead. Check all three against the live example on screen. An ordinary pop typically fails at least one: modest beat, in-line guide, or a gap that opens inside the base where sellers are waiting. Three for three or it is not a PEG — that is a gate, not a judgment call.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, May 2023 with the three separators annotated: beat size, raised guide, gap clearing the full base

chapters.beat: known leader versus neglected name, and how that single difference changes the hold horizon from a day-one trend trade to a position add on a stock the market already trusts.
chapters.speaker_notes: One difference drives everything: the EP is a NEGLECTED name — nobody owns it, the surprise creates a brand-new crowd, and you are trading day one of a trend that did not exist yesterday. The PEG is a KNOWN leader — the market already trusts the business, institutions already own it, and the gap is them adding at a new valuation. That single difference changes the hold horizon and the job of the trade. The EP is a trend-initiation trade managed on the 10/20-day trail from a standing start. The PEG behaves like a position add on an existing story: the base below is real support, the shakeouts are shallower, and it slots naturally into a book that may already hold the name. Same gap on the surface, different trade underneath — name which one you are in before you size it.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: SMCI January 2024 (neglected-name EP) beside NVDA May 2023 (known-leader PEG)

chapters.marker: One real earnings morning, print to entry
chapters.beat: walk the actual sequence on screen: the numbers hit, the premarket gap forms above the base, the open, and the exact entry with stop and size from the formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the sequence in real order. After the close, the numbers hit: a blowout beat and a guidance raise far above the street. Premarket, the stock builds a gap that sits clear above the entire base — separator three confirmed before the open. At the bell, let the opening range form; the entry is the break of the opening-range high on volume, exactly the EP mechanic, because the intraday entry logic is shared across this family. Stop under the day low. Size it through the formula: if the stop distance works out to 5%, then at 1% account risk the position is 0.01 ÷ 0.05 = 20% of the account — at the top of the GREEN + A+ table cell, and only there because this is an A+ setup in a permissive tape. Say each step as you mark it: print, gap, range, trigger, stop, size.
chapters.on_screen: That earnings morning's 5-minute chart — premarket gap, opening range, entry, and day-low stop marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute, May 25, 2023 — the morning after the May 24 guidance blowout (prices split-adjusted for the 10:1 of June 2024 — ≈10× these at the time). Walk the real order: after-hours print and a raise far above the street; the premarket gap sits clear above the entire base — prior close ≈$30.55, opens ≈$38.52, a +26.1% gap (separator three before the bell). Opening range forms: early flush to the ≈$36.60 day low, opening-range high ≈$38.90–39.20 (read exact prints); entry on the ORH break on volume ≈$39.20; stop under the day low ≈$36.60 — ≈6.6% distance, so ≈15% position at 1% risk. Day one closes ≈$37.98 on ≈3× volume; the 10/20-day trail rode the trend to ≈$47 by late August, ≈+3R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: put the ordinary earnings pop beside the PEG, show it failing the separators (small beat, no raise, gap dies inside the base), and close with the rule: if it doesn't clear the base on a raised guide, it's not a PEG, skip it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the counter-example, and grade it out loud against the three separators. The beat is small — a penny or two, no estimate-changing surprise. The guide is in-line — nothing forces anyone to reprice tomorrow. And the gap opens INSIDE the base, underneath a shelf of holders who have been waiting weeks to sell at breakeven. Watch what the tape does: an opening pop, then supply leans on it all day, and the gap is fully faded by the close. Nothing broke — the market correctly decided nothing changed. Close with the rule stated as a sentence the member can repeat: if it doesn't clear the base on a raised guide, it's not a PEG — skip it. No partial credit, no 'but the beat was decent.' The separators are the gate.
chapters.on_screen: A same-season ordinary earnings pop that faded back into its base, beside the NVDA PEG (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: GOOGL daily plus a 15-minute inset, April 26, 2023 — same season as the NVDA PEG. Grade the separators aloud: modest beat, effectively in-line guide, and the gap opens INSIDE the multi-month ≈$101–108 base beneath weeks of trapped overhead — it never even registers as a 5% gap in the data. Walk the tape: prior close ≈$104, opening pop toward ≈$106–107, supply leans on it all session, close ≈flat-to-red ≈$104 — fully faded back into the base on unremarkable volume. Nothing broke; the market decided nothing changed. A forced ORH entry stopped at the day low for ≈−1R; the rule says skip. Beside it, NVDA's May 25 gap opened ≈$38.52 (split-adjusted) clear above its whole ≈$30 base and never returned. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: News/Earnings Gapper: Trade the First Pullback and Reclaim, Not the Open
lessons.note: The headline-driven gap that holds its range, entered off the first controlled pullback and reclaim rather than the emotional open — the exact reclaim trigger and stop marked on one worked example. The number-one gapper mistake shown on a real chased-open loser with the R damage computed.

chapters.beat: replay the first fifteen minutes of a real headline gap whipsawing both directions, and state the doctrine: the emotional open is where amateurs pay; your trade is the first controlled pullback and reclaim.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the first fifteen minutes of a real headline gap and just let the tape make the argument: up 4% in two minutes, down to flat, back up — both sides getting stopped out of positions they took on emotion. The open of a news gap is a collision of market orders from people who have not thought: shorts covering in panic, FOMO buyers paying any price, funds unloading into the liquidity. Nobody in that scrum has an edge, and the spreads and slippage are the worst of the day. State the doctrine plainly: the emotional open is where amateurs pay; your trade is the first controlled pullback and reclaim, after the crowd has exhausted itself and the real auction begins. Patience here is not a temperament trait — it is the setup's entry rule.
chapters.on_screen: 5-minute chart of a major headline gap's first 15 minutes, whipsawing both directions (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: META 5-minute, February 2, 2023, first fifteen minutes — the earnings-and-buyback headline gap. Prior close ≈$153.07; opens ≈$183.38, a +19.8% gap on ≈5× average volume, the heaviest print in the name since 2022. Let the tape argue: immediate thrust, a hard flush back toward the ≈$182–183 opening low within minutes, snap back through the open — shorts covering in panic, FOMO buyers paying any price, funds unloading into the liquidity, spreads at their worst. Mark both cohorts' stop-outs. The session resolved higher, closing ≈$188.77 near the day's upper end (read the exact high), but nobody trading minute one had an edge — the patient reclaim later paid ≈+1R (chapter 3) while the open's entrants churned. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: a headline-driven gap that HOLDS its range on real volume versus one that starts bleeding immediately, and the tell that separates them before you ever plan an entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two gaps side by side. The one that qualifies HOLDS its opening range: after the first thrust, price consolidates in the upper portion of the day's range on real, sustained volume — dips get bought, the low of the day never revisits, the volume stays elevated instead of evaporating after the first candle. That is a crowd that wants in. The one that fails starts bleeding immediately: lower highs from the first ten minutes, each bounce weaker, volume front-loaded into the open and then gone — sellers using the headline as an exit. The tell, before you ever plan an entry, is where price spends its time: upper third of the range on volume means qualified; sliding off the open's high on fading volume means walk away. You are filtering, not predicting — most gaps fail this test and that is fine.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: a gap holding the top of its range on volume vs. one bleeding from the open (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Split screen. Qualifier: META 5-minute, February 2, 2023 — after the opening thrust from ≈$183.38, price consolidates all morning in the upper third of the day's range (≈$185–190), dips get bought, the ≈$182–183 opening low never revisits, volume stays elevated bar after bar, and the day closes ≈$188.77 on ≈5× average. Failure: SPCE 5-minute, July 12, 2021 — opens ≈$52, lower highs from the first ten minutes, each bounce weaker, volume front-loaded into the open then gone, closes ≈$40.70 (SPCE reverse-split 1-for-20 in 2024; a current chart shows ≈20× those prices). Annotate the tell on each: where price spends its time. The qualifier's reclaim paid ≈+1R; the bleeder round-tripped ≈−1R or worse for anyone who chased. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The reclaim trigger, marked to the tick
chapters.beat: on the worked example, mark the first controlled pullback, the exact reclaim trigger, and the stop under the pullback low, then size it through the Module 5 formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: On the worked example, mark the sequence to the tick. The gap holds its range, then makes its first CONTROLLED pullback — orderly, on declining volume, no panic bars. Mark the level it pulled back through, then the trigger: the reclaim of that level on expanding volume. That reclaim is the entry — you are buying proof that the pullback was digestion, not distribution. The stop goes under the pullback low: if price trades back below the pullback's floor, the reclaim failed and the thesis is dead. Now the formula. Entry $31.20, pullback low $29.95 — stop distance 4%. At 1% account risk: 0.01 ÷ 0.04 = a 25% position by formula, capped at the table's ceiling for your regime and grade. The reclaim structure is what makes the stop tight enough for the trade to pay.
chapters.on_screen: The qualifying gapper's 5-minute chart with pullback, reclaim trigger, and stop marked to the tick (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: META 5-minute, February 2, 2023. Mark the sequence to the tick on your platform: the gap opens ≈$183.38 and holds its range; the morning thrust tops ≈$190 (read the exact high); the first CONTROLLED pullback — orderly, declining volume, no panic bars — eases back toward ≈$185; mark the level it pulled back through (≈$187); the trigger is the reclaim of ≈$187 on expanding volume; the stop goes under the pullback low ≈$184.50 — ≈1.5–2% stop distance, so the 1%-risk formula gives a huge position the regime/grade table must cap. The close ≈$188.77 is ≈+0.7R the same day and the day's high ≈+1.2R; February chops back to ≈$175 before the mid-March reclaim carries it to ≈$212 by month-end. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The number-one gapper mistake, in R
chapters.beat: a real chased-open loser on screen with the damage computed in R terms against what the patient reclaim entry on the same chart would have paid.
chapters.speaker_notes: The number-one gapper mistake is buying the open, and here it is on a real loser with the damage priced in R. The chaser bought the opening spike at $32.50 with no structure to stop against — the nearest honest invalidation was the gap fill near $29, a 10.8% stop, so either he oversized against a mental stop or sized correctly for a trade that couldn't pay. Price faded to $30; he sold in disgust for about a 1.6R loss against his planned risk. Now the same chart, the patient entry: the reclaim at $31.20, stop $29.95, and the afternoon run to $34 — a gain of $2.80 against $1.25 of risk, +2.2R. Same stock, same day, same headline. The difference between minus 1.6R and plus 2.2R was nothing but WHERE the entry happened. The chase doesn't just risk more — it shrinks the payoff before the trade begins.
chapters.on_screen: The same gapper's full session chart, chased-open entry vs. reclaim entry, both R outcomes annotated
chapters.example_spec: META full session, February 2, 2023, 5-minute. The chaser: buys the first-minutes spike ≈$190 with no structure beneath — the nearest honest invalidation is the ≈$182–183 opening low, ≈4% away — and the flush back through ≈$185 shakes him out in disgust for ≈−1R or worse against his planned risk. The patient entry, same chart: reclaim ≈$187, stop ≈$184.50, close ≈$188.77 — ≈$1.80 gained against ≈$2.50 risked, ≈+0.7R day one and ≈+1.2R at the day's high, in a position that keeps working. Annotate both entries and both R outcomes side by side: same stock, same day, same headline — only the entry location differs. Read exact prints off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: fill context, pattern, trigger, stop, and failure mode for the gapper on camera, closing on the one-line rule the member repeats: never the open, always the reclaim.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the card on camera, field by field, so the setup exists as five falsifiable blanks. Context: a genuine headline catalyst, gap holding the upper portion of its opening range on sustained volume. Pattern: first controlled pullback on declining volume after the opening drive. Trigger: the reclaim of the pullback level on expanding volume — a PREV DAY HIGH BREAK or RED TO GREEN depending on where the structure sits, marked to the tick. Stop: under the pullback low, the price where the reclaim is objectively dead. Failure mode: the reclaim prints and then price loses the pullback low again — exit, no averaging, no second chances on a failed reclaim. Then the one-line rule the member repeats until it is reflex: never the open, always the reclaim.
chapters.on_screen: The Five-Field Setup Card toolkit artifact, filled live for the News/Earnings Gapper

lessons.title: The Level the Tape Remembers: High Volume Edge & Gap Support
lessons.note: One principle, two flavors: a high-conviction event creates a line price must defend. The highest-volume day's close and the prior up-gap zone, each traded the same way — the candle that holds the zone, entry over its high, stop under the zone, invalidated when the level fully fails. Two real charts, one per flavor, with the institutional-memory logic that makes both work.

chapters.beat: open with the principle both flavors share: a high-conviction event creates a line price must defend, because the institutions who acted there defend their own cost.
chapters.speaker_notes: One principle carries this whole lesson: a high-conviction event creates a line price must defend. When enormous volume trades at a price — an earnings day, a gap, a breakout — that volume is real positions with real cost bases. The institutions who bought there will defend their own cost, because letting it fail means marking losses on size they cannot exit quickly. So the level is not a line on YOUR chart; it is a line on THEIR blotter. That is institutional memory: the tape remembers where the size traded, and price behaves differently when it returns there. Today you learn two flavors of the same principle — the highest-volume day's close, and the prior up-gap zone — and one trade template that covers both. Different chart shapes, identical logic, identical execution.
chapters.on_screen: A daily chart with its highest-volume bar highlighted and a horizontal line at that day's close
chapters.example_spec: META daily, 2023 — the lesson's own example, introduced generically. Highlight the February 2, 2023 bar: volume ≈5× average, the heaviest up-day print since the 2022 collapse (only the October 2022 and February 2022 earnings crashes traded more); draw the horizontal line at that day's close ≈$188.77. Narrate the blotter logic while the line sits there: that volume is real institutional cost basis clustered around ≈$189 — a line on THEIR blotter, not just your chart. Pan forward: late February probes below it toward ≈$168–175, then the mid-March reclaim, after which every return is defended with shrinking down-bars (worked next chapter, ≈+1.5R). No trade here — mark the level the day the volume prints, then wait. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: on a real chart, mark the highest-volume day's close as the level, and watch price return to it and hold, with the who-bought-there logic narrated.
chapters.speaker_notes: Flavor one: find the highest-volume day of the move — usually the earnings reaction or the day of the news — and mark its CLOSE. That close is the fairest single print of what the big buyers paid, because the heaviest volume clustered around it. Now watch what happens when price pulls back to it weeks later: the decline slows, the down-bars shrink, and buyers appear at almost exactly the level. Narrate the who-bought-there logic as it holds: the funds that built positions on that high-volume day are adding at their cost, not selling — defending it costs them nothing and protects everything. You are not predicting support; you are locating the one price where a known, motivated buyer already exists. Mark the level the day the volume prints, then wait — sometimes weeks — for the tape to come back to it.
chapters.on_screen: META daily, February 2023 — the huge-volume earnings day's close acting as the defended level on later pullbacks (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: META daily, February–April 2023. Mark the highest-volume day of the move — February 2, 2023, ≈5× average — and its close ≈$188.77. Walk the return trip: the late-February drift probes below the line toward ≈$168–175 (read exact) — watch down-bars shrink and volume dry as buyers appear; the mid-March layoff-news reclaim retakes ≈$189 decisively, and price never trades below it again — late-March and April dips hold ≈$194–207 above the defended close. Template: entry over the mid-March reclaim/holding candle ≈$195, stop under the defended zone ≈$166, run into the April 27 earnings gap that opened ≈$239.89 and closed ≈$238.56 — ≈+1.5R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: on a second real chart, mark the prior up-gap zone, and show the first controlled pullback into it holding, the same defended-line logic in gap clothing.
chapters.speaker_notes: Flavor two: the prior up-gap zone — the empty space between the pre-gap close and the gap-day open. That zone printed no volume on the way up, but the gap EVENT was the high-conviction moment: everyone who bought the gap day has a cost basis at or above it. So when the first controlled pullback comes, the gap zone is where their defense shows up. Shade the zone on a second real chart and watch the pullback enter it and hold: wicks into the zone, closes back above it, volume drying as sellers finish. Same defended-line logic in gap clothing — the only difference from Flavor one is that the level is a zone, not a single close, so you use the zone's boundaries. Top of the zone is where defense begins; bottom of the zone is where the claim of support is fully broken.
chapters.on_screen: A daily chart with the up-gap zone shaded and the first pullback holding it (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, May–August 2023 (prices split-adjusted for the 10:1 of June 2024 — ≈10× these at the time). Shade the up-gap zone: May 24 pre-gap close ≈$30.55 to the May 25 open ≈$38.52 — no volume printed there, but every gap-day buyer's cost sits at or above it. First controlled pullback runs into June 7: the low ≈$37.36 wicks into the zone's top, then closes recover above ≈$38 as sell volume dries — the defense arriving. Boundaries: top of zone = where defense begins; bottom ≈$30.55 = support fully broken. Later summer dips never test it. Template: holding candle ≈June 8, entry over its high ≈$39.50, stop under the pullback low ≈$37.20, run to the ≈$47.16 August 24 close, ≈+3R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the candle that holds the zone, entry over its high, stop under the zone, sized through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %.
chapters.speaker_notes: One template covers both flavors, three parts. Part one, the signal: price returns to the level and prints a candle that HOLDS the zone — a low that tests it, a close back above it. That candle is the defense showing up on schedule. Part two, the entry: over that holding candle's high — you buy the proof, not the touch. Part three, the stop: under the zone, where the defense has objectively failed. Then size it. Entry $47.50 over the holding candle, stop $45.60 under the zone — a 4% stop distance. Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, so at 1% account risk: 0.01 ÷ 0.04 = 25% position, subject to the regime table's cap — 20-25% only in GREEN with an A+ grade, 15% in YELLOW, 8% in ORANGE. The template never changes; only which flavor drew the line does.
chapters.on_screen: The holding candle, entry-over-its-high, and under-the-zone stop marked on the Gap Support example, sizing worked in the margin

chapters.beat: walk a zone break where the defense never shows up, name it as the invalidation (not a dip to average into), and close by restating the principle: one line, two flavors, same trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the honest ending: sometimes the defense never shows up. Walk a zone break — price enters the level, the holding candle never prints, and instead it closes decisively below the zone on expanding volume. Name that for what it is: the invalidation. The institutions either finished distributing or chose not to defend, and either way the premise of the trade is gone. This is NOT a dip to average into — 'it held last time' is exactly the sentence that precedes the worst losses in this setup, because a broken high-volume level flips from support to overhead supply, with every defender now trapped. If you are in from the holding-candle entry, the stop under the zone takes you out mechanically. If you were waiting, you simply never got a signal. Restate the close: one line, two flavors, same trade — and when the line breaks, no trade at all.
chapters.on_screen: A counter-example daily chart where the high-volume level breaks cleanly on expanding volume (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, April–September 2024 (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). The level: the high-volume support shelf ≈$68–75 that held the April and May pullbacks. The failure: late July re-enters the level and no holding candle ever prints; the August 7 earnings reaction gaps −13.7% and closes decisively below on expanding volume (≈$61.70 to ≈$49.27), and the August 28 10-K-delay bar (≈−19% close-to-close, closing ≈$44.35 on ≈5× average — the heaviest day of the period) confirms. Name it: invalidation — the broken level flips to overhead supply and the stock more than halves into autumn, ≈$29.11 at the October close and ≈$17.25 at the November 15 low. Holding-candle entries exited mechanically at the under-zone stop for ≈−1R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Kicker Candle: The Trap That Closes Above Yesterday's High
lessons.note: The prior day closes weak and looks broken — then a catalyst gaps the stock to close above that day's high, trapping every short who leaned on the breakdown; the cleanest RED TO GREEN entry in the catalog. One real squeeze with the short-interest context and the short-covering fuel visible in the volume.

chapters.beat: open on the prior day's weak close on a real chart and voice the short seller's thesis out loud, because their conviction is the fuel for this setup.
chapters.speaker_notes: Start on yesterday's chart and argue the SHORT side out loud, sincerely, because their conviction is this setup's fuel. Yesterday closed weak — bottom of its range, below the level everyone was watching, on real volume. The short seller's thesis writes itself: the stock is broken, the breakdown is confirmed, lean on it with a stop just above yesterday's high. Thousands of traders took exactly that position at the close and overnight, and the heavier the short interest already in the name, the bigger that leaning crowd is. Hold on this: nothing about their read was stupid. The chart really did look broken. That is precisely what makes what happens next so violent — the more reasonable the short looked, the more trapped money there is when the gap invalidates it before the open even prints.
chapters.on_screen: The prior day's weak close on the daily chart, with the short's stop level marked above (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: ANF daily, August 2023 — a heavily-shorted mall retailer into its August 23 report. Show August 22's close ≈$41.16: red, near the bottom of a week-long pullback ≈$41–45 after the broad-market slide, below the level swing traders were watching (read exact levels). Argue the short case sincerely: broken chart, failed summer breakout, stop just above yesterday's high ≈$42.50 — mark that stop level on screen, and note the elevated short interest already in the name. Nothing about the read was stupid — which is exactly why the next morning's candle is so violent: that reasonable-looking cluster became the fuel for a +20.8% gap and a ≈+24% close-to-close overnight invalidation (chapter 2). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the catalyst gaps the stock up to CLOSE above that weak day's high, trapping every short who leaned on the breakdown, with the trapped cohort circled on the chart.
chapters.speaker_notes: Overnight, the catalyst lands — earnings, guidance, a contract — and the stock gaps up so hard it opens above yesterday's HIGH and holds there into the close. That is the kicker candle: no retest, no warning, no chance for the shorts to exit near their entries. Circle the trapped cohort on the chart: everyone who shorted yesterday's weakness is now underwater from the first print of the day, their stops sitting right where price already is. Every tick higher forces more of them to buy to cover, and their buying pushes price into the next layer of stops. The candle's shape tells you the trap is sprung — a close above the weak day's high means the breakdown thesis has been invalidated at the daily level, not just intraday noise. You are not reading the news; you are reading the trapped positioning the news detonated.
chapters.on_screen: The kicker candle gapping and closing above the weak day's high, with the trapped-short zone shaded
chapters.example_spec: Same chart, one day forward: ANF daily, August 23, 2023. The blowout quarter with raised guidance gaps the stock so hard it OPENS at ≈$49.72 — far above the prior day's ≈$42.50 high — and holds, closing ≈$50.86, a +20.8% gap and ≈+24% close-to-close, on ≈7× average volume, the heaviest print of the year. Shade the trapped-short zone (entries ≈$41–43); their stops sat where price opened, so covering is forced from the first print. Annotate the candle: gap, no retest, close above the weak day's high — breakdown thesis invalidated at the daily level. Entry over the kicker's high ≈$52 against its midpoint ≈$50 paid ≈+4R by the ≈$61 October close and double-digit R into the ≈$78 late-November high. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The cleanest RED TO GREEN in the catalog
chapters.beat: map the kicker to its entry type from the Module 7 table, mark the trigger and the stop, and size it through the formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: Map it to the entry-trigger table from Module 7: the kicker is the cleanest RED TO GREEN in the catalog — yesterday printed red and broken, today reclaims and closes above it, and the trigger is price proving the flip is real. Mark the trigger at the push through the opening consolidation or yesterday's high, whichever the structure gives you, exact to the tick. The stop goes under the reclaim structure — the level where, if price trades back below it, the trap has failed and the shorts were right after all. Then the formula, out loud: entry $24.30, stop $22.85 — a 6% stop distance. Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, so at 1% account risk: 0.01 ÷ 0.06 ≈ a 16.7% position. Within the GREEN + A+ 20-25% ceiling, so the formula's answer stands. Stop first, distance second, size last.
chapters.on_screen: The setup-to-entry-type mapping table (RED TO GREEN row highlighted) beside the marked trigger and stop

chapters.beat: replay the squeeze with the short-interest context stated up front and the short-covering fuel pointed out bar by bar in the volume pane.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the real squeeze with the context stated before the first bar: short interest in the name was enormous — a large fraction of the float sold short — so the trapped cohort was not a few day traders, it was a crowded institutional position. Now walk the volume pane bar by bar and point at the fuel: the surge on the gap open is shorts covering at market; the follow-through bars where price rises on RISING volume with barely a pullback are forced buying, not fresh conviction — covering buyers don't wait for dips, they pay whatever the tape asks. Note how long the squeeze persists: crowded shorts cannot all exit in a day any more than institutions can build a position in one. This is the same repricing logic as the PEG, inverted — the buyers are involuntary, and involuntary buyers are the most reliable kind.
chapters.on_screen: CVNA daily, June 2023 — the high-short-interest guidance-surprise squeeze, volume pane annotated (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: CVNA daily, June 2023 (prices split-adjusted — ≈5× these at the time). State context before bar one: short interest was enormous, widely reported near half the float. June 7 close ≈$3.11; June 8 the record-EBITDA pre-announcement opens ≈$3.76 (+20.9%) and closes ≈$4.85, up ≈56%, on ≈8× average volume — the heaviest day of the period. Walk the volume pane: the open surge is market-order covering; the following sessions rising on RISING volume with barely a pullback are involuntary buyers, not fresh conviction. Note persistence — crowded shorts cannot all exit in a day: ≈$5.18 by the June close, ≈$11.16 at the July 19 debt-deal gap. A June 8 opening-range entry ≈$3.95 with a day-low stop ≈$3.60 paid ≈+2.5R day one and 20R+ by July. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: fill the five-field card, flag the failure mode (a kicker that closes back inside yesterday's range is dead), and close on the doctrine: you're not buying news, you're buying trapped shorts.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the five-field card. Context: a weak, broken-looking prior close in a name with meaningful short interest — check the short interest before the open; it is the fuel gauge. Pattern: overnight catalyst gaps price above the weak day's high. Trigger: RED TO GREEN, the reclaim priced to the tick. Stop: under the reclaim structure. Failure mode — and flag this one hard: a kicker that closes back INSIDE yesterday's range is dead. If the shorts absorb the gap and push price back into the prior day's range by the close, there was no trap, just a headline they sold into, and holding it hoping is how a squeeze trade becomes a bagholding. Close on the doctrine sentence: you're not buying news, you're buying trapped shorts. If the trap isn't visible in the positioning and the volume, there is no trade — however loud the headline.
chapters.on_screen: The Five-Field Setup Card toolkit artifact, filled live for the Kicker Candle, failure-mode line highlighted

lessons.title: Catalyst Taxonomy + the Earnings-Season Game Plan + 15 Gap Reps
lessons.note: Which catalysts have legs — earnings, FDA, contracts, guidance raises — versus PR fluff that fades by 10:30, ranked by historical follow-through so the member stops treating all gaps as equal. Artifact: the earnings-season prep sheet; closes with 15 mixed gap reps, answer covered, recycling one RS-line question from Module 4. Then the field week: one week live — scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry/stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome vs plan. 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next family.

chapters.beat: rank the catalysts by historical follow-through on screen: earnings, FDA, contracts, and guidance raises have legs; PR fluff fades by 10:30, with one real fluff-fade chart as proof.
chapters.speaker_notes: Rank the catalysts by historical follow-through, top to bottom, and make the member memorize the order. Tier one, the catalysts with legs: earnings surprises with raised guidance, FDA approvals, major contract wins, guidance raises — events that change what the business is WORTH, forcing multi-day institutional repricing. Tier two, tradeable but weaker: analyst upgrades, index inclusion, partnership announcements. Bottom tier, the fade fuel: PR fluff — vague 'strategic initiatives,' crypto or AI pivots from companies with no revenue in either, letters of intent. Those gaps are typically faded by 10:30 because no institution needs to reprice anything. Show one real fluff-fade as proof: the open pop, the 10:30 rollover, the full round trip. The lesson's job in one line: stop treating all gaps as equal — the catalyst's tier sets the trade's grade before the chart gets a vote.
chapters.on_screen: The catalyst follow-through ranking table, beside one real PR-fluff gap faded by 10:30 (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: Beside the ranking table, show TSLA 5-minute plus daily, July 13, 2020 (NKLA is delisted since its 2025 bankruptcy — no chart to pull). Prices split-adjusted for the 2020 5:1 and 2022 3:1 — ≈15× these at the time. Textbook bottom-tier catalyst: no numbers, just price-target chatter after a parabolic run. Prior close ≈$102.98; opens ≈$110.60 (+7.4%), spikes to ≈$120 in the first hour (read the exact high), rolls over by late morning and closes ≈$99.80 — RED on the day, the entire pop surrendered same session on ≈3× volume that was all front-loaded churn, no institutional repricing. Any opening-range entry stopped for ≈−1R by lunch. Contrast aloud with tier-one catalysts — earnings plus raised guides — that reprice for weeks. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: fill the earnings-season prep sheet live against the actual upcoming reporting calendar: which names, which nights, and which gap setups each could produce.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now turn the taxonomy into a weekly operating plan. Open the actual upcoming reporting calendar and fill the earnings-season prep sheet live, three columns. Which names: your A-list and B-list holdings first, then the leaders of your two ranked hunting-ground themes, then high-short-interest names where a surprise means a kicker. Which nights: map each name to its report date and time — before the open or after the close — because that decides which MORNING you show up prepared. Which setups: for each name, write the gap setup it could produce — a neglected name is an EP candidate, an established leader is a PEG candidate, a crowded short is a kicker candidate, anything else is a first-pullback gapper at best. This sheet is filled every season, and the premarket homework from the flagship lesson runs against it every reporting morning. Preparation is the position.
chapters.on_screen: The earnings-season prep sheet artifact, filled live against the Calendar's upcoming reporting weeks

chapters.beat: recycle one RS-line question from Module 4 cold, then show why a gap without the RS and volume witness is a lower-grade trade no matter how loud the headline.
chapters.speaker_notes: Cold quiz, no warning — one RS-line question straight from Module 4: here is a stock printing new price highs; the RS line versus SPY is flat-to-down; leader or laggard? The answer is laggard — the price high has no relative-strength witness, and the missing witness disqualifies it. Now apply the same court to gaps: a gap without the RS and volume witness is a lower-grade trade no matter how loud the headline. A tier-one catalyst on a name whose RS line was already rising and whose gap volume runs multiples of average is an A+ candidate. The same catalyst on a laggard with ordinary volume is a B at best — and remember what the sizing table says about a B: 15% ceiling territory shrinks fast, and a B in ORANGE is a skip, always. Confirmation is not a separate skill you learned once in Module 4; it is a gate every gap must pass.
chapters.on_screen: Covered-answer RS-line chart from the Module 4 drill, then a gap graded with and without the RS/volume witness
chapters.example_spec: After the covered-answer RS quiz, grade one gap twice with an RS-vs-SPY subpane. With the witness: NVDA daily, May 25, 2023 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time) — the RS line was already at new highs before the gap (NVDA ≈+110% YTD against SPY ≈+9%), and the gap opened ≈$38.52, +26.1%, on ≈3× average volume: tier-one catalyst plus rising RS plus volume = A+ candidate, and the trail paid ≈+3R. Without the witness (NKLA is delisted — use META instead): META daily, April 28, 2022 — a loud beat gaps +16.0% to open ≈$202.92 and close ≈$205.73 on ≈3.5× volume, but the RS history is a laggard's. B at best, and a B in ORANGE is a skip — META closed ≈$93 six months later. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run the reps across EP, PEG, gapper, HVE/Gap Support, and Kicker: name the setup, the entry, and the stop before each reveal.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fifteen charts, answer covered, all five family setups interleaved: Episodic Pivot, Power Earnings Gap, News/Earnings Gapper, High Volume Edge or Gap Support, Kicker. For every chart the member must commit to three things BEFORE the reveal: the setup name, the entry, and the stop. Enforce the tells while grading: neglected name plus 10%+ surprise gap equals EP; established leader clearing its whole base on a raised guide equals PEG; headline gap holding range equals gapper, entered on the reclaim, never the open; price returning to a heavy-volume close or up-gap zone equals HVE or Gap Support; a gap closing above a weak prior day's high in a shorted name equals kicker. Include two deliberate no-trades — a fluff catalyst and a gap opening inside its base — because 'skip' is a correct answer and the deck must reward it. Review every miss by naming which tell was misread.
chapters.on_screen: The 15-chart cover-the-answer rep deck — mixed real gap charts, labels hidden until each reveal

chapters.marker: The gate and the field week
chapters.beat: state the pass bar (80% on the reps), then the field week mechanics: scan nightly, card 2-3 live candidates of THIS family with entry and stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome versus plan — drill plus completed field log opens the next family.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the gate: 80% on the reps — twelve of fifteen — to pass this module. A miss means targeted rewatch of the lesson whose setup you misread, then retake with fresh charts. Then the field week, the part that makes it real. For one week, live: run the nightly scan every night; find two to three genuine candidates of THIS family — gaps and catalyst names, which means the reporting calendar is your scan's co-pilot this week; write the five-field card for each with exact entry and stop; log every one in the Journal whether it triggers or not; and when the week closes, grade each outcome against plan — not against P&L, against PLAN. Pilot size or paper only, per the standing guardrail, until both the M5 sizing gate and this family's drill are cleared. Eighty percent on the drill plus the completed field log opens Family IV.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal's trade log with a field-week entry template open, the 80% pass bar stated on a slide

modules.label: M10 · Setup Family IV: Reversals & Reclaims — and the Short-Side Mirror

lessons.title: FLAGSHIP — U&R (Undercut & Rally): The Shakeout You Buy
lessons.note: Price briefly undercuts a prominent prior low — stopping out weak holders, luring shorts — then reclaims it: the PREV LOW RECLAIM entry with the stop back under the undercut low, the tightest stop in the playbook, and the family-wide rule that counter-trend trades size smallest. Two winners with the trapped-participant logic narrated bar by bar, plus one reclaim that failed the same day, exited at plan.

chapters.beat: open on a real prominent prior low and narrate what lives there: resting stops below, shorts waiting to press, and the family doctrine up front — counter-trend trades size smallest.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a prominent prior low and narrate what actually lives at that price. Below it: a shelf of resting sell-stops from every holder who bought the base and placed their stop 'under the low,' exactly as they were taught. Around it: short sellers waiting for the break, ready to press. A prominent low is not a line — it is a pile of standing orders, and when price undercuts it, all of them fire at once. The U&R is the trade that buys that liquidation. And lead with the family doctrine before any mechanics: this is the Reversals & Reclaims family, and counter-trend trades size SMALLEST. Everything in the first three families traded with the trend; this family trades against the immediate move, so the burden of proof is higher and the size is lower. Say it now, repeat it every lesson: counter-trend trades size smallest.
chapters.on_screen: A daily chart with a prominent prior low marked and the resting stop cluster + short entries annotated below it
chapters.example_spec: QQQ daily, 2022 — this lesson's own tape, one chapter early. Mark the prominent prior lows: the June 16 low ≈$269.28 and the late-September/early-October shelf ≈$262–263. Annotate what lives beneath them: resting sell-stops from every base buyer taught to stop 'under the low,' plus shorts waiting to press the break — a pile of standing orders, not a line. Then show October 13 undercutting to ≈$254.26, every order firing at once, before the massive reclaim (next chapter) that closed ≈$268.82 the same day for ≈+2R, on the heaviest volume of the whole window. State the family doctrine over this chart: counter-trend trades size smallest. Read exact levels off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the undercut candle in slow motion: weak holders stopped out, shorts lured in below the low, and then the reclaim that turns both crowds into forced buyers.
chapters.speaker_notes: Slow the undercut candle down to a bar-by-bar narration. Price dips below the prior low: the resting sell-stops trigger — weak holders are ejected at the worst price of the move, and their market sells accelerate the dip. Shorts see the breakdown confirm and pile in below the low, stops just overhead. For a moment, everyone bearish is right. Then the selling exhausts — the stops are done firing, there is no one left to sell — and price reclaims the low. Now walk the two trapped crowds: the stopped-out holders watching the stock trade back above where they were forced out, many buying back in; and the shorts who entered below the low, now underwater within hours, whose covering is market BUYING. The reclaim converts both crowds into forced or eager buyers simultaneously. That double conversion is the fuel, and it is why the rally leg is often faster than the undercut was.
chapters.on_screen: QQQ daily, October 13 2022 — the CPI-morning undercut of the prior low and the massive same-day reclaim

chapters.marker: PREV LOW RECLAIM, the tightest stop in the playbook
chapters.beat: mark the entry as the reclaim of the undercut low, the stop just back under it, and show how that tiny stop distance sizes through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %.
chapters.speaker_notes: The entry is the trigger from the Module 7 table: PREV LOW RECLAIM — you buy as price reclaims the undercut prior low, to the tick. The stop goes just back under the undercut low: if price loses that low again, the shakeout thesis is dead and you are out. That is the tightest stop in the playbook — often 2-3% — and here is the trap inside the gift. Run the formula: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. At 1% account risk with a 2% stop, the formula says 0.01 ÷ 0.02 = a 50% position. The formula is not the last word — the table is. GREEN + A+ caps you at 20-25%, and this family's own doctrine pushes below even that, because a tight stop cannot catch an overnight gap and counter-trend trades size smallest. Cap it. A tight stop never licenses a monster position.
chapters.on_screen: The reclaim entry and back-under-the-low stop marked to the tick, with the formula-vs-table cap worked in the margin
chapters.example_spec: QQQ daily plus 5-minute, October 13, 2022. Mark to the tick on your platform: undercut prior low = the late-September shelf ≈$262–263; CPI-morning flush ≈$254.26, the low of the whole window; PREV LOW RECLAIM entry as price trades back up through ≈$263 mid-morning on the period's heaviest volume (≈2× average); stop just back under the undercut low ≈$260.50 — roughly a 1% stop, the tightest in the playbook. Run the trap-inside-the-gift math: 1% account risk ÷ 1% stop = a 100% position by formula — then cap it hard by the table and the family doctrine. Same-day close ≈$268.82 (≈+2R); ≈$277.95 at the October close (≈+6R) and ≈$282.75 by November 10 (≈+8R by uncapped math — which is why the cap exists). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: replay both real U&R winners with the trapped-participant logic voiced at every bar: who is being squeezed, who is covering, and where the fuel runs out.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay both winners with the trapped-participant logic voiced at every single bar — this narration IS the skill being transferred. Bar one after the reclaim: who is buying? Shorts covering, paying up because their stop is hit. Next bars: stopped-out holders re-entering, plus breakout buyers as price retakes the broken level. Where does the fuel run out? When the covering is done — watch the volume taper and the bars narrow; that is where the first-third partial at 2-3R comes off into strength. Manage the rest by the standard rules: breakeven stop at roughly +1R or the first higher low, then trail. On both charts, point at the moment the trade stopped being a squeeze and became an ordinary uptrend — because that is when the U&R's edge is spent and the normal management rules fully take over. Two different charts, identical crowd mechanics.

chapters.marker: The reclaim that failed the same day
chapters.beat: the third chart loses the low again within hours and is exited exactly at plan, closing on the point: the tight stop is WHY you can afford to be wrong fast and small.
chapters.speaker_notes: The third chart is the honest one. The undercut prints, the reclaim triggers, the entry fills — and within hours price rolls back over and loses the low again. The stop just under the undercut low takes you out the same day, at plan, for the planned fraction of 1R. No hesitation, no 'give it until tomorrow' — losing the low again means the sellers were not done and the shakeout read was wrong. Now close on the point this chart exists to make: the tight stop is WHY you can afford to be wrong fast and small. A 2% stop that fails costs you a scratch; the same failed read with a wide stop or a moved stop is a real wound. This family gives you the best-priced invalidations in the whole catalog — the entire discipline is taking them instantly when they hit. Wrong fast and small is a fine business. Wrong slow and big is the end of one.

Then the sequel: two weeks later a deeper flush to the ≈$348.11 October 13 low produced the real U&R off the same shelf. Wrong fast and small. Read exact levels off the chart.
