lessons.title: 2B Reversal — and Oops, Its Gap-Open Variant
lessons.note: The trap skeleton taught once: a break of a prior extreme that fails and snaps back through it — trapped cohort as fuel, the reclaim as trigger, the stop just beyond the trap's extreme. Then Oops as the gap-open variant of the identical mechanics: gap below the prior low, close back above it, same entry and stop logic. One real 2B and one real Oops, both with the trapped-volume read.

chapters.beat: teach the mechanics once on a clean diagram: price breaks a prior extreme, fails to follow through, and snaps back through it, with the trapped cohort named as the fuel.
chapters.speaker_notes: Teach the skeleton once, on a clean diagram, before any real chart: price breaks a prior extreme — a prior low for the long version — FAILS to follow through, and snaps back through the broken level. Three beats: break, fail, snap-back. The trapped cohort is the fuel, name them precisely: everyone who traded the BREAK. Breakdown sellers who shorted the new low, momentum sellers who dumped on the violation — all of them are positioned for follow-through that never comes, and the snap-back puts every one of them underwater within bars. This is the same crowd mechanics as the U&R — in fact the U&R is this skeleton applied to a prominent prior low. The 2B generalizes it: ANY prior extreme that breaks and fails builds the same trap. Learn the skeleton once and you will recognize it in every costume the market puts on it.
chapters.on_screen: A clean whiteboard-style diagram: break of prior extreme → failure → snap-back, trapped cohort labeled

chapters.beat: the reclaim of the broken extreme is the trigger, the stop sits just beyond the trap's extreme, and both are marked to the tick before any real chart appears.
chapters.speaker_notes: Mechanics before charts, marked to the tick on the diagram. The trigger is the RECLAIM of the broken extreme — for the long version, price trading back above the prior low it undercut. Not the undercut itself; bottom-fishing the break is guessing. The reclaim is proof the break failed, and proof is what you buy. From the Module 7 table this is the PREV LOW RECLAIM trigger. The stop sits just BEYOND the trap's extreme — below the lowest tick of the failed break. Logic: if price returns past the point of maximum trap, the break did not fail after all, the thesis is dead, and the shorts were right. That gives another tight-stop structure, so run the sequence in order: stop first, distance second, size last, through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, capped by the regime table and by this family's size-smallest doctrine — never the formula's raw output on a 2-3% stop.
chapters.on_screen: The same diagram with reclaim trigger and beyond-the-extreme stop marked to the tick

chapters.beat: work the trade on a real chart with the trapped-volume read: the heavy volume on the failed break IS the trapped crowd, and their unwinding drives the snap-back.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now a real chart, and teach the volume read that upgrades this from pattern-matching to evidence. Find the failed break bar and look at its volume: HEAVY. That heavy volume is not abstract — it is the trapped crowd, measured. Every share that traded on the breakdown bar below the prior low is a position that is wrong the moment the reclaim prints, and the bigger that volume, the bigger the forced unwinding that follows. Walk the trade: undercut on heavy volume, reclaim trigger fills, stop just beyond the trap's low, and then the snap-back leg — rising price on solid volume as the breakdown sellers cover and buyers front-run them. Point at where the fuel gauge reads empty: volume tapering as the covering completes, which is where partials come off at 2-3R into strength per the standard management rules. Heavy volume on the failed break is the setup's witness; without it, the trap is small and so is the trade.
chapters.on_screen: A real daily 2B: heavy-volume failed break, reclaim entry, stop, and the snap-back leg annotated (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SPY daily, August–October 2011. Prior extreme: the August 9 panic low ≈$110.27 (that bar closed ≈$117.48 on the heaviest volume of the period). Failed break: October 3 closes below it, October 4 flushes to ≈$107.43 on HEAVY volume — point at that bar: the trapped crowd, measured; every share traded down there is wrong the moment the reclaim prints. Failure and snap-back: October 4's final hour rips back through the prior extreme to close ≈$112.30. Trade: reclaim trigger ≈$110.40; stop just beyond the trap's low ≈$107.30 (risk ≈$3.10); snap-back leg on solid volume to ≈$120 within a week (≈+3R) and ≈$128–129 by October 27 (≈+6R) — partials 2–3R as covering volume tapers. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the gap opens below the prior day's low and closes back above it, and every rule maps one-to-one: same trapped cohort, same reclaim trigger, same beyond-the-extreme stop.
chapters.speaker_notes: Oops is the identical skeleton delivered by a gap. The stock gaps OPEN below the prior day's low — overnight fear, a scary headline, a margin-call morning — and then closes back above that low. Map every rule one-to-one and let the member see there is nothing new to learn. Trapped cohort: everyone who sold or shorted the gap open below the prior low — panicked at the worst print of the day. Trigger: the reclaim of the prior day's low, same PREV LOW RECLAIM logic. Stop: just beyond the trap's extreme — under the gap morning's low. The only difference is speed: the gap compresses the break-and-fail into the opening minutes instead of days, so the trap springs faster and the entry usually comes the same session. Same skeleton, gapped costume. If the member can trade a 2B, they can already trade an Oops — this chapter just proves it.
chapters.on_screen: Side-by-side diagram: 2B skeleton vs. Oops gap variant, each rule mapped one-to-one

chapters.marker: One real Oops, then the card
chapters.beat: work the real Oops with its trapped-volume read, then close by filling one five-field card that covers both: one skeleton, two costumes, identical trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the real Oops with the trapped-volume read: a panic morning where the stock gaps well below the prior day's low on enormous opening volume — that opening volume IS the trapped crowd, sellers ejected at the low of the move — then reclaims the prior low and closes strong. Entry on the reclaim, stop under the morning's extreme, sized small per family doctrine. Then close by filling ONE five-field card that covers both setups. Context: an extreme break of a prior low on heavy volume — multi-day for 2B, gap-open for Oops. Pattern: the break fails to follow through. Trigger: PREV LOW RECLAIM, to the tick. Stop: just beyond the trap's extreme. Failure mode: price loses the extreme again — out immediately, the break was real. One skeleton, two costumes, identical trade — and one card is all it takes to carry both.

lessons.title: Remount: Shake Out Below the Line, Retake It with Authority
lessons.note: A leader slips below its moving average, flushes weak hands, then remounts with a wide-range candle — 'with authority' defined numerically by range and volume thresholds on the remount bar, and explicitly contrasted with the 20 EMA Pullback: this is loss-and-RECLAIM of the line, a different trigger with a different stop. One authoritative remount against one feeble drift-back that failed.

chapters.marker: The leader that loses its line
chapters.beat: open on a real leader slipping below its moving average and pose the only question that matters: is this a shakeout flushing weak hands, or the start of the decline?
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a real leader — a stock that has ridden its moving average for months — slipping below the line, and pose the only question that matters: is this a shakeout flushing weak hands, or the start of the decline? Sit in the discomfort honestly, because at the moment it happens you cannot know. Every holder is asking the same question; the ones with weak conviction answer it by selling, and their selling is the flush. The Remount setup exists because the market itself answers the question — not with opinion but with the CHARACTER of the move back above the line. A violent, high-volume retake says institutions used the flush to buy. A quiet drift back says nobody cared. This lesson teaches you to wait for the answer instead of guessing at it, and to define 'answer' numerically so it cannot be argued with in the moment.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, August 2024 — the leader flushing below its 50 SMA after months above it (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, June–October 2024 — the era's leader, above its 50 SMA for months. Walk the loss of the line: July 30–August 5 the flush accelerates through the 50-day ≈$115 to the August 5 panic low ≈$90.69 — that bar gapped −14.2% to open ≈$92.06 and closed ≈$100.45 on ≈2× volume — then a retest ≈$99 on August 7: weak hands ejected, and genuinely unknowable in the moment whether shakeout or top. Then let the market answer: the mid-August remount (≈August 13, a +6.5% wide-range bar on heavy volume) drives price back through the line — a violent retake, institutions buying the flush — versus the quiet drift that would have said nobody cared. The worked trade (chapter 4) paid ≈+1R–1.7R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: define the remount bar numerically on screen: the range and volume thresholds it must clear, because a wide-range high-volume retake is institutions, and a quiet drift is nobody.
chapters.speaker_notes: 'With authority' is not a vibe — define it numerically on screen so the remount bar is a pass/fail check. Two thresholds on the retake bar. Range: a wide-range candle — the bar's range meaningfully larger than the recent average, on the order of one and a half to two times the average daily range of the pullback bars, closing in the top of its range and back above the line. Volume: expansion — clearly above average, ideally the heaviest bar of the whole pullback. The logic behind the numbers: a wide-range, heavy-volume retake is institutions absorbing every share the flush shook loose and paying up for more — size leaves footprints. A narrow, quiet drift back above the line is nobody; it is the absence of demand wearing the costume of recovery. Both thresholds or it is not a Remount. Write them on the card as numbers, and grade every candidate bar against them.
chapters.on_screen: The remount bar with range and volume thresholds annotated, pass/fail checked against each

chapters.marker: This is NOT the 20 EMA Pullback
chapters.beat: side-by-side with Module 8's flagship: the pullback HOLDS the line, the Remount LOSES and RECLAIMS it — a different trigger with a different stop below the shakeout low.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put this setup side by side with Module 8's flagship and draw the line hard, because confusing them costs money. The 20 EMA Pullback HOLDS the line: price touches or kisses the moving average, never meaningfully loses it, and resumes — the trigger is the resumption off a level that held, and the stop hides under that held level. The Remount LOSES the line and RECLAIMS it: price breaks below, flushes the weak hands, then retakes it with authority — the trigger is the authoritative retake bar, and the stop goes below the SHAKEOUT LOW, the flush's extreme, because that is the new invalidation. Different event, different trigger, different stop. Practical consequence: the Remount's stop is wider — the flush low is further away than a held level — so by the formula the position is smaller. Same line on the chart, two different trades. Name which one you are in before you touch the order ticket.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: a 20 EMA Pullback holding the line vs. the Remount losing and reclaiming it, triggers and stops contrasted
chapters.example_spec: Left panel: META daily, May–July 2023 — the 20 EMA Pullback HOLDING the line: successive dips tag the rising 20 EMA (≈$230 at the May 5 low, ≈$262 in early June — read exact) and never meaningfully lose it, the months closing ≈$264.72, ≈$286.98, ≈$318.60; trigger = resumption off the held level, stop hides just under it. Right panel: NVDA daily, July–August 2024 — the Remount LOSING the line: two-plus weeks below the 50-day, flush to ≈$90.69, then the authoritative mid-August retake; trigger = the remount bar's high ≈$117, stop = below the shakeout low ≈$99. Annotate the consequence: the Remount's wider stop means a smaller position; META's held-line trades paid 2–3R partials, NVDA's remount ≈+1R–1.7R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: entry over the remount bar, stop below the flush low, sized through the formula, and managed to its first target on a real chart.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work the real trade end to end. The flush: several sessions below the moving average, weak hands ejected. The remount bar: wide range, heavy volume, closing back above the line — both thresholds pass on screen. Entry: over the remount bar's high, buying the proof of authority, not the hope of it. Stop: below the flush low. Now the math with real numbers. Entry $126.50 over the remount bar; flush low puts the stop at $117.60 — a 7% stop distance. Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, so at 1% account risk: 0.01 ÷ 0.07 ≈ a 14.3% position. On $50,000 that is roughly $7,150, 56 shares, about $500 at risk. Under the GREEN + A+ ceiling, so the formula stands. Then manage to the first target by the standard rules — breakeven at about +1R, first third off at 2-3R into strength.
chapters.on_screen: The full remount trade on the daily chart — flush, remount bar, entry, flush-low stop — with the sizing arithmetic in the margin
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, August 2024, end to end. Flush: two-plus weeks below the 50-day, the August 5 low ≈$90.69 (gap −14.2%, close ≈$100.45), retest ≈$99 on August 7. Remount bar: ≈August 13 — wide range, heavy volume, closing back at the line ≈$116; both thresholds pass on screen. Entry: over the remount bar's high ≈$117. Stop: below the flush/retest low ≈$99 — ≈15% distance, so 1% account risk gives ≈a 6–7% position; write the arithmetic in the margin and note how the wide stop shrinks size versus the notes' 7% example. Outcome: late-August high ≈$131, then the ≈$132.76 October close and the ≈$152.89 November 21 high — ≈+1R to +1.7R on the trail. The prize is re-boarding the leader with defined risk. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the counter-example crawls back above the line on shrinking volume and rolls over, closing on the rule: no authority, no trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: The counter-example, graded against the same two thresholds. Price crawls back above the line — but the bars are narrow, the closes are mid-range, and the volume is SHRINKING as it rises. Range test: fail. Volume test: fail. That is not institutions absorbing a flush; it is a market with no sellers left and no buyers either, drifting on air. Watch what happens next: the drift stalls at the first overhead supply and rolls over, and everyone who bought the 'recovery' is trapped in a lower high. The trader who required authority never entered and lost nothing. Close on the rule as a flat sentence: no authority, no trade. The moving average being reclaimed is not the signal — the CHARACTER of the reclaim is. Two thresholds, both numeric, both checkable before entry. The chart either shows you size coming back in, or it shows you nothing — and you do not pay for nothing.
chapters.on_screen: A counter-example: low-volume narrow-bar drift back above the MA that rolls over into a lower high (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: QQQ daily, February–April 2022. After the March 14 low ≈$318, price crawls back above the falling 50-day ≈$350–358 in late March — grade it against both thresholds on screen: the final bars into the March 29 high ≈$371.83 are NARROW with mid-range closes (range test: fail) and volume SHRINKS as it rises (volume test: fail) — no institutions absorbing, a market drifting on air. The consequence: the drift stalls at overhead supply, rolls over into a lower high (≈$371.83 versus the ≈$404 early-January peak and the ≈$408.71 November 2021 record), loses the line in early April, and slides to the ≈$269.28 June 16 low. Buyers of the 'recovery' ≈$362 were stopped for −1R within days. No authority, no trade. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Slingshot: Recapture the 4-EMA of the Highs — Buy Momentum Resuming, Not the Low
lessons.note: A strong uptrend pulls back, stabilizes, then recaptures the 4-EMA of the highs — the entry is the resumption, never the guess at the bottom. Configures the non-standard 4-EMA-of-highs overlay on screen, then one clean recapture plus the anticipation entry that got run over.

chapters.marker: You are not buying the low
chapters.beat: open with the doctrine: bottom-guessers get run over, and the Slingshot's entire design is to buy momentum RESUMING, never the guess at the turn.
chapters.speaker_notes: Doctrine first: bottom-guessers get run over. Every trader feels the pull of buying the pullback low — it prices best, it feels smartest, and it is a guess with no evidence behind it, which is why the same pullback that 'looked done' keeps not being done. The Slingshot's entire design is to remove the guess: you buy momentum RESUMING, never the turn itself. In a strong uptrend, the pullback ends when price proves it has ended — by recapturing a fast reference line — and that proof is the entry. Yes, you pay a slightly worse price than the fantasy low-tick entry. In exchange you get an entry with evidence, a defined invalidation just below, and a structure where being wrong costs a controlled fraction of 1R instead of an averaging-down spiral. In this family the sequence is always the same: the market moves first, then you do. Never the reverse.
chapters.on_screen: A strong-uptrend pullback with three failed 'buy the low' guesses marked, each run over
chapters.example_spec: TSLA daily, September 2020 (prices split-adjusted for BOTH the 2020 5:1 and the 2022 3:1 — a 2020-era chart showed ≈3× these). The uptrend is undeniably strong — ≈$79 in early July to the ≈$167 September 1 high — then the September pullback down to ≈$110 by September 8. Mark three 'buy the low' guesses on the way down, each run over: the September 3 dip-buy ≈$136–140 into that day's −9% gap; the September 4 close ≈$139.45 that looked like a bounce; the September 8 open ≈$118.67, which closed ≈$110.07, −21% on the day. Each felt smart, priced 'best,' and carried zero evidence — each cost −1R or worse. The evidence entry paid ≈+4R (chapter 4). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: build the non-standard overlay live on the dashboard chart (an EMA on the HIGHS, not the closes) so every member leaves with the exact same line on their screen.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build the overlay live so every member leaves with the identical line. This is a NON-standard configuration: a 4-period exponential moving average calculated on the HIGHS, not the closes. On the dashboard chart, open the MA overlay slots, set period 4, type EMA, and switch the source field from close to high — walk the clicks on screen. Why the highs: in a strong uptrend the highs are the momentum frontier — the line hugs the advance tightly, and during a pullback price falls BELOW it by construction, since the line tracks where the highs were. That makes the recapture unambiguous: price closing back above a 4-EMA of the highs means the stock is printing at the frontier of its own recent strength again. A close-based line blurs that signal. Four periods keeps it fast — this is a resumption timer, not a trend filter; your trend filter is still the 9/20/50/200 stack underneath.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard chart's MA overlay settings — period 4, EMA, source = High — configured live on screen

chapters.beat: a strong uptrend pulls back, stabilizes below the line, and the RECAPTURE of the 4-EMA of the highs is the entry, with the stop under the stabilization low.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three phases, in order, all required. Phase one: a strong uptrend — the 9/20/50/200 stack in rising order, real momentum behind the name; the Slingshot only exists inside strength, never as a knife-catch in a downtrend. Phase two: the pullback stabilizes BELOW the 4-EMA of the highs — down-bars shrink, volume dries up, price stops making meaningful lower lows and chops sideways. Stabilization matters: a pullback still falling hard has no business being bought under any name. Phase three: the RECAPTURE — price closes back above the 4-EMA of the highs. That close is the entry signal; the entry is over that recapture bar. The stop goes under the stabilization low — the floor the pullback built. If price returns below that floor, the stabilization was false, the pullback is still alive, and the trade is dead. Trend, stabilization, recapture — miss any phase and there is no Slingshot.
chapters.on_screen: The three-phase anatomy annotated on one chart: rising MA stack, stabilization below the 4-EMA of highs, recapture bar

chapters.beat: the real trade entry-to-target with the stop and size run through Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, narrating why the recapture proves the buyers are back.
chapters.speaker_notes: The real trade, entry to target. The uptrend is established, the pullback stabilizes below the line for several sessions, then the recapture bar closes above the 4-EMA of the highs. Entry over that bar at $58.40; the stabilization low puts the stop at $55.50 — a 5% stop distance. Run it: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, so at 1% account risk, 0.01 ÷ 0.05 = a 20% position. On $50,000: $10,000, 171 shares, about $500 at risk — inside the GREEN + A+ 20-25% cell, legal only because this is an A+ chart in a permissive tape. As the trade works, narrate WHY the recapture proved the buyers were back: the very next bars ride the reclaimed line higher, exactly the behavior the frontier line predicts when demand returns. Breakeven at roughly +1R, first third off at 2-3R into strength, standard rules the rest of the way.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily, November–December 2020 — a pullback-and-recapture leg with entry, stop, and sizing worked (or substitute a firm trade)

Established uptrend: the November breakout ≈$136 runs to ≈$217 by December 8. Pullback: December 9–14 — price loses the 4-EMA of highs and stabilizes below it for ≈four sessions, low ≈$187 (read exact). Recapture bar ≈December 14–15, closing back above the line; entry over its high ≈$208; stop at the stabilization low ≈$187 — ≈10% distance, ≈a 10% position at 1% account risk (work it in the margin). The next bars ride the reclaimed line into the December 18 S&P-inclusion close ≈$231.67 on ≈5.6× volume (≈+1R fast) and the January high ≈$300 (≈+4R on the trail). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The anticipation entry that got run over
chapters.beat: the counter-example bought DURING the pullback before any recapture, stopped out as the low broke, closing on the line: the recapture is the permission slip.
chapters.speaker_notes: The counter-example is the same chart pattern traded one phase early. This trader bought DURING the pullback — below the 4-EMA of the highs, before any recapture — because the price 'looked cheap' and the stabilization 'looked close.' Then the stabilization failed: the low broke, the pullback resumed, and the anticipation entry was stopped out — or worse, held and averaged, the classic spiral this course's one commandment forbids. Put the two entries side by side on the same chart: the anticipator lost a full stop on a guess; the Slingshot trader entered two days later, a point higher, on evidence — and kept the entire move. The price difference between them was trivial; the evidence difference was the whole trade. Close on the line the member repeats: the recapture is the permission slip. No recapture, no entry — the market has not signed off yet, and you do not trade on its behalf.
chapters.on_screen: The same chart with both entries marked: the run-over anticipation buy vs. the recapture entry two days later

lessons.title: Failed H&S / Rounded Top: When the Breakdown Everyone Sees Never Comes
lessons.note: The most-watched topping pattern fails to break down and the crowded short becomes squeeze fuel for the next leg up — entry over the right-shoulder high. One famous historical example with the short-covering volume signature marked: the clearest lesson in trading other people's textbooks against them.

chapters.marker: The most-watched pattern in the textbook
chapters.beat: draw the head-and-shoulders every retail short is staring at, and state the setup's premise: when EVERYONE sees the top, the trade is on the other side.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the head-and-shoulders exactly the way every textbook does — left shoulder, head, right shoulder, neckline — because that familiarity is the point. This is the most-watched topping pattern in existence: every retail short, every chart blog, every trading forum is staring at the same neckline, and most of them are positioning short against it before it even breaks. Now state the setup's premise, which cuts against everything intuitive: when EVERYONE sees the top, the trade is on the other side. A pattern's power comes from who is positioned around it, and a universally-watched breakdown means a universally crowded short. If the breakdown delivers, fine — they win a crowded trade. But if it fails, the crowd itself becomes the setup. You are not trading the pattern; you are trading the positioning the pattern created. That reframe is the whole lesson.
chapters.on_screen: A textbook head-and-shoulders drawn on a real chart, neckline marked, with the crowded-short positioning annotated
chapters.example_spec: S&P 500 daily, May–August 2009 (SPX; SPY at ≈one-tenth works — its July 8 low was ≈$87.00). Draw it exactly as the textbook does: left shoulder ≈930 (early May), head ≈956 (June 11), right shoulder ≈931 (July 1), neckline ≈878–888. Annotate the crowd: in mid-2009 every blog and desk note stared at this neckline, shorts positioned before it broke. Pre-mark for later chapters: the July 8 break to ≈869.32 that never confirms, the July 13–15 reclaim, entry over the right-shoulder high ≈932, stop back inside ≈875 (risk ≈57 points), and the run to the ≈1,010 August 7 close (high ≈1,018, ≈+1.5R) and ≈1,101 by late October (≈+3R). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the mechanics: the neckline break never comes, the crowded short is trapped at bad prices, and their forced covering becomes the buying power for the next leg up.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the mechanics of the failure. The neckline break everyone is waiting for never comes — or breaks intraday and closes back above, no follow-through. Now inventory the trapped: shorts who pre-positioned in the right shoulder anticipating the break, shorts who sold the intraday violation, all of them at bad prices with stops clustered just above the right-shoulder high. Every bar that holds above the neckline increases their pain, and none of them planned for the pattern to simply... not work. When price turns up through the pattern, their forced covering becomes the buying power for the next leg — involuntary buyers, the most reliable kind, exactly the kicker-candle logic from Module 9 at pattern scale. The equation to write on screen: the more crowded the short, the bigger the fuel tank. A failed pattern nobody watched moves nothing. A failed pattern EVERYONE watched launches legs.
chapters.on_screen: The same chart: the neckline break that never confirms, trapped-short zones and their stop cluster marked above the right shoulder

chapters.beat: mark the trigger, place the stop back inside the pattern, and size it through the formula — you are long the moment the pattern officially fails.
chapters.speaker_notes: The trigger is the price that makes the failure official: the right-shoulder high. Above that level, the pattern's own geometry is broken — a head-and-shoulders cannot exist once price exceeds the right shoulder, so every short in the structure is now provably wrong, and their stops are firing into your entry. Mark the buy-stop just above the right-shoulder high, to the tick. The stop goes back INSIDE the pattern — below the structure that triggered the entry — because if price falls back into the pattern's body, the failure failed and the top may be real after all. Then size it through the formula: say entry $91.50, stop $85.10 back inside the pattern — a 7% stop distance; at 1% account risk that is 0.01 ÷ 0.07 ≈ a 14% position, checked against the regime table's cell before the order goes in. You are long the moment the pattern officially fails — not before, not on a hunch, on the geometry.
chapters.on_screen: The entry over the right-shoulder high and the back-inside-the-pattern stop, marked to the tick with sizing worked

chapters.beat: replay the historical example with the short-covering volume signature marked bar by bar: the surge that isn't new buyers, it's trapped shorts paying any price to leave.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the famous historical example: the S&P 500 in the summer of 2009. Coming off the March low, the index carved what the entire financial world identified as a textbook head-and-shoulders — it was discussed on television, in every newsletter, by every bear who believed the rally was a mirage. The neckline broke intraday in July 2009... and the breakdown never followed through. Price reclaimed the neckline, then took out the right-shoulder high, and the most-watched top of the era failed in public. Mark the volume signature bar by bar as it runs: the surge off the failure is not new bulls arriving with fresh conviction — it is trapped shorts paying any price to leave, covering that feeds on itself as each layer of stops triggers the next. The market ran for months afterward. The bigger the audience a pattern has, the more spectacular its failure — and 2009 had the biggest audience a pattern ever drew.
chapters.on_screen: S&P 500 daily, June–August 2009 — the famous failed head-and-shoulders, short-covering volume signature marked

chapters.marker: Trading other people's textbooks against them
chapters.beat: close with the transferable lesson and the five-field card: the more obvious the topping pattern, the more explosive its failure.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the transferable lesson, because it is bigger than this one pattern: the more obvious the topping pattern, the more explosive its failure. That principle generalizes to every crowded structure — obvious support everyone buys, obvious breakdowns everyone shorts. The crowd's textbook is your positioning map. Then fill the five-field card. Context: a widely-watched topping pattern in an otherwise healthy name, visible crowded short positioning. Pattern: the neckline break that never confirms. Trigger: buy-stop over the right-shoulder high — the price where the pattern is geometrically dead. Stop: back inside the pattern body. Failure mode: price re-enters the pattern and holds there — the top may be real; exit without argument. And the family reminder one more time: this is a Reversals & Reclaims trade, so it sizes small. You are trading other people's textbooks against them — do it with a stop, at modest size, or not at all.
chapters.on_screen: The Five-Field Setup Card toolkit artifact, filled live for the Failed H&S

lessons.title: Parabolic Long: Riding the Vertical, Bar by Bar
lessons.note: The runaway move managed candle by candle as the angle goes vertical — no fixed target, a pre-agreed give-back rule decided before entry, exits keyed to climax signals (largest spread, biggest gap, heaviest volume of the run). One full parabolic ridden from base to blow-off with each daily hold/trim decision narrated.

chapters.beat: open on a real parabolic in progress and name why every normal tool breaks here: no base, no fixed target, an angle going vertical, and a crowd in full euphoria.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on a real parabolic mid-flight and name why every tool in the first nine modules breaks here. No base — the stock left its last consolidation weeks ago, so there is no pattern to measure. No fixed target — a stock going vertical has no resistance map; it is in price discovery driven by crowd psychology, up 50-100% in days. The angle itself keeps steepening, which means any moving-average trail lags hopelessly. And the crowd is in full euphoria — the news is everywhere, your barber owns it, and every fiber of the position wants you to believe this time is different. The Parabolic Long is the setup for riding that move anyway — but only with a management system built for it, decided in advance, executed bar by bar. This lesson is almost entirely about exits, because in a parabola the entry is the easy part and the exit is the entire trade.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily, January 2020 — the vertical run in progress, angle steepening, no base in sight

chapters.marker: The give-back rule, decided BEFORE entry
chapters.beat: pre-commit on camera to the exact give-back that ends the trade, because the one decision you cannot make honestly mid-parabola is when to leave.
chapters.speaker_notes: Pre-commit on camera to the exact give-back that ends the trade, and explain why it must happen BEFORE entry: the one decision you cannot make honestly mid-parabola is when to leave. Once you are up huge and the crowd is euphoric, your judgment is part of the crowd's — every fresh high resets your anchor and 'I'll sell if it pulls back' quietly becomes 'it always bounces.' So the rule is written now, while calm: a fixed give-back — for example, surrendering a set fraction of the open profit, or a close below the prior two days' low — and it is an appointment, not a debate, exactly like every stop in this course. Write the specific rule on the trade card before the order. The give-back rule is not there to catch the top; nothing catches the top. It exists to guarantee that whenever the end comes, you leave with most of the move instead of donating it back.
chapters.on_screen: A trade card with the give-back rule written and dated BEFORE the entry, shown on camera

chapters.beat: the three exit signals defined and drawn: the largest spread of the run, the biggest gap of the run, the heaviest volume of the run — any of them means the crowd's last buy is in.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three exit signals, defined and drawn, each measured against the run itself — not against averages, against THIS move's own history. One: the largest spread of the run — a daily bar whose range exceeds every prior bar of the advance. Two: the biggest gap of the run — an opening gap larger than any gap the move has printed. Three: the heaviest volume of the run — the highest-volume day of the entire advance. Any one of them firing means the same thing: the crowd's last buyer is in. Climaxes are maximum-intensity events — the widest bar, biggest gap, and heaviest volume happen when the greatest number of people capitulate INTO the stock at once, and when the last buyer has bought, there is only one direction left. These are not sell-some signals; combined with the give-back rule they are the exit. Draw all three on the example so the member sees each superlative printing at the end, not the middle.
chapters.on_screen: The blow-off region of the same parabolic with largest spread, biggest gap, and heaviest volume each labeled

chapters.beat: replay one complete parabolic from base to blow-off with every daily hold-or-trim decision spoken: what the bar showed, what the rule said, what was done.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay one complete parabolic from base to blow-off, and narrate every single session in the same three-beat cadence: what the bar showed, what the rule said, what was done. Early: normal up-bars, no climax signals, give-back untouched — hold. Mid-run: a wide bar, but not the widest of the run — checklist says no signal; hold, trail mentally against the give-back line. As the angle steepens: partials into strength are legitimate — a third off into an accelerating move banks the trade's cost basis while the rules keep the rest working. Late: gaps appearing, spreads widening, volume building — checklist tightening but not fired; hold, knuckles white, rules doing the holding for you. The narration teaches the real skill of this setup: subordinating a screaming emotional environment to a three-item checklist and a pre-written give-back line, one daily decision at a time, no improvisation anywhere.
chapters.on_screen: The full parabolic, base to blow-off, with a hold/trim decision annotation on every daily bar

chapters.beat: the exit fires on the climax signals, the give-back rule caps the damage of imperfect timing, and the close compares what was kept versus the round-trip the euphoric holder took.
chapters.speaker_notes: The final day: the checklist fires — say the run's biggest gap at the open, then its widest spread and heaviest volume by the close. The exit executes on the signals, and the give-back rule is standing behind them as the backstop either way. Be honest on camera about the imperfection: the exit is not the top tick — nobody sells the top tick of a parabola — and the give-back rule's job was to cap the cost of that imperfect timing, which it did. Now run the comparison that makes the lesson permanent: what the rules-trader kept versus the round trip the euphoric holder took. The holder who had no give-back rule and no climax checklist watched the same stock give back most of the entire advance in a fraction of the time it took to build — parabolas retrace as violently as they rise. Kept most of a monster with rules, or round-tripped it with hope. That is the entire argument for this lesson.
chapters.on_screen: TSLA daily, February 2020 — the blow-off and the violent retrace, exit-on-signals vs. round-trip holder marked

lessons.title: Parabolic Short: Shorting the Crack of a 3-5 Day Blow-Off
lessons.note: The hardest setup in the book and the true short-side mirror: a 3-5 day blow-off stretched miles above the averages, shorted only as it cracks — never into strength — with buy-stop protection above and the snap back to the 9 EMA as target, every long rule inverted on screen one at a time. States the patience rules: appears a handful of times a year, smallest size in the catalog. Artifact: the long-rules/short-rules mirror table.

chapters.marker: The hardest setup in the book
chapters.beat: open with the honest framing: a 3-5 day blow-off stretched miles above the averages, a handful of appearances a year, and the smallest size in the entire catalog.
chapters.speaker_notes: Frame it honestly before any mechanics: this is the hardest setup in the book, and it earns that title three ways. The qualifying structure is rare and specific — a 3-5 day terminal blow-off, stretched miles above the moving averages, at the end of a longer run; not every hot stock, THAT structure. It appears a handful of times a year across the whole market — this is not a weekly tool. And it carries the smallest size in the entire catalog, because the short side's risk is structurally different: a long's worst case is bounded, a short squeezed against you accelerates. So set expectations to camera: most members should paper this setup for a long time; some should simply know it exists and never trade it. It is in the course because it completes the education — it is the true short-side mirror of everything the long playbook taught — not because it is a regular income stream. Respect it accordingly.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI daily, February 2024 — the 3-5 day terminal blow-off stretched far above the 9/20/50/200 stack (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, January–February 2024 (prices split-adjusted for the 10:1 of October 2024 — ≈10× these at the time). Show the qualifying structure precisely: after the January 19 EP and a month-long run, the FINAL 3–5 days (≈February 12–16) go terminal — ≈$74 to the February 16 intraday high ≈$107.70, stretched far above the whole 9/20/50/200 stack. Mark the blow-off ingredients for later chapters: largest spread, biggest gap and heaviest volume all clustering at the end — February 16 traded ≈4× average, the heaviest day of the window — then that same bar reverses to close ≈$80.33: the crack, which paid ≈+0.3–0.5R to the snap-back (chapter 3). Keep the March 8 rebound to ≈$122.90 on the same chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the iron rule on a real blow-off: you short ONLY as it cracks, and every early short into the vertical is shown getting squeezed carried out on the same chart.
chapters.speaker_notes: The iron rule: you short ONLY as it cracks — never into strength. On the real blow-off, mark every place an early short 'knew' it was too high: day two of the vertical, day three, day four — and show each one getting squeezed out, because a parabolic's defining feature is that it goes further than any rational estimate. Shorting into strength is fighting the exact climax mechanics you learned in the Parabolic Long: while the last buyers are still arriving, there is no ceiling, and every early short's forced covering is literally part of the fuel that extends the move. The crack is the signal that the last buyer is in: the first heavy-volume reversal — a high-volume outside day, a gap-up that closes red, a wide bar that gives up its gains. Until the crack prints, there is no trade — only a stock going up and a graveyard of tops that were 'obvious' three days early. The crack is to this setup what the reclaim was to the U&R: the proof you wait for.
chapters.on_screen: The same blow-off with three early-short entries marked and squeezed out, then the crack bar highlighted

chapters.beat: the crack entry, buy-stop protection placed ABOVE (the short side's stop is a buy), the snap back to the 9 EMA as the target, and the smallest-size rule run through the 2% formula.
chapters.speaker_notes: Mechanics, with every element inverted from the long side. Entry: as the crack confirms — the break of the reversal bar's low. Protection: a BUY-stop placed ABOVE — the short side's stop is a buy order, sitting above the reversal high, because being wrong means the parabola has another leg and you must be taken out mechanically before the squeeze compounds. Target: the snap back to the 9 EMA — a parabolic stretches an extreme distance above even its fastest average, and the violent mean-reversion to the 9 EMA is the trade; you are not shorting a bear market, you are shorting an elastic band. Size: the smallest in the catalog, through the same formula. At 0.5% account risk with an 8% stop distance: 0.005 ÷ 0.08 ≈ a 6.25% position — half the usual account risk, deliberately, and never more than the 2% hard max under any argument. Wide stop, small size, defined target, mechanical exit both directions.
chapters.on_screen: The crack entry, buy-stop above the reversal high, and 9 EMA snap-back target marked, sizing worked at 0.5% risk
chapters.example_spec: Same chart: SMCI daily, February 2024 (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). Mechanics, never into strength: the crack bar is February 16 — spike ≈$107.70, close ≈$80.33 on ≈4× volume, the period's heaviest. Entry: short the crack's confirmation, the break of the crack bar's low ≈$78.60 on February 20 (that session closed ≈$78.76). Buy-stop above the reversal's upper supply zone ≈$94 (the literal ≈$107.70 extreme is the by-the-book stop). Target: the rising 9/20 EMA snap-back, tagged at the ≈$73.43 February 21 close — cover there for ≈+0.3–0.5R against that wide stop; at 0.5% account risk the ≈18% stop sizes to ≈a 3% position. Overstaying is punished: February 22 gapped +17.8% to open ≈$86.50 and close ≈$97.55. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The mirror, one rule at a time
chapters.beat: invert every long rule on screen while building the long-rules/short-rules mirror table live: trigger, stop direction, target, sizing, each flipped and written into its row.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build the long-rules/short-rules mirror table live, one row at a time, because seeing the inversions written down is what makes the short side stop feeling alien. Trigger: long buys proof of strength — a breakout, a reclaim; short sells proof of failure — the crack, never the anticipation of it. Stop direction: long's stop is a sell below invalidation; short's stop is a BUY above it — and it must be a hard order, because squeezes move faster than decisions. Target: long trails an open-ended trend on the 10/20-day; short takes a defined snap-back to the 9 EMA — the short is a mean-reversion trade, not a trend trade, so it is take-profit, not trail-and-hope. Sizing: long sizes by the table up to 20-25% in GREEN + A+; short sizes smallest in the catalog at reduced account risk. Time: longs can compound for months; shorts resolve in days. Same formula, same discipline, opposite reflexes — the table is the map between them.
chapters.on_screen: The long-rules/short-rules mirror table being filled row by row on screen

chapters.beat: close with the patience doctrine (it appears a handful of times a year; forcing it is how shorts blow up) and hand off the completed mirror table as the lesson's artifact.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the patience doctrine, stated as the setup's most important rule. This structure appears a handful of times a year — which means the correct position in this setup, almost all year, is NO position. Forcing it is how shorts blow up: the trader who shorts every strong stock because it 'looks parabolic' is fighting uptrends with the catalog's most dangerous tool, dying by a thousand squeezes while waiting for the one real blow-off. The discipline is inverted from everything else you have practiced: the skill is not execution, it is declining — months of watching hot stocks run without touching them, until the rare 3-5 day terminal vertical actually prints and then cracks. When it does, the mirror table is the checklist and the smallest-size rule is the seatbelt. Hand off the completed mirror table as the lesson's artifact, and repeat the family doctrine one last time: counter-trend trades size smallest — and this one sizes smallest of all.
chapters.on_screen: The completed long-rules/short-rules mirror table artifact, with the a-handful-of-times-a-year patience rule stated beneath it

lessons.title: Four-Family Placement Drill: 20 Mixed Charts
lessons.note: The setup tier's capstone gate: 20 cover-the-answer charts interleaving all four swing families — name the family, then the setup, then the entry type, before naming the trade — graded at 80% to proceed. Deliberately recycles two Winners Gallery charts from Module 2 and one regime question from Module 3, because mastery is perishable. Then the field week: one week live — scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry/stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome vs plan. 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next family.

chapters.beat: open with the perishability point: you can ace each family in isolation and still freeze on a live chart, so this gate mixes all four swing families in one deck.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the training-science point that justifies this gate: you can ace each family in isolation and still freeze on a live chart, because the live market never tells you which chapter it is quoting. Studying setups family by family builds recognition WITHIN a category; the real skill is discrimination BETWEEN categories — is this coil a flat base or a flag? Is this gap an EP, a PEG, or fluff? Is this dip a pullback that held the line or a Remount that lost it? Interleaved practice — mixing all four swing families in one shuffled deck — is measurably harder and measurably better at building exactly that discrimination, which is why this capstone gate refuses to sort the charts for you. Twenty charts, four families — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — in random order, answer covered. The market interleaves; so does the exam.
chapters.on_screen: A slide: the four family names over a shuffled 20-chart deck, 'the market never tells you the chapter'

chapters.beat: work three charts on camera in the strict order: name the FAMILY, then the SETUP, then the ENTRY TYPE (BASE BREAKOUT / PREV DAY HIGH BREAK / PREV LOW RECLAIM / RED TO GREEN), and only then the trade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Demonstrate the strict order on three charts before the member touches the deck, because the ORDER is the skill. First: name the FAMILY — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, or Reversals & Reclaims. The family tells you what kind of trade this even is: trend-following or counter-trend, and therefore how it sizes. Second: name the SETUP from the catalog — the specific play inside that family. Third: name the ENTRY TYPE from the four triggers — BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN. Only then, fourth, describe the trade: the tick-level trigger, the stop, the size. Coarse to fine, always — a trader who jumps straight to 'buy here' with no family and no name has skipped the classification that makes the trade reviewable, sizeable, and gradeable. Say the sequence out loud on all three demonstrations: family, setup, entry type, trade.
chapters.on_screen: Three worked charts with the four-step sequence stamped on each: FAMILY → SETUP → ENTRY TYPE → trade
chapters.example_spec: Use three course-familiar charts, one per family, and stamp FAMILY → SETUP → ENTRY TYPE → trade on each. (1) Bases & Breakouts: NVDA daily, October 2023–January 2024 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time) — flat base under ≈$50.50; BASE BREAKOUT January 8, entry ≈$50.50 over the base high, stop ≈$46.50 under the last contraction; ran to the ≈$97.40 March 8 high, ≈+10R. (2) Gaps & Catalysts: SMCI daily, January 19, 2024 (≈10× at the time) — Episodic Pivot; opening-range-high entry ≈$38.60, day-low stop ≈$34.50, close ≈$42.35, ≈+10R on the trail. (3) Reversals & Reclaims: QQQ daily, October 13, 2022 — U&R; PREV LOW RECLAIM ≈$263, stop ≈$260.50, close ≈$268.82, ≈+2R same day — counter-trend, so it sizes smallest. Say the four-step order aloud on all three. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run the drill guess-before-you-check, deliberately recycling two Winners Gallery charts from Module 2 and one regime question from Module 3, because mastery is perishable.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the deck guess-before-you-check: twenty charts, answer covered, the member commits family, setup, and entry type in writing before every reveal. Tell them up front that the deck deliberately recycles: two charts come straight from the Module 2 Winners Gallery — charts they have seen and annotated before — and one question is a regime call from Module 3, a dial reading they must band and interpret before the chart question counts. Name why: mastery is perishable. Recognizing a chart in week three and failing it in week ten is the norm, not the exception, and the recycled items measure retention, not just this module's freshness. Expect the misses to cluster at the family boundaries — flag versus flat base, pullback versus Remount, EP versus PEG — because those discriminations are exactly what interleaving trains. Every miss gets reviewed by naming the tell that was misread, in writing, before the next chart.
chapters.on_screen: The covered-answer drill deck running — Model Book charts with labels hidden, two Winners Gallery repeats included

chapters.beat: score against the printed rubric on camera, and show what a miss means: not a retake-loop, but targeted remediation back to the family whose reps failed.
chapters.speaker_notes: Score it on camera against the printed rubric: each chart is right only when family, setup, AND entry type are all correct — partial placement is a miss, because a right setup in the wrong family sizes wrong. The pass bar is 80% — sixteen of twenty. Then show what a miss actually means, because it is not a retake-loop: it is targeted remediation back to the family whose reps failed. Missed both Reversals & Reclaims charts? The prescription is that family's lessons and its drill again — not re-running this whole deck until the answers are memorized. The distinction matters: re-grinding the same twenty charts teaches the deck; remediating the weak family teaches the skill, and then a fresh deck proves it. Log the score and the per-family miss pattern in the Journal — the capstone in the final module reads this exact page back when it asks which families your own playbook should be built from.
chapters.on_screen: The printed grading rubric with a per-family miss tally, score circled against the 80% bar

chapters.marker: The field week that closes the tier
chapters.beat: the mechanics and the pass bar: one week live, scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates with entry and stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome versus plan — 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next tier.
chapters.speaker_notes: The mechanics one final time, because this field week closes the entire setup tier. One week, live: run the nightly scan every night; find two to three real candidates of this family — Reversals & Reclaims, which means you are hunting undercuts of prominent lows, lost-and-retaken moving averages, failed breakdowns, and stabilized pullbacks near recapture; write the five-field card for each with exact entry and stop; log every one in the Journal, triggered or not; grade each outcome against PLAN at week's end — did you follow the card, win or lose — because P&L is not a grade. The standing guardrail holds: pilot size or paper until the M5 sizing gate and this family's drill are both cleared, and this family sizes smallest even after that. Eighty percent on the drill plus the completed field log opens the next tier. Four families are now in the toolkit; what remains is timing, risk at the portfolio level, and making the playbook YOURS.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal's field-week log template beside the nightly Screener scan, the tier-gate requirements on a closing slide

modules.label: M11 · The Intraday Toolkit: Timing the Swing Entry

lessons.title: Reading the Open: ORB and the 30-Minute Pivot — Two Range-Break Timers
lessons.note: Read the first minutes of the session, then the two range-break entry timers on one replayed open: the aggressive opening-range break and its patient sibling — consolidate under the first half-hour high, break with volume. When each fits a swing entry, the pass case, and the chase case that violates both. Includes the volume-confirmation bar both timers share.

chapters.marker: An execution timer, not a day trade
chapters.beat: open on the trap: the swing was picked last night on the daily chart, and the only question the first 30 minutes answers is whether today puts the day's trend behind the entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: This lesson exists to prevent a specific failure: the member who learns intraday charts and quietly becomes a day trader. Say it plainly — nothing about the trade changes this morning. The name came off last night's scan, the dial granted permission, the setup has a catalog name and family, and the entry trigger and stop are already written on the five-field card. The first 30 minutes answer exactly one question: does today's session put the day's trend behind that entry, or against it? That's it. ORB and the 30-Minute Pivot are execution timers on a swing entry that was already earned on the daily chart. If the daily work isn't done — no card, no stop, no catalog name — then no intraday pattern, however clean, authorizes a trade. Timer, not trade idea.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: the swing candidate's daily chart with last night's entry/stop marked beside its 5-minute opening bars — NVDA daily + 5-min, May 25 2023 (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily plus 5-minute, May 25 2023 — the session after record Q1 guidance (prices split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time; May 24 close ≈ $30.5). Left panel, the daily: the March–May base ≈ $27–31 (March and April both close ≈ $27.8), with the card written the prior evening — EP entry on gap confirmation ≈ $38.5–39.0, stop just under the developing gap-day low ≈ $36.5; read exact levels off the chart. chapters.beat: run the replayed open bar by bar and narrate the auction live: the opening range drawing itself, where the volume is landing, and what a real bid looks like versus churn.
chapters.speaker_notes: Run the replay bar by bar and narrate the auction out loud. The opening range is drawing itself: the high and low of the first minutes of trade. Watch three things. One — where the range sets: above yesterday's high, inside yesterday's body, or below it. Two — where the volume lands: a real bid shows up as expanding volume on the up bars and shrinking volume on the dips, with dips getting bought before they reach the low of the range. Three — churn: heavy volume with no price progress, closes in the middle of the bars. Churn means supply is absorbing every buy. Don't predict anything yet — the whole skill of this chapter is describing what the tape is doing without forming an opinion. The two timers in the next chapters are just structured ways of acting on this read.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA 5-minute with volume pane, May 25 2023, 9:30–10:00 ET replayed bar by bar (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute with volume pane, May 25 2023, 9:30–10:00 ET (split-adjusted — ≈10× these prices at the time). Replay bar by bar and narrate only what prints. Find, in order: where the opening range sets — roughly $37.0–39.2, far above the prior close ≈ $30.5 and prior high ≈ $31.2; where volume lands — this is the heaviest-volume session of the whole spring at 3.1× average, and its biggest bars print in this half hour, so mark which side they close on; dips getting bought before tagging the range low; any churn bars — heavy volume, mid-bar closes, no progress. Draw the first-30-minute high/low exactly as printed (≈ $39.2 / ≈ $37.0 — verify). No opinion yet. Reference outcome: the swing timed off this open ran ≈ +2R to the ≈ $42.3 June close. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: on the same replayed open, draw the opening-range high and take the break with momentum: the pass case, entry the tick it clears, and why this timer fits a swing entry only when the daily setup work was already done.
chapters.speaker_notes: Draw the opening-range high on the replayed open. The ORB entry is the tick that clears it with momentum — price through the level, volume expanding, no hesitation. It's the aggressive timer because you're paying up early for the chance to have the whole day's trend behind you. Three conditions, all mandatory: the daily setup work is already done and this price is at or through the trigger written on your card; the tape has permission — the dial's band allows new buys today; and the break comes with the volume-confirmation bar we define in chapter five. The stop does not move — it stays where the daily structure put it, and the size came from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % before the open. ORB times the fill. It never widens the stop and never adds size.
chapters.on_screen: Same replayed open with the opening-range high drawn and the ORB entry tick marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Same NVDA 5-minute open, May 25 2023 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time). Draw the opening-range high ≈ $39.2 — read the exact printed level off your feed. Find the first bar that clears it with volume clearly expanded above the morning's prior bars — it comes out of the recovery after the early flush; verify the exact bar on your platform. Mark the ORB entry tick just above ≈ $39.3. The stop stays daily structure ≈ $36.5, under the gap-day low ≈ $36.63 — never an intraday level — and size was fixed pre-open. Outcome: the daily stop is never tested (session low $36.63, close $38.0); NVDA prints ≈ $40.5 within three sessions, ≈ $42.3 at the June close (+1.1R on ≈ $2.8 risk) and ≈ $46.7 by the July close — ≈ +2.6R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: mark the first half-hour's high, show price consolidating UNDER it, then the break with volume; name when patience beats aggression: gappy opens, thinner names, a YELLOW tape.
chapters.speaker_notes: Mark the high of the first half-hour — that's the pivot. The patient timer wants price to consolidate UNDER that level: a tight sideways drift, higher lows pressing against it, volume quieting while it coils. Then the break of the pivot, with volume, is the entry. What you've bought is proof: the open's sellers had thirty minutes plus the coil to knock it down and couldn't. Choose patience over aggression in three situations. Gappy, whippy opens — where ORB fills you at the high of a shakeout bar. Thinner names — where the first prints are noise, not auction. And a YELLOW tape — reduced rights mean you demand more proof before committing capital. Same stop, same size, same card. The only thing patience changes is which bar you pay.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI 5-minute, Jan 19 2024 — price coiling under the first half-hour high, then the volume break of the pivot (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI 5-minute, January 19 2024 — the morning after pre-announced blowout Q2 guidance (January 18 close ≈ $31.15; split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the gap open ≈ $34.76, +11.6% on 3–4× volume; the first half-hour high ≈ $35.5–36 — mark it as the pivot; the coil UNDER it — higher lows pressing the level, volume quieting; then the break bar through the pivot on clearly expanded volume — entry tick ≈ $36 (read exact levels off the chart). Stop stays daily structure ≈ $31, just under the prior close; 1R ≈ $5. Outcome: SMCI closes ≈ $42.34, +36% on the day — ≈ +1.3R — and reaches ≈ $80.33 by the February 16 close, ≈ +9R for the patient timer. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: show the volume-confirmation bar both timers share (the break bar must expand clearly above the morning's prior bars), then the chase case that violates both — extended, mid-range, no volume — and the walk-away rule.
chapters.speaker_notes: Both timers share one volume test: the break bar must expand clearly above the morning's prior bars — visibly bigger than anything the session has printed so far, not marginally bigger. No expansion, no witness, no entry. Now the chase case, and be blunt about it: price is extended past the range, sitting mid-air between levels on quiet volume — and the member buys anyway because it 'got away.' That entry violates both timers at once: there's no range structure behind it, so the logical stop is far away, and Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % says a wide stop forces either a tiny position or an oversized loss. The walk-away rule: if the break traded without you, you missed it. Set the alert at the next valid trigger — the prev day high, the next coil — and wait. Missing a trade costs nothing. Chasing one costs R.

Nearest logical stop is the OR low ≈ $129 — ≈ 3% away with nothing in between, so the formula forces a tiny position or an oversized loss. Then the proof: AMD reverses off ≈ $132.83 into the event and closes ≈ $124.53, −3.6% on 2.1× volume — the chase entry is ≈ −2R by the bell; the walk-away costs 0R. lessons.title: Go Signal: The Catalyst Gap That Digests into the 9 EMA, Then Engulfs
lessons.note: A catalyst gap digests into the 9 EMA, then one wide candle engulfs the pullback and closes above the catalyst high — the intraday confirmation layer for EP and Power Earnings Gap entries. One day where it fired and one where it never came, both annotated.

chapters.marker: Why EP entries need a go signal
chapters.beat: open with the blind-open buy that gets shaken out at the day's lows, and frame the Go Signal as the intraday confirmation layer that sits under Episodic Pivot and Power Earnings Gap entries.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on the failure this signal prevents: the blind open buy. A stock gaps 10%+ on real news, the member market-buys the open, the gap digests for two hours, and he's shaken out at the day's lows — right before it trends. The Go Signal is the intraday confirmation layer that sits underneath Episodic Pivot and Power Earnings Gap entries in the Gaps & Catalysts family. The daily thesis is already in place — surprise catalyst, gap clearing the base, pre-market homework done. What's missing is proof that TODAY's buyers can absorb the profit-takers. The Go Signal is that proof, in three parts you'll see across this lesson: the gap holds its range, the pullback digests into the 9 EMA, and one engulfing candle reclaims the catalyst high. Until all three print, you have a watchlist entry, not a position.
chapters.on_screen: META 5-minute, Feb 2 2023 post-earnings gap — the blind open buy marked at the high before the shakeout (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: META 5-minute, February 2 2023 — the post-earnings gap (February 1 close ≈ $153.1; opens ≈ $183.4, +19.8%, on 5.2× volume, the heaviest session of the window). Find, in order: the blind chase — mark an entry arrow on the early spike into the catalyst high ≈ $196–197 (read the exact print off your feed); then the multi-hour digestion bleeding back toward ≈ $185–188, where that buyer — no stop logic, no structure — is down ≈ 5% and gets shaken out; finally the ≈ $188.8 close, roughly 4% under the high, with the gap itself never once threatened. Outcome: the blind buy turns a day the gap never failed into ≈ a −1R-equivalent hit; the Go Signal exists to replace exactly this entry. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: annotate the catalyst gap holding its range and drifting back into the 9 EMA on fading volume, and name it correctly: the market re-loading, not the gap failing.
chapters.speaker_notes: Annotate the digestion. After the gap opens, price drifts back — and the first thing to check is character: the pullback holds inside the gap's range and slides into the rising intraday 9 EMA on FADING volume. Each dip prints smaller volume bars than the open did. That's the market re-loading — early sellers cashing out while stronger hands absorb quietly — not the gap failing. Failure looks different: expanding volume on the down moves, closes below the 9 EMA that stick, price threatening the gap fill. Teach the 9 EMA as the digestion's spine — the intraday cousin of the 9/20 pair the daily work leans on. As long as the pullback respects it on quiet volume, the setup is alive and you do nothing. The discipline in this chapter is watching a strong stock pull back and not touching it.
chapters.on_screen: 5-minute chart with the intraday 9 EMA overlaid — gap holding its range, pullback drifting into the 9 EMA on fading volume (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute, February 22 2024 — the session after the blowout Q4 FY24 report — with the intraday 9 EMA overlaid (split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these prices at the time). Find, in order: the gap open ≈ $75.0 against the ≈ $67.5 prior close, +11.2% on 1.8× volume — the range that must hold; the morning push into the catalyst high ≈ $76–77 (verify off your feed); then the digestion leg — price drifting back into the rising 9 EMA around ≈ $75.5–76 on visibly fading volume, each dip's bars smaller than the open's; dips holding at or above the line with no sticky closes below it; the gap never threatening a fill. Annotate: market re-loading, not failing. Do nothing here — the trigger is next chapter. The session closed ≈ $78.5, at its high. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The engulf above the catalyst high
chapters.beat: freeze on the trigger bar: one wide candle that engulfs the entire pullback and closes above the catalyst high — entry there, stop under the digestion low, sized by the normal R math.
chapters.speaker_notes: Freeze on the trigger bar. One wide-range candle engulfs the entire pullback — its body swallows the digestion — and closes above the catalyst high, the high of the move the news created. That candle is the Go Signal: entry there, at the close of the engulf or the tick it takes out the catalyst high. The stop goes under the digestion low — the structural point where the reclaim is disproven. Then normal R math, nothing special because it's intraday: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. Worked: entry $52.00, digestion low $49.92 — a 4% stop. At 1% account risk, 1% ÷ 4% = a 25% position, which sits right at the GREEN + A+ cap of 20-25%; in YELLOW you'd cut it to 15%. The signal times the entry. The table still sizes it.
chapters.on_screen: Frozen trigger bar on the 5-minute: the engulfing candle swallowing the digestion, with catalyst-high and digestion-low stop lines drawn
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute, February 22 2024, frozen on the trigger (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time). Find: the digestion into the intraday 9 EMA ≈ $75.5–76; then the single wide-range candle whose body swallows that pullback and closes above the catalyst high ≈ $77 — verify the exact bar and level on your feed. Draw the two lines: catalyst high ≈ $77 (entry) and the gap-day/digestion low ≈ $74.6 (stop), 1R ≈ $2.5 — read exact levels off the chart. Keep the script's $52.00/$49.92 sizing arithmetic as the on-screen worked overlay; the chart supplies the pattern. Outcome: the session closes ≈ $78.5, its own high, gap fully held, and the swing runs ≈ +4R to the ≈ $87.5 March 8 close. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: replay a real annotated session start to finish: gap, digestion, engulfing trigger, the fill, and where the swing stop and first target sat by the closing bell.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay the whole session start to finish with the annotations on. The gap: up huge on the catalyst, opening well above the prior base. The digestion: two hours of drift into the 9 EMA on shrinking volume — narrate how bad it feels to wait through it. The trigger: the wide engulfing candle that swallows the pullback and closes through the catalyst high — the fill goes here, stop under the digestion low. Then the day finishes the argument: trend up into the close. End the chapter at the closing bell with the swing plan on screen: stop under the digestion low, first partial planned at 2-3R, and the runner handed to the 10/20-day trail on the daily chart — because this is an EP entry now, and EPs trail the 10/20-day. One session of patience bought a swing with the day's whole trend behind it.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA 5-minute full session, May 25 2023 — gap, 9 EMA digestion, engulfing trigger, trend close, with the swing stop and 2-3R target annotated (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA 5-minute full session, February 22 2024 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time; prior close ≈ $67.5). Walk it start to finish: the +11.2% gap open ≈ $75.0 on 1.8× volume, clearing the whole January base; the early push into the catalyst high ≈ $76–77; the mid-session digestion into the rising 9 EMA ≈ $75.5–76 on shrinking volume — narrate the discomfort; then the wide engulfing candle reclaiming ≈ $77 (verify the exact bar on your feed); close ≈ $78.5 at the session high, gap fully held. At the bell, annotate the swing plan: stop under the gap-day low ≈ $74.6 (1R ≈ $2.5), first partial 2–3R ≈ $82–85, runner handed to the 10/20-day trail — which carried it to the ≈ $87.5 March 8 close, ≈ +4R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: replay a real annotated session where the digestion broke the 9 EMA and the engulf never printed: the no-trade IS the win, and the card reads one line — no engulf, no entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Same annotations, opposite outcome. The gap opens, the digestion starts — and then the character breaks: the pullback closes below the 9 EMA and stays there, volume expanding on the down moves instead of fading. The engulf never prints. Walk forward bar by bar and let the lesson land: there was never an entry. No signal, no fill, no loss — while the blind open buyer bleeds all day. Say the punchline exactly the way the card reads: no engulf, no entry. One line. The no-trade IS the win here — you risked nothing on a gap that couldn't prove itself, and the same catalyst often offers a second, better entry days later when a real daily setup forms. Close by logging the non-trade in the journal as a rep: setup watched, rule held, zero R spent.
chapters.on_screen: COIN 5-minute, Apr 14 2021 — digestion losing the 9 EMA on expanding volume, 'no engulf, no entry' stamped on the chart (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: COIN 5-minute, April 14 2021 — direct-listing day, so trading opens ≈ 1:25 PM ET against a $250 reference price. Find, in order: the open ≈ $381 and the immediate spike to the catalyst high ≈ $429.54 — the highest print COIN made all year; then the failed digestion — closes below the intraday 9 EMA that STICK, volume expanding on the down legs (the session runs 11× average), every bounce dying under the line; no engulfing candle ever reclaiming ≈ $429; the slide into the ≈ $328.28 close near the session low. Stamp 'no engulf, no entry' on the chart. Outcome: 0R risked — the rule-follower never had a fill, while the blind ≈ $400 buyer is down ≈ 18% by the bell. Log the non-trade as a rep. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Selling Because You Were Wrong: The Stop Is an Appointment, Not a Debate
lessons.note: Pre-commitment mechanics (hard GTC stops versus alert-and-act) and the base re-entry rule: cut at least half the moment a breakout falls back into its base. One narrated real stop-out taken exactly at plan — presented as a WIN of process — with the counterfactual computed on screen: the same trade at −2.5R when the stop gets moved once.

chapters.beat: open on the split that organizes this whole module: selling because you were wrong is its own psychological event, and the stop is an appointment you made before the trade, not a debate you hold during it.
chapters.speaker_notes: This module splits selling by intent, and the split matters because the psychology differs even when the mechanical action is identical. Selling because you were RIGHT — next lesson — is a fight against greed. Selling because you were WRONG — this lesson — is a fight against hope, and hope is the more expensive opponent. The frame that wins the fight: the stop is an appointment, not a debate. You made the appointment before you entered — when you were calm, objective, and had no money at stake. The moment the trade is on, you are the least qualified person in the world to renegotiate it. Every rule in this lesson is a way of making sure the calm version of you — the one who wrote the stop on the card — is the one who executes the exit, not the version watching red numbers.
chapters.on_screen: THE LOOP CARD with station 5 MANAGE highlighted: 'The stop is an appointment, not a debate'

chapters.marker: Pre-commitment mechanics: hard GTC versus alert-and-act
chapters.beat: show both order setups on screen, who each style fits, and the non-negotiable they share: the exit price exists in writing before the entry order does.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two mechanics, both legitimate, one non-negotiable. Hard GTC: the stop order rests at the broker from the moment the entry fills — good-till-cancelled, executes without you. This fits almost everyone: anyone with a day job, anyone who has ever frozen at the moment of truth, anyone whose journal shows a moved stop. Alert-and-act: an alert fires at the stop price and you execute manually. This one is earned, not chosen — it fits only a trader at the screen all session whose journal proves the appointment is always kept, and its single advantage is dodging the stop-run wick that tags resting orders. Show both on screen: the GTC ticket at the broker, and the dashboard price alert set at the identical level. The non-negotiable they share: the exit price exists in writing before the entry order does. Stop first, entry second — never the reverse.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen: broker GTC stop-order ticket beside the dashboard Watchlists price-alert popover set at the identical stop price

chapters.beat: the moment a breakout falls back into its base you cut at least half, without waiting for the stop; draw the base boundary on a real chart and mark the exact bar that triggers the cut.
chapters.speaker_notes: One exit rule fires BEFORE the stop, and it's specific to breakouts: the moment a breakout falls back inside its base, you cut at least half — without waiting for the stop. The logic: you bought the breakout because the stock left the base on volume. When price closes back inside the base, the thing you paid for no longer exists. The stop under the base low protects your capital; the re-entry rule protects your R — it takes half the risk off at a small loss instead of riding the full position to −1R on a pattern that's already dead. Draw the base boundary on the chart — the pivot line it broke through — and mark the exact bar: the first close back below the pivot, inside the range. That bar cuts half. If price then reclaims, you still hold half. If it keeps failing, the stop handles the rest.
chapters.on_screen: DKNG daily, March 2021 — breakout over the base pivot that closed back inside; base boundary drawn, cut-half bar marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: DKNG daily, February–March 2021 (no split, prices as charted). Find, in order: the base — the ≈ $52–64 range from early February into March; the pivot line ≈ $64.5 across the range highs (the March 9 gap opens right at ≈ $64.0 and closes back at ≈ $62.2); the mid-March breakout through it, running to the ≈ $74.38 all-time high on March 22; then the failure — the first daily close back BELOW ≈ $64.5, inside the base, in late March (the month closes ≈ $61.33). Mark that exact bar as the cut-half bar. Trade frame: entry ≈ $65.5, stop ≈ $56 under the last higher low inside the base (1R ≈ $9.5 — read exact levels off the chart). Cutting half ≈ $63 books ≈ −0.25R on that half versus riding it to −1R; DKNG hit ≈ $39.93 by May 13, confirming the pattern was dead. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: A real stop-out, narrated as a win
chapters.beat: replay the actual trade taken out precisely at plan for −1R, and grade it on camera as an A trade: right size, right stop, appointment kept.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay a real trade taken out precisely at plan, and grade it on camera as an A — because it is one. Walk it: sized from the formula, under the 2% ceiling.
