Stop placed at the structural invalidation, written before entry. The trade went against the thesis, the appointment was kept, and the loss is exactly −1R — the number chosen in advance, while calm. Then fill in the journal entry on screen: Exit-vs-plan reads YES, and the three-axis grade — Idea, Execution, Preparation — comes back high on all three. Say the doctrine straight: P&L is not a grade. A planned 1R loss taken on rule is the system working, not the system breaking. The expectancy math REQUIRES these losses — a 45% win rate with 2R winners prints money only if the losers stay at 1R. This trade is what that looks like.
chapters.on_screen: A firm stop-out trade's chart beside its finished 7-field Journal entry with Exit-vs-plan = YES (owner to supply — any clean −1R exit-at-plan)
chapters.example_spec: SHOP daily, October–December 2021 (split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the autumn base under the prior ≈ $165 summer high; the mid-November breakout — entry ≈ $166 as price clears the pivot, running to the ≈ $176.29 all-time high on November 19 (max excursion only ≈ +0.6R); the stop ≈ $148 under the November 10 reaction low, written before entry (1R ≈ $18 — read exact levels off the chart); then the growth-stock reversal from November 22 — November still closes ≈ $152.18, and the slide fills the stop in the first days of December (the month closes ≈ $137.74). Loss: ≈ −1R exactly, appointment kept. Postscript for the grade: SHOP traded ≈ $37 by May 2022 — the kept stop cost 1R; hope was offering ≈ −7R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: recompute the same trade live with the stop moved just once: −1R becomes −2.5R on screen, and that single number is why the appointment can never become a debate.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now recompute the same trade with the stop moved once. The plan: entry $50.00, stop $47.50 — $2.50 of risk per share, that's 1R, a 5% stop, sized to 1% of the account as a 20% position. The move: price approaches $47.50 and the trader 'gives it room' down to $43.75. It keeps going and fills there. The loss is now $6.25 per share — $6.25 ÷ $2.50 = 2.5R. One decision turned a 1% hit into 2.5% of the account, past the 2% hard max the whole system is built never to breach. And that's the polite version — the reflex that moved it once moves it twice. Put the two numbers side by side on screen: −1R versus −2.5R. That gap is the entire argument. The appointment can never become a debate, because the debate has a house edge — and the house is your hope.
chapters.on_screen: Same trade's chart with both exits marked and the arithmetic overlaid: $2.50 planned risk → −1R versus $6.25 moved-stop exit → −2.5R
chapters.example_spec: Same SHOP daily, November 2021–March 2022 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time): entry ≈ $166, planned stop ≈ $148, 1R ≈ $18. Mark both exits. Exit one: the planned fill ≈ $148 in the first days of December — −1R. Exit two, the counterfactual: the stop 'given room' once, down to ≈ $130 — filled in the December–January slide (December closes ≈ $137.74, January ≈ $96.42); loss ≈ $36 ÷ $18 ≈ −2R, double the plan on one decision. Then extend the reflex: January closes ≈ $96, March prints a ≈ $51 low, May ≈ $37 — the debate's house edge, drawn on real bars. Keep the script's $50.00 / $47.50 / $43.75 arithmetic as the on-screen overlay; the chart shows the same trade wearing both endings. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Selling Because You Were Right: Partials into Strength, Trailing into Weakness
lessons.note: Two distinct skills with two different feelings: a third off into strength at 2-3R while the crowd is euphoric, trail the remainder into weakness. The same real winner worked three ways (all-out early, all-or-nothing hold, partials) with the final R of each path compared. Artifact: the partials playbook card (first third, second third, runner rules).

chapters.beat: open on the paradox: selling because you were right splits into selling into euphoria (feels too early) and holding into weakness (feels too late), and the two are trained as separate skills.
chapters.speaker_notes: Selling because you were right splits into two skills with opposite feelings, and traders who master one usually fail the other. Skill one: selling a piece into strength — taking the 2-3R partial while the stock is ripping, the crowd is euphoric, and every instinct says higher. It always feels too early. Skill two: holding the remainder into weakness — letting the runner pull back to its moving average and trusting the trail while open profit shrinks. It always feels too late. The paradox to state up front: the feelings are the evidence you're doing it right. Selling into strength feels premature because strength is when buyers pay you top price. Holding into weakness feels wrong because give-back is the fee for catching a trend's whole body. Train them as separate skills — this lesson drills each, then proves the combination wins.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, May–September 2023 — the winner this lesson reworks, entry and stop marked (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, May–September 2023 (split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Mark the trade this lesson reworks: EP entry ≈ $38.5 on the May 25 earnings gap (+26.1%, prior close ≈ $30.5), stop ≈ $36.5 under the gap-day low ≈ $36.63 — 1R ≈ $2.0, ≈ 5%; read exact levels off the chart. Then survey the road ahead on the same chart: the June push into the ≈ $44 high (June closes ≈ $42.3), the June 26 shakeout toward ≈ $40, the July high ≈ $48 (July closes ≈ $46.7), the August flush toward ≈ $41–43.5, the August 24 post-earnings spike to ≈ $50.27 that closed ≈ $47.16, and the September fade to a ≈ $43.5 close. Every later chapter prices its rules off this map; the partials path finishes ≈ +3R blended. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the 2-3R partial taken while the crowd is euphoric: show what strength looks like on the tape, place the exact order, and explain how that sale funds the patience for everything after it.
chapters.speaker_notes: The first third comes off at 2-3R, into strength. Work the arithmetic on screen: entry $50.00, stop $47.50, so 1R is $2.50 per share. The 2R level is $55.00, 3R is $57.50 — that band is the partial zone. What 'into strength' looks like on the tape: a wide-range up move, volume expanding, the stock stretched above its short moving averages — the exact moment everyone else is buying. Place the order precisely: sell one third of the shares, limit, into that move — never on a pullback. Two things this sale buys. First, banked R — with a third off at +2.5R, the trade is now mathematically hard to lose money on. Second, and more valuable: patience. The banked profit is what lets you sit through the runner's pullbacks without flinching. The partial doesn't cap the trade — it funds the hold.
chapters.on_screen: Same daily chart with the 1R/2R/3R ladder drawn from the $2.50 risk and the partial-zone strength bar highlighted
chapters.example_spec: Same NVDA daily (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time): entry ≈ $38.5, stop ≈ $36.5, 1R ≈ $2.0. Draw the ladder: 2R ≈ $42.5, 3R ≈ $44.5 — the partial zone. Find the strength bar to highlight: the mid-June advance (roughly June 13–20) running from ≈ $41 into the ≈ $44 area on wide range and expanding volume, stretched above the short moving averages — the crowd-euphoria moment. Mark the limit sell of one third ≈ $42.5–44, into that move, never on a pullback. Keep the script's $50.00/$47.50/$55.00 arithmetic as the on-screen worked overlay. Outcome: ≈ +2.5R banked on the third — the profit that funds sitting through the June 26 and August shakeouts that follow (June closes ≈ $42.3). (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: hand the runner to the moving average and let the market close the trade: what a normal give-back looks like, and why the trail exit always feels worse and pays better.
chapters.speaker_notes: The remainder gets handed to a moving average, and from that moment the market closes the trade — not you. The trail matches the setup family that produced the trade: 10-day for fast movers, 10/20-day for EPs, 20/50-day for position holds. The rule is mechanical — hold while price closes above the line, exit on the close that breaks it. Show what a normal give-back looks like: a leader can pull back hard from its high and never violate its trail line; that retreat is not a sell signal, it's the cost of the seat. Then say the truth out loud: the trail exit always feels worse and pays better. You will never sell the top — the trail guarantees you give the last piece back. In exchange, it keeps you in the trades that double while everyone who 'felt' the top sold at +3R.
chapters.on_screen: Same chart with the 10/20-day trail overlaid — normal give-backs circled, the trail-break exit close marked
chapters.example_spec: Same NVDA daily with the 10/20-day pair overlaid (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time; entry ≈ $38.5, 1R ≈ $2.0). Circle the normal give-backs the trail survives: the June 26 dip toward ≈ $40 that tags the 20-day and holds; the August 7–18 flush toward ≈ $41–43.5 pressing the trail without a decisive break; the August 24 spike to ≈ $50.27 (closing ≈ $47.16) the trail lets run. Then mark the exit: the first decisive September close below the 20-day, ≈ $45 area — read the exact bar off the chart (September closes ≈ $43.5). Remainder result: ≈ +3.3R on ≈ $2.0 risk, kept only because no give-back was 'felt' into a sale. The trail never sells the ≈ $50.27 top — it feels worse and pays better. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: rework the same real winner three times on screen — all-out early, all-or-nothing hold, partials — and put the final R of each path side by side to show why partials win the long game.
chapters.speaker_notes: Take one real winner and work it three ways on screen — same entry, same stop. Path one, all-out early: the whole position sold into the first surge around +3R. Feels great, banks 3R, misses the entire trend. Path two, all-or-nothing hold: every share held for the full trail — on paper it can beat everything, but live it fails psychologically; with nothing banked, the first sharp pullback shakes the whole position out around +1R. Path three, partials: a third off at 2-3R, the remainder trailed on the moving average. Put the three final R numbers side by side. The partial path rarely wins any single trade — all-out wins the ones that die early, the full hold wins the monsters — but across twenty trades it wins the long game, because it's the only path a human actually executes repeatedly. The playbook optimizes for the trader, not the trade.
chapters.on_screen: Three-panel view of the same winner: all-out at +3R, all-or-nothing hold, partials — final R of each path side by side
chapters.example_spec: Three-panel view of the same NVDA winner (entry ≈ $38.5, stop ≈ $36.5, 1R ≈ $2.0; split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time). Panel one, all-out early: everything sold into the mid-June surge ≈ $44 — final ≈ +2.8R, misses the entire summer. Panel two, all-or-nothing hold: nothing banked, so the August 7–18 flush toward ≈ $41–43.5 shakes the full position out ≈ $41.5 — final ≈ +1.5R despite the ≈ $50.27 August 24 spike that follows. Panel three, partials: a third off ≈ $43.5 (≈ +2.5R), remainder trailed to the September 20-day break ≈ $45 (≈ +3.3R) — blended ≈ +3R. Put the three finals side by side: partials wins no panel decisively, but it is the only path a human executes twenty times running. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close on the artifact: first-third rules (2-3R into strength), second-third rules (trail or structure break), runner rules for the piece you let run — the card members trade from.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close on the artifact — the partials playbook card, the card members trade from. First-third rules: sell one third at 2-3R, into strength, limit order into an up move, never into a pullback. Second-third rules: hold until either the trail line breaks — 10-day fast mover, 10/20-day EP, 20/50-day position hold — or structure breaks: a lower low, a close back below the breakout pivot, whichever the setup family defines. Runner rules for the final piece: it belongs to the trend; it exits only on the trail, it is never sold on feel, and its stop never leaves breakeven once the first third is banked. Every open trade should map onto exactly one line of this card at all times — if you can't say which third you're managing and which rule governs it, the trade is being managed by mood, and mood is what the card exists to replace.
chapters.on_screen: The partials playbook card artifact: first-third rules (2-3R into strength), second-third rules (trail or structure break), runner rules

lessons.title: The Rules Between Entry and Exit: Breakeven Rule, Trails by Timeframe, Time Stops
lessons.note: The point after which a trade must never again become a loser (roughly +1R or the first higher low); trails matched to the setup family that produced the trade — 10-day for fast movers, 10/20-day for EPs, 20/50-day for position holds, with the wrong trail's give-back quantified; and the N-day dead-money rule where nothing happening is itself the exit signal. Each rule stamped on a real chart at the bar where it fired.

chapters.beat: open on the dead zone between entry and exit where unmanaged winners round-trip to zero, and name the three mid-trade rules this lesson installs: breakeven, trails by timeframe, time stops.
chapters.speaker_notes: Between entry and exit sits a dead zone where most R quietly leaks out. The stop handles being wrong, the partial handles being right — but the middle of the trade, where an open winner stalls, wobbles, and round-trips to zero, has no rule yet. Show the chart of the round-trip: a position runs to +2R, no partial level hit, and drifts all the way back to entry — then through it. Nothing 'happened,' and that's exactly the problem: no rule fired. This lesson installs the three mid-trade rules that close the leak. The breakeven rule — the point after which the trade must never again become a loser. Trails by timeframe — the right moving average for the setup family that produced the trade. And time stops — where nothing happening is itself the exit signal. Each one gets stamped on a real chart at the bar it fired.
chapters.on_screen: A round-trip chart: a +2R open gain drifting all the way back through entry with no rule fired — MARA daily, Feb–Mar 2021 (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: MARA daily, February–May 2021 — the crypto-miner mania leg. Find, in order: the February 8 gap — open ≈ $26.94, close ≈ $32.07, +19.6% on 2.8× volume; an entry ≈ $32.5 over that bar, stop ≈ $26.9 under its low (1R ≈ $5.6 — read exact levels off the chart); the advance through February (February 22 closes ≈ $37.1) and March (month closes ≈ $48.0) into the ≈ $57.75 high on April 6 — label it '≈ +4.5R open, no partial filled'; then the round trip — April closes ≈ $36.8, May trades ≈ $24.8, back through entry and through the stop with no rule ever firing. ≈ +4.5R becomes −1R. Annotate the missing rules: breakeven ≈ $32.5 in March, a fast-trail exit ≈ $45–48 in early April — ≈ 3R saved. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: the point after which a trade must never again become a loser — roughly +1R or the first higher low — stamped on a real chart at the exact bar where the stop moves up.
chapters.speaker_notes: The breakeven rule: there is a point after which this trade must never again become a loser. That point is roughly +1R — open profit equal to the planned risk — or the first higher low the new trend prints, whichever the chart gives you first. At that bar, the stop moves up to entry. Stamp it: entry $50.00, stop $47.50, and the day price tags $52.50 — that's +1R — the stop rises to $50.00. From that moment the trade is a free position: worst case is zero, not −1R. Two disciplines live inside the rule. First, breakeven is the ONLY early stop move allowed — stops move up, never down, and only to entry, not trailed tick-by-tick. Second, don't jump it: moving to breakeven at +0.3R just donates the position to normal noise. Earn the move at +1R or the higher low, then make it mechanically.
chapters.on_screen: Daily chart with the breakeven bar stamped: price tagging +1R at $52.50 and the stop line stepping up from $47.50 to $50.00
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, January–March 2024 (split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time): entry ≈ $36 off the January 19 guidance-gap pivot, stop ≈ $31, 1R ≈ $5. Find the breakeven bar: the gap day itself closes ≈ $42.34, +36% — through +1R ≈ $41 — and completes the first higher-low structure. Stamp that bar and step the stop up from ≈ $31 to ≈ $36 — the only early stop move allowed, up and only to entry. Then show the rule earning its keep: the January 30 gap-and-reverse (opens ≈ $54.73, closes ≈ $51.30) and the February 16 outside day (≈ $107.8 high, ≈ $80.33 close on 4× volume) never come near ≈ $36, and the trade runs to the ≈ $122.90 March 8 top. Keep the script's $50.00/$47.50/$52.50 arithmetic as the overlay. Worst case after the stamp: 0R, never −1R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Trails matched to the setup family
chapters.beat: 10-day for fast movers, 10/20-day for EPs, 20/50-day for position holds: the trail is chosen by the setup family that produced the trade, each one stamped on a real chart at the bar it fired.
chapters.speaker_notes: The trail is not a preference — it's chosen by the setup family that produced the trade. Fast movers — the high-velocity Momentum & Trend runs and parabolic legs — trail the 10-day: they move too fast for anything slower to protect the gain. Episodic Pivots trail the 10/20-day — the post-gap trend needs a bit more room than a pure momentum burst, and the 10/20 pair is its lane. Position holds — the multi-month Bases & Breakouts campaigns — trail the 20/50-day: their pullbacks routinely test the 20 and hold the 50, and a tighter line would eject you from the middle of the move. Stamp each on its own chart at the bar the trail fired — the close below the line that ended the trade. One sentence to anchor it: the setup told you how to enter; the same setup tells you which line carries you out.
chapters.on_screen: Three charts side by side: SMCI early 2024 on the 10-day, NVDA May 2023 EP on the 10/20-day, META 2023 on the 20/50-day (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Three charts side by side; read exact bars off each. Fast mover, 10-day: SMCI January–February 2024 (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time) — entry ≈ $36 off the January 19 guidance-gap pivot (that day opened ≈ $34.76), stop ≈ $31 (1R ≈ $5); the 10-day hugs the vertical run to the ≈ $107.8 high on February 16; exit at that day's ≈ $80.33 close below the line — ≈ +8.9R. EP, 10/20-day: NVDA May–September 2023 (split-adjusted) — entry ≈ $38.5, stop ≈ $36.5; exit on the first decisive September close below the 20-day ≈ $45 — ≈ +3.3R. Position hold, 20/50-day: META March–August 2023 — entry ≈ $200 over the ≈ $197 February gap high, stop ≈ $178; spring pullbacks test the 20 and hold the 50; exit on the mid-August close below the 50-day ≈ $290 — ≈ +4R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: run the fast mover on the slow 50-day trail and compute the give-back in R on screen, then overlay the 10-day exit bar that would have kept it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now quantify what the wrong trail costs. Take the fast mover and run it on the slow 50-day. The move: a vertical run where the 10-day hugs the advance and the 50-day lags far below. When the run breaks, price slices most of the way to the 50-day before the slow trail ever fires — compute the give-back on screen in R: the 10-day exit banked the move near the highs; the 50-day exit surrendered a third or more of the entire gain, often several R on a single trade. Overlay the 10-day exit bar on the same chart so the difference is visual, not abstract. Then state the symmetric error: trailing a slow position hold on the 10-day ejects you at the first normal pullback of a six-month move. Wrong-fast costs opportunity; wrong-slow costs banked R. The family match from the last chapter prevents both.
chapters.on_screen: SMCI daily, Jan–Apr 2024 with both trails overlaid — the 10-day exit bar versus the 50-day's give-back computed in R on screen (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI daily, January–April 2024, both trails overlaid (split-adjusted for the 10:1 — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the vertical February–March leg into the ≈ $122.90 top on March 8, the 10-day hugging the advance while the 50-day lags near ≈ $60–70; then the first close below the 10-day — mid-March, ≈ $100–105 (mark the bar; March 19 gaps −11.2% to a ≈ $91.10 close); and the first close below the 50-day — mid-April ≈ $80, confirmed by the April 19 collapse to ≈ $71.4 (April closes ≈ $85.88). Compute on screen from the ≈ $36 January entry (1R ≈ $5): 10-day exit ≈ +13R versus 50-day exit ≈ +8.8R — roughly 4–5R of banked profit surrendered to the wrong line. Read exact closes off the chart. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Time stops: when nothing happening is the signal
chapters.beat: the N-day dead-money rule stamped at the bar it fired, closing with the three rules assembled into one mid-trade checklist the member runs on every open position.
chapters.speaker_notes: The third rule covers the trade where nothing happens at all. Every setup implies a schedule: a breakout should make progress within days of clearing the pivot; an EP should trend within sessions of its gap. The time stop: if N days pass and the trade has done nothing — no follow-through, no +1R, just sideways drift — the absence of progress IS the signal, and the exit is taken at market, not at the stop. Dead money is not neutral: it occupies a slot in your 5-10 name book, ties up heat under the 10% cap, and decays your attention. Stamp the bar where it fired: day N, price still churning at entry, out. Then assemble the full mid-trade checklist the member runs on every open position: Is breakeven earned and moved? Is the family-correct trail on? Is the time-stop clock inside its window? Three questions, every day, every position.
chapters.on_screen: A dead-money chart with the time-stop bar stamped at day N, beside the three-question mid-trade checklist
chapters.example_spec: MSFT daily, February–April 2024 (no split, prices as charted). Find, in order: the multi-week shelf under ≈ $420–430 after the January-earnings run (January closes ≈ $397.6, February ≈ $413.6); a breakout entry ≈ $421 in mid-March, stop ≈ $398 under the range low (1R ≈ $23 — read exact levels off the chart); then the nothing — two-to-three weeks drifting ≈ $415–430 (March closes ≈ $420.7), never tagging +1R ≈ $444, no follow-through bar, flat volume. Stamp the time-stop bar at roughly day 10–15 (early April, price ≈ $420): exit at market, ≈ 0R. Postscript that pays the rule twice: late April breaks the range to the ≈ $388.03 April 25 low — the −1R the time stop pre-empted — while the freed slot and heat went hunting. Close beside the three-question mid-trade checklist. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The Earnings Decision: Hold Through, Trim, or Step Aside
lessons.note: The most recurring swing decision the course must answer: you hold a +2R winner and it reports in three days. The mechanical rule set: check the implied move on the Calendar, compare it to your open profit cushion in R, then hold-full / trim-to-house-money / exit-and-re-enter by rule, never by feel. Two real positions worked — one held through with a cushion, one stepped aside — plus the hard rule for NEW entries inside the pre-report window.

chapters.marker: The decision every swing trader keeps meeting
chapters.beat: open on the live scenario: you hold a +2R winner and it reports in three days, and the answer must come from a rule set, never from feel.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here's the scenario that never stops recurring: you hold a +2R winner, and it reports earnings in three days. Every swing trader meets this decision monthly, and most meet it with feelings — 'it's strong, it'll beat' or 'I can't watch it gap against me.' Both are guesses about an unknowable print. The rule set this lesson installs refuses to guess. It compares two numbers you can actually know: what the options market says the stock will move on the report, and how much cushion in R you're carrying into it. Then it routes you down one of three branches — hold full, trim to house money, or exit and re-enter — mechanically. Frame the stakes honestly: earnings gaps do not respect stops. A stop cannot protect you through a gap; only position size and cushion can. That's why this decision gets its own rule set.
chapters.on_screen: Journal open-position view showing a +2R winner beside the Calendar entry with its report date three days out

chapters.marker: Implied move versus cushion, in R
chapters.beat: pull the implied move off the Calendar on camera and convert your open profit cushion into R, so the whole decision collapses into two numbers side by side.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two numbers, both on screen. First, the implied move: pull it off the Calendar — the dashboard surfaces the options-implied expected move right next to the report date. That's the market's own estimate of the post-earnings swing, in percent. Second, your cushion, converted to R. Worked example: entry $100.00, stop $95.00 — 1R is $5.00, which is 5% of entry. The stock now trades at $112.00, so open profit is 12%, and 12 ÷ 5 = +2.4R of cushion. The implied move reads 8% — and 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6R. Now the entire decision has collapsed into one comparison: 2.4R of cushion against a 1.6R expected swing. A full implied-move gap against you still leaves the trade positive. No feelings entered the room — two numbers did, and the next chapter routes them.
chapters.on_screen: The dashboard Calendar with the ticker's implied move displayed, and the conversion worked on screen: 12% ÷ 5% = +2.4R cushion versus 8% ÷ 5% = 1.6R implied

chapters.beat: cushion clears the implied move: hold full; partial cover: trim to house money; no cover: exit and re-enter by rule after the print — each branch stated as a mechanical threshold, not a judgment call.
chapters.speaker_notes: Three branches, each a mechanical threshold. Branch one — the cushion clears the implied move, like 2.4R against 1.6R: hold full. A worst-case ordinary gap still leaves you profitable; the position has earned its ticket through the print. Branch two — partial cover: the cushion is real but smaller than the implied move. Trim to house money: sell enough shares that a full implied-move gap against the remainder cannot take the whole trade negative. You're risking only profit, never principal. Branch three — no cover: cushion near zero against the implied move. Exit before the report, full position, and re-enter by rule after the print if the setup re-forms — the Power Earnings Gap entry exists precisely for that re-entry. State the discipline plainly: the branch is computed, not chosen. If you find yourself arguing with the branch, you're trading feelings again.
chapters.on_screen: The three-branch decision tree: cushion clears → HOLD FULL · partial cover → TRIM TO HOUSE MONEY · no cover → EXIT & RE-ENTER AFTER THE PRINT

chapters.beat: replay one position held through with a cushion and one stepped aside, show what the report did to each, and prove both were the RIGHT call at decision time regardless of outcome.
chapters.speaker_notes: Work two real positions at their decision moments — and grade the decisions, not the outcomes. Position one: held through with a cushion that cleared the implied move. Show what the report did; with that cushion, even an adverse gap would have left the trade green. Position two: stepped aside — thin cushion, branch three, exited before the report. Maybe the stock then gapped UP without you. Say it anyway: both were the RIGHT call at decision time, because a decision is graded against the information available when it was made, not against the coin flip that followed. This is the journal's three-axis grading applied live — Idea, Execution, Preparation — and P&L is not a grade. Run twenty earnings decisions through the branches and the math wins; judge any single one by its outcome and you'll be back to guessing by next season.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily held into the Aug 23 2023 report with cushion marked, beside a thin-cushion position exited pre-report (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Two decision moments. Held through: NVDA daily into the August 23 2023 report (split-adjusted — ≈10× at the time) — May EP position, entry ≈ $38.5, stop ≈ $36.5, 1R ≈ $2.0; the August 23 close ≈ $47.1 gives cushion ≈ +4.3R against an ≈ 10% implied move ≈ 2.4R — cushion clears, hold full. The print: gap to ≈ $50.2, high ≈ $50.27, close ≈ $47.16; even a full adverse ≈ 10% gap to ≈ $42.4 leaves ≈ +2R. Stepped aside: TSLA daily, July 2023 — entry ≈ $284 over the ≈ $282 two-week flag, stop ≈ $266 (1R ≈ $18); July 19 prints the ≈ $299.29 period high and closes ≈ $291 — cushion ≈ +0.4R against ≈ 7% implied ≈ 1.1R, so branch three, exit pre-print. TSLA opened lower next day and closed ≈ −10% at ≈ $263; grade the branch, not the coin flip. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The hard rule for new entries
chapters.beat: no NEW position inside the pre-report window, full stop; close with the earnings-decision card: check the date, check the implied move, run the branch.
chapters.speaker_notes: New entries get a harder rule than holds: no NEW position inside the pre-report window. Full stop, no branches. A hold carries cushion into the print — profit that absorbs the gap. A fresh entry has none; you'd be placing your entire 1R on a binary event your stop cannot protect you through, because gaps don't stop at stops. So the pre-trade routine gains one mandatory check: before any entry, check the report date on the Calendar. Inside the window — no trade, regardless of how clean the chart looks. The setup will still exist after the print, and the Power Earnings Gap gives you the sanctioned way in if the report goes well. Close on the earnings-decision card, three lines: check the date, check the implied move, run the branch. Holds get the branches. New money waits.
chapters.on_screen: The earnings-decision card — check the date, check the implied move, run the branch — with NO NEW ENTRIES IN THE PRE-REPORT WINDOW as the footer rule

lessons.title: Two Complete Trades, Candle by Candle — Plus the Post-Exit Protocol
lessons.note: The module's mini-capstone: a winner and a loser replayed full-cycle with the sizing math, a mid-trade regime check, partial exits, and the finished journal entry for each — the loser managed exactly as well as the winner. Closes by performing the 60-second post-exit ritual (screenshot, setup tag, one-line verdict) on both exits, installing the habit before Module 14 formalizes it. Script in three chaptered segments with a micro-check between each — one recording, three sittings if needed.

chapters.beat: segment one opens the mini-capstone: run the sizing math on camera (Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, under the 2% ceiling), check the regime dial, and take the entry candle by candle.
chapters.speaker_notes: Segment one of the mini-capstone: everything the module taught, run on one real winner, candle by candle. Start where every trade starts — the dial: read the band on camera and confirm new buys are authorized. Then the sizing math out loud, no shortcuts: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. This trade: entry $50.00, structural stop $47.50 — a 5% stop. At 1% account risk, 1% ÷ 5% = a 20% position; on a $10,000 account that's $2,000, 40 shares, $100 at risk — comfortably under the 2% hard max and inside the GREEN + A+ cell of 20-25%. Name the setup from the catalog, name its trigger from the four, and take the entry at the tick the trigger fires. Every number on screen existed before the fill: stop first, distance second, size last.
chapters.on_screen: The dial reading on the dashboard, then the sizing math written on screen — 1% ÷ 5% = 20% → $2,000 → 40 shares → $100 at risk — beside the winner's entry candle
chapters.example_spec: Winner: PLTR daily, February–March 2024 (no split, prices as charted). February 5 closes ≈ $16.72; the Q4 print and AI-platform demand gap it +21.4% open to ≈ $20.30 on February 6, and it closes ≈ $21.87 — up ≈ 31% on the day on 7.5× volume, the heaviest bar of the window. Entry ≈ $21.50 as the trigger fires over the catalyst high on the gap day; structural stop ≈ $19.90 under the gap-day low (1R ≈ $1.60 — read exact levels off the chart). Run the script's $50.00/$47.50 sizing arithmetic as the on-screen overlay; beside it show this chart's real card: EP from the catalog, engulf-over-catalyst-high trigger, dial GREEN in the February 2024 tape. Segment preview: ≈ +3.7R at the ≈ $27.50 March 7 high, finishing ≈ +2R blended after the partial and trail. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: partial a third at 2-3R into strength, trail the remainder into weakness, then fill in the finished journal entry on screen; micro-check one before moving to the loser.
chapters.speaker_notes: Manage the winner with the module's own rules, candle by candle. At +1R the breakeven rule fires — stamp the bar, the stop moves to entry. Into the surge at 2-3R, the first third comes off into strength: the limit sell prints while the crowd is chasing. The remainder goes to its family-matched trail, and you hold through the pullbacks that used to shake you out — narrating each 'this is normal give-back' candle — until the close that breaks the line ends the trade. Then the part most traders skip: fill in the finished journal entry on screen, all seven fields — Date, Setup tag, Entry type, Planned R, Exit-vs-plan, the three-axis grade, annotated screenshot. Zero blank fields. Micro-check one before the loser: state your entry, your 1R, and which rule closed the trade. If you can't, rewatch this segment before starting segment two.
chapters.on_screen: The winner's daily chart with breakeven bar, 2-3R partial, and trail-break exit marked, then the 7-field Journal entry filled in live
chapters.example_spec: Same PLTR daily (entry ≈ $21.50, stop ≈ $19.90, 1R ≈ $1.60). Find, in order: the breakeven bar — the very next session, February 7, closes ≈ $23.60, through +1R ≈ $23.10 on 4.5× volume; stamp the stop stepping up to ≈ $21.50. The partial — the early-March surge into the ≈ $27.50 high on March 7: limit-sell one third in the ≈ $24.70–26.30 zone (2–3R), into strength, never on a pullback. The trail — 10/20-day, EP family: narrate the give-back candles (the February 13 −6.1% gap that closes green), then mark the first decisive mid-March close below the 20-day ≈ $24 (March closes ≈ $23.01 — read the exact bar off the chart). Remainder ≈ +1.6R; blended ≈ +2R, and worst case after breakeven was 0R. Fill all seven journal fields on screen — zero blanks. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The loser, entered with identical rigor
chapters.beat: segment two: same sizing math, same checklist, a perfectly valid entry — then the mid-trade regime check that dims from GREEN toward YELLOW while the trade stalls.
chapters.speaker_notes: Segment two: the loser — entered with identical rigor, because that's the point. Same dial read, same catalog name, same formula: the stop set at the structural invalidation, the size derived from it, the risk under the ceiling. This entry was VALID — nothing about the process distinguishes it from the winner's entry, and that must be visible on screen. Then the mid-trade regime check, the habit that separates graduates from chart-watchers: while the trade stalls, re-read the dial — and it's dimming from GREEN toward YELLOW. The market's permission structure is weakening underneath the position. That doesn't trigger a panic exit; it changes posture: no adds, no new exposure elsewhere in the book, and the exit rules get enforced without a millimeter of grace. A stalling trade in a weakening band is exactly the trade the next chapter's stop exists for.
chapters.on_screen: The loser's daily chart with the identical sizing math on screen and the dial shown dimming from GREEN toward YELLOW mid-trade
chapters.example_spec: Loser: DKNG daily, March–April 2024, entered with identical rigor. Find, in order: the March range under ≈ $46.5; the late-March breakout — entry ≈ $47 over the range high on March 27, a bar that spikes to ≈ $49.57 on 2.9× volume and closes back at ≈ $45.35; stop ≈ $43 under the last contraction (1R ≈ $4 — read exact levels off the chart). Then the stall — roughly two weeks drifting ≈ $43–48 with no +1R follow-through (+1R ≈ $51 is never touched, $49.57 is the highest print of the year) while the tape deteriorates beneath it: breadth rolling over, the dial dimming GREEN toward YELLOW — show the regime read beside the chart. Posture change only: no adds, exits enforced without grace. The stop hits ≈ April 12–15 at ≈ $43 for −1R at plan; DKNG closed April ≈ $41.6 and May ≈ $35 — the rule was early, and right. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The loser, managed exactly as well
chapters.beat: the stop taken at plan candle by candle, and the finished journal entry graded as highly as the winner's: the outcome differed, the process did not; micro-check two.
chapters.speaker_notes: The stop hits, candle by candle, taken exactly at plan: −1R, the number chosen before entry. No freeze at the moment of truth, no 'give it room' — the appointment kept. Then fill in the loser's journal entry with the same care as the winner's — and grade it just as highly: Idea strong, Execution clean, Preparation complete. Say the module's central sentence while both entries sit on screen: the outcome differed; the process did not. One trade paid, one trade cost, and the system is indifferent — expectancy is built from exactly these two trades repeating: winners paid at 2-3R and beyond, losers capped at 1R, every time. Micro-check two: pull up your own most recent loser. Does its journal entry exist? Was the exit at plan? If either answer is no, that trade — not this video — is your homework.
chapters.on_screen: The two finished Journal entries side by side — winner and loser, both graded high on Idea / Execution / Preparation

chapters.beat: segment three, performed live on BOTH exits: screenshot the chart, tag the setup, write the one-line verdict — installing the habit Module 14 will formalize into the review engine.
chapters.speaker_notes: Segment three, performed live on BOTH exits, sixty seconds each. One: screenshot the chart — exit bar visible, annotations on. Two: tag the setup — the exact catalog name, so this trade aggregates into your per-setup statistics. Three: write the one-line verdict — a single honest sentence: 'Kept the appointment, clean −1R,' or 'Sold the third late; the trail did its job.' That's the whole ritual: screenshot, setup tag, one-line verdict — sixty seconds, before you look at another chart. Do it while the trade is fresh: accuracy dies within the hour, and the version of events your memory writes tomorrow will flatter you. Module 14 formalizes this into the full review engine — weekly stats, per-setup expectancy, the three-axis grades trending over time — but the engine only works if the raw material exists. This habit, installed today on these two exits, is that raw material.
chapters.on_screen: Live performance of the ritual on both exits — annotated screenshot, setup tag, one-line verdict — with a 60-second timer on screen

modules.label: M13 · Portfolio Command: Sizing, Second Pass

lessons.title: Grading the Setup: A+, A, B, C — The Grade That Keys the Table
lessons.note: The rubric that turns 'I like this chart' into a letter with reasons — regime alignment, family-rubric score, RS rank, catalyst quality, cleanliness of the stop — because the firm's sizing table cannot be used until a setup has a grade. Six real candidates graded and defended live, including one seductive B that a beginner would call an A+.

chapters.marker: Two charts, one feeling, two very different sizes
chapters.beat: open on two real candidates the gut would size identically, then reveal the firm's sizing table and show that neither can be sized at all until it carries a letter grade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here are two charts. Both are up-trending, both carry a tight pattern, and if you sized by feel you'd buy the same amount of each. That feeling is the most expensive instrument you own. In this shop, position size does not come from conviction — it comes from a table with a row for the market and a column for the setup. GREEN plus A+ pays 20-25% of the account. YELLOW plus A+ pays 15%. ORANGE plus A+ pays 8%. A B-grade setup in ORANGE pays nothing — it's a skip. Now notice what that means for these two charts: neither one can be sized at all yet, because neither one carries a letter. The grade is the key that opens a cell. This lesson builds the rubric that earns the letter.
chapters.on_screen: Side-by-side daily charts: NVDA May 2023 pre-earnings flat base vs COIN Oct-Nov 2021 late-stage base, sizing table revealed mid-chapter (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Left: NVDA daily, March–May 2023 (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time): the April contractions tightening under ≈$28 off the ≈$22.30 March 13 low, volume dry-up, RS line at highs, May 24 earnings ahead; entry ≈$28.10 over the base high, stop ≈$26.20 under the last shelf (≈7%) — read exact levels off the chart. Right: COIN daily, September–October 2021 — an equally tight-looking late-stage base ≈$220–$270, fading RS, no structural stop nearer than ≈$240 (≈11%). Outcome: NVDA gapped May 25, opening ≈$38.52, +26.1% on ≈3× volume, ≈+5R and beyond. COIN broke out in October, topped ≈$369 on Nov 9 earnings, gapped −8.4% the next day, lost ≈$240 by early January and closed January ≈$190. Same gut feel, opposite grades. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The five rubric lines that earn the letter
chapters.beat: walk regime alignment, family-rubric score, RS rank, catalyst quality, and cleanliness of the stop one at a time, stating what an A+ demands on each line and what drops it to a B or C.
chapters.speaker_notes: Five lines earn the letter. One: regime alignment — an A+ trades WITH the band; a great chart in a hostile tape drops a grade immediately. Two: family-rubric score — the setup nails its family checklist: tightening contractions, volume dry-up, pivot drawn to the tick; sloppy structure is a B at best. Three: RS rank — the relative-strength line at or near highs, leading price; fading RS under a pretty pattern is a C tell. Four: catalyst quality — earnings, guidance, a story with legs beats no catalyst at all. Five: cleanliness of the stop — a structural invalidation close enough that the size stays meaningful; if the honest stop sits 15% away, the trade can't be sized and the grade can't be an A. An A+ passes all five. Fail one line, drop to A. Fail two, it's a B. Fail on regime or on the stop, it's a skip.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the five rubric lines (regime alignment · family-rubric score · RS rank · catalyst quality · clean stop) as printed in THE PLAYBOOK TEMPLATE + DEFENSE RUBRIC, row 3 · SETUP

chapters.marker: Six real candidates, graded and defended
chapters.beat: pull six live watchlist charts and assign each its letter on camera, naming the rubric line that decided the grade out loud before moving to the next.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now we grade for real. Pull six names off the current A-list and give each its letter on camera — and name the rubric line that decided it before moving to the next. That habit is the whole drill: the grade must come with a reason from the rubric, never a vibe. Expect the spread to look like this: one true A+ that passes all five lines; two or three A's, each dinged on a single line — an RS rank that's merely good, a catalyst that's thin; a B with two flaws; and at least one C where the stop simply isn't clean. Speak the deciding line out loud every time — 'A, docked on catalyst,' 'B, structure is loose and RS is flat.' When a letter gets challenged, defend it from the rubric line, never from how much you like the chart.
chapters.on_screen: Screener A-list — six live candidates pulled one at a time into the chart panel, letter typed beside each
chapters.example_spec: Grade six charts frozen at the May 15, 2023 close (NVDA split-adjusted — ≈10× these then). NVDA — base under ≈$28, RS at highs, May 24 earnings ahead, clean stop ≈$26.20: A+, all five lines pass. META — tight flag holding its April 27 earnings gap ≈$240, no near catalyst: A, docked on catalyst. AMD — base ≈$81–$89 off the May 3 flush, pivot ≈$89.50, RS merely good: A, docked on RS. ELF — coiling under ≈$93 into May 24 earnings: A. DKNG ≈$23.50, ≈20% past its ≈$19.50 pivot, nearest shelf ≈$21: B, two flaws. COIN ≈$60, ≈22% under its March high after the −19.8% March 23 gap, RS at lows: C, skip. Rolled forward the A+ gapped +26.1% (≈+5R); the C gapped −19.8% again on June 6. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: dissect the one chart a beginner would stamp A+ and show the two lines that quietly fail it: a stop that isn't clean and an RS rank that's already fading under the pretty pattern.
chapters.speaker_notes: This is the chart a beginner stamps A+. Big prior run, recognizable pattern, headline name — everything the eye loves. Now run the rubric. Line five: where is the honest structural stop? Under a shelf 11% below the pivot — at 1% account risk that's a 9% position, and there is no cleaner invalidation without inventing one inside the noise. That's a fail. Line three: pull up the RS line — it put in its high three weeks ago and has made lower highs while price flattened. The leadership is already leaking out underneath the pretty pattern. Two failed lines makes this a B, and the table sizes a B smaller in every band and skips it entirely in ORANGE. The lesson: the most dangerous charts aren't ugly — they're beautiful with two quiet fails.
chapters.on_screen: COIN daily, Oct-Nov 2021 — the pretty base with a sloppy 11% stop and an RS line already fading (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: COIN daily, September 2021–January 2022. Find, in order: the headline-name aura after the spring IPO run; the pretty two-month base ≈$220–$270; the pivot ≈$270, taken out in mid-October on ≈3× volume; the only honest structural stop — the September shelf ≈$240, ≈11% below the pivot (fail, line five: at 1% risk that is a ≈9% position). Roll forward: the move tagged ≈$369 on Nov 9 earnings (≈+3.3R open), gapped −8.4% the next day, then broke ≈$240 in early January — an untrailed B hands the whole thing back at −1R. RS proof (fail, line three): COIN closed January ≈$190, −48% off the high, while SPX printed a record 4,818 on Jan 4. Grade: B; sized smaller everywhere, skipped in ORANGE. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close by grading tonight's actual watchlist and installing the standing rule the next lesson runs on: the grade is the key that opens a cell in the sizing table, and an ungraded chart opens nothing.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close with the standing rule this module runs on: no letter, no size. An ungraded chart opens nothing — not a pilot, not a probe, nothing. Tonight, take your actual watchlist and grade every name: five rubric lines, one letter, and write the deciding line next to each grade. That letter is not decoration; it is the key that opens exactly one cell of the sizing table in the next lesson — GREEN+A+ opens 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ opens 15%, ORANGE+A+ opens 8%, and B-in-ORANGE opens a locked door. From here forward, every A-list candidate carries its grade before any alert is armed. If you're about to size something and you can't state its letter and the rubric line that earned it, you've already left the system.
chapters.on_screen: Tonight's actual watchlist in the Screener with a letter-grade column, sizing table pinned beside it
chapters.example_spec: If recording without a live watchlist, reuse the six May 15, 2023 candidates from chapter three as the 'tonight' list in the Screener: NVDA A+, META A, AMD A, ELF A, DKNG B, COIN C — each with its deciding line typed in the grade column ('A+, all five pass'; 'A, docked on catalyst'; 'A, docked on RS'; 'B, extended + loose stop'; 'C, no clean stop'). Pin the sizing table beside the list and map letters to cells at the current band — under YELLOW, NVDA opens 15%, the A's open reduced size, DKNG and COIN open nothing. Rolled forward, the A+ gapped +26.1% on May 25 — ≈+5R from ≈$28.10 (split-adjusted — ≈10× that at the time) — while the C gapped −19.8% to ≈$46 on June 6. The letter earned its keep. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: The Table, Verbatim: GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-in-ORANGE = Skip
lessons.note: The firm's sizing table stated exactly and worked live: the same A+ setup sized on a fixed account once under GREEN and once under ORANGE with the dollar-risk difference computed, plus the universal floor restated in every cell — Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, 2% max, prefer under 1%. Includes what pulls you out of a cell mid-trade: a regime downgrade or the −5%/−10% equity triggers firing.

chapters.marker: The table, read aloud cell by cell
chapters.beat: put the full grid on screen and state it verbatim: GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-in-ORANGE = skip, and no cell is negotiable.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here is the table, verbatim, and none of it is negotiable. GREEN band plus an A+ setup: 20 to 25 percent of the account in the position — full playbook authorized. YELLOW plus A+: 15 percent — rights reduced, trim the count and the size. ORANGE plus A+: 8 percent — best names only, smallest size. A B-grade setup in ORANGE: skip. No cell, no trade. Read what the table is actually saying: the market's permission band sets the row, your setup's grade sets the column, and the intersection is your MAXIMUM single-position size. Not a target — a ceiling. There is no cell for 'I really like this one.' There is no cell for a B in ORANGE at reduced size. The table is the entire negotiation, and it happened before the open.
chapters.on_screen: THE MONDAY MAX-EXPOSURE PLAN card, section 3 — THE REGIME SIZING TABLE, full screen

chapters.beat: restate the universal law, Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, 2% max and prefer under 1%, then prove on screen that even a 25% GREEN+A+ position obeys it when the stop is tight.
chapters.speaker_notes: Under every cell sits the universal law: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %. Hard maximum 2% of the account at risk per trade; under 1% is the preference. Now prove the biggest cell obeys it. Take the top of the table — a 25% GREEN+A+ position with a tight 4% stop: 25% × 4% = 1.0% account risk. Legal and comfortable. Push the stop to 8%: 25% × 8% = 2.0% — exactly at the hard max, and nothing may be added. Wider than that and the formula forces the position below the ceiling. That's the design: the table caps the position, the formula caps the damage, and both must agree before shares are bought. And when a tight stop invites a monster position — 1.5% risk on a 3% stop solves to 50% — the ceiling outranks the formula: cap it at 25%, because a stop cannot catch an overnight gap.
chapters.on_screen: THE SIZING GATE card — the formula line plus worked problems 5 and 9 (the 25% cell at 1.0% risk; the tight-stop trade capped by the ceiling)

chapters.marker: Same A+ setup, GREEN versus ORANGE
chapters.beat: size the identical chart on the same fixed account twice, compute shares and dollar risk both ways on camera, and let the dollar difference make the regime argument better than any speech.
chapters.speaker_notes: Same chart, same $50,000 account, same A+ grade, sized twice. Entry $80.00, structural stop $76.80 — a 4% stop. Under GREEN: the cell allows 25%, so the position is $12,500 — 156 shares. Risk: 156 × $3.20 ≈ $499, right at 1% of the account. Under ORANGE: the cell allows 8%, so the position is $4,000 — 50 shares. Risk: 50 × $3.20 = $160, roughly 0.32%. Identical chart, identical trigger, identical stop — and the ORANGE version carries less than a third of the exposure and a third of the dollar risk. That is the regime argument in dollars: the market's condition, not the chart's beauty, decides how much of your money stands in the road. When the tape is hostile, the same great setup is a small trade — not caution for its own sake, but math applied to a lower win-rate environment.
chapters.on_screen: One A+ chart — e.g. AMD daily, May 2023 flat base — with the dial shown GREEN then ORANGE and the share/dollar math worked beside it (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: AMD daily, May 2023. Find: the May 3 post-earnings gap-down (−7.1%) closing ≈$81.60; the two-week flat base ≈$81–$89; the trigger ≈$89.50 over the base high mid-May; the structural stop ≈$86 under the last contraction (≈4%) — or keep the script's round $80.00/$76.80 numbers in the side panel and use AMD purely as the visual. Size it twice on the $50,000 account per the notes: GREEN cell 25% ≈ $12,500, ≈1.0% risk; ORANGE cell 8% ≈ $4,000, ≈0.32% risk. Outcome: AMD rode the May 25 NVDA-sympathy gap (+8.3%, closing ≈$120.35) and reached ≈$132.83 on June 13 — roughly +8.8R to +12R on the ≈$3.50 stop, identical setup in both bands; only the dollars at risk differ. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: What pulls you out of a cell mid-trade
chapters.beat: walk the two evictions live: a regime downgrade while you hold, and the −5%/−10% equity triggers firing, with exactly what happens to open positions and new buys in each case.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two things evict you from a cell while you hold. First, a regime downgrade. A distribution-day cluster — four to six inside roughly 25 sessions — legally ends an uptrend, and a mid-week band drop re-keys every ceiling immediately: new-buy rights are revoked, pending orders get cancelled, and open positions get managed to their existing plans. You don't panic-sell — you stop adding and let the stops do their job. Second, the equity triggers, and these fire regardless of band. At minus 5% of equity from your high-water mark, halve all new position sizes. At minus 10%, pilot-size or paper only. Those thresholds were decided while you were calm — that's the point. A cell is permission granted under conditions; when the conditions die, the permission dies with them — mid-week, mid-trade, no appeal.
chapters.on_screen: The dial mid-band-flip beside THE MONDAY MAX-EXPOSURE PLAN section 6 — BAND-FLIP TRIGGERS (distribution cluster, −5%/−10% equity triggers)

chapters.marker: Print it, pin it, size only from it
chapters.beat: close with the table as the take-home artifact and the drill: re-size your last three real trades from the correct cell and log the delta between what you took and what the table allowed.
chapters.speaker_notes: The take-home is physical: print the table, pin it beside the platform, and size only from it. Then run the drill that makes it real: pull your last three actual trades and re-size each one from the correct cell. Write three numbers per trade — the size you took, the size the table allowed, and the delta. Most traders find the same pattern: oversized in YELLOW and ORANGE, strangely undersized in GREEN — big when scared money should be small, timid when the tape was paying. The delta column is your personal tuition bill: what trading by feel cost against trading by table. From this lesson forward, every position gets sized from a cell — band, grade, ceiling, formula check, done. If you can't name the cell, you can't place the order.
chapters.on_screen: The printed sizing table beside three re-sized past trades: size taken · size the table allowed · delta

lessons.title: Portfolio Heat: All Open Risk as One Number, Capped at 10%
lessons.note: Sum of (entry − stop) × shares over equity computed on a real five-position book against the 10% aggregate heat cap, plus why 5-10 names beats 30 for momentum swing. Then the correlation check: five AI names is one trade wearing five tickers — the same book computed naive and correlation-adjusted. Artifact: the heat worksheet.

chapters.marker: Five safe trades, one dangerous account
chapters.beat: open with a book where every position honors the 2% ceiling individually yet the account is one bad gap from a brutal morning, and name the number that was never computed: heat.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here's a book where every position is individually perfect and the account is a loaded gun. Five positions, $50,000 account, each sized by the formula, each risking the full 2% — $1,000 apiece. Every row passes the single-trade law. Now add them: $5,000 of open risk. If one bad morning takes out every stop — a gap, a sector shock, a red tape — this account gives back 10% of its equity before breakfast, and slippage through gapped stops makes it worse. Nobody broke a rule, because nobody computed the one number that was never on screen: total open risk. That number has a name — portfolio heat — and it has a cap. This lesson installs both. Per-trade risk protects you from one bad trade; heat protects you from one bad day.
chapters.on_screen: Journal open-positions view — a five-position demo book, each row individually inside the 2% law
chapters.example_spec: Build the demo book dated late June 2024, $50,000 equity, five positions each sized to exactly $1,000 risk — the full 2% single-trade law: NVDA entry ≈$124, stop ≈$118, 165 sh; META ≈$504 / $484, 50 sh; AMD ≈$162 / $152, 100 sh; AVGO ≈$162 / $152, 100 sh (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time); SMCI ≈$82 / $77, 200 sh (also split-adjusted — ≈10× then). Walk the rows in order, showing each passes the formula individually; keep the sum off screen until the reveal: $5,000 of open risk — 10% of equity, −5R if one correlated gap sweeps every stop before breakfast. Read exact prices off the chart for the entry/stop columns. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The heat formula on a real book
chapters.beat: compute sum of (entry − stop) × shares over equity across an actual five-position book on camera and check the result against the 10% aggregate cap.
chapters.speaker_notes: Heat is one formula: the sum of (entry minus stop) times shares, across every open position, divided by equity. Run it on this five-position book, $50,000 account. NVDA: 30 shares, $6 to the stop — $180. META: 10 shares, $25 to the stop — $250. AMD: 60 shares, $8 to the stop — $480. Then $600 and $490 on the last two. Total open risk: $2,000. Divide by $50,000: 4.0% heat. The cap is 10% — hard. This book has room for more risk, if the table and the grades authorize it. Recompute after every fill and every stop move: raising a stop to breakeven takes that position's line to zero and refunds headroom. Heat is a live number, not a Monday number — and no new buy goes on while it reads above 10.
chapters.on_screen: THE MONDAY MAX-EXPOSURE PLAN section 4 — PORTFOLIO HEAT vs THE 10% CAP, computed live on the demo book
chapters.example_spec: Second demo book, same late-June 2024 pricing, matching the scripted rows exactly: NVDA 30 sh, $6 to the stop (≈$124 / $118) = $180; META 10 sh, $25 (≈$504 / $479) = $250; AMD 60 sh, $8 (≈$162 / $154) = $480; name the two unnamed rows AVGO — 40 sh, $15 (≈$162 / $147) = $600 — and SMCI — 70 sh, $7 (≈$82 / $75) = $490; both split-adjusted, ≈10× these at the time. Total open risk $2,000 ÷ $50,000 = 4.0% heat versus the 10% cap; worst case, all stops hit = −4% of equity. Then demo the refund: raise NVDA's stop to breakeven, its $180 line zeroes, heat re-reads ≈3.6% live. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: make the concentration case for momentum swing: attention per name, the quality of the marginal idea, and the truth that 30 names is closet-indexing with none of the index's safety.
chapters.speaker_notes: Five to ten names is the right book for momentum swing; thirty is closet-indexing with none of the index's safety. Three reasons. Attention: every open name demands nightly chart work, stop management, and a fresh read at the open — at thirty names you do none of it well, and the trade that needed your eyes at 9:45 didn't get them. Marginal idea quality: your capital should live in your best five graded setups; the twenty-fifth-best idea on your list is, by your own rubric, a C — why does it own capital? And concentration is how this style pays: a season's return usually comes from two or three leaders sized properly, not thirty slivers. Meanwhile thirty scattered names still gap down together in a correction — you kept the correlation and gave away the edge. Fewer names, bigger attention, table-sized.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: a 30-name closet-index book beside an 8-name focus book — attention, marginal idea quality, correlation

chapters.marker: Five AI names is one trade wearing five tickers
chapters.beat: rerun the same book correlation-adjusted, watch the heat number jump past the cap, and set the rule that correlated positions share one risk budget.
chapters.speaker_notes: Re-run the same book with honest eyes. NVDA, AMD, AVGO, SMCI, VRT — the tickers differ, the trade doesn't: they all answer to the same AI tape, and on the day that theme breaks they hit their stops together. Naive heat said five separate risks of $1,000 each — 10% total, at the cap and technically legal. Correlation-adjusted, this is one trade risking $5,000 — 10% of the account on a single idea, five times the 2% single-trade ceiling. That's the rule: correlated positions share one risk budget. Same theme, same catalyst chain, same gap risk — one budget, sized like one position. If you want five AI names, their combined open risk gets treated as a single line on the worksheet, and the adjusted heat is the number the 10% cap governs. This book was legal ticker by ticker and reckless as a whole.
chapters.on_screen: The heat worksheet re-run on five AI names (NVDA/AMD/AVGO/SMCI/VRT, spring 2024) collapsed into one shared risk budget (or substitute firm positions)
chapters.example_spec: Date the correlation book early March 2024, each row ≈$1,000 risk (NVDA, AVGO and SMCI split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time): NVDA ≈$88 / $83, 200 sh; AMD ≈$205 / $195, 100 sh; AVGO ≈$132 / $127, 200 sh; SMCI ≈$105 / $95, 100 sh; VRT ≈$80 / $75, 200 sh (verify on chart). Naive heat: five separate $1,000 risks = 10%, at the cap and 'legal.' Collapse them — one AI tape, one catalyst chain — into a single $5,000 line: one trade at five times the 2% ceiling. Forward proof: all broke together into the April 19 low — AMD −30% from ≈$227.30, SMCI −30% from ≈$122.90, NVDA −20% to ≈$75.61, AVGO to ≈$119.76 — −5R as one idea wearing five tickers. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The heat worksheet, filled and armed
chapters.beat: complete the artifact on the demo book, then install the nightly habit and its gate: compute your book's heat before every session, and no new buy while the number reads above 10%.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the worksheet on the demo book, top to bottom. Equity today. Open risk: sum of (entry minus stop) times shares, every position. Heat: open risk over equity — cap 10%. Then the correlation line: same-theme names collapsed into one risk budget, and the adjusted heat that results. Last line: headroom — 10% minus adjusted heat — the only number that authorizes a new buy. Now install the habit: this worksheet gets computed before every session, every day, no exceptions; it takes ninety seconds on a five-name book. And arm the gate: while adjusted heat reads above 10%, no new buy — not a pilot, not an add, not the best A+ chart in GREEN. Heat headroom is a precondition of permission, exactly like the band and the grade. Three keys open a trade: cell, formula, headroom.
chapters.on_screen: The completed heat worksheet — adjusted heat plus the headroom line (10% − adjusted heat), no-new-buy gate highlighted

lessons.title: Progressive Exposure and the Drawdown Protocol: Pilot → Half → Full → Overweight; De-Risk at −5% and −10%
lessons.note: The confirmation-gated ladder where every rung must be paid for by the rung below — the follow-through-day pilot-buy protocol after a regime turn, expanding only after the last rung paid — and the mirror-image down-ladder: at −5% of equity halve all new sizes, at −10% pilot-or-paper only, decided now while calm because it cannot be decided during. Artifact: the signed drawdown-protocol card plus a season-long equity curve showing the ladder expanding and the protocol contracting.

chapters.beat: open by laying the exposure ladder over a base breakout: contract, confirm, then expand is the same move at chart level, position level, and now account level, which is why full size on day one of a regime turn is a category error.
chapters.speaker_notes: One shape runs this whole system: contract, confirm, then expand. On the chart, it's a base — price contracts, the breakout confirms, the trend expands. At the position level, it's how you build a line — start small, let the trade prove itself, add only into proof. And at the account level — today's lesson — it's the exposure ladder: pilot, half, full, overweight, each rung gated by confirmation. Which is why full size on day one of a regime turn is a category error, not a bold call. The market just printed the equivalent of the first green candle off a low: that's a contraction ending, not a trend confirmed. You wouldn't buy a full position on the first tick above a pivot with no volume; don't run a full book on the first day the dial improves. Same shape, three altitudes.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: one base-breakout chart beside the exposure ladder — contract → confirm → expand at chart, position, and account level
chapters.example_spec: Use NVDA daily, October 2022–March 2023 as the slide's one chart (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the contraction — the multi-month base off the ≈$10.81 October 13 low, ranges tightening into December–January; the confirmation — the late-January breakout through the ≈$18.50 December pivot on expanding volume, weeks after the Jan 6 Nasdaq follow-through day; the expansion — the trend to the ≈$27.78 March close. Levels: entry ≈$18.60 over the pivot, stop ≈$16.80 under the last contraction low — read exact prices off the chart; the run to ≈$27.80 is roughly +5R. Draw the exposure ladder beside it and label the same three phases at account level: pilot at confirmation, rungs added only as the trend pays. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Pilot → Half → Full → Overweight, every rung paid for
chapters.beat: teach the confirmation-gated up-ladder with the follow-through-day pilot-buy protocol after a regime turn: pilots go on first, and the next rung is bought only after the last rung's open profit is paying for it.
chapters.speaker_notes: The up-ladder has four rungs — pilot, half, full, overweight — and one law: every rung must be paid for by the rung below it. It starts with the follow-through day: day four to seven off the low, a big up day on higher volume. That re-opens buying at PILOT size only — small probes in the best graded names, table-capped. Then the gate: you buy the next rung only after the last rung's open profit is paying for it — pilots working, sitting on gains that finance the added risk. Pilots green, move to half. Halves working, go full. Overweight is earned only when a fully expanded book is being carried by open profit. If the pilots get stopped instead, the market answered: back down the ladder, cheaply — probes cost fractions of a percent. You never wish your way up a rung; the book's own P&L is the ticket.
chapters.on_screen: The Pilot → Half → Full → Overweight ladder diagram with the follow-through-day rule labeled (day 4-7 off the low, up big on higher volume)

chapters.marker: A real season up the ladder
chapters.beat: narrate the season-long equity curve as pilots confirm and exposure expands rung by rung, marking on the curve exactly where each expansion was earned rather than wished for.
chapters.speaker_notes: Watch a real season climb it. The follow-through day prints — buying re-opens at pilot size: two or three probes in the best A+ names, each a fraction of normal risk. Ten days later the pilots sit up 2R-plus and the dial is improving: their open profit pays for the half rung, and the book widens to five names. The leaders base and break again; halves are financing fulls now, heat runs 6-7% against the 10% cap, all of it funded by the market's own money. By mid-season the book is fully expanded — and the overweight rung goes on only in the names that led the whole way up. Mark each expansion on the curve and say it out loud: earned here, not wished for. Then note what never happened — no rung was bought on hope, and every added dollar of risk was underwritten by profit already on the screen.
chapters.on_screen: Season-long equity curve — e.g. the January 2023 Nasdaq follow-through day into the spring AI run — with each rung expansion marked (or substitute a firm season)
chapters.example_spec: Build the demo equity curve on a $50,000 account over January–July 2023. Mark, in order: the Jan 6, 2023 Nasdaq follow-through day — two pilots go on, NVDA ≈$15.00 (split-adjusted — ≈10× that at the time) and META ≈$130, ≈0.3% risk each; late January — pilots up +2R-plus as NVDA closes the month ≈$19.54 and META ≈$148.97, halves added, curve ≈+2%; February–April — META's Feb 2 +19.8% and Apr 27 +14.6% earnings gaps let halves finance fulls, heat runs 6–7%, curve ≈+6%; May 25 — NVDA's +26.1% earnings gap, book fully expanded, curve ≈+12%; June — overweight only in the season's leaders (NVDA ≈$42.30, META ≈$287), curve ≈+16–18%. Annotate every rung 'earned here — paid for by open profit.' (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: The mirror down-ladder, decided while calm
chapters.beat: state the drawdown protocol verbatim (at −5% of equity halve all new sizes, at −10% pilot-or-paper only) and show the same curve's drawdown leg contracting on schedule, against the trader who tried to decide it during.
chapters.speaker_notes: The down-ladder is the same shape inverted, and it is decided now, while calm, because it cannot be decided during. Verbatim: at minus 5% of equity from your high-water mark, halve all new position sizes. At minus 10%, pilot-size or paper trades only. No third threshold, no discretion clause. Watch the drawdown leg of the same equity curve: the protocol trader's risk shrinks on schedule — half-size new positions after the first trigger, token probes after the second — so the curve flattens instead of accelerating downhill. Against it, the trader who tried to decide in the moment: sizing UP to win it back, converting a 10% drawdown into a 25% one — which then needs plus 33% just to get even. Drawdown math is asymmetric; the protocol exists because the person at minus 10% is the least qualified person alive to set their own size.
chapters.on_screen: The same equity curve's drawdown leg with the −5% and −10% trigger lines drawn, per THE MONDAY MAX-EXPOSURE PLAN section 6
chapters.example_spec: Extend the same demo curve into the August–October 2023 correction. Mark, in order: the high-water mark ≈$58,000 in late July; the early-August Nasdaq distribution cluster that drops the band; the −5% trigger line at ≈$55,100 — hit mid-August, all new sizes halved from there; the −10% line at ≈$52,200 — hit late September as the tape grinds toward the October 26 low, pilot-or-paper only from there. The protocol leg flattens near ≈−11%. Overlay the counter-example path — sizing up after each loss — turning the identical stop-out sequence into ≈−25%, which needs +33% to recover. One chart, two endings, the asymmetry drawn in R. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close by filling in and signing the drawdown-protocol card on camera with thresholds written in real dollars for the member's actual account, because a protocol you didn't pre-sign is just an opinion under stress.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill in the card and sign it on camera, and have the member do the same with real numbers. Not percentages — dollars. On a $50,000 account: high-water mark $50,000; first trigger $47,500 — from there, all new sizes are halved; second trigger $45,000 — from there, pilot or paper only, until equity recovers the threshold. Write the actual figures, because 'minus five percent' is an abstraction and $47,500 is a tripwire you'll recognize on the screen. Then sign it and date it. The signature matters: a protocol you didn't pre-sign is just an opinion under stress, and opinions under stress lose. When the trigger hits, there is no meeting and no re-litigation — the calm version of you already voted, and that vote outranks the tilted one. This card, the sizing table, and the heat worksheet are the whole portfolio-command kit.
chapters.on_screen: The drawdown-protocol card filled in with real dollar thresholds ($47,500 / $45,000 on a $50k account) and signed on camera

modules.label: M14 · The Inner Game and the Review Engine

lessons.title: Map Your Pattern First: The Trader's Self-Diagnostic
lessons.note: The 10-question diagnostic that locates each member's dominant failure pattern (fear family, tilt family, discipline family) before any fix is offered — with the instructor mapping one of his own real historical leaks on camera. Artifact: the completed pattern map the next two lessons and the capstone read from.

chapters.marker: You can't fix a leak you haven't found
chapters.beat: open with two traders running the identical system to opposite P&L, and state this module's doctrine: diagnosis before any fix, self-assessment before any technique, every lesson.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two traders run the identical system — same dial, same table, same setups — and finish the year on opposite sides of zero. The system didn't diverge; the operator did. One followed the plan under stress; the other paid a leak — a repeated, predictable behavior that taxes every trade it touches. This module's doctrine, applied in every lesson: diagnosis before any fix, self-assessment before any technique. We will not hand you a breathing exercise for a problem we haven't located. First you find YOUR pattern — the specific failure that fires under specific conditions — with evidence from your own trades. Then, and only then, we correct it. Generic mindset content is what the rest of the industry sells; a mapped leak with a named trigger is something you can actually plug. You cannot fix a leak you haven't found — and most traders have never looked.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: two equity curves from the identical system — one compounding, one bleeding — over the doctrine line 'diagnosis before any fix'

chapters.beat: draw the map of fear, tilt, and discipline with the signature behaviors of each, so members hear their own trading described before a single question is asked.
chapters.speaker_notes: Every trading leak lives in one of three families. The fear family: FOMO chases, valid setups seen and not taken, the trigger that couldn't be pulled, winners cut early to make the discomfort stop. Fear pays a tax on entries and steals the right tail of your winners. The tilt family: revenge trades after a stop-out, size escalating after losses, rapid-fire entries, the loss that spirals into a session-wrecker. Tilt shows up as your worst three days destroying your best thirty. The discipline family: stops moved and widened, plans abandoned mid-trade, the journal skipped, rules followed only while winning. Discipline leaks are quiet — no drama, just steady erosion. Listen for which description made you uncomfortable; that flinch is data. The diagnostic will score it properly, but most traders already know their family — they've just never said it out loud.
chapters.on_screen: Whiteboard map: three failure families — fear, tilt, discipline — with signature behaviors listed under each

chapters.beat: run all ten questions on camera pause-and-answer style, showing which family each answer scores toward and why honest scoring beats flattering scoring.
chapters.speaker_notes: Ten questions, taken live, pause-and-answer — and each answer scores toward a family. When a setup runs without you, do you chase it late? Fear. After two stop-outs, is your next size bigger or smaller? Bigger scores tilt. Have you moved a stop farther from entry in the last twenty trades? Discipline. Do you skip valid triggers after a losing streak? Fear. Has one session ever cost more than your five best combined? Tilt. Is your journal current through your last closed trade? Discipline. Answer against your last twenty real trades — pull the journal, not the memory. And score honestly: the flattering answer sends the wrong leak into the next two lessons and the capstone, so the correction you practice will be aimed at a problem you don't have. A gamed diagnostic has negative value. Tally the columns; the tallest one is your family.
chapters.on_screen: The 10-question self-diagnostic worksheet answered live, each answer scored to its family column

chapters.beat: work one of my real historical failure patterns through the same diagnostic using my own journaled trades, landing on the family and the exact trigger that used to fire it.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the same diagnostic pointed at me — one of my own real historical failure patterns, worked from my own journaled trades. [Presenter: use your own documented leak, or the firm's worked example.] The honest tally lands in the tilt family, and the journal proves it: after two stop-outs in a session, my third trade averaged well above normal size — the win-it-back trade — and that third trade's expectancy was disastrous. The trigger wasn't losing money; it was two losses in sequence, fast. That's the point of this exercise: the family is only the category — the map isn't done until you find the exact trigger that fires it, a specific observable condition, not a mood. Two consecutive stop-outs: that's a tripwire you can build a mechanical rule around, and two lessons from now, we will. Your map needs the same precision: family, trigger, evidence.
chapters.on_screen: Journal trade log filtered to the evidence trades — oversized third trades after back-to-back stop-outs (presenter substitutes their own or a firm-documented leak)
