chapters.example_spec: If no personally documented leak exists, use this firm-style worked example as the filtered journal evidence. Session one — April 19, 2024, a heavy red tape: NVDA red-to-green try ≈$84, −1R; QQQ bounce long as it set its ≈$413 low on 2× volume, −1R twenty minutes later; eight minutes on, an untagged NVDA long at double size into the ≈$76.20 close (a −10% day on 2.2× volume), −3.1R. Session two — August 1, 2024, the post-Fed reversal: AMD breakout ≈$144, −1R; META long ≈$505 as it faded from its ≈$521 gap open, −1R; untagged QQQ long at 2× size, −2.8R. Read the tally aloud: family = tilt; trigger = two fast stop-outs; third trades run double size with disastrous expectancy — the tripwire the circuit-breaker lesson arms. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: fill in the artifact with the member's dominant family, its trigger, and two evidence trades attached, and state the dependency out loud: the next two lessons and the capstone all read from this page.
chapters.speaker_notes: Complete the artifact before you leave this lesson. Three entries. One: your dominant family — fear, tilt, or discipline — from the honest tally. Two: the trigger, stated as an observable condition — 'after two consecutive losses,' 'when a watchlist name gaps without me,' 'when I'm up big by 10:30' — not a feeling. Three: two evidence trades attached — ticker, date, and what each cost in R — because a map without evidence is a guess. Then hear the dependency out loud: the next two lessons read from this page. The fear lesson corrects fear-family entries; the tilt lesson builds your circuit breaker around YOUR trigger; and the capstone playbook requires the leak plugged, with journal proof. A blank or flattered pattern map doesn't just waste this lesson — it silently aims the rest of the module at the wrong target. Fill it honestly.
chapters.on_screen: The pattern-map artifact filled in: dominant family · trigger · two evidence trades with their R cost

lessons.title: FOMO and the Fear Family: Signs, Subtypes, Corrections
lessons.note: The fear emotions on one template — nature, signs, subtypes, correction — with the FOMO tax quantified from journal data (average fill vs trigger price in basis points) and the two-candle wait rule as the correction. Includes one journaled real example: the trade seen, not taken, and what the tape did after.

chapters.marker: The FOMO tax, in basis points
chapters.beat: open by quantifying it from real journal data, average fill versus trigger price on chased entries, so the fear has a dollar cost before it has a name.
chapters.speaker_notes: Before the fear gets a name, it gets a price. Pull the journal data: every chased entry — where the fill came after the trigger because you hesitated, then paid up — and compute fill versus trigger in basis points. This sample's average: 90 basis points of chase. Sounds small. Now run it through the risk math: planned entry $50.00, stop $47.50 — $2.50 of planned risk per share. A chased fill at $50.45 means $2.95 of actual risk — 18% more than planned — and the 2R target you mapped from $50 just became about 1.7R from your real fill. FOMO isn't a feeling; it's a per-trade tax on your expectancy, paid at entry and compounded across every chase in the ledger. A trader with a 0.35R edge donating chunks of it to chases has no edge. Quantify first: a fear with a dollar cost is a fear you'll take seriously.
chapters.on_screen: Journal analytics — chased entries with fill-vs-trigger in basis points, plus the $50.00-trigger / $50.45-fill worked math

chapters.beat: install the fixed structure (nature, signs, subtypes, correction) and run the fear family through it: FOMO, fear of loss, and fear of pulling the trigger as subtypes of the same emotion.
chapters.speaker_notes: Every fear emotion gets processed on the same fixed template — nature, signs, subtypes, correction — so the work is systematic, not therapeutic. Nature: fear in trading is the brain treating a missed gain or an open loss as a threat, and it acts through urgency. Signs — yours are physical and specific: the lean toward the screen when a name rips, the hover over the buy button, the stomach drop when a position goes red. Learn your two or three tells; they fire before the bad click. Subtypes — all one emotion wearing different clothes: FOMO, where the pain of missing overrides the plan; fear of loss, where winners get cut at the first wiggle to make the discomfort stop; fear of pulling the trigger — valid setup, armed alert, no fill. Correction comes mechanically in the next chapters. Note the order: nature, signs, subtypes FIRST — you can't interrupt a pattern you can't recognize mid-flight.
chapters.on_screen: The fear-family template (nature · signs · subtypes · correction) with FOMO, fear of loss, and fear of pulling the trigger slotted as subtypes

chapters.marker: The trade seen and not taken
chapters.beat: replay one journaled real example of a valid setup skipped out of fear, then roll the tape forward and read honestly what it did after, because the answer is the cure either way.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here's a journaled one: a valid A-grade setup, alert armed at the trigger, everything the checklist demands — and no fill, because the last two trades were stop-outs and the hand wouldn't move. Now roll the tape forward and read it honestly, because the answer is the cure either way. Path one — the common one: the setup worked. Count the R that walked away and write it in the ledger as a real cost; skipped valid trades are losses the P&L never shows you, and a trader who only takes setups when feeling brave is running a worse system than the one they built. Path two: the setup failed. The process still failed — you refused a positive-expectancy bet for the wrong reason, and next time the same fear will skip a winner. Either way the lesson is identical: the checklist decides, not the nervous system. The journal makes the invisible cost visible.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, May 2023 — the earnings-gap EP seen and not taken, tape rolled forward to show it never looked back (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: NVDA daily, April–July 2023 (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time). Find, in order: the base under ≈$28; the May 24 after-hours earnings guidance shock; the May 25 gap — open ≈$38.52, +26.1%, ≈3× volume, straight to new highs; the EP trigger ≈$39.00 over the first-hour high; the stop ≈$36.60 under the gap-day low (≈6%) — read exact levels off the chart. Roll the tape forward: that gap-day low was never revisited — ≈$43.99 on June 20 (+2R), ≈$49–50 in late August (+3.7R to +4.7R), and past +20R by March 2024's ≈$90 close. Frame it as scripted: alert armed, two prior stop-outs froze the hand, and the walked-away R goes in the ledger as a real cost. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: teach the correction mechanically: when the urgency spikes you may still take the trade, but only after two full candles close and the checklist re-passes, then show it defusing a chase on replay.
chapters.speaker_notes: The correction is mechanical, because in the moment you cannot out-reason urgency. The rule: when the urgency spikes — the name is ripping, the lean toward the screen starts — you may still take the trade, but only after two full candles close and the checklist re-passes. On a 5-minute chart, that's up to ten minutes of enforced waiting. Not a ban — a toll gate. Two things happen behind it. Most chases die: the spike that manufactured the urgency stalls or pulls back, the checklist no longer passes, and the rule just saved you the 90-basis-point tax plus a bad entry. And the trades that survive it are real: still valid two candles later, trigger intact, volume confirming — take them, at table size, without guilt. Watch the replay: urge marked at the vertical line, two candles counted out, checklist re-run — the 'must buy NOW' candidate is now below the urge price. Urgency is information that something moved fast; it is never a reason.
chapters.on_screen: 5-minute replay of a spiking name — e.g. SMCI, January 2024 — with two full candles counted out before the re-checked entry (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: SMCI 5-minute replay, January 19, 2024 — the pre-announcement day (prices split-adjusted — ≈10× these at the time; it gapped +11.6% and closed +36%). Find, in order: the gap open ≈$34.76 on ≈3× volume; the vertical first-30-minute spike — draw the urge line at the ≈9:45 high; the next two full 5-minute candles pulling back below it — the chase died behind the toll gate, saving roughly a full R of slippage; the checklist re-run — above VWAP, volume confirming; the fresh trigger over the consolidation high, stop under the 10:00 low, roughly $2 of risk. Outcome: closes ≈$42.34 (≈+1.9R same day), ≈$55 by the Jan 30 gap (≈+8R) and ≈$122.90 on March 8 (≈+40R). Verify exact prints on platform replay. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: Your fear entry on the template
chapters.beat: close with the member filling the fear-family template from their own pattern map, plus the standing measurement: log fill-versus-trigger in basis points on your next ten entries and watch your personal FOMO tax shrink.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the member fills their own fear-family template from the pattern map. Nature: which subtype is yours — FOMO, fear of loss, or fear of pulling the trigger — in your own words, with the trigger condition from the map. Signs: your two or three physical tells, the ones that fire before the click. Evidence: the two trades from your map, with their cost in R. Correction: the two-candle wait rule, plus your subtype's specific variant — trigger-fear traders pre-commit with armed buy-stops at the exact price so the hand isn't in the loop; loss-fear traders write the stop as the only exit before entry. Then the standing measurement: on your next ten entries, log fill-versus-trigger in basis points, every trade, in the journal. Ten entries is enough to watch your personal FOMO tax move. The template names the fear; the measurement proves the correction is working. Numbers, not affirmations.
chapters.on_screen: The member's fear-family template beside the standing measurement: fill-vs-trigger in bps logged on the next ten entries

lessons.title: Tilt and Revenge: The Circuit Breaker and the Mental Hand History
lessons.note: The tilt subtypes and one hard mechanical rule — two consecutive stop-outs = flat for the rest of the day, platform closed, no appeal — plus the next-morning re-entry protocol so the breaker never becomes a week of avoidance, and the five-step written mental hand history that dismantles a recurring mistake at its logic error. Artifact: the circuit-breaker card and one complete worked hand history.

chapters.marker: The third trade is the expensive one
chapters.beat: open with a real sequence where two ordinary stop-outs led to an oversized revenge trade, then name the tilt subtypes so each member can spot which one is theirs.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here's the real sequence. Trade one: a planned setup, stopped for minus 1R. Fine — that's the system working. Trade two, twenty minutes later: another valid trigger, stopped again, minus 1R. Still fine on paper. Trade three, eight minutes after that: no setup tag, double normal size, entered on a green candle to win the morning back — minus 3.4R. Two ordinary stop-outs, one catastrophic response. The third trade is the expensive one, always. Now name the tilt subtypes so each member can spot theirs: revenge tilt — attacking the ticker that stopped you; entitlement tilt — 'I'm up huge this month, this can't happen to me'; desperation tilt — size escalating to get back to even before the close; injustice tilt — the market 'cheated,' so the rules stop applying. Different flavors, one signature: after losses, size goes UP while setup quality goes DOWN. That inversion is the tell.
chapters.on_screen: Journal trade log — the real three-trade sequence: −1R, −1R, then the oversized −3.4R revenge trade (or substitute a firm sequence)
chapters.example_spec: Stage the demo log on August 1, 2024 — the post-Fed reversal day (Nasdaq ≈−2.3%). Trade one, 9:52: AMD base-breakout trigger ≈$144 after the prior day's +8.9% gap, stopped ≈$141.20, −1R — planned, tagged. Trade two, 10:14: META long ≈$505 as it faded from its ≈$521 gap open, stopped ≈$500, −1R — still planned, still tagged; it closed ≈$497.74. Trade three, 10:22, eight minutes later: NVDA long ≈$114 on a green 5-minute candle, no setup tag, double normal size, sold ≈$109.50 into the afternoon slide — −3.4R. Show the size column doubling while the setup-tag column goes blank: the inversion tell. Session total −5.4R, of which −3.4R is the third trade the circuit breaker would have deleted. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: state the hard rule with no softening: two consecutive stop-outs means flat for the rest of the day, platform closed, no appeal, and explain why it must be mechanical precisely because you are least rational when it fires.
chapters.speaker_notes: The rule, verbatim, with no softening: two consecutive stop-outs means flat for the rest of the day. Platform closed. No appeal. Not 'smaller size after two losses.' Not 'one more if it's an A+.' Flat, closed, done until tomorrow. Why must it be mechanical? Because the moment it fires is precisely the moment you are least rational — the win-it-back urge is a physiological state, not a reasoning error, and you cannot out-argue your own adrenaline in real time. Any discretion clause becomes the door tilt walks through, every time. And notice what the rule costs: nothing that matters. If the tape is good tomorrow, it's good without your third trade today — and two stop-outs in one session usually means your read and the tape are out of sync anyway, so the breaker exits you from your worst conditions. It caps the tilt sequence at minus 2R. The third trade, the expensive one, never exists.
chapters.on_screen: The circuit-breaker card full screen: two consecutive stop-outs = flat for the day · platform closed · no appeal

chapters.beat: walk the specific return steps for the following open (review both stops, re-grade the setups, resume at normal size) so the breaker resets you for a day and never metastasizes into a week of avoidance.
chapters.speaker_notes: A breaker without a re-entry protocol becomes a week of avoidance — the trader flattened Tuesday who is still 'being careful' the following Monday has swapped tilt for fear. So the return steps are specific, for the very next open. One: review both stop-outs in the journal — were they valid setups that simply lost, or was something off in the reads? Ten minutes, written. Two: re-grade today's candidates cold — full rubric, letters assigned, as if yesterday didn't happen. Three: resume at normal size — the table's size, from the correct cell, not a fear-discounted half position. That third step is the one traders flinch on, and it's deliberate: cutting size after a breaker day punishes you for following your own rule and teaches your brain that the breaker is a fine. It isn't. Two stop-outs were the system working; the breaker was the system working; today is a normal day, sized normally.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: the next-morning re-entry protocol — review both stops · re-grade the setups · resume at normal size

chapters.marker: One mental hand history, worked complete
chapters.beat: write the five steps live on a real recurring mistake, drilling down to the logic error underneath it and the corrected logic that replaces it.
chapters.speaker_notes: The hand history is five written steps that dismantle a recurring mistake at its logic error, not its symptom. Worked live on a real one — moving stops lower mid-trade. Step one, describe the problem in detail: when price nears my stop, I cancel it and re-place it lower, telling myself I'm avoiding the wick-out. Step two, the logic behind it — why it makes sense in the moment: 'the level will hold; I'm protecting a good trade from noise.' Step three, why that logic is flawed: the stop WAS the structural invalidation, priced calmly at entry; if price reached it, the thesis is dead by my own definition — 'noise' is the name I give evidence I don't like. Step four, the correction: stops are set at entry and move only in my favor. Step five, why the correction is correct: it makes every loss the planned minus 1R — the number my entire expectancy math depends on. Written, not thought — writing is the tool.
chapters.on_screen: A blank mental hand history worksheet filled in live, five steps top to bottom, on the moved-stop mistake

chapters.marker: Sign the breaker, write the history
chapters.beat: close with the two artifacts and the pass bar: the signed circuit-breaker card posted by the platform, and one complete written hand history on the dominant mistake from your pattern map.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two artifacts leave this lesson, and both are pass bars. First, the circuit-breaker card, signed and physically posted by the platform — the rule verbatim: two consecutive stop-outs, flat for the day, platform closed, no appeal; with the next-morning protocol on the back: review both stops, re-grade, resume normal size. Sign it while calm, for the same reason as the drawdown card — the calm signature outranks the tilted argument, and a rule that lives only in your head is negotiable in exactly the moment it matters. Second, one complete written mental hand history on the dominant mistake from your pattern map — all five steps, full sentences, down to the logic error and the corrected logic. Not a mistake in general; YOUR mistake, with the evidence trades attached. The card handles the acute failure in real time; the hand history dismantles the chronic one at its root. Both filed, both dated, before the journal lesson.
chapters.on_screen: The signed circuit-breaker card beside the completed five-step hand history — the lesson's two pass-bar artifacts

lessons.title: The Fixed-Field Journal: Seven Fields, Three Grades — No Free-Form
lessons.note: The firm's journal schema — date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-vs-plan, the three-axis grade (idea, execution, preparation), annotated screenshot — set up live in the UCT Journal, because free-form notes cannot be aggregated into diagnosis and P&L is not a grade. One winner that grades poorly and one loser that grades well, entered on camera.

chapters.beat: open with a page of eloquent free-form notes that cannot answer one aggregate question, and state the two doctrines: unstructured notes cannot be diagnosed, and P&L is not a grade.
chapters.speaker_notes: Here's a page of genuinely good free-form journaling — thoughtful, honest, well-written. Now ask it one aggregate question: what's my win rate on breakout entries in YELLOW bands this quarter? Silence. Eloquence doesn't aggregate. Two doctrines drive this lesson. First: unstructured notes cannot be diagnosed. A diagnosis needs the same fields, filled the same way, across every trade — only then can twenty entries become a statistic and a statistic become a fix. Free-form prose turns 'I traded poorly' into a feeling; fixed fields turn it into a named, countable failure category. Second: P&L is not a grade. A reckless trade that got paid and a perfect trade that got stopped will both be graded on process — the journal's whole design exists to keep the money result from writing the review. Structure is the price of self-knowledge. From today: no free-form, seven fields, every trade.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: a page of eloquent free-form journal notes with the unanswerable question overlaid — 'win rate on breakouts in YELLOW this quarter?'

chapters.marker: The seven fields, one by one
chapters.beat: walk the schema on screen (date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-vs-plan, the three-axis grade, annotated screenshot) with what each field lets you aggregate later.
chapters.speaker_notes: Seven fields, and each earns its place by what it lets you aggregate later. Date — turns entries into a time series; slumps and streaks become visible. Setup tag — the catalog name, exactly, so weekly stats can roll up win rate and average R per setup. Entry type — which of the four triggers fired: BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN — so you learn which trigger YOU execute best. Planned R — the dollar risk fixed before entry; without it, no result can be priced in R. Exit-versus-plan — did the exit follow the written plan, yes or no; the single most diagnostic field in the schema. The three-axis grade — idea, execution, preparation, each scored separately, because a trade can be a good idea, poorly executed, well prepared. And the annotated screenshot — the chart at entry, marked up, because in review the picture recalls what prose forgets. Seven fields, one row, aggregatable forever.
chapters.on_screen: The seven-field schema on screen — date · setup tag · entry type · planned R · exit-vs-plan · three-axis grade · annotated screenshot — highlighted one at a time

chapters.marker: Set up live in the UCT Journal
chapters.beat: build the fixed-field template inside the actual UCT Journal on camera, with setup tags matched to the catalog names so weekly stats can roll up by setup.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build it live in the UCT Journal so the member leaves with the machine running. Create the entry template: the seven fields as the standard for every closed trade. The one that demands care is the setup tag — it must match the catalog name exactly, letter for letter, because the weekly rollup groups by tag: 'Flat Base Breakout' and 'flat base' are different buckets to a computer, and mismatched tags quietly destroy your per-setup statistics. Pull tags from the setup catalog, never from memory. Set planned R as a required numeric field. Set the three grades — idea, execution, preparation — as separate entries, never one blended score. Attach the screenshot slot and actually use it: mark the entry, the stop, and the reason on the chart itself. Two minutes of setup, and every future trade drops into a structure the review-cadence lesson can compute on.
chapters.on_screen: The UCT Journal — building the fixed-field template live, setup tags matched exactly to catalog names

chapters.marker: The winner that grades poorly, the loser that grades well
chapters.beat: enter both real trades on camera with idea, execution, and preparation graded separately, and let the inversion land: the loss was a good trade and the win was a bad one.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two real trades, entered on camera, and the inversion is the lesson. Trade one: a winner, plus 2.1R. Grade it honestly. Idea: C — no clean catalog fit, chased off a hot open, RS mediocre. Execution: C — filled above the plan price, no volume confirmation, stop widened intraday. Preparation: B — the name wasn't on the A-list; it appeared mid-session. This trade made money and was bad on every axis that repeats. Trade two: a loser, minus 1R. Idea: A — A-grade setup, GREEN band, catalog-clean. Execution: A — trigger to the tick, stop honored exactly where planned. Preparation: A — graded the night before, alert armed. The loss was a good trade; the win was a bad one. Run either pattern a hundred times and the 'loser' compounds while the 'winner' bleeds out. P&L is not a grade — this is what that doctrine looks like in rows.
chapters.on_screen: UCT Journal — two real entries side by side: the +2.1R winner graded C/C/B and the −1R loser graded A/A/A (or substitute firm trades)
chapters.example_spec: Winner: COIN, late February 2024 — bought ≈$185 mid-session on the bitcoin-through-$60k headline pop, not on the A-list, no catalog fit, filled ≈90 bps above the level, stop widened once from ≈$176 to ≈$172, lucky exit ≈$205 into the ≈$203.56 month-end close: +2.2R on the original risk, graded C (idea) / C (execution) / B (preparation). Loser: CELH, mid-March 2024 — late-stage flat-base breakout, pivot ≈$99.60, the March 14 all-time high, GREEN band, RS leading, graded the night before, alert armed, entered at the trigger, stopped exactly at the planned ≈$93: −1R, graded A / A / A. Roll forward: CELH never made a new high — ≈$82.92 by month-end, ≈$57 by June, −43%. The good loss dodged a collapse; the bad win is the pattern that eventually ruins. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: close with the standing rule and pass bar: every trade journaled the day it closes, all seven fields filled, ten consecutive complete entries before the review cadence lesson has anything to review.
chapters.speaker_notes: The standing rule: every trade is journaled the day it closes, all seven fields filled, zero blanks. Same-day matters — by tomorrow the memory has been edited by the outcome, and exit-versus-plan becomes fiction. A blank field is not a small omission; it's a hole in every future statistic that row touches — one missing setup tag and that trade vanishes from your per-setup win rates forever. The pass bar for this lesson is concrete: ten consecutive complete entries — ten trades, seventy fields, no gaps — before the review-cadence lesson has anything to review. Not your next ten good trades; your next ten trades, including the ugly ones, especially the ugly ones, because rule-break trades are the highest-value rows in the whole ledger. The journal is the raw material for everything downstream: weekly stats, the monthly audit, the capstone playbook. An incomplete journal doesn't slow that engine — it starves it.
chapters.on_screen: A completed seven-field entry beside the pass bar: ten consecutive complete entries, zero blanks

lessons.title: The Review Cadence: Daily Tag, Weekly Stats, Monthly Audit — Narrated on a Real Month
lessons.note: Three nested loops feeding one artifact: daily tag at exit, weekly setup-level win-rate/avg-R rollup, and an actual month reviewed end-to-end on camera — equity curve, per-setup statistics, mistake-tag frequency, converted into next month's single focus — closed by the 21-mistakes audit scored against the last 20 trades. Artifact: the 4-pillar monthly review template.

chapters.marker: The engine that outlives the course
chapters.beat: open with the claim this module exists to prove: three nested loops (daily tag, weekly stats, monthly audit) feeding one artifact are what turn your own trades into next month's curriculum.
chapters.speaker_notes: This module ends with a claim, and this lesson proves it: three nested loops feeding one artifact are what turn your own trades into next month's curriculum. Loop one, daily: a sixty-second tag at every exit. Loop two, weekly: the setup-level rollup — win rate and average R per catalog tag — the first view that tells you which setups deserve your size. Loop three, monthly: the full audit — equity curve, per-setup statistics, mistake-tag frequency — converted into one focus item and filed on the 4-pillar template. Each loop feeds the next: tags make the weekly computable, weeklies make the monthly readable, monthlies write next month's single focus. When the course ends, the videos stop — this engine doesn't. A trader running these three loops is generating their own coaching from their own data, forever. That is the difference between finishing a course and installing a system.
chapters.on_screen: Slide: three nested loops — daily tag → weekly stats → monthly audit — feeding the single 4-pillar artifact

chapters.marker: The daily tag and the weekly rollup
chapters.beat: demo the two fast loops live: the sixty-second tag at exit, then the weekly setup-level win-rate and average-R rollup that starts telling you which setups deserve your size.
chapters.speaker_notes: The two fast loops, demonstrated live. The daily tag: sixty seconds at exit, while the trade is still warm — the seven fields, plus a mistake tag if a rule bent. Sixty seconds is a design constraint, not an estimate: a review habit that costs ten minutes dies in a week; one that costs a minute survives. Then the weekly rollup, computed from those tags: group the week's closed trades by setup tag and read two numbers per setup — win rate, and average R. Even three weeks in, the table starts talking: Flat Base Breakouts running 55% winners at plus 0.6R average; EP entries at 30% winners but plus 1.4R — both profitable, differently shaped. Twenty trades per tag is when the numbers deserve real trust, but the direction shows early. This is the first honest answer to 'which setups deserve my size' — and it comes from your ledger, not your memory of it.
chapters.on_screen: UCT Journal — the sixty-second exit tag, then the weekly per-setup win-rate / average-R rollup

chapters.marker: A real month, end to end
chapters.beat: narrate an actual month's review on camera in order: the equity curve, the per-setup statistics, and the mistake-tag frequency table, reading what each layer says the others can't.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now a full month, reviewed end to end, in order, because each layer says what the others can't. First the equity curve: shape, not endpoint — a steady climb with a mid-month dip, or one monster day carrying twenty mediocre ones? The curve shows the experience of the month. Second, per-setup statistics: the month's trades grouped by catalog tag — one setup did the earning, one broke even, and one lost money at a 25% win rate and should arguably lose its capital next month. The stats show where the P&L actually came from, which the curve can't tell you. Third, the mistake-tag frequency table: 'moved stop' twice, 'chased entry' four times, 'no setup tag' once. The mistakes show what the trader did, which the stats can't. Read in order — curve, setups, mistakes — the month becomes a diagnosis: what happened, what caused it, what it cost. That diagnosis is next month's raw material.
chapters.on_screen: A real month in the Journal: equity curve, per-setup statistics table, mistake-tag frequency table (or substitute a firm month)
chapters.example_spec: If no personal month exists, load the firm demo month: March 2024, 14 closed trades, $50,000 start. Equity curve: climb to ≈+5R by March 8, mid-month dip to ≈+2.5R on three straight losers March 12–15, recovery to ≈+4.2R (≈+4.6%) — narrate shape before endpoint. Per-setup table: Flat Base Breakout — 6 trades, 4 wins, ≈+0.7R average, with NVDA (≈$79 to ≈$90 on the month, split-adjusted — ≈10× that at the time) doing the earning and AVGO roughly flat; Prev-Day-High Break — 5 trades, ≈0.0R; Gap/EP — 3 trades, 1 win, ≈−0.4R average, exemplified by CRWD's March 6 gap that opened ≈$90.01 and closed ≈$82.39 on 5.5× volume — the setup that should lose its capital. Mistake tags: chased entry ×4 (≈−1.8R), moved stop ×2, missing tag ×1. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: convert the month's data into next month's single focus item against the counter-example of the five-fix list that fixes nothing, then run the 21-mistakes audit scored against the last 20 trades to choose that focus honestly.
chapters.speaker_notes: The counter-example first: the five-fix list. 'Stop chasing, honor stops, size correctly, journal daily, trade less' — five fixes is zero fixes; attention doesn't divide that way, and February's list reappears verbatim in March. The rule: one month, one focus. To choose it honestly, run the 21-mistakes audit — score your last 20 trades against the catalog of classic errors, tallying every one each trade committed. The frequency column does the arguing: if 'chased entry' fired four times and cost more R than everything else combined, the focus writes itself — next month, every entry at trigger or through the two-candle rule, measured in fill-versus-trigger basis points. A proper focus item has three parts: the behavior, the mechanical rule that constrains it, and the number that will prove it moved. Not 'be more disciplined' — a measured behavior with a target. Twelve months of one-focus beats a decade of five-fix lists.
chapters.on_screen: The 21-mistakes audit sheet scored against the last 20 trades, with the single chosen focus circled

chapters.beat: close by filling the artifact (results versus target, setup-level stats, goal reflection, forward plan) from the month just reviewed, with the pass bar: one complete monthly review submitted before capstone entry.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close by filling the artifact from the month just reviewed. Pillar one — results versus target: the month's R and P&L against what the plan called for, gap noted without drama. Pillar two — setup-level stats: the per-tag win-rate and average-R table carried straight over, with the size-deserving setups marked. Pillar three — goal reflection: last month's single focus item, and the number that says whether it moved — this is where the one-focus system holds itself accountable. Pillar four — forward plan: next month's focus, chosen by the 21-mistakes audit, written as behavior, rule, and measurement. One page, four pillars, filed where the next review will read it back. And the pass bar, stated plainly: one complete monthly review submitted before capstone entry. The capstone builds your playbook from this data — a trader who hasn't produced one honest month of it has nothing to build from.
chapters.on_screen: The 4-pillar monthly review template — results vs target · setup-level stats · goal reflection · forward plan — filled from the month just reviewed

modules.label: M15 · The Options and Flow Overlay

lessons.title: Reading the Flow Tape — and the Veto Hierarchy: Confirmation, Never Signal
lessons.note: The Options Flow tab end-to-end — sweeps versus blocks, at-the-ask aggression, and unusual-versus-baseline — with ten real prints classified on camera into signal, hedge, and noise. Then the standing order of authority: regime and chart outrank flow, always — flow can upgrade conviction on a setup you already have, but hot flow on a failed-gate chart correctly stays a no-trade.

chapters.beat: open on a real screaming call sweep whose stock went nowhere, and name the trap this whole module exists to prevent: signal-chasing.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open cold on the print: a $1.9 million call sweep, at the ask, filled across four exchanges — and then the daily chart: the stock went nowhere for two weeks. That contradiction is why this module sits second-to-last in the course. Options flow is our flashiest data, and taught first it manufactures signal-chasers — people who buy prints instead of setups. So state the standing order before anything else: flow is confirmation, never signal. The dial grants permission, the chart supplies the trade, and only then does flow get a vote — and never the deciding vote. Big prints have many mothers: hedges, spread legs, closing trades, and someone else's information you cannot verify. This module teaches you to read the tape precisely so you can rank it properly — below regime, below the chart.
chapters.on_screen: Options Flow tab — an archived large at-the-ask call sweep beside the underlying's flat daily chart over the following two weeks (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Use AT&T (T), March–April 2024. Pull an archived multi-million-dollar at-the-ask call print off the flow tape — T routinely prints $1–3M call orders that are really covered-call and hedge flow. Beside it, show T's daily chart for the two weeks after the print: price pinned in a roughly one-dollar band around ≈$16.50–$17.50, flat 20-day, no base, no breakout. Walk it in order: the headline premium, the apparent fill urgency, then the going-nowhere chart. Read the exact print premium (≈$2M) and the forward drift (under ±3% over ten sessions) off the archived tape on recording day. Outcome: 0R — no setup ever existed, so no trade; the print was somebody's hedge. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk the Options Flow tab end-to-end and define the vocabulary live on the tape: sweep versus block, at-the-ask aggression versus mid-fill, size and premium.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the tab column by column with the live tape running. A sweep is one order split across multiple exchanges to hit every offer at once — it screams urgency; the buyer paid up to be filled now. A block is a single negotiated print, usually institutional, often a hedge or a rolled position — patience, not urgency. Fill location is the aggression read: at-the-ask means the buyer lifted the offer — aggressive; a mid-fill was negotiated between bid and ask and tells you far less about direction. Then size and premium: contracts times price times 100 — a 2,000-lot at $9.50 is $1.9 million of premium. Read every print in that order: sweep or block, ask or mid, how much money, which expiry. Short-dated at-the-ask sweeps are the urgency end of the spectrum; far-dated mid-fill blocks are the patience end.
chapters.on_screen: Options Flow tab, live tape, with the sweep/block, fill-side, size, and premium columns highlighted in turn

chapters.beat: show the same $2M print landing on SPY and on a sleepy mid-cap, and teach that 'unusual' is always measured against that ticker's normal tape, never an absolute number.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the identical $2 million call print on two tickers. On SPY it is a rounding error — SPY trades billions in premium every session, so $2 million moves nothing and means nothing. On a sleepy mid-cap that averages $200,000 of call premium a day, that same print is ten times the ticker's normal tape — somebody suddenly wants ten days of ordinary interest in one order. That is the whole lesson: 'unusual' is always measured against that ticker's own baseline, never against an absolute dollar number. No premium threshold means anything by itself. So the reading discipline is two questions, in order: what does this name's tape normally look like, and how many multiples of normal is today? A modest print at five times baseline outranks a headline print at one times baseline, every day of the week.
chapters.on_screen: Options Flow tab split view — the same ~$2M call print shown landing on SPY versus a low-baseline mid-cap
chapters.example_spec: Left panel: SPY, January 2022 — price ≈$440–465, average volume ≈92M shares. A $2M call print against SPY's multi-billion-dollar daily premium is under 1× baseline; the tape swallows it. Right panel: Activision (ATVI), Jan 12–14, 2022 — the documented burst of short-dated call buying before Microsoft's Jan 18 bid, running ≈10×+ the name's ordinary call premium. Walk in order: the SPY print drowning; the ATVI prints stacking — same direction, near-dated, at the ask, repeated. ATVI ≈$63–65 before, gapping to ≈$82 on the news (+26%). ATVI was delisted in October 2023, so pull the archived chart and tape. Outcome: baseline multiples, not dollars, carried the information — several R on the gap. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: pull ten real prints off today's tape and sort each on camera into signal, hedge, or noise, saying the tell out loud before revealing the verdict.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now reps. Pull ten real prints off today's tape and, for each one, say the tell out loud before the verdict. Signal tells: at-the-ask sweep, multiples of the ticker's baseline, dated tightly enough to imply a timeline, and repeated prints stacking the same direction — urgency plus size plus repetition. Hedge tells: puts bought in a name or sector that just ran, deep-in-the-money prints paired against stock, or one visible leg of a spread — protection, not prediction. Noise tells: mid-fills, small lots, and anything on a high-baseline ticker at one times normal. Expect roughly this split on an ordinary day: most of the tape is noise, a meaningful minority is hedging, and genuine directional signal is rare — which is exactly why it never outranks the chart. Ten prints, ten spoken verdicts: signal, hedge, or noise.
chapters.on_screen: Options Flow tab — today's live tape, ten prints flagged and classified one at a time

chapters.beat: state the standing order of authority (regime and chart outrank flow, always), then show hot call flow on a failed-gate chart and let it correctly die as a no-trade: flow's only legal job is upgrading conviction on a setup you already have.
chapters.speaker_notes: State the standing order of authority and never soften it: regime and chart outrank flow, always. Flow's only legal job is upgrading conviction on a setup you already have — a valid base, a passed Stage-2 gate, a band that grants permission. Then show the test case: hot call flow, five times baseline, at-the-ask sweeps — sitting on a chart that fails the gates, a Stage-4 name below its declining moving averages with no base. The verdict is a no-trade, and it is correct. Flow cannot create a trade, cannot rescue a failed gate, and cannot overrule an ORANGE band. It can raise conviction inside the sizing table's cell; it cannot mint a cell that doesn't exist. If your chart says no and the tape says yes, the answer is no — you trade the setup, not the print.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen — heavy call-flow prints beside a failed-gate Stage-4 chart, e.g. CVNA daily, mid-2022, heavy call speculation all the way down (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Keep CVNA, daily, May–October 2022 (levels as today's adjusted chart shows them). Features in order: Stage-4 downtrend from the ≈$12.19 high on May 2 to the ≈$2.58 low on Oct 24; monthly closes stepping down ≈$5.89 → $4.52 → $5.83 → $6.60 → $4.06 → $2.71; price under a declining 50-day the whole stretch; every bounce dying — the May 16 +11% gap opening ≈$8.50 and closing weak at ≈$7.68 on 2.4× volume, the Sept 12 +9.8% gap erased next day by Sept 13's −12.1% gap. Beside it, that era's tape: repeated at-the-ask call sweeps at multiples of baseline, all the way down. A flow-chased bounce entry near the Aug 5 ≈$9.40 close was −57% by late September. Outcome: the no-trade verdict saved ≈ −3R to −5R per attempt. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Expressing a Swing with Calls: Strike, Expiry, Delta — Same 2% Math
lessons.note: The defined-risk stock substitute with hard rules: roughly 0.70+ delta, expiry at least twice the expected holding period, and total premium at risk inside the same risk budget the formula would have allowed for shares. One identical swing built twice — shares versus calls — with risk, breakeven, and both P&L paths compared line by line at exit.

chapters.marker: The lottery ticket and the substitute
chapters.beat: put a cheap OTM weekly next to a 0.70-delta three-month call on screen and name which one funds the options industry and which one is a defined-risk stock substitute.
chapters.speaker_notes: Two contracts, same underlying, on one screen. Left: the cheap out-of-the-money weekly — a 0.10-delta call for forty cents. It needs the stock to be right on direction, magnitude, and week, and it bleeds value every session; this ticket funds the options industry. Right: a 0.70-delta call, three months out. It is mostly intrinsic value, moves about seventy cents for every dollar the stock moves, and gives the swing time to work — a defined-risk stock substitute, not a lottery ticket. That is the only options trade this course teaches: same chart, same setup, same stop logic as shares, but the maximum loss is written on the ticket the moment you buy it. If the stock gaps through your stop overnight, shares eat the whole gap; the call can never lose more than its premium.
chapters.on_screen: Options chain side by side — e.g. AAPL: the 5%-OTM weekly call versus the 0.70-delta call three months out

chapters.beat: write the non-negotiables before any chain is opened: roughly 0.70+ delta, expiry at least twice the expected holding period, and total premium at risk inside the same risk budget the formula would have allowed for shares.
chapters.speaker_notes: Write the three hard rules before any chain is opened, because the chain is where discipline dies. Rule one: roughly 0.70-plus delta — below that you own a decaying probability bet, not a stock substitute. Rule two: expiry at least twice the expected holding period — planning a three-week swing, buy no less than six weeks out, in practice the two-to-three-month contract, so theta never forces your hand while the setup is still valid. Rule three: total premium at risk stays inside the same risk budget the formula would have allowed for shares — the instrument changes, the risk budget does not. Each rule kills a specific failure: the delta rule kills lottery tickets, the expiry rule kills being right about the stock and losing on the clock, the budget rule kills the classic 'it's only premium' oversize blowup.
chapters.on_screen: The call-substitution checklist card — the three hard rules written as three lines

chapters.beat: re-run Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % for the share version of the trade, then cap total call premium at that identical dollar risk so the 2% ceiling never moves when the instrument changes.
chapters.speaker_notes: Re-run the formula exactly as Module 5 taught it. Account $50,000, target risk 1% — that is $500. Entry $50.00, structural stop $47.50: stop distance 5%. Position Size % = Account Risk % ÷ Stop Distance % = 1% ÷ 5% = 20% — a $10,000 position, 200 shares, and 200 × $2.50 = $500 at risk. That $500 is the number that carries over. For the call version you cap total premium at risk at that identical $500 — not at some larger number because 'options are cheap.' The 2% hard max and the under-1% preference never move when the instrument changes; the formula priced the trade's risk budget, and the budget is instrument-blind. If the premium for even one contract exceeds the budget, the answer is fewer contracts or no trade — never a bigger budget.
chapters.on_screen: The Sizing Gate toolkit card — Problem 1's arithmetic re-run on a $50,000 account

chapters.beat: construct the identical real swing as shares and as calls on camera: same chart, same entry and stop, contract count sized against the budget, breakeven marked on both tickets.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build the same real swing twice on camera. The chart: a base breakout through $50 with the structural stop at $47.50. Ticket one, shares: 200 shares at $50.00, stop $47.50, $500 at risk on the $50,000 account — 1%. Ticket two, calls: the $45-strike call about 90 days out, roughly 0.75 delta, offered at $5.00. One contract is $500 of premium — the entire budget — so the size is exactly one contract, controlling 100 shares' worth of exposure at about 75 deltas. Mark breakeven on both tickets: shares break even at $50.00; the call at expiry breaks even at strike plus premium, $45 + $5 = $50.00 — the same level. Same chart, same trigger, same invalidation, same $500 maximum planned loss. The difference is capital: $10,000 committed versus $500, and the call's loss stays capped even through a gap.
chapters.on_screen: UBER daily, Nov 2023 — base breakout through $50, both tickets built on the same chart (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Keep UBER, daily, October–December 2023. Features in order: the Oct 26 low ≈$40.09 forming the left side under the ≈$50 pivot; the Nov 7 earnings bar closing ≈$49.92 on ≈3.3× average volume, right at the pivot; the mid-November push through ≈$50 that carried November to a ≈$56.38 close; the pre-breakout contraction just under the pivot anchoring the stop. Build both tickets on it: shares — entry ≈$50.00, stop ≈$47.50 (5% distance); calls — the ≈$45-strike, ~90-day, ≈0.70–0.75-delta contract offered near ≈$5.00, breakeven ≈$50. S&P 500 inclusion news drives Dec 4 to ≈$58.63 and Dec 15 to ≈$61.86 on ≈14× volume. Outcome: ≈+2.4R on shares at the $56 target; the call ≈+120% on capped premium. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: replay both versions to the exit and compare the P&L paths side by side on the target-hit path and the stop-hit path, showing where calls outrun stock and where theta and the premium cap bite; members leave with the call-substitution checklist.
chapters.speaker_notes: Replay both tickets to the exit, line by line. Target path — stock to $56, up 12%: shares make 200 × $6 = $1,200, +2.4R on $10,000 committed. The call is worth at least its $11 intrinsic, so +$600 or better, +1.2R — fewer deltas because the premium cap bought one contract, but +120% on $500 of capital versus +12% on $10,000. Stop path — stock to $47.50: shares lose the planned $500, and an overnight gap to $45 would cost $1,000; the call still has salvage value when you exit at the stop, and its absolute worst case is the $500 premium, gap or no gap. Where calls lag: a stalling stock pays theta every day, and the premium cap means smaller absolute wins. Hand over the call-substitution checklist — delta, expiry, budget, breakeven — and close.

lessons.title: Dealer Positioning and Gamma: Pins, Slingshots, and the Flow + EP Combination
lessons.note: Gamma context on the GEX view as the map of where dealers dampen versus accelerate price — one real pinned expiry and one slingshot through a level, both annotated, explicitly bounded as context for exits, never an entry system. Closes with the highest-conviction combination in the playbook: unusual call flow stacked on a qualifying Episodic Pivot, traced through all six LOOP stations.

chapters.marker: Why price sticks to some strikes
chapters.beat: open on an expiry-Friday chart glued to a round strike all afternoon and name the invisible hand behind it: dealer hedging.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open on an expiry Friday afternoon: the index glued to a round strike for four hours, every push sold, every dip bought, closing almost exactly on the number. That is not coincidence and it is not conspiracy — it is dealer hedging, done mechanically and in public. Market makers who take the other side of options must hedge with shares; how they hedge depends on their gamma position, and near a strike loaded with open interest their hedging flows press price back toward it. The invisible hand has a map, and our dashboard draws it. Two warnings before we start: this is context, not a crystal ball, and it matters most in the days around expiry and in index products and huge single names — a thin mid-cap's gamma map is barely a sketch.
chapters.on_screen: SPY 15-minute chart, a triple-witching opex Friday — e.g. Dec 15, 2023, price glued to the heavy round strike into the close (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: Keep SPY, 15-minute, Friday December 15, 2023 — triple-witching opex, and the heaviest-volume session of that whole stretch at ≈1.8× average. Features in order: the morning drift toward the ≈$470 strike, that expiry's heaviest open-interest shelf; midday oscillation — pushes above ≈$470.50 sold, dips toward ≈$468.50 bought; the range visibly tightening after 2 PM ET; the official close $469.33, within $0.70 of the strike. Annotate the rejections 'dealer supply' and the dip-buys 'dealer demand.' Verify the $470 open interest and the exact intraday prints on your platform. Outcome: 0R by design — this is context, not a trade; breakout attempts into a heavy strike stalled all afternoon while enormous premium expired at the pin. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: read the GEX view as the map of where dealers dampen versus accelerate price: positive-gamma zones absorb moves, negative-gamma zones amplify them.
chapters.speaker_notes: Read the GEX view as a terrain map of dealer hedging pressure. Positive-gamma zones: dealers are net long gamma, so their hedging leans against price — they sell into rallies and buy into dips. Moves get absorbed, ranges compress, and heavy positive strikes act like magnets; that is where pins live. Negative-gamma zones: dealers are net short gamma, so their hedging chases price — they must sell as the market falls and buy as it rises. Moves get amplified; that is where slingshots live. The flip point where net gamma changes sign is the boundary between the two regimes. So the read is three items: where is price relative to the flip point, which strikes carry the heavy positive gamma, and what sits below in negative territory. Dampen above, accelerate below — that is the whole map.
chapters.on_screen: The GEX view on the dashboard — net gamma by strike, flip point and heavy strikes annotated
chapters.example_spec: Capture the dashboard's GEX view on SPY during a monthly opex week (any third week of the month; the Dec 15, 2023 expiry if archived data exists — spot closed ≈$469.33 that day). Features in order: the net-gamma-by-strike bars; the flip point where net gamma changes sign — typically ≈1–3% below spot in an uptrend; the two heaviest positive-gamma strikes, clustered at round 5-point SPY levels at and just above spot — label both; the negative-gamma shelf below the flip. Annotate 'dampen' across the positive zone and 'accelerate' below the flip. Read the actual bar heights and strikes off the view — they change daily. Outcome: 0R, context only — this map places targets, partials and stop urgency; it never creates an entry. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk one real pinned expiry bar by bar, showing dealer hedging pressing price back into the heavy strike into the close.
chapters.speaker_notes: Annotate a real pin bar by bar. Morning: price drifts toward the heavy strike — the biggest positive-gamma concentration on the board. Midday: every rally of a few points meets dealer selling — long-gamma dealers sell rallies to stay hedged — and every dip meets their buying. The range tightens hour by hour like a closing vise. Last hour: the magnet wins; price closes within a fraction of the strike, and enormous premium expires worthless around it. Two honest caveats while annotating: pins are a tendency, not a law — strong enough news snaps any pin — and the effect concentrates in the final session before expiry. The tradable takeaway is modest and real: do not count on a breakout launching into a heavy positive-gamma strike on expiry day; that is where moves go to stall, so partials belong in front of it.
chapters.on_screen: The same SPY opex Friday walked bar by bar with the GEX heavy strike overlaid (or substitute a firm example)
chapters.example_spec: Keep SPY, 15-minute, December 15, 2023, with the ≈$470 heavy positive-gamma strike overlaid as a horizontal band. Bar-by-bar: 9:30–11 AM drift into ≈$470 from below; midday — mark three rally bars sold within ≈$0.75 above the strike and three dip bars bought within ≈$1.50 below it; the hourly range contracting like a vise after 1 PM; the final hour closing $469.33 — $0.67 from the strike — on the heaviest volume of the stretch (≈1.8× average), as the magnet wins. State the caveats on screen: pins are tendency, not law, and concentrate in the last session before expiry. Outcome: 0R context — the tradable takeaway is taking partials in front of heavy positive-gamma strikes on expiry day. Verify bars on your platform. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: walk one real break through a negative-gamma level that accelerated instead of stalling, then bound the tool explicitly: gamma is context for exits and targets, never an entry system.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the mirror image. Walk a break through a level sitting in negative-gamma territory: price breaks it, short-gamma dealers must sell into the fall to stay hedged, which pushes price lower, which forces more selling — the move accelerates exactly where a chart reader expected support to slow it. August 5, 2024 is the textbook print: SPY gapping down through negative-gamma territory in the yen-carry unwind, levels slicing instead of holding. Then bound the tool, explicitly and permanently: gamma is context for exits and targets, never an entry system. Use it two ways only — expect stall risk into heavy positive strikes near expiry when placing targets and partials, and expect acceleration rather than support when price trades below the flip point, which argues for honoring stops instantly. Nobody at this firm enters a trade because of a GEX chart.
chapters.on_screen: SPY hourly, Aug 5, 2024 — the yen-carry unwind slicing through negative-gamma levels, GEX overlay annotated

chapters.beat: stack unusual call flow on a qualifying Episodic Pivot (the neglected stock gapping on a true surprise) and trace the trade through all six LOOP stations, regime to review — the highest-conviction pattern in the playbook.
chapters.speaker_notes: Close the module with the highest-conviction combination in the playbook. Start with a qualifying Episodic Pivot — the neglected stock gapping 10%-plus on huge volume from a true surprise the market has not priced. Then stack unusual call flow on it: at-the-ask sweeps at multiples of that ticker's baseline, confirming institutions are paying up for the same thesis. Trace it through all six LOOP stations. Regime: the dial's band grants permission. Scan: the gap scan surfaces the name at the open. Setup: Episodic Pivot, Gaps & Catalysts family, graded on the card. Size: Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, capped by the regime × grade cell, 2% hard max. Manage: partials into strength, trail the rest on the 10/20-day. Review: the 7-field journal entry. Flow confirmed the trade; it never created it. That ordering is the whole module.
chapters.on_screen: NVDA daily, May 2023 — the earnings-gap EP with record call premium behind it, traced station by station (or substitute a firm trade)
chapters.example_spec: Keep NVDA, daily, March–August 2023 — prices split-adjusted, ≈10× these at the time. Features in order: months of consolidation ≈$25–30 after the 2022 bear (March close ≈$27.78, April ≈$27.75); the May 24 guidance shock at earnings; the May 25 gap — open ≈$38.52 from a ≈$30.54 close, +26.1% on ≈3.1× average volume, the heaviest day of the stretch and a true unpriced surprise; record single-day call premium, at-the-ask sweeps at many multiples of baseline. Trace the LOOP: GREEN dial; gap scan surfaces it at the open; EP, Gaps & Catalysts, grade A+; entry ≈$38.50 over the first-hour high, stop ≈$36.50 (≈5%); partials into ≈$42 ≈+1.7R; 10/20-day trail to ≈$47 by Aug 24 ≈+4R. Flow confirmed; the gap created the trade. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

lessons.title: Choose Your Two: Match the Families to Your Drill Data — and Sign the Specialization Contract
lessons.note: The member mines their own family-drill scores, placement-drill results, and journal statistics from Modules 7-14 to pick a primary family and two setups — selection by data, not preference, with the anti-hopping doctrine stated plainly: traders fail by jumping between setups, not by picking the wrong one. Ends by signing the specialization contract on camera: one primary setup, two full earnings seasons, 40 journal-logged reps before any expansion. Artifact: the family-fit scorecard and the signed contract. Uses your own logged drill and field-week results as the data — the choice is read off your numbers, not your mood. This capstone is the single graduation gate for BOTH courses (UCT Foundations points here).

chapters.beat: open with the diagnosis that kills most traders: they fail by jumping between setups, not by picking the wrong one, so today the data picks and you commit.
chapters.speaker_notes: Open with the diagnosis, because it explains this entire lesson: traders fail by jumping between setups, not by picking the wrong one. Every family in the catalog works — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims all carry edge when executed. None of them works for a hopper, because edge lives in accumulated reps, and a trader who touches three setups in six weeks never banks twenty reps in any of them. You saw this leak in Module 1's Placement Diagnostic — question 4 asked exactly that. So today the selection method changes: your preferences don't vote, your mood doesn't vote, your data votes. You will mine your own logged record from Modules 7 through 14, read the answer off a scorecard, and then sign a contract that makes the choice binding. Commitment is the edge.
chapters.on_screen: The Placement Diagnostic toolkit card — the setup-hopping leak row (Q4 + Q9) highlighted

chapters.beat: pull up your family-drill scores, your four-family placement-drill results, and your journal statistics from Modules 7 through 14: these logged numbers, not your mood, are the electorate.
chapters.speaker_notes: Pull up the record — yours, not an example. Three sources, all logged during Modules 7 through 14. First, family-drill scores: the graded replay drills, twenty reps per family, answer covered — your accuracy identifying and executing each family's flagship in replay. Second, the four-family placement-drill results — how you scored when the families competed head-to-head on the same charts. Third, journal statistics: every field-week trade tagged by setup, with wins, losses, and average R per tag, straight from your Journal. These logged numbers are the electorate; your mood is not on the ballot. If a source is thin — a family with only six logged reps — record that honestly too, because a thin sample is itself data: you cannot claim a family you have not repped. Lay all three sources on the desk before any conclusion is drawn.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal — statistics view filtered by setup tag across the Module 7-14 field weeks

chapters.beat: fill the scorecard live on camera (accuracy per family, average R per family, reps per family) and read the primary family straight off the totals.
chapters.speaker_notes: Fill the family-fit scorecard live, one row per family, three columns per row: accuracy per family, average R per family, reps per family. Accuracy comes from the drills — how often you called the pattern and its trigger correctly with the answer covered. Average R comes from the journal's field-week trades — what the family actually paid you per unit of risk. Reps is the sample size that tells you how much to trust the first two columns. Then read the primary family straight off the totals — no interpretation, no negotiation. A family with 78% drill accuracy, +0.4R average, and thirty logged reps beats a family with 55% accuracy and +0.1R, no matter which is more exciting to trade. If two families genuinely tie, the tiebreak is reps: go where your sample is deepest, because that is where your evidence is real.
chapters.on_screen: The family-fit scorecard — four family rows, three columns, being filled in on camera

chapters.beat: pick the primary and second setup inside the winning family, and work the honest case where data contradicts the heart (you love EPs, your numbers say pullbacks) — the data wins.
chapters.speaker_notes: Inside the winning family, pick two: the primary setup and the second. Same electorate — drill accuracy and journal R per setup tag, not affection. Then work the honest case out loud, because it is most members' actual case: you love EPs. They are cinematic, fast, and the crown combination from Module 15 made them glamorous. But your numbers say pullbacks — your Gaps & Catalysts drill accuracy sits in the fifties while your pullback executions grade in the high seventies with better average R. The data wins. And remember the mastery clock: EP mastery is honestly priced at three to four earnings seasons — a family your record does not support yet is not banned forever, it is deferred until your logged reps earn it. Write both chosen setups on the scorecard. The heart gets a vote in what you drill next year; it gets no vote today.
chapters.on_screen: The completed scorecard beside the four family names — the loved family losing to the evidenced one

chapters.beat: one primary setup, two full earnings seasons, 40 journal-logged reps before any expansion; the signed specialization contract plus the completed family-fit scorecard is the artifact, and this choice goes into your capstone folder — graduation itself hangs on the defended trade plan two lessons from now, the single gate both courses share.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now sign it, on camera, because a commitment witnessed is a commitment kept. The specialization contract reads: one primary setup, two full earnings seasons, forty journal-logged reps before any expansion. Two earnings seasons because setup mastery is paced in market cycles, not weeks — the pattern must be seen across different tapes. Forty logged reps because that is a sample large enough for your expectancy math to mean something. Before any expansion — not 'unless bored,' not 'unless a hot streak.' The artifact leaving this lesson is the signed specialization contract plus the completed family-fit scorecard, and both go into your capstone folder. Be clear about what is ahead: graduation itself hangs on the defended trade plan two lessons from now — the single gate both courses share; UCT Foundations members arrive at this same door. The contract you just signed is what that defense is built from.
chapters.on_screen: The Playbook Template + Defense Rubric card — the 'Specialization contract signed: one primary setup · two full earnings seasons · 40 journal-logged reps' checklist line

lessons.title: Write Your Playbook: The Five-Field Entries for Your Two Setups
lessons.note: Authoring both playbook entries on the firm's five-field card, extended with your size rule and management plan — template — context and regime conditions, entry trigger, stop and size rule, management plan, failure modes — modeled by the instructor writing one complete entry live. This document is the course's terminal artifact and the thing reviewed for graduation. Authored as a real artifact in the Journal's Notebook — not a worksheet that dies in a download folder. One playbook serves both courses.

chapters.marker: A playbook you wrote beats one you read
chapters.beat: open with why this document is the course's terminal artifact and the thing actually reviewed for graduation, not a worksheet that dies in a download folder.
chapters.speaker_notes: Say what this document is before writing a word of it: your playbook is the course's terminal artifact — the thing actually reviewed for graduation — not a worksheet that dies in a download folder. That is why it gets authored inside the Journal's Notebook, where it lives next to the trades it will govern, not in a PDF you never reopen. And say why writing beats reading: a playbook you wrote beats one you read because the writing is the learning — every number you commit to is a decision made now, while calm, instead of mid-trade, while bleeding. The firm hands you the template; the numbers must be yours, mined from your two contracted setups and your own logged stats. The pass bar, stated up front so nobody is surprised: every field numeric and falsifiable — a document a stranger could trade from.
chapters.on_screen: The Playbook Template + Defense Rubric toolkit card — the two five-field entry sections, blank

chapters.beat: walk the firm's template field by field: context and regime conditions, entry trigger, stop and size rule, management plan, failure modes — and the standard each must meet: numeric and falsifiable.
chapters.speaker_notes: Walk the firm's template field by field. Field one: context and regime conditions — what the chart must show before the trade exists, plus the minimum permission band, GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE. Field two: entry trigger — exact price logic, to the tick, with a volume threshold, expressed as one of the four triggers: BASE BREAKOUT, PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, or RED TO GREEN. Field three: stop and size rule — the invalidation price plus Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, 2% hard max, prefer under 1%. Field four: management plan — breakeven at roughly +1R, a third off at 2-3R into strength, and the named trail: 10-day for a fast mover, 20- or 50-day for a position hold. Field five: failure modes — the two ways the setup dies and the tell for each. The standard every field must meet: numeric and falsifiable.
chapters.on_screen: The five-field template — SETUP 1 section of the Playbook card, each field highlighted as it is named

chapters.beat: the instructor authors a complete entry for a flagship setup in real time inside the Journal's Notebook, narrating every number as it lands on the page.
chapters.speaker_notes: The instructor authors one complete entry in real time — the Flat Base Breakout, the course's flagship — narrating every number as it lands in the Notebook. Context and regime: GREEN band minimum, Stage-2 stock, RS line at highs, a five-week flat base with volume drying up into it. Entry trigger: BASE BREAKOUT — buy-stop $50.10, valid only on expanding volume through the $50.00 pivot. Stop and size: $47.50, under the final contraction low, where the pattern is objectively broken — 5.2% stop distance, so at 1% account risk, 1% ÷ 5.2% ≈ 19% position, inside the GREEN + A+ 20-25% cap. Management: breakeven at roughly +1R, a third off at 2-3R, trail the 20-day. Failure modes: a close back inside the base within three days on rising volume — exit, don't argue — and a breakout whose volume never expands. Every line a number.
chapters.on_screen: The Journal's Notebook — the flagship entry typed live, the worked flat-base chart alongside
chapters.example_spec: Use UBER, daily, September–December 2023 — the same chart as Module 15's call lesson, so the narrated numbers ($50.10 / $47.50) sit on real tape. Features in order: the base under the ≈$50.00 pivot (September close ≈$45.99, the Oct 26 low ≈$40.09 as the left side); the tight early-November shelf with volume drying up; RS line at highs against a firming market; the Nov 7 earnings bar closing ≈$49.92 on ≈3.2× volume, then the mid-November push through $50 into a ≈$56.38 November close. Author the entry live: buy-stop ≈$50.10, stop ≈$47.50 (≈5.2% distance), 1% ÷ 5.2% ≈ 19% position. Outcome: the December run — ≈$58.63 on Dec 4, ≈$61.86 on Dec 15 — pays ≈+2.3R to the first trail exit near $56. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.marker: What a weak entry looks like
chapters.beat: contrast with a vague entry ('buy strength, stop below support') and show how every unfalsifiable line becomes a mid-trade argument with yourself at the worst possible moment.
chapters.speaker_notes: Now the contrast that makes the standard stick. Put a vague entry on screen: 'buy strength, stop below support, take profits when extended.' Read it as your future self, mid-trade, down 3% at 3:50 PM. Is this strength? Which support — the intraday low, the 20-day, the base low? Extended by whose measure? Every unfalsifiable line becomes a mid-trade argument with yourself at the worst possible moment — and you will lose that argument, because the arguing self wants comfort, not process. Line it up against the live entry from the last chapter: $50.10 is not debatable. $47.50 is not debatable. 19% is arithmetic. The vague entry fails review not because it is short but because a stranger could not trade it — and in a drawdown, you are the stranger. Falsifiable numbers are the only defense against the person you become inside a losing trade.
chapters.on_screen: Split screen — the vague 'buy strength, stop below support' entry beside the fully numeric flagship entry

chapters.beat: write both entries for your two contracted setups in the Journal's Notebook; pass bar: all five fields on both entries filled with numbers a stranger could trade from — this one document goes to graduation review and serves both courses.
chapters.speaker_notes: Your turn, and this is the lesson's deliverable: author both entries — your two contracted setups from the specialization contract — in the Journal's Notebook, on the firm's template. Fill all five fields on both: context and regime conditions, entry trigger, stop and size rule, management plan, failure modes. Then complete the two lines the card adds: 'When I do NOT take it' — band too low, grade below the table's cell, B in ORANGE, extended, inside the pre-report earnings window, book heat at 10% — and 'My stats,' pulled from your drill scores and field-week logs. The pass bar: all five fields on both entries filled with numbers a stranger could trade from — zero vague lines. This one document goes to graduation review, and it serves both courses; Foundations members submit the same artifact. Next lesson you defend a live plan built from it.

lessons.title: The Trade-Plan Defense: One Full Plan Through All Six Stations, Stress-Tested
lessons.note: The graduation gate: present one complete current-market trade plan — today's dial score and GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, the scan source, the setup name and grade, the size from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % and the regime × grade table, both exit paths, and the review commitment — then defend it against the standard challenge rubric. Graduation hands off to the live loop: Morning Wire as your daily scorecard, Sunday Scans as your weekly review, and the Desk as the rep room where the 40 contracted reps happen. Submitted against a published rubric with a named grader: the plan goes to the owner for async review (Compass pre-grades it), and a pass is what graduation actually certifies — for this course and for UCT Foundations, which shares this gate.

chapters.beat: put the published challenge rubric on screen first and say plainly what graduation certifies: a defended trade plan that passes a named grader's review, never percent-watched.
chapters.speaker_notes: Put the rubric on screen before anything else, because a gate you can see is a gate you can pass. Six rows, one per LOOP station — REGIME, SCAN, SETUP, SIZE, MANAGE, REVIEW/STRESS — each graded pass/fail, and all six must read PASS to graduate; five of six is a fail, with remediation and resubmission. The grader is named: Compass pre-grades your submission, and the plan goes to the owner for async review. Then say plainly what graduation certifies: a defended trade plan that passes a named grader's review — never percent-watched. Nobody graduates this course by finishing videos; completion percentage measures attendance, and attendance was never the product. The plan you build today is a real, current-market plan — today's dial, today's tape, a name you could actually trade tomorrow. That is the standard, face up, before we build.
chapters.on_screen: The TRADE-PLAN DEFENSE RUBRIC — six pass/fail rows on the Playbook Template + Defense Rubric card

chapters.marker: Stations one through four, on today's tape
chapters.beat: build the plan live: today's dial score and GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, the scan source that surfaced the name, the setup name and grade, and the size from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % plus the regime × grade table.
chapters.speaker_notes: Build stations one through four live on today's tape. Regime: write today's actual dial score and the band the dashboard shows beside it — say the dial reads 112 of 150, GREEN — today's reading, not 'the market looks good.' Scan: cite the real source that surfaced the name — the nightly Screener run, the A-list, or the weekend deep scan; a candidate that came from Twitter fails row two. Setup: name it from the catalog, family included, and grade it A+/A/B/C citing the rubric line that decided the letter — regime alignment, family score, RS rank, catalyst, clean stop. Size: show it both ways and make them agree, down to the share count. Example: 1% account risk, 4% stop distance → 1% ÷ 4% = 25% position — check the cell: GREEN + A+ allows 20-25%, so it stands. On $100,000 that is $25,000 — 250 shares of a $100 stock, $1,000 at risk, exactly 1%.
chapters.on_screen: Dashboard split — today's dial reading, the scanner A-list, and the plan document filling in station by station
chapters.example_spec: Build stations one through four on the recording day's real tape: read the live dial and band, open the nightly Screener A-list, take its highest-graded Stage-2 name. If the day offers no clean A/A+ candidate, use the archived fallback: ELF, daily, June–August 2023 — a two-month flat base ≈$110–117 (June close ≈$114.23, July ≈$116.72), then the Aug 2 earnings gap that opened ≈$134.60, +15.5% on ≈3.2× volume, closing ≈$133.19. Note it out loud: the gap priced through any $120 buy-stop, so this is an EP entry, not a pivot breakout — entry ≈$134, stop ≈$127.50 (≈5% → 1% ÷ 5% = 20% position, the GREEN + A+ cell). Scale the speaker-notes share math to the actual price. Outcome: the Aug 31 high ≈$139.85 pays ≈+1R before the 20-day trail exits in September. (Upgrade: swap in a firm trade of the same setup if available.)

chapters.beat: write both exit paths (the wrong-path stop as an appointment, the right-path partials-and-trail plan) and the review commitment that closes the LOOP before a single share is bought.
chapters.speaker_notes: Stations five and six get written before a single share is bought — that is the point of a plan. Manage, the wrong path first: the stop price, written as an appointment, not a debate — the price where the thesis is dead and the exit is mechanical. Then the right path: a third off at 2-3R into strength, and the named trail for the rest — 10-day for a fast mover, 10/20-day for an EP, 20- or 50-day for a position hold. Name the line now; you do not choose it mid-trade. Add the heat check: this entry's open risk joins the book, and portfolio heat — the sum of entry-minus-stop times shares across every open position, divided by equity — must stay at or under the 10% cap, with correlated names sharing one risk budget. Review: commit to the 7-field journal entry the day the trade closes, win or lose. Both paths written, the LOOP closed on paper first.

chapters.speaker_notes: Now the defense. Run the standard challenges against the model plan on camera and answer each with a number, not a posture. 'What if it gaps through your stop?' — the position is 25% with a 4% stop; a gap to twice the stop distance costs 2%, survivable by design, which is exactly why the ceiling table caps size even when a tight stop would license more. 'Why this size in YELLOW?' — it would not be: YELLOW + A+ caps at 15%, and the plan re-sizes or dies. 'What invalidates the thesis?' — something specific: the close back inside the base, the band downgrading, a distribution-day cluster — never 'if it goes down.' 'Correlation to your open positions?' — same-theme names share one risk budget; three AI longs are one trade. Then show a plan failing the same rubric — 'it's going up, I'll watch it closely' — so the difference between a defense and a hope is visible.
